profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-11T21:22:19.003+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: In the past, the State of Zhōu was on the verge of decline.
Six powerful states rose in contention,
and eight states vied for invasion.
To the south was King Píng of Chǔguó,
who was a ruler who brought peace to the people and fostered civilization.
The King then held court for myriad states,
his divine prestige reverberating far and wide,
commanding all the states.
Externally, he made clear his grand platform;
internally, he elevated his palaces.
To the south, he made Tiānmén his stronghold;
to the north, he took Huáihǎi as his pass;
to the east, the sun and moon marked his borders;
to the west, he neighbored the Buddhist lands.
He opened mountains and rivers, setting the earth's axis,
and harmonized the *lǜ-lǚ* to distinguish *yīn* and *yáng*.
He rode to the Purple 極 (Pole) to establish the celestial gate,
and moved the Yellow Dragon to come and bear his wings.
Six dragons descended with auspicious signs,
the earth bore abundant crops,
the wind did not rustle the branches,
and the rain did not break the clods.
The streets and roads
were bustling and orderly,
broad and smooth,
leaving a name for ten thousand generations.
The Grand Chancellor of Chǔ,
named Wǔ Shē,
possessed both civil and military talents,
and his heart was devoted to the state.
He wielded a three-foot sword,
committing his six-foot body.
Myriad states received his commands,
his character was pure and upright,
his demeanor loyal and steadfast,
his will like wind and clouds,
his heart like iron and stone.
He constantly harbored no slackness,
and was vigilant day and night.
Serving his lord, he aimed for excellence by compliance
and achieving things smoothly;
if the lord had any transgressions,
he would admonish him even if it meant offending him.
Wǔ Shē had two sons
who served the King.
The younger was Zǐxū,
the elder named Zǐshàng.
One served the State of Liáng,
the other served the State of Zhèng,
both equally loyal and steadfast,
and astute in understanding people.
The Crown Prince of Chǔ,
having grown up, had not yet taken a wife.
The King asked his officials, "Who has a daughter suitable to be a consort?
I have heard that if a state has no Crown Prince,
half the state is like barren land;
if the springs of the eastern sea overflow,
and a tree has no branches,
half the tree dies.
The Crown Prince is the revered lord of half the state,
yet he has no wife.
What do you, my lords, think?"
Grand Master Wèi Líng reported to the King, "Your subject has heard that the daughter of Duke Mù of Qín,
at the age of sixteen,
is surpassingly beautiful.
Her eyebrows are like the full moon,
her cheeks like congealed light,
her eyes like shooting stars,
her complexion like flowers.
Her hair is seven feet long,
her nose straight, her forehead square,
her ears like dangling pearls,
her hands hang below her knees,
her ten fingers slender and long.
May Your Majesty issue an edict
to arrange a marriage with the Crown Prince.
If it pleases your sacred heart,
it will be a good deed that harmonizes all states."
So Wèi Líng was dispatched
to summon the daughter of Duke Qín.
King Chǔ called Wèi Líng and said, "I trouble you, my lord, on this long journey,
braving wind and frost."
When the King saw the maiden,
her graceful and beautiful appearance
suddenly stirred a wolf-like, tiger-like desire in him.
Wèi Líng subtly catered to the King's feelings: "May Your Majesty take her as your own consort.
The Crown Prince
can seek a wife elsewhere.
Beautiful women are countless;
how could this hinder the great Way?"
When the King heard Wèi Líng's words,
he was overjoyed, unable to control himself,
and immediately took the Qín maiden as his consort,
remaining in the palace without holding court for three days.
Wǔ Shē, hearing of this, was enraged.
Unafraid of the might of thunder and lightning,
he disheveled his hair and went straight to the palace hall,
offending the sacred heart with his direct remonstrance.
The King was immediately startled and fearful,
asking, "What inauspicious event has occurred?"
Wǔ Shē replied, "Your subject now sees the King as lawless,
and fears that the state will be lost and the nation ruined.
If the state suddenly descends into chaos and subjects flee,
will it not be due to the daughter of Duke Qín!
To marry a wife for your son,
and then take her yourself as your consort,
contending with your son for a wife,
can this not be shameful before heaven and earth!
This is a law of chaos,
overturning proper rites.
Your subject wishes to admonish,
fearing that the state cannot endure!"
The King, blushing with shame,
was too embarrassed to face his officials: "Grand Chancellor,
have you not heard the saying: 'A completed plan cannot be unsaid,
spilled water cannot be recovered'?
Since the matter is already so,
do not admonish me again!"
Wǔ Shē saw the King was lawless,
having taken the Qín maiden as his consort.
Unafraid of the might of thunder and lightning,
he offended the sacred heart with his direct remonstrance: "Your Majesty is the lord of ten thousand people,
commanding all states.
How can you believe and accept Wèi Líng's words!
(The following passage is missing))
(The preceding passage is missing)) filial piety,
[missing character] to save me from this difficulty,
the realms of the living and dead are far apart.
" Zǐshàng, having received his father's distant letter summoning him,
tearfully imprisoned King Píng.
A distant letter commanding him,
wishing to save his compassionate father.
The King said, "Your father is now under severe torture,
imprisoned in the dungeon.
If you do not save your father,
what kind of filial son are you called?
You must go quickly,
and do not hesitate further."
Zǐshàng immediately bade farewell to King Zhèng,
and rushed to the State of Liáng by night,
to see his younger brother Zǐxū,
and fully explained the letter's meaning.
"Now, due to King Píng's lawlessness,
believing the words of a treacherous minister,
our compassionate father has been imprisoned,
intended for severe punishment.
I have come from afar
to summon you, my brother, to come with me.
This matter cannot be delayed;
I wish, brother, that you prepare yourself quickly."
Zǐxū, hearing what his brother said,
remotely knew his father was detained.
He reasoned out the circumstances,
believing the letter must be largely fabricated.
He replied to his brother, "King Píng is lawless,
using the words of a wicked minister,
imprisoning our father,
intending to execute him.
Seeing us brothers are outside,
he fears future enmity,
so he fabricated our compassionate father's letter,
falsely sending it from afar to lure us.
This situation
is enough to warrant a swift execution.
The letter summoning us
must be a deceptive trick.
If we go, we will be captured and unable to escape,
like a dull bird entangled in a net,
or a spring fish (
(The following passage is missing))
(The preceding passage is missing)) now returned to fully recount Zǐxū's words.
I was somewhat clumsy just now,
please, my lord, do not blame me."
The messenger, having delivered the words,
immediately returned,
bound himself with rope,
and went to see King Píng.
He reported to King Píng,
"I was commanded to serve as an urgent envoy,
traveling day and night through several provinces.
I caught up with him south of Mount Kuàijī,
where he drew his sword, intending to cut off my head.
I feared Zǐxū's sword,
and Zǐxū feared that both of us would perish.
We stood facing each other but did not approach,
speaking our reasons from afar.
He told me to return and report to you, King Píng: 'Today I will raise an army to avenge my father!'"
King Chǔ heard these words
and slammed the steps of the throne, greatly enraged: "Rebellious little men,
how can they be endured?
A blade of grass
is hardly fit to measure the heavens;
a single strand of hair
attempts to resist a furnace's coals.
Wǔ Zīxū's crazy words
are not worth considering;
wild talk in the wind
need not be collected!"
King Chǔ then summoned Wǔ Shē and his son Wǔ Shàng from prison,
to be punished by penal servitude.
When Wǔ Shàng was about to die,
he looked up to heaven and sighed, saying: "I should not have disregarded my brother's words
and come from afar to be executed with my father.
What can be done, what can be done?
What other path is there to know?
After my death,
I wish my brother may survive.
Should Heaven's path suddenly open,
may he avenge my father's grievances by killing Chǔ."
Having finished these last words,
he was immediately killed.
Father and son,
were executed at the same time.
King Chǔ came forth
and immediately sought to seize Wǔ Zīxū. How was it done?
It was proclaimed: "A minister of the state of Liáng,
the rebellious villain Wǔ Zīxū,
whose father served the sovereign,
failed to be loyal and diligent,
plotted against the altars of earth and grain,
and was cruel, tyrannical, and greedy.
Wǔ Shàng, a minister of the state of Zhèng,
was killed along with his father;
only Wǔ Zīxū has escaped and fled,
and is not yet apprehended.
If he can be captured and delivered,
a reward of one thousand catties of gold
and a fief of ten thousand households will be granted.
Those who conceal him
will suffer the customary penalty of the law:
first their own body will be executed,
then their nine familial generations will be exterminated.
Officials who leniently overlook
or release him will be removed from office and investigated,
and their daily reports will be brought forth
for their bodies to be imprisoned and sent up."
Once this decree was issued,
the roads were impenetrable,
and prefectures and counties were informed,
with notices posted along the roads.
Villages and hamlets were searched thoroughly;
who would dare to conceal him?
Everyone vied to pursue and capture him
to covet the great reward.
Wǔ Zīxū traveled to the boundless wilderness of Mǎngdàngshān,
leaned on his sword, sang a mournful song, and sighed:
Wǔ Zīxū, filled with indignation, sighed deeply,
"A true man, enduring hardship, why sigh thus?
Heaven's net is vast, the road is blocked,
leaving me distraught, with nowhere to flee.
Thirsty and hungry, with no food to fill my belly,
in the desolate wilds, I wander alone, having lost my companions.
Afar I hear the Heavenly Chasm, full of wind and waves,
with towering mountains reaching the Milky Way.
The desolate river bend has no boats;
how can I reach the southern bank of the Jiāng?
If the Azure Heaven goes against human will,
I cannot avoid being trapped and stranded here."
Having finished his mournful song,
he continued forward,
letting fate guide him
until he reached the Yǐngshuǐ.
The wind brought whispers to his ears,
and he heard the sound of pounding silk.
He dared not move forward,
but crouched and stood back.
Wǔ Zīxū reached the bank of the Yǐngshuǐ,
thirsty and famished, finding it hard to proceed.
Afar he heard the sound of pounding silk in the air;
he bent his knee and body diagonally, then stopped.
Fearing that someone might ambush him here,
he tiptoed and pressed himself against a tree.
After a long while, feeling secure and no longer startled,
he gradually peered from between the trees.
By the ford, there was no man,
only a light and graceful girl pounding silk.
She dipped her head into the water a hundred times,
and raised her jade-like wrists above the waves a thousand times.
He wanted to go forward and beg for food,
but his mind was filled with doubt and hesitation.
He dared not advance or retreat to consult,
and lingered, almost turning to leave.
The girl, pounding silk in the water,
suddenly looked up and saw a man
walking erratically,
his spirit dazed and confused,
his face showing hunger,
and a sword at his waist.
She knew it was Wǔ Zīxū
and, filled with sorrow, said: "I have heard that a single meal among the mulberry trees
led Líng Zhé to support the carriage wheel;
a yellow sparrow, healed of its wound with medicine,
brought a white jade ring in return.
Though I am pure and chaste,
my simple character is unblemished.
Now, pounding silk by the water,
I am fortunate to meet a gentleman.
Though my family is not wealthy,
why should I begrudge this one meal?"
She walked slowly to the bank
and called out: "Traveler, please stop!
Swordsman, from what land are you, noble sir?
From what state, talented hero?
Your appearance and spirit,
your bearing, are imposing.
For what urgent matter
do you journey a long road?
Lost and confused,
your spirit is dazed.
Judging by your complexion,
you must have some request in mind.
If not a knight harboring a grievance,
then surely you are being pursued by King Píng.
I have a small offering from my poor home;
dare I invite you to dine?
How do you feel about this?
I hope you will grace me with your presence."
Wǔ Zīxū replied: "I am a man of Chǔ,
serving as an envoy to Yuè.
Recently, on account of tribute,
I journeyed west to King Chǔ,
and to the states of Liáng and Zhèng to discuss military and state affairs.
Returning on a stout horse,
I reached a small river,
and was attacked and ambushed by crazy bandits.
Fortunately, I survived.
Today, climbing mountains and crossing ridges,
my provisions are exhausted.
I heard the sound of your pounding silk in the air,
and followed the sound to seek you out.
My humble self is like this,
clumsy as a person.
I fear I may miss the king's schedule;
my hurried journey is real.
Now, traveling on the road to Kuàijī,
how can I pass through?
Please guide me,
I dare not even hope for food!"
The girl replied: "I have heard the words of the ancients,
and they are truly not empty.
When affection is gone, it is hard to retain true feelings;
a broken string can still be reattached.
Your journey
is quite evident.
I see you looking back and forth,
with a sorrowful expression as you travel,
across vast rivers and mountains,
covered in dust and wind.
Now, I do not despise my low status,
and dare to invite you to a meal:
My family originally lives in Nányáng Xiàn;
my youthful beauty is like pure silk.
Pounding silk in the deep pool, my red makeup is reflected,
and the lotus flowers on the water are not as fair as my face.
A traveler is like a boat drifting on the sea,
fearing the late evening as dusk falls to return home.
If you do not despise my humble status,
I urge you to eat your fill."
Wǔ Zīxū was about to proceed,
but was repeatedly and earnestly held back.
It was truly hard to refuse human kindness,
so he sat by the water's edge
and ate.
After three mouthfuls, he stopped eating,
feeling indebted to the woman,
and wanted to depart.
But the girl further urged him
to eat his fill.
His shame grew deeper,
so he confessed his true feelings.
Wǔ Zīxū replied:
"I am Wǔ Zīxū,
fleeing Chǔ to take refuge in southern Wú.
Fearing King Píng's pursuit and capture,
I have journeyed through this desolate path day and night.
I am grateful for the meal that has filled me;
I wonder how I can repay you!
My body is light and strong, my eyes sharp;
I wish to take my leave and embark on the long road.
I am an exile who abandoned the imperial capital,
now sought by King Píng.
My benefactor's kindness should not be told to others;
I hope, young lady, you understand my feelings."
After Wǔ Zīxū spoke, he walked forward,
and the girl cried out in lamentation:
“The traveler, so forlorn, is truly pitiable.
Crawling on the ground in fear of death, yet clinging to life.
One meal from me is not enough;
The wife’s heart does not accord with the husband’s will.
Though you, sir, are noble and I must respectfully decline,
My daughter's intention is to not lightly shame you.”
Having spoken, she shed tears and wiped them: “Your noble appearance has suddenly grown gaunt and haggard.
If, later on, you are pursued and captured,
They will surely say that a woman burdened you.
For thirty years, I have not spoken with a man.
Living with my mother in this neighborhood,
Her cherished beauty is before my eyes.
The loyal and chaste woman's steadfastness is idly abandoned.”
Then she called out, “Wǔ Xiàng, do not doubt!”
And immediately embraced a stone and threw herself into the river to her death.
Zǐxū turned his head and gazed for a long while,
Pitying the woman, filled with sorrow.
He saw her afar, embracing a stone and drowning in the river,
And could not help but cry out in injustice.
Without cause, the Yǐngshǔi swallowed a human trace,
His tears fell, his lamentations were doubly mournful:
“If, later on, I achieve high promotion,
I will surely present a hundred catties of gold for her burial!”
After Zǐxū had wept,
He continued on his journey.
Dust and wind sullied his face,
Dust covered the sky,
His spirit was restless,
When suddenly he arrived at a deep river.
The spring water was bottomless,
The banks were boundless,
He climbed mountains, entered valleys, circled ravines, and sought the source.
Dragons and snakes blocked the path,
He drew his sword and cleared the way.
Tigers and wolves filled the road,
He immediately strung his bow.
Hungry, he ate grass among the reeds;
Thirsty, he drank from the flowing spring beneath the cliffs.
A man, driven by enmity,
Approached death as if it were sleep.
In the river valley, he suddenly encountered a household,
And immediately knocked on the door to beg for food.
A woman came out to answer,
And from afar, concealed the sound of her younger brother's voice,
Knowing from afar that it was her younger brother Zǐxū.
She spoke urgently of her longing and comfort,
But Zǐxū kept his mouth shut and said nothing.
Knowing her brother had been thirsty and exhausted for a long time,
She then took a gourd and filled it with rice,
And also made a pickle from bitter lettuce (kǔjù).
Zǐxū, a wise scholar,
Perceived his elder sister’s feelings in advance,
And after careful consideration,
Understood and said: “Filling the gourd with rice means bitter on the inside, sweet on the outside;
Making a pickle from bitter lettuce means mixing bitterness with bitterness.
This means you are sending me away;
Go quickly, go quickly,
I cannot stay long.”
Then he took his leave.
His sister asked her brother, “Now that you are setting off,
Where do you intend to go?”
Zǐxū replied, “I intend to go to the state of Yuè.
My father and elder brother were killed;
I cannot fail to avenge them.”
His elder sister embraced her brother’s head,
Choking and with a hoarse voice,
Not daring to cry loudly,
She sighed: “Alas, how painful!
How bitter!”
She threw herself down and beat her chest,
Asking, “What sin did my brother and I commit in our past lives,
To suffer such loneliness and misery?
What sin did we commit over the vast kalpas,
To now betray our father and mother?
Though we have achieved human form and wealth,
Father in the south, son in the north, each separated.
Suddenly remembering my father and brother, I sit and cry,
Making my guts tear inch by inch.
I don't know where my brother is going now,
Leaving me alone to suffer anxiety and fear.
Now I have no other attachments,
I regret not destroying myself!”
Zǐxū bid his sister farewell, saying, “Live well,
There is no need for tears to flow in thousands of streams.
My father and brother were unjustly executed,
My heart burns like boiling soup.
A man now has no place under heaven,
My heroic spirit is filled with bitter resentment against the vast sky.
If the day comes when Heaven's way opens,
I swear I will capture King Píng of Chǔ alive.
I will gouge out his heart and cut his flesh into pieces,
All nine generations of his clan must perish.
If I do not do this,
I swear I will not return home!”
After saying these words,
He then traveled south.
After traveling more than twenty *lǐ*,
His eyes twitched and his ears felt hot.
He immediately drew on the ground and divined,
And saw that his nephews were coming to pursue him.
He made an offering with water at the water's edge,
Inserted bamboo into his waist,
Wore his wooden clogs backward,
And also drew a 'ground-door' and 'heaven-gate' on the ground.
Then he lay down in the reeds,
And chanted a curse, saying: “Those who seize me shall suffer misfortune,
Those who pursue me shall perish.
Hurry, as if by imperial decree!”
Zǐxū had two nephews, Zǐ’ān and Zǐyǒng.
When they arrived home, they saw evidence of someone having eaten,
And knew it was their maternal uncle Zǐxū.
Disregarding their mother's deep affection for her brother,
They immediately harbored evil intentions and set off in pursuit.
“If I see the Emperor of Chǔ and receive a reward,
I will surely attain high promotion.
Since the rebel has now reached the door,
Why not capture him?”
After walking about ten *lǐ*,
They stopped by the roadside to rest.
Zǐyǒng, having a slight understanding of *yīnyáng*,
Immediately drew on the ground and divined.
He saw that his maternal uncle had water above his head,
Meaning he would surely fall by a river;
Bamboo at his waist,
Meaning his tomb would become overgrown;
Wooden clogs worn backward,
Meaning he would not advance but wander.
If this divination is true,
He will surely die.
I will not search for him anymore,
I will give up and return home.
Zǐxū, having humbled himself to observe the divination,
Saw that his nephews were not pursuing him,
And immediately ran,
Unceasingly day and night.
In the river valley, he again encountered a household,
Whose walls were unusually stately and beautiful.
A solitary dwelling, standing alone,
With no one around for miles.
Not shaming his eight-foot stature,
He immediately knocked on the door to beg for food.
Zǐxū knocked on the door to beg for food,
And his wife came out with a composed expression to answer.
She immediately recognized her own husband,
And was about to speak and acknowledge him.
The woman stood upright, thinking carefully,
Not daring to approach him closely,
She greeted him with a respectful bow,
And with sorrowful tears, she asked:
“My family lives on the edge of the desolate wilderness,
Alone and secluded, without neighbors for miles.
From where has this gentleman come to this place,
With a face full of sorrow and signs of hunger?
Wild and panicked like a startled deer,
Humbly bending and shrinking to beg for food.
Although I am confined deep in my chambers,
I feel as if I vaguely recognize you, sir.”
Zǐxū replied to the lady, saying:
“I am a messenger from Chǔ on a distant mission,
Having traversed mountains and rivers to return to my homeland.
On the way, I lost my way and became confused,
Unknowingly wandering until I arrived here.
My homeland is far away, on the western side of the sea,
Separated by the distant waters of the three rivers.
Just now I acted presumptuously and interfered,
Putting myself in a truly awkward position.
Noble people are often forgetful and mistake others,
I do not recall ever having known you, lady.
Now I wish to travel to the east of the river,
I hope you will kindly show me the way.”
His wife then composed a poem using names of medicinal herbs and asked: "I am a 細辛, wife of 仵茄 (五加).
Early appointed to office in 梁,
I have not yet been able to return home (當歸) to perform the rites,
leaving me to live alone (獨活) in idleness.
The 薑芥 of 粔莨 (高良),
澤瀉 has no pity.
I gaze up and sigh for the 檳榔,
when will you be far-sighted (遠志)?
Recently, I heard that the King of 楚 is without principle,
and thus I felt a heart of 柴胡,
destroying my family, making it 芒消,
and forcing me to bend my body like 苷.
葳蕤 is timid and weak,
石膽 is hard to bear.
My husband fears the fugitive,
茱萸 managed to escape.
Hiding my form like 菌草,
concealing my shadow like 藜蘆,
I am like a wild jackal (野干) being pursued,
making my mad husband 莨菪.
I recall my tears staining 赤石,
and my hatred knotted like 青葙.
At night, it is difficult to see clearly (決明) in sleep,
by day, my tongue is dry and curled like 卷柏 from thinking.
Hearing your voice begging for 厚朴,
I involuntarily hesitate (躑躅) before you.
I thought my husband was 麥門,
and so I walked slowly (蓯蓉).
Looking at your 龍齒,
it resembles my 狼牙.
If this is 桔梗,
I wish to explain my 枳殻."
Wǔ Zixū replied: "I am not the son of 仵茄 (五加),
nor am I a fugitive escaping disaster.
Listen to my story.
I was born in 巴蜀,
grew up in 藿鄉.
My father was 蜈公,
born to 貝母.
He sent 金牙 to gather treasures,
and 支子 to travel far.
Liú Jìnú is my humble friend,
Xú Chángqīng is his noble friend.
Together we crossed the 蘘河,
our bodies harmed by the cold water.
Two companions became 芒消,
only I remained alone (獨活).
Daily, my intestines are suspended (續斷),
my thoughts drifting.
Walking alone on 恒山,
石膏 is difficult to cross.
Scaling the cliffs of 巴戟,
I frequently encountered 柴胡.
I intended to rest for winter (款冬),
when I suddenly met 鍾乳.
I lingered for half a summer (半夏),
but did not see 鬱金.
So I returned home (當歸),
arriving here through 芎藭.
My teeth (羊齒)
are not wolf's teeth (狼牙).
Regarding your 桔梗-like feelings,
I wish to know their meaning."
His wife replied: "Sir, do not be so hasty (急急),
the road is still long.
Even if we have never known each other before,
what harm is there in a mistaken recognition?
I am the daughter of a public servant with a noble family (公孫鍾鼎女),
matched with a gentleman of integrity and goodness.
My husband's surname is Wǔ, and he is a minister,
having served the king for a thousand li since he came of age.
Since our separation, letters have ceased,
I miss you so much my sorrowful heart almost breaks.
The distant path is dark and desolate,
my family is unaccustomed to long partings.
My youthful face is wasted and not as it used to be,
when have my tears of longing ever stopped?
Youthful years are wasted guarding an empty boudoir,
who can endure such a blooming season?
My beauty fades day and night in the green chamber,
only because my wandering husband serves in 梁.
I am too lazy to look at the bright moon in the courtyard,
and sorrowfully return to my tent to embrace the mandarin ducks.
A distant letter sent by goose (雁書) may not arrive,
the cold weather blocks the long road.
I wish to weave on the half-finished loom, but I am not pleased,
I am ashamed to paint my eyebrows and face myself in the mirror.
I especially pity the magpies chirping on the grape arbor,
and think of the swallows nesting in pairs in the white jade hall.
You act like Qiū Hú, not recognizing me,
I also have no intention of learning to pick mulberries.
Seeing the two front teeth in your mouth,
I recognize you by this, and our intentions align.
I will not begrudge even a coarse meal,
I wish you would stay for a while and not hurry."
Wǔ Zixū, being recognized, politely declined,
and with gentle words wrote back:
"My lady, do not mistakenly interfere,
there are many similar people in the world.
Your husband's surname is Wǔ and he is a minister,
while I am from a humble family, living in the wilds.
If you happen to see your husband, please convey to him,
and persuade him with reason to return home.
I must now hurry to 江東 for urgent matters,
and cannot stay day and night."
The woman knew he was planning something great,
and dared not disturb him further.
She provided for him appropriately,
and sent him off with proper reasoning.
Wǔ Zixū, having been recognized by the woman,
said nothing more.
A great man had not yet achieved his goal,
but was recognized by a woman;
how could he, for a small matter,
spoil his great mission?
The resolute man picked up a stone and acted,
and immediately knocked out his teeth.
By day he watched the sun,
by night he observed the stars,
running without stopping,
until he reached the northern bank of 吴江.
Fearing someone might ambush him,
he hid himself in the reeds,
clutching his sword, he sang a mournful song and sighed:
The waters of the river 吴江 are vast, waves rise and fall,
reaching the sky, sometimes turbulent, sometimes shallow or deep.
Flying sand rises vigorously, obscuring the Milky Way,
the clear wind stirs up waves, likened to destroying forests.
White grass covers the plains everywhere,
green willows line both banks.
Magpies gather food, crisscrossing everywhere,
fish and dragons leap and churn in disorder.
Water cats and playful otters compete in a rush,
a thousand times I sigh endlessly.
Suddenly remembering my father and brother were unjustly executed,
my five internal organs immediately feel rotten.
Pondering the hatred and pain, I lament,
today we meet, and I will not let it go.
If my life ends in this river's depths,
life or death, it all depends on this night.
I do not regret my bones being covered by the long waves,
the revenge for my father and brother will never cease.
All withered grass under the heavens follows the wind,
it is still the manifestation of the power of all devas.
After the mournful song was finished,
he walked to the riverbank and gazed into the distance.
He saw only the vastness of the river and its depths—
how could he cross?
He stretched his neck among the reeds,
then turned his head back, finding only silence.
He met no one to ferry him across,
and forever lacked a traveler by raft.
He saw only river crows leaving the bank,
while egrets soared in competition;
fish and turtles crisscrossed,
and cormorants congregated.
He also saw the immense expanse of the long sandbar,
the waves of the silent inlet,
the mist thick and dark,
and the clouds dense and shadowy.
Trees were toppled on the ancient bank,
the moon shone on a solitary mountain.
Dragons roared, turtles were startled,
and the river, turbid, made waves.
It was as if a homesick traveler,
ascending the mountain peaks to yearn for home;
or a traveler by raft,
pointing to the constellations Shēn and Chén as a guide.
The single peak of Mínshān,
like tigers and wolves circling,
rumbling like the sound of drums and horns,
yet there was no boat to cross.
After two more nights,
he remained hidden among the reeds.
On the waves, he saw only one person,
singing a folk song and rowing,
holding a fishing reel
like a fisherman.
Immediately he emerged from the reeds
and called out, "Sir, you who hold the hook and steer the boat,
please condescend to come to the bank for a moment so I may see you.
Do not decline for lack of effort;
I earnestly hope you will be kind enough to grant me a glance."
The fisherman heard the call
and immediately sought the sound;
suddenly seeing a person in the reeds,
he at once rowed his boat to the bank.
He reeled in his line, coiled his rope,
stopped his oar and rested his pole,
then glided gracefully with the current
and, singing to the clear wind, asked, "Where does the gentleman wish to go now?
You are far out by the riverbank and inlet,
without a boat to ride or a passenger,
nor any companion in this desolate place.
Are you a wanderer, adrift like a tumbleweed?
Standing alone on a desolate islet by the bank.
Even if you seek a boat and a crossing,
here there are no boats at all.
Do not disdain a humble, foolish man;
I beg you to fully relate your concerns."
Wú Zǐxū replied, "I have heard that people know each other by their principles,
just as fish look to each other in rivers and lakes.
I am but a wandering traveler;
how dare I speak falsely to you!
Now, because of some urgent business,
I wish to travel south of the Jiāng.
I am clumsy in my ways;
I hope, sir, you will understand.
If I am granted passage,
your kindness would be worth my life;
if it is not permitted,
I will naturally give up the idea."
The fisherman replied, "Just now I observed your appearance and discerned your demeanor,
and found you different from ordinary folk.
What the gentleman harbors in his heart is clear;
there is no need for further explanation.
I have heard that not despising others is not ignoble,
and not despising jade is not poor.
Qín Mùgōng, having been granted wine and favored,
could speak and halt three armies,
and received a great reward for an empty cage.
I see that you have suffered hardships for a long time,
and have been thirsty and weary for much time;
you cannot cross the river on an empty stomach.
I wish to provide a meal for you.
My home is more than ten *lǐ* round trip from here;
I will be a little late in coming and going,
so please do not be surprised or doubt me."
Wú Zǐxū replied, "I only ask for a boat to cross;
how dare I hope for a meal!"
The fisherman replied, "I have heard that a *qílín*, having eaten,
travels a thousand *lǐ* a day;
a *fènghuáng*, having eaten,
soars across the four seas."
Having finished speaking,
he left the boat and departed immediately.
He went home to fetch food.
Wú Zǐxū heard these words
and watched the boat with the fisherman.
Wú Zǐxū pondered in his heart: "This man told me he was going home to fetch food.
Will he not summon people to come and seize me?"
So he abandoned the boat and ran,
then hid himself among the reeds.
In a moment, the fisherman
arrived at the boat.
The fisherman had brought a flask of fine wine,
five *jīn* of fish and meat,
ten flatbreads,
and a pot of rice.
He arrived at the boat
but did not see the man from the reeds,
only an empty boat on the bank.
His feelings of attachment and longing
made him grieve endlessly.
The fisherman sang and called out, "Man in the reeds,
why have you hidden yourself?
Come out here so I may see you.
I harbor no ill intentions whatsoever;
there is no need for suspicion or worry,
do not make it difficult for yourself.
I have brought food for you;
why do you not come to eat?"
Wú Zǐxū heard these words from the boatman
and knew he had no ill intentions,
so he immediately emerged from the reeds,
ashamed and grateful for the hardship taken to fetch food,
and humbly offered his thanks.
At that moment, a spread was laid out,
and they both ate.
Then the boatman plied his oars and rowed the boat,
reaching the middle of the river.
Wú Zǐxū, having eaten his fill,
thought to himself: "An ordinary person, receiving one meal from another,
is shamed by it;
receiving two meals,
he ought to exert himself for them."
He offered the jade disc from his bosom as a gift,
but the boatman, fearing greed,
did not accept the item.
Wú Zǐxū worried that he was suspected of being untrustworthy due to the smallness of the gift,
so he took off his precious sword to offer it in return.
The fisherman stopped his oar and turned around,
then spoke to Wú Zǐxū, saying, "Sir, do not be so hasty;
you must think thrice.
A single charitable meal,
what is it worth?
When a man is in distress,
fish and turtles are his companions;
when a gentleman is in difficulty,
dragons and snakes share his abode.
The King of Chǔ pursues you,
offering a thousand gold pieces for your capture;
those who harbor you
will have their lives and clans destroyed.
I do not covet the heavy reward of an enlightened ruler above,
nor do I shun the blame of execution below.
You wish to repay me with a precious sword;
how is it different from the property of King Píng?
This *Lóngquán* precious sword
is for you to protect yourself;
this jade disc, a treasure of Jīng,
is to be cherished by you.
If you later rise to high office and wealth,
do not forget this one morning.
I regret my advanced age,
that I met you so late.
Regarding the sword and jade,
please do not insist further.
If you truly wish to show your gratitude,
there is no need for further thanks."
Wú Zǐxū saw that the fisherman would not accept,
and his heart gradually felt uneasy.
He pondered in his heart,
worried that the boatman suspected his token of gratitude was too small.
Though they were precious royal treasures,
what could he do?
So he threw the sword into the river,
and it emitted a brilliant, dazzling divine light.
The sword rose and sank three times,
gliding gracefully on the water.
The river god, hearing the sword's roar from afar,
shook with fear, causing surging, boiling waves;
fish and turtles, terrified, burrowed into the mud;
fish-dragons rushed forth.
The river god held it in his hand,
and in fear, delivered it.
Once the sword left the water,
fish and turtles leaped;
the sun and moon shone brightly,
mountains and forests were clear and bright,
clouds dispersed and mists cleared,
auras scattered and smoke flowed.
Trees on the bank welcomed the guest,
river winds bade farewell to the traveler.
Looking far off, white egrets by the sand
were preparing to return to their nests at dusk.
By the inlet, no boat was seen,
and the traveling passenger had no companion.
Only the vast, solitary mountain could be seen.
He looked back at his homeland,
wiping tears that moistened his clothes,
his heart filled with deep melancholy.
Crossing the river, they were about to reach the south bank,
Wú Zǐxū then asked the boatman, "Sir, what is your surname and name?
Where in which prefecture and county is your ancestral home located?”
The fisherman replied: “I also have no surname and no given name,
dwelling long by the river as my companion.
I cross the Mò Pǔ,
and sheathe my sword in the deep pool.
Today, two rogues meet,
what need is there to state our names?
You are the scholar among the reeds,
I am the man on the boat.
The meaning is sufficiently clear,
there is no need to forget wealth and status.”
Wǔ Zǐxū said: “I have received this assistance from you, sir,
and will never forget it.
A snake that has been healed by medicine
is still able to repay the kindness.”
The fisherman asked: “Now that you are fleeing,
to which state do you intend to go?”
Wǔ Zǐxū said: “I intend to go to the state of Yuè.”
The fisherman said: “If you go to the state of Yuè,
Yuè and Chǔ are harmonious,
they have never engaged in war.
I fear they might capture you and hand you over,
and your heart for revenge will not be realized.
If you go to the state of Wú,
you will surely find an open path.
The King of Wú is always an enemy of Chǔ,
the two states are not harmonious.
Wú and Chǔ have frequently engaged in warfare,
and Wú has no wise ministers.
They will greatly need you if they get you.”
Wǔ Zǐxū asked the boatman: “How can I successfully go to the state of Wú?”
The boatman said: “When you arrive in the state of Wú,
enter the city,
smear your face with mud,
dishevel your hair like a roebuck,
and run wildly east and west,
crying out three times.”
Wǔ Zǐxū said: “I fortunately wish for an explanation of this method.”
The boatman replied: “Smearing your face with mud
means outwardly defiled but inwardly pure;
crying out three times
and running wildly east and west
means seeking a sagacious ruler;
having disheveled hair in the market
is simply as it should be.
I am not a sage,
but I have experienced many things.”
Wǔ Zǐxū received his instruction,
and immediately bowed in thanks to the fisherman.
Fearing an encounter with Chǔ envoys,
he could not linger,
and departed as soon as he reached the shore.
His voice choked with sobs,
like four birds separating in flight,
resembling the parting of the three Jīng.
He then parted from the fisherman and headed south,
his feelings of attachment
and sorrow unending.
Turning his head to look afar,
he suddenly saw the fisherman overturn his boat and die.
Wǔ Zǐxū was deeply indebted to the fisherman,
and choked with endless tears of sorrow,
then sang a mournful song and sighed:
“Oh, the great river's waters are vast and boundless,
clouds and waters connected together.
Oh, the pain, oh, the pain, unbearable,
oh, the bitterness, oh, the bitterness, injustice upon injustice.
Since ancient times, human feelings have known parting,
life, death, wealth, and status are all matters of Heaven.
Sir, what did I do to displease you,
that you overturned your boat in the river?
Waves and boat, floating, submerging, sinking,
singing of injustice, deep and piercing pain.
An inch of sorrowful intestines feels like knife-cuts,
along the way, I cannot stop tears from drenching my lapels.
I gaze at the state of Wú, yet cannot reach it,
I think of my imperial homeland, harboring deep resentment.
If I chance upon a sagacious ruler and achieve advancement,
I will display my hero's full heart.
The mournful song finished,
he pressed onward again,
still filled with sorrow.
Husband and wife separated,
what great misfortunes?
With loyal heart, I served my lord for nine years,
day and night without slack,
morning and evening, helpless.
Now facing destitution,
what more can be said?
Having spoken, filled with resentment,
anger surged to his throat,
karma, fate,
all are determined by Heaven.
Climbing mountains, traversing ridges,
crossing waters, seeking streams.
Seeking retreat, yet unable to retreat;
seeking advancement, yet unable to advance.
Every move risks starvation,
life turning precarious.
King Píng was too extreme,
singing and crying out injustices.
Wǔ Zǐxū carried his sword,
and walked forward.
He arrived in the vast and wild mountains,
where stone cliffs touched the sky,
and plunged ten thousand *zhàng* into the earth.
Vines and bamboos crisscrossed,
from afar, pine and moss were visible,
mountain cliffs were darkly shadowed.
Insects and wolves gathered and dispersed,
a hundred birds sang their calls.
Thinking of his imperial homeland,
he then sang:
“The road I ponder is long,
crossing the river waters to enter Wú's land.
My father and elder brother, lost in darkness, where are they?
Alone and left behind, I am desolate and anxious.
A husband drifts, following his karma and fate,
life, death, wealth, and status, what constancy do they hold?
King Píng wrongly accepted Wèi Líng's words,
trusting sycophants and slanderers, killing loyal and good men.
Thinking of my homeland, sorrow is hard to stop,
facing water and climbing mountains, my feelings are endless.
The Emperor of Chǔ, light and graceful, doted on slender waists,
many beautiful women in the palace died of starvation.
Qín Mùgōng's daughter, her face like jade,
her youthful beauty like peach and plum blossoms.
Seeing her figure, he took her as a concubine,
how could a king rightfully do such a thing?
Since fleeing, I have constantly harbored worry,
leaving me orphaned with nowhere to turn.
By day, I seek ghostly paths along the road,
treading lightly and hiding my form, always traveling at night.
When will the achievements on Yānshān be carved?
My temples are stained with dust and have turned autumn-gray.
I do not fear the east and west, defying the celestial barrier,
I only worry about thirst and exhaustion crossing barren lands.
May I safely reach my destination,
traveling without hindrance, flowing smoothly.
If I chance upon a sagacious ruler in Wú,
I will raise an army and first behead Wèi Líng.”
The mournful song finished,
he still harbored indignation.
With his back to the Chǔ pass in the north,
he ascended the Wú meeting-place in the south.
He encountered the darkening sky,
clouds thick and dense.
Lost and wandering,
the mountains and forests obstructed him.
Strange birds formed flocks,
insects and wolves formed packs.
Birds cried out "xìng xìng",
beasts named "fèi fèi".
Suddenly, his heart was startled,
he drew his sword and continued.
Light emanated from its scabbard,
illuminating the entire wilderness with brilliant clarity,
containing the sun and moon,
and the Big Dipper constellation.
His heart was heroic and fierce,
fearing no thousand soldiers.
King Píng captured me,
the matter is not yet settled.
If I were to be captured,
I would die a hundred deaths with no chance of survival.
Sneaking and stealing paths,
holding his breath and swallowing his voice,
if the wind stirred the grass,
he would immediately hide his form.
The sword-song finished,
he pressed onward again.
Crossing Guǎnglíng in the north,
ascending Wú Huì in the south,
the passes and fords were urgent,
prefectures and counties were strictly guarded,
posts and stations crisscrossed,
garrisons followed one after another.
He concealed his body and avoided shadows,
one step at a time.
Within not many days or months,
he arrived in the state of Wú.
Completely following the fisherman's instructions,
he disheveled his hair and entered the market,
smeared mud on his face as he walked,
and like a roebuck, cried out three times,
running wildly east and west.
Ministers and assistants of Wú,
riding horses, toured the market,
and just saw a man of unusual appearance and extraordinary talent,
eight *chǐ* tall.
Knowing it was Wǔ Zǐxū,
he bade farewell to the others:
“All are children of good families,
coming together to share hardships.
We look at each other, our feelings unsatisfied,
how can we bear to part ways?
When will we meet again,
our parting hearts are like dearest kin.”
From this point on, once we were separated,
we both became people of a foreign land.
The worthy man, Guìzǎi,
hastened to report to Wú Wáng: "Having just parted from the Dragon Visage,
I was strolling in the market,
and saw a gentleman from a foreign country,
covered in mud and acting wildly,
with dishevelled hair, weeping mournfully,
running hither and thither.
I observed him carefully from the side,
and by his appearance, I could tell
that Your Majesty should pursue and question him thoroughly;
he must be a knight harbouring a grievance!"
When Wú Wáng heard the minister's words,
joy arose in his heart,
so he gathered his ministers,
and pushed aside the pearl curtain to speak of a dream: "Last night at the third watch,
I dreamt that a worthy man entered my country,
whereupon my body became light and healthy,
and I leaped with boundless joy.
You gentlemen, discuss this in detail,
and interpret its good or ill for me."
When the officials heard the King's words,
they all danced and laughed heartily at once,
singing of peace,
and all proclaiming "Long live the King!"
"There is a gentleman eight feet tall in the market,
who perfectly accords with Your Majesty's heart.
Now that he is among the ministers,
we cannot but express our joyful congratulations!"
Wú Wáng immediately ordered a swift envoy
to go to the market to invite the worthy minister.
"Convey my words to him:
although we have not met before,
I wish to see him
and express my feelings face to face."
The envoy received his instructions,
and galloped straight into the market,
where he found Zǐxū and fully relayed Wú Wáng's words.
Zǐxū, obeying the King's command,
dared not delay,
and immediately set off with the envoy.
Upon arriving at Wú Wáng's palace,
he prostrated himself on the ground,
choking with sobs until his voice was hoarse,
and after a long while, he rose.
Wú Wáng knew it was Zǐxū,
and immediately, with sorrow, commiserated: "The King of Chǔ did not accept loyal remonstrance,
but perversely listened to the words of sycophantic ministers,
and unjustly killed your father and elder brother.
How terrible was the suffering,
too grievous to discuss,
and how bitter the pain!
Who could endure it?
Mountains and rivers separate us,
you travelled far through wind and cloud.
My country is small,
I trouble you to have come so far."
After a long while, Zǐxū
clasped his hair and spoke: "My father and elder brother did not serve their lord diligently,
and were thus executed by the Chǔ Emperor.
I then did not succeed my family,
abandoning my father and leaving my lord to flee.
I have heard that when a country is about to perish,
disasters arise in succession.
When a tree is about to be broken,
wind and frost press upon it together.
A lone sentiment is hard to establish;
seeing this hardship,
white and black are hard to distinguish,
dragons and snakes are mixed.
I wished to commit suicide by slitting my throat,
but below ground, I would be ashamed to see my ancestors.
Therefore, I sought refuge with an enlightened king,
and I beg Your Majesty to know my true heart.
I dwelt in the wilds,
long lived in a humble abode,
unfit to serve and establish a king,
yet fortunately received Your Majesty's acceptance."
Wú Wáng replied, saying: "My country is narrow,
lacking loyal and good men.
I wish to establish you as my minister now;
will bending your will not be considered a disgrace?"
Zǐxū said: "I am a humble person,
who undeservedly received great favour;
to be accepted by the King
is already an extraordinary grace.
To be further raised and established as a minister,
I would rather die than dare accept!"
Wú Wáng asked his attendants: "What do you gentlemen think?"
The assembled ranks all spoke in agreement,
all saying: "The enlightened King has been moved;
a man from a foreign country has come to pledge allegiance."
So he was appointed as a minister to assist the King,
and the whole country together proclaimed "Long live the King!"
Wǔ Zǐxū's ambition and integrity as a minister
constantly harbored a spirit of unflagging diligence.
Day and night, he was vigilant and cautious,
serving his lord with unwavering loyalty.
His words did not wound feelings,
his speech was harmonious and illuminating,
and people from far and near gathered abundantly,
officials were numerous and prosperous.
Heavenly troops remained still,
warhorses halted their whips,
all four borders returned to peace,
the eight directions were tranquil.
Calamities did not arise,
disasters did not occur,
the common people rejoiced,
songs filled the roads,
just like in the years of Yáo and Shùn.
All said, "Our Emperor has been touched
by the sacred and majestic sun,
and Heaven and Earth are bright again."
Wǔ Zǐxū governed the state for one year:
the wind did not rustle the branches,
the rain did not break the clods.
He governed the state for two years:
the granaries overflowed,
the world was peaceful and prosperous,
officials ceased to be greedy and cruel,
and administrators ended their tyranny.
He governed the state for three years:
the six barbarian tribes offered their submission,
and all nations pledged allegiance.
He governed the state for four years:
he moved Heaven to manifest auspicious signs with the Jǐnglóng,
red sparrows carried books in their mouths,
Ganoderma lucidum grew everywhere,
and auspicious grains bore joint ears.
Farmers yielded their boundaries,
and nothing was picked up from the roads.
The three teachings flourished together,
and city gates were left open.
There were no more shouts,
and people lived without forced labor.
Wǔ Zǐxū governed the state for five years:
the sun and moon shone brightly again,
there were no two prices in the market,
cats and mice shared the same hole,
rice and wheat were sold by weight,
and prisons were empty of inmates.
Everyone said that the ruler and minister were in perfect harmony,
and from far and near, praises were spread,
honoring the achievements of Chancellor Wǔ.
The common people all went to Wǔ Zǐxū's gate, saying: "We wish to be soldiers for Chancellor Wǔ and attack Chǔ!"
Wǔ Zǐxū saw brave men volunteering,
but dared not act on his own initiative.
So he addressed the King of Wú, saying: "I am but a humble man,
undeservedly favored with your grace.
Having accomplished nothing yet,
how dare I harbor such a thought?
I assess myself as incapable,
and certainly dare not undertake this."
The King of Wú replied: "I have heard that raising children is to prepare for old age,
and accumulating good deeds is to prepare for decline.
Last year, I intended to send you to avenge,
but I feared your desire for revenge had not yet fully awakened.
This year's peace and prosperity
are all due to Chancellor Wǔ's efforts.
If we do not avenge this injustice now,
how can I be called a filial son?
It is precisely the right time
for my state to raise an army and attack Chǔ."
He summoned brave men from within the state,
to avenge with Chancellor Wǔ.
The proclamation read: "Chancellor Wǔ's father and brother
were unjustly executed by King Píng.
Now I wish to dispatch the heavenly army to subjugate Chǔ,
and recruit people to contribute their strength.
If anyone is willing to risk their life and follow,
they must immediately come and volunteer.
Great rewards will be given first,
and meritorious service will not be lightly compensated.
If there are such valiant and fierce warriors,
come quickly to consult and explain,
and register."
Once this was issued,
everyone, far and near, knew,
and each came to register their names,
eagerly competing to volunteer.
The Ministry of War rigorously selected,
tested, and assessed,
choosing those whose courage surpassed the three armies,
and who could decide victory a thousand *lǐ* away.
There were also those who could lift gate bars and wield logs,
grasping square beams with their hands,
leaping into the air while carrying stones,
and bending bows of seven *zhá*.
The recruitment notice was displayed for seven days,
and ninety thousand elite soldiers were recruited.
They were rewarded with scarlet and granted green (robes),
each receiving a thousand bolts of silk.
Those who were about to pass outside the city
lined up in a geese-formation.
When the King of Wú saw the battle-ready soldiers arranged south of the city,
he immediately offered comfort and encouragement to the warriors.
The King of Wú asked Wǔ Zǐxū: "Now that we wish to attack Chǔ,
how many troops should we use?"
Wǔ Zǐxū replied to the King of Wú: "We only need ten thousand troops."
The King of Wú asked: "Are ten thousand troops not too few?"
Wǔ Zǐxū said: "I have heard that if one man is determined to die,
a hundred men cannot defeat him;
if a hundred men are of one mind,
they can march unhindered across the world."
The King of Wú said: "No,
we must take nine hundred thousand men,
only then can we attack them."
The King of Wú then appointed Wǔ Zǐxū as Grand Marshal and Commander-in-Chief, with full authority over military operations.
He was to act according to the Emperor's decree,
to avenge his father's wrong.
Thereupon, many cattle and sheep were slaughtered,
and a feast was set up south of the city.
There were a thousand *hú* of wine,
and ten thousand *jīn* of meat,
all equally distributed,
with no distinction in who ate what.
The King of Wú went out of the city to see Wǔ Zǐxū off, saying: "My lord, just put in your effort,
be cautious on the road ahead,
Heaven will favor you,
and your desire for revenge will surely be granted.
I will have no worries about the state,
and you will not fail the departed souls.
Return early when the matter is concluded,
do not cause me worry."
Wǔ Zǐxū replied to the King of Wú: "I am now leading troops to attack Chǔ,
and I will surely achieve what I desire.
May Your Majesty not worry or think anxiously of me from afar;
my journey will not be long.
