I also request Lú Wǎn to accompany me."
Having taken leave of the King,
he walked out of the military gate,
and before ten days had passed,
he arrived at the border between the two armies.
Wáng Líng's eyes twitched and his ears burned.
He temporarily requested Lú Wǎn to enter Chǔ
to check on his mother: "If my mother is alive,
I will enter Chǔ to rescue my kind mother;
if my mother is no more,
then I will return to the Hàn court with the Grandee [Lú Wǎn]
to serve the sagely ruler."
Wáng Líng's mother saw Lú Wǎn, who had delivered the letter,
return again,
and feared her son would come. If her son came,
her son would die,
and she would also die.
She instructed Lú Wǎn to report back to Wáng Líng.
Before Bawang, Wáng Líng's mother
verbally agreed to write a letter to summon her son.
Bawang, hearing her words,
was greatly pleased.
"To summon Wáng Líng's mother,
what is needed for consultation?"
"No other object is needed;
I request the precious sword Tài'ē from Your Majesty's waist!"
"Since it is for summoning your son,
and you need my precious sword,
what will you use it for?"
"I have written letters to summon my son before,
but my son does not believe them.
If I borrow Your Majesty's precious sword,
cut off a strand of my hair,
and seal it in the letter,
when my son sees the hair,
he will travel day and night, doubling his speed, to enter Chǔ and rescue his mother."
Bawang, hearing her words,
drew the Tài'ē sword
and handed it to Wáng Líng's mother.
Wáng Líng's mother received the sword,
moved more than thirty paces away from Bawang,
and said, "Report this to my King!"
Then Wáng Líng's mother committed suicide.
At that time, heaven and earth lost their radiant light
and thus turned to tell the tale.
At that time, winds and clouds were all bleak and sorrowful,
and all the birds saw it and cried tears of blood.
The border guards first reported to Wáng Líng,
and then fully reported to Gāohuáng, saying:
"You were instructed by the general to visit your kin,
and entered the camp to see the Grand Matron again.
Upon hearing the general was at the border,
she looked south, occupying a position of anger.
In a hurry, she devised a plan like a sudden calm,
fearing that the matter would not be true when the time came.
She turned and sent a message: 'Go back south and serve the Hàn ruler.
If one day you ascend to the golden palace,
do not forget your mother's kindness of nurturing!
Do not be surprised by the sorrow I report to your face:
The Madam committed suicide at the Chǔ camp gate.'"
When Wáng Líng heard the envoy's words,
his heart and guts were torn apart as if by knives.
He threw himself down like a collapsing mountain,
and blood spurted from his ears and nose.
"Mother, why must it come to this?
It is your rebellious son's clumsy actions.
If one day the Hàn dynasty prospers,
I will first raise my hand to behead Zhōng Lí Mò!"
Lú Wǎn報 (bào)哀 (āi) was already finished,
then went with Wáng Líng to the border of Hàn.
A gatekeeper reported: “Wáng Líng saved his mother and has returned.”
So he was summoned to the front of the palace.
After bowing and dancing were completed,
the Hàn Wáng said: “I allowed you into Chǔ to save your kind mother.
Have you saved her yet?”
Wáng Líng reported: “Upon reaching the border, my spirit became confused,
my thoughts uneasy,
so I temporarily asked Lú Wǎn to enter Chǔ
to visit my mother.
When my mother saw Lú Wǎn arrive,
she drew the Bā Wáng’s sword and committed suicide.”
The Emperor heard the report,
slapped the table in great shock: “Summon Zhāng Liáng to come near the front of the palace.”
He ordered the Grand Historian to inscribe his wife’s spirit on a golden tablet,
facing three hundred generals,
forty thousand officials,
and held a grand feast,
with delicacies and rare dishes laid out,
to sacrifice to Wáng Líng’s loyal mother,
bestowing upon her the title of Guó Tàifūrén (國太夫人).
Wáng Líng was so moved that before the Son of Heaven,
he let down his hair and wept for his kind mother.
Wáng Líng’s mother, from the Chǔ camp,
rode a black cloud,
and in the air, expressed her shame and gratitude to the Emperor.
The sacrificial ceremony was arranged as follows:
Alas, how bitter was the general’s mother,
bearing hardship with a resentful heart.
How fortunate am I, the lonely one, to have such
loyal officials always assisting me.
At this time, Wáng Líng wept for his mother and said: “Looking far at the Chǔ camp, verdant and lush,
yesterday you joined Xiàng to recruit children,
your fame in the world is countless.
Wáng Líng will not be worried later,
he will certainly be granted a fief of ten thousand households.”
"Hàn Bā Nián Chǔ Miè Hàn Xīng Wáng Líng Biàn (漢八年楚滅漢興王陵變)" - a narrative.
Written by Registrar Yán Wùchéng on the sixteenth day of the eighth month of Tiānfú (天福) fourth year.
"Dà Hàn Sān Nián Chǔ Jiàng Jì Bù Mà Zhèn Hàn Wáng Xiūrǔ Qúnchén Bá Mǎ Shōu Jūn Cí Wén (大漢三年楚將季布駡陣漢王羞恥群臣拔馬收軍詞文)":
In ancient times, Chǔ and Hàn settled Xī Qín,
not yet distinguishing dragon from snake, establishing two monarchs.
Continuous years of battle made rivers boil,
prolonged confrontation made sun and moon dim.
Hàn’s strategists were truly like rain,
Chǔ’s fierce generals exactly like clouds.
Each aided their king to contend for the state,
several years of clashes, no supreme ruler established.
Then, in the tenth month of winter of the third year,
armies were raised again by the Suī River.
Chǔ and Hàn both arrayed their formations,
observing the wind and sensing the atmosphere, ready to devour each other.
Horses reined with jade bells, men girded in armor,
each worried about victory or defeat in the hesitation.
Jì Bù of Chǔ was eloquent,
holding the office of Grandee Censor.
He then reported to the Bā Wáng, boasting of his quick wit,
saying: “I have a good plan for an auspicious moment.
I see that both sides have arrayed their formations,
a tiger-dragon fight will surely cause casualties.
I will curse the Hàn Wáng three or five times,
without using bows and arrows, I will make them withdraw their troops.”
The Bā Wáng heard such words and said: “According to your report, a great loyal official!
Spears and halberds clashing still do not make them retreat,
how can they withdraw troops just by hearing curses?
Since your tongue possesses quick wit,
do not mislead me, the lonely one, with deceptive words!”
Jì Bù, having received the king’s permission to curse,
his intent was like a fierce dragon about to emit clouds.
He then called upon the general Zhōnglí Mò,
each with light cavalry following close behind.
They came out of the formation, throwing flags a hundred paces forward,
halted their horses, hooves gathered, raising no dust.
At his waist was a wolf-tooth halberd with four plumes,
on his arm a Wū Háo bow weighing six jūn.
With the wind, his banners were held high, his yak-tail flags low,
(against) the arrow, his long skirt of chainmail hung low.
From afar, he waved his hand to the Hàn Wáng and cursed,
his words capable of moving heaven and earth.
In a loud voice, he directly called out: “Liú Jì!
You are from Fēng Xiàn in Xúzhōu.
Your mother unravelled hemp and lived in a village,
your father herded livestock and lived in a rural area.
You once served as a village head in Sìshuǐ,
long suffering hunger and poverty in the marketplace.
After taking advantage of Qín’s chaos,
you called yourself king, feigning truth.
How can a crow wear phoenix wings?
How dare a turtle display dragon scales?
A hundred battles, a hundred losses, heaven does not bless you,
two-thirds of your soldiers are lost.
Why don’t you bind yourself with straw ropes,
surrender to my lord and beg for mercy?
If you remain stubborn and boast of fighting the enemy,
you will be captured alive, without any cause for release.”
Drums were not beaten, flags were not unfurled,
his loud and high words were heard one by one.
The Hàn Wáng, being cursed and having his ancestors insulted,
was ashamed to look at his left and right, shamed before his officials.
A phoenix fears a cold crow and dislikes a noisy tree,
a dragon fears common fish and avoids murky water.
He pulled back his horse, whipped it, and immediately fled,
the formation like a collapsing mountain, raising dust across the field.
He reached a slope and rested,
rearranged his spears and banners, and asked his ministers:
“Yesterday, the two armies arrayed for battle,
suddenly I heard two generals speaking confusedly,
who was that person standing on horseback in front of the formation, waving a whip,
cursing in a loud voice?”
After asking, Xiāo Hé reported: “Yesterday, the two generals were audacious and unruly,
insulting Your Majesty and disgracing us, your humble servants,
their curses touched the dragon’s face, angering heaven and earth.
With fine horses and carved saddles, wearing chainmail,
under the flags, they could be clearly recognized.
They were none other than Jì Bù and Zhōnglí Mò,
we definitively know it was no one else.”
The Hàn Wáng heard the words and was deeply enraged,
slapping the table and furrowing his brows, unable to bear the anger:
“Unable to help Hàn eliminate the mad rebels,
you falsely govern to aid the state and harm me, the lonely one.
If I, the lonely one, have no heavenly destiny,
then all matters will truly not be discussed;
but if a patch of cloud covers my head,
all Chǔ generals who surrender will be safe,
only Jì Bù and Zhōnglí Mò,
even being roasted by fire and fried in oil would not be a sufficient misfortune.
You and I, the lonely one, remember this together,
copy their names and record them, do not delay.
When the day comes that I face south and claim supreme power,
I will capture them alive, pulverize their bones, and scatter the dust.”
Later, in the tenth month of winter of the fifth year,
at Gāixià, Chǔ was destroyed, and the smoke and dust settled.
Xiàng Yǔ committed suicide at Wūjiāng,
at that time, the four borders were clear of weeds.
Chǔ’s defeated generals came to surrender to Hàn,
the Hàn Wáng bestowed rewards and extended his grace to all.
Only Jì Bù and Zhōnglí Mò
finally realized that the mouth is the gate of misfortune.
They dared not reveal their names in the enlightened age,
parting ways to flee and hide themselves.
At this time, the Hàn Emperor established his imperial enterprise,
ascended the throne in Cháng'ān, solely claiming supreme power.
The four people were content in their work, the three borders were quiet,
the eight directions revived, and the myriad people rejoiced.
His sagely virtue was majestic, ending military conflicts,
his imperial benevolence vast, cultivating culture.
He often thought of not having punished Jì Bù,
his dragon face always with furrowed brows.
So he issued a decree throughout the land,
sending out to capture vicious villains and search for rebellious ministers.
Whoever captured them would be rewarded with a thousand households and gold,
whoever concealed them would have their family executed.
Within ten days, the document was spread throughout the world,
regardless of prefecture, county, or village.
When Jì Bù learned of the Emperor’s hatred,
he was frantic, almost losing his spirit.
He only sighed that there was nowhere to hide in the world,
heaven was wide but earth was narrow, causing great sorrow.
So he entered the valleys and ravines of Lì Shān,
stealthily living and hiding from death.
At night, he would steal meals from villages,
at dawn, he would enter the mountains to accompany beasts.
He disliked the sun and moon,
loved the stars,
hiding by day and emerging at dusk, fearing encounters with people.
A true man encountering such hardship,
all because he did not recognize the wise and enlightened ruler.
Like this, day and night filled with sorrow and danger,
constantly sighing, his worries like clouds.
Ever since the Hàn Wáng ascended to the supreme position,
the common people revived, and the myriad people rejoiced.
Only I, whose sin is grave, worry for my life,
ultimately, what will become of this body?
Suicide or execution by others will surely come one day,
soaring to heaven or burrowing into the earth is bitterly impossible.
Enduring hunger and thirst is ultimately unbearable,
I must seek refuge with old friends and relatives of integrity.
In the early first watch, when it was just dark and few people walked,
he directly climbed over the wall into the stable gate.
Deep in the night, he stealthily reached the foot of the hall steps,
his shadow a tree in the flower and herb garden.
As Zhōu Shì (周氏) and his wife were eating,
in an instant, they felt a stirring of spirit.
They stopped eating, startled by a burning sensation in their ears,
holding their chopsticks and setting aside their spoons, surprised by a twitch in their eyes.
Suddenly, they stood up and looked towards the gate, asking: “At the foot of the steps, could it be ghosts or spirits?
If it is a living person, speak early,
if it is a ghost, flee to the tombs.
If you are asked and do not speak, you will alarm my servants,
and sharp swords and steel knives will surely harm you!”
Jì Bù secretly and softly reported: “It can be assumed there are no ghosts or spirits at the foot of the steps,
“It was merely an old friendship and duty,
that I came tonight to give you a thousand gold pieces.”
Zhōu Yì [周謚] inquired with a tone: “Every thousand gold pieces must come from a kindness received,
suddenly you say you’ve come from afar to repay a friendship;
this statement must be false, let’s not discuss it further.”
He added: “It’s deep night, you came over the wall into my house,
the night is quiet and no one is around, just speak the truth.”
Jì Bù [季布] replied in a low voice: “Do not speak loudly and disturb the neighbors.
If you hadn’t asked, I couldn’t have spoken,
but since you’ve condescended to ask, I will explain.
There’s no need to ask my name in the dead of night,
I am the man who cursed the battle formation the year before last!”
Zhōu Shì [周氏] then knew it was Jì Bù,
and went down the steps to greet him and exchange pleasantries.
He then asked: “Ever since Dàfū [大夫] has been separated from us,
many springs and autumns have passed.
Since the imperial decree for your capture was issued,
where you have hidden yourself, we have not heard.”
Jì Bù heard these words and wept: “Do not speak of the hardships I have endured.
Ever since I cursed Gāo Huáng’s [高皇] formation,
I have been hiding in mountains and lurking in grass, suffering hardships.
Like a bird in a net, I worried about my wings,
like a fish heading for a cauldron, I cherished my fins.
I have specifically entrusted my remaining life to my kind younger brother,
how can I beg for safety and survival from you?”
Zhōu Shì saw that his words were sincere: “Dàfū, please calm your mind.
From the moment we became friends, it was like Guǎn [管] and Bào [鮑],
our deep friendship and old relationship were once beyond reproach.
Now you are in distress, and the world is small,
where else can you turn to a wild man?
Even if my nine generations of kinsmen were to suffer the crime of defying an imperial edict,
we must live and die together, so do not worry about your life.”
He took his hand and they went up to the hall to sit opposite each other,
ordered food and they ate together, and drank several rounds of wine.
Zhōu Shì explained the details to his wife,
saying: “This is an old friend with whom I have a deep affection.
Now he is in national difficulty and has come to seek refuge with me,
so do not speak of it publicly to the neighbors.”
Jì Bù was then hidden in a double wall,
where even spirits could not know, and people could not hear.
Zhōu Shì’s reputation and position were in the county,
so every morning he wore his cap and entered the public office.
He instructed his wife to prepare and deliver meals,
treating him with the same diligent reverence as an elder.
But Gāo Huáng’s [高皇] desire for revenge was urgent,
so he opened the fan and rolled up the curtain, asking his ministers:
“I sent officials to all the prefectures to search for Jì Bù,
how is it that for months there has been no news?
It must be that the officials are negligent,
for the rebel has not yet hidden himself.”
So he dispatched the relevant authorities to go out again,
changing regulations and revising methods, becoming even more diligent.
They instructed people to brush walls with white clay and paint his likeness,
and then paint even more realistic portraits.
In every locality, two households were grouped into one ‘bǎo’ [保] (mutual surveillance unit),
to report any discoveries or lack thereof.
First, they were to dismantle multi-layered sheds and remove double walls,
then scatter the earth and raise dust.
They searched mountains and followed rivers, fumigating caves,
tramping through grass and scouring forests, blocking tomb entrances.
Whoever was captured by examining appearance and checking names,
would be rewarded with gold and jade, and appointed to a new official position.
Hiding him for even one meal or one night,
would lead to the extermination of one’s clan, the killing of one’s family, and the execution of all six degrees of kin.
He also sent Zhū Jiě [朱解] as an envoy to Qí [齊],
who departed from the imperial court and passed through the national gate.
He rode quickly, shaking his whip, arriving within ten days,
hoping to capture the treacherous villain and his esteemed descendants.
Arriving at the official residence in Púyáng [濮陽],
he fully conveyed the Emperor’s will and declared the edict.
All the prefectural and county officials were worried and afraid,
fearing that failing to capture him would lead to losing imperial favor.
At that time, Zhōu Shì heard the proclamation,
it was like a huge stone pressing on his heart.
Since Jì Bù had been hidden for so long in his house,
he felt chills in his bones, his hair stood on end, and he lost his composure.
Returning to the wall, he looked at Jì Bù,
whose face was ashen, and he frowned repeatedly.
After a long silence, he had no other words,
only saying that disaster was imminent.
Jì Bù did not know the new envoy had arrived,
and instead spoke words of blame to his host:
“Director, you don’t need to scare me.
I often hear the common saying:
‘Living long in one place makes one despised,’
and it’s also said, ‘Troubled waters become turbid.’
If you dislike my imposition and disdain me,
it will be difficult for my guilty self to find peace elsewhere.
If our friendship is broken and human sentiment is thin,
I should kill myself this very morning.”
Zhōu Shì replied in a low voice: “Brother, please listen and do not be angry.
The Emperor’s hatred for you is urgent,
a special envoy has just arrived to proclaim the edict.
The yellow imperial decree is clearly posted in the market,
offering a new large reward of gold.
First, they are to dismantle multi-layered sheds and remove double walls,
then scatter the earth and raise dust.
With such strict and rapid search and capture orders,
it will be extremely difficult for your life and my life to be preserved.
You, brother, were once an imperial censor,
with great virtue, high office, and peerless skill.
My family is willing to face the cauldron and chopping block,
but it would be a pity for your body to turn to dust.”
Jì Bù was alarmed and worried, and asked: “Who is this envoy today?”
Zhōu Shì reported: “He is an Imperial Censor,
named Zhū Jiě, who has received imperial favor.”
At that moment, Jì Bù heard Zhū Jiě’s name,
nodded slightly and smiled, his eyebrows parting.
“If it were anyone else, I would worry for my life,
but why even speak of a fellow like Zhū Jiě?
It is said he is incompetent and receives emoluments in vain,
with a coarse mind, lacking martial prowess and literary skill.
Even if they piled up a thousand gold pieces as a reward,
or amassed ten thousand taels of silver,
the imperial edict, though severe,
scattering dust and raising earth, would be useless.
Since Zhū Jiě has been sent to search and capture,
I have a plan to change my clothes and escape.”
Zhōu Shì heard these words with great astonishment,
speaking as if mocking the emperor with such ease.
“The envoy was specifically dispatched to search and capture,
how then, brother, can you escape?”
Jì Bù then said: “I now have a plan,
just watch me escape, younger brother.
I will cut my hair and wear short coarse clothes,
pretending to be a lowly servant born into the family.
Just say I am a guest from the estate in Yǎnzhōu [兗州],
frequently accompanying you in and out.
When Zhū Jiě returns,
you will sell me as a servant with a mount at the front of the line.
If Zhū Jiě suddenly comes to buy a servant,
discuss it and do not argue vehemently.
If he suddenly buys me and takes me away,
I will hold his whip and carry his hat without complaining of hardship.
If heaven allows me to see Gāo Huáng’s [高皇] face,
it will be like a sick crane soaring into the clouds again.”
He then asked for scissors, about to cut,
changing his form and altering his appearance, deeply distressing his spirit.
[Untying] his hair, grasping the knife, about to cut,
his chest filled with emotion and tears flowed.
He sighed and confessed to Director Zhōu: “I regret my dim mind and eyes in the past,
vainly studying poetry and books, futilely learning swordsmanship,
merely knowing how to discern climates and winds.
I assisted the unrighteous lord in Jiāngdōng [江東],
and reviled the righteous ruler in Xiányáng [咸陽].
This caused me to disregard my own flesh and skin,
ashamed to face the sun and moon, and disgraced by the stars.
Originally, I served my lord, boasting of my loyalty and integrity,
but I have become unfilial and disgraced my family.”
Having said this, he grasped the knife and cut with tears,
making his hair of uniform length, covering his head and eyebrows.
He blackened his skin with charcoal to resemble a wound and smoke-stained flesh,
and swallowed charcoal to alter his voice, making his speech unclear.
He went in and out with Zhōu Shì,
and the neighbors believed him to be a warehouse keeper.
Zhū Jiě, the Imperial Censor from Dōngqí [東齊],
took a rest during his travels and entered the city gate.
He saw a low-status person, six feet tall,
with skin all over like it had been smoked.
Bewildered and entranced, he decided to buy him,
intending to show him off to the people of Luòyáng [洛陽].
He asked, “Who is the master of this lowly person?
I intend to discuss buying him for a few strings of cash.”
Zhōu Shì came forward on horseback and saluted,
and according to the previous plan, he explained:
“This one was bought as a warehouse keeper due to a lack of funds,
I will sell him for one hundred gold pieces to relieve my family’s poverty.
If Dàfū wishes to discuss purchasing him,
I will follow your instructions without argument.”
Zhū Jiě asked Zhōu Shì: “What virtue or skill does he possess to be worth a thousand gold pieces?”
Zhōu Shì then praised his skills: “Although he is lowly, he is extraordinary.
From childhood, his parents doted on him,
as he was born and raised in our household.
He is particularly skilled at massaging, making one soft and pliant,
and folding clothes nicely, perfuming them.
He can deliver messages and also read characters,
and can accompany and teach children to enter the school.
As for riding, he is skilled at saddling and bridling,
having once herded horses on the estate.
“I, the Emperor, for old feuds, laid waste the land,
letting them, year after year, impoverish the four seas.
As you, my esteemed minister, have advised, cease the search and capture,
dissolve the grievances, release the knots, and end the discourse!”
Hóu Yīng prostrated himself, bowed, and departed the golden hall,
going to see Jì Bù and share the joyful news.
“The Emperor has pardoned you;
you may now live a carefree and unburdened life!”
Jì Bù’s heart swelled upon hearing these words,
“I have long suffered hardships and bitterness.
Although the decree for cessation of search and capture has been issued,
I should still lie low and guard the dust.
If not for the 'thousand gold' imperial edict,
I would rather be executed than show myself in vain.”
Hóu Yīng heard these words and felt a surge of anger: “How could one issue a 'thousand gold' edict to a rebellious minister!”
Jì Bù bowed again and respectfully replied: “Another memorial should seek to open the benevolence of Yáo and Shùn.
Just say that Jì Bù’s heart is stubborn and hard,
unashamed of the sagely virtue and disloyal to imperial favor.
Knowing his crimes are grave and fearing the cauldrons of punishment,
he fears fleeing to the Róng Dí beyond the river ford.
If he gathers wild soldiers to invade Hàn territory,
the border regions will inevitably be stirred with war.
One concern is like Xiàng Yǔ being reborn in the East,
the second concern is Qín being re-established in the West.
If Your Majesty summons him with a 'thousand gold' edict,
he will surely be able to assist and become a loyal minister.”
Hóu Yīng heard such words and said: “According to you, one can move the stars.
I shall go and present another memorial for you,
but when the memorial is presented, Emperor Pān might be angered.”
Awaiting the early court, he entered the palace
and presented the aforementioned memorial to the Emperor:
“Yesterday, by Your Majesty’s sacred compassion, Jì Bù was pardoned,
bringing peace to the country and its people, and fresh joy.
Your servant fears that Jì Bù is still obstinate and rebellious,
unashamed of Your sacred grace and disloyal to imperial favor.
If Your Majesty ceases the search and capture,
he might flee to the Róng Dí beyond the river ford.
He might gather wild soldiers to invade Hàn territory,
and the border regions will inevitably be stirred with war.
One concern is like Xiàng Yǔ being reborn in the East,
the second concern is Qín being re-established in the West.
Your servant has heard that Jì Bù is resourceful,
skillful in strategy and adept at military command.
His attack breaks the vanguard like frost withering leaves,
his charge through formations is like wind sweeping clouds.
If only a 'thousand gold' edict is issued to summon him,
he will surely demonstrate loyalty in gratitude for the national benevolence.”
The Emperor heard these words and was greatly pleased: “I am grateful for your frequent loyal remonstrances!
I, the Emperor, suffered injuries during the struggle for the throne,
my body covered in boils from arrow wounds.
I still dream of the battles against the Chǔ family,
let alone my concern that Jì Bù might disturb the universe.
As you have advised, I shall issue a 'thousand gold' edict,
swearing by the mountains and rivers to record his meritorious service.”
Since Jì Bù received the scarlet edict,
he immediately cast off his worries and drafted a memorial.
The memorial read: “Your servant, in service to Heaven, should be pulverized!
Your servant lived in Dōngqí, simple and true,
residing in a humble alley, growing up with a thatched gate.
Unaware of Your Majesty's dragon fate,
I assisted the wolf-tiger ruler of Jiāngdōng.
My reckless schemes and abusive taunts of the ancestors
have led me to the boiling cauldrons of affliction.
Now Your Majesty ascends the throne, broadening the sacred era,
greatly opening the benevolent sun of Shùn and spreading the auspicious clouds of Yáo.
That this sinful servant is not slain but given a 'thousand gold' edict,
my gratitude is overwhelming and difficult to express fully.
I beg that your servant’s remaining life be dedicated to agriculture,
so that my family, including all nine generations, may rejoice in life, death, glory, and prosperity.”
At that time, he was led to the imperial court,
and the officials in charge ushered him through the golden gate.
The Emperor rolled up the screen to look at Jì Bù,
and remembering his abusive taunts, suddenly grew angry.
He immediately ordered the warriors to seize him: “Boil him for me; he is not to live!”
As he was being seized and led outside the palace,
Jì Bù shouted loudly, his voice reaching the hall:
“A sagely and enlightened Son of Heaven is worthy of assistance,
but what's the point of discussing a king who speaks falsely!
You clearly issued a 'thousand gold' edict,
lured your servant to the court gate, and now you kill him.
Though it is my due to suffer execution for my crimes,
how can Your Majesty bear to be remembered thus by future generations!”
The Emperor heard these words instantly,
turned his anger into joy, and ordered him to be spared.
“I pity your resourceful and strategic mind,
let us not speak of those past minor offenses.
I bestow upon you brocade, silk, and precious jades,

so do not say that the poet's song is untrue.

Gǔsǒu called out to Shùnzi: "Your father sees the granary in the back courtyard,

He mixed a pile of muddy water,

His stepmother asked Gǔsǒu: "That enemy of yours is repairing the granary,

As soon as Shùnzi ascended the granary,

Shùnzi feared for his life,

Shùnzi was a sagely monarch,

"Since my husband went to Liáoyáng,

The stepwife replied to Gǔsǒu: "If we don't humiliate him, all matters will be cut off;

Gǔsǒu replied to his wife: "Although you are a woman,

He loudly called out to Shùnzi: "Your father's dry well in front of the hall
has been without water for two or three years.
If you can clean the well until water comes out,
would that not be a matter accomplished for the family by my son?"
Shùn heard about cleaning the well,
and knew in his heart,
so he took off his clothes,
knelt by the well,
and entered the well to dig out the mud.
Di-shì from the upper realm
secretly sent down five hundred silver coins,
into the well.
Shùnzi then placed the silver coins in the mud bucket,
and had his stepmother pull it out.
After several times,
he reported to his father and stepmother: "The well is full of water and the money is gone.
If you let me come out,
and give me a plate of food,
would that not be my stepmother's virtue?"
When his stepmother heard this,
she falsely said to Gǔsǒu: "That enemy of yours said
I must not use my silver coins;
if I use my silver coins,
he will go out and report to the authorities,
and the whole family will not survive."
Gǔsǒu then immediately filled the well with large stones.
His stepmother's daughter held onto her father: "If you kill the older brother from the previous marriage,
where will he resurface?"
His father did not listen,
pulled her hand away and buried the well.
Di-shì transformed into a yellow dragon,
and led Shùn through a tunnel,
emerging from the well of the eastern neighbor.
Shùn called out, reporting his presence,
just as an old woman was fetching water,
and she responded: "Who is calling from the well?"
Shùnzi replied: "I am the unfilial son from the western house."
The old woman immediately knew it was Shùn,
and pulled him out.
Shùn immediately wept and bowed,
the old woman then gave him clothes,
which he put on,
and a plate of food which he ate.
She told Shùn: "Do not return home,
but go to the tomb of your birth mother,
and you will surely see your mother appear."
Having finished speaking,
Shùn immediately searched for his mother's tomb.
He saw his mother's true form,
and wept tears of blood.
His mother told Shùnzi: "Son, do not return home;
your great tribulation is not yet over.
Instead, go cultivate the fields on Mount Lì in the southwest corner;
you will surely become noble."
Shùn took leave of his mother,
and they parted ways. He walked into the mountains
and saw over a hundred *qǐng* of empty fields.
His heart was choked with emotion,
for he had no seeds or plowing oxen
and nowhere to obtain them.
Heaven, knowing his supreme filial piety,
provided a herd of pigs that used their snouts to plow the land and open furrows.
Hundreds of birds carried seeds (and scattered them) in the fields,
and heaven sent rain to irrigate them.
That year, the whole world suffered from poor harvests,
but Shùnzi alone had an abundant yield,
obtaining several hundred *shí* of grain.
His heart yearned for his homeland,
intending to repay his parents' kindness.
As he journeyed, he came to a river.
Shùn saw a herd of deer
and sighed, saying, "Though I am in human form,
I am not like these wandering deer."
As he wept and sighed,
he again saw several merchants.
Shùnzi asked, "Are the people of the Yáo family in Jìjùn
all well and good?"
The merchants replied, "There are tens of thousands of Yáo families.
Who would know your relatives?
There is one family named Yáo
who said they sent their son to dig a well.
His stepmother, out of jealousy,
colluded with her husband to fill the well and (kill) the child.
Since then, Āyé's eyes have been blind,
and the mother became stupid (or foolish),
carrying firewood to the market.
There is also a younger brother,
who is also crazy and demented,
suffering extreme poverty,
with no way to beg for food.
We only know this one family;
as for other families named Yáo,
we do not know who they are."
Shùnzi immediately knew that these were his parents and younger brother.
He pondered in his heart,
but did not speak.
Shùn came to Lìshān,
and after ten years had passed,
he took his rice to his home province.
When he arrived at the market,
he saw his stepmother carrying firewood
to the market to exchange for rice.
It happened that Shùn was selling rice at the market.
Shùn recognized her
and sold it to her.
Shùn, having received the mother's money, pretended to forget it,
placed it in her rice sack, and left.
This happened more than once.
Gǔsǒu found it strange
and said to his second wife, "Is that not our son Shùnzi?"
His wife replied, "He was buried at the bottom of a hundred-foot well,
crushed with large stones,
and filled with earth.
How could he still be alive?"
Gǔsǒu said, "You try leading me to the market."
His wife led Sǒu to the market,
where they again saw the young man selling rice.
Sǒu said to him, "What virtuous person are you,
who has repeatedly shown such generosity?"
Shùn said, "Seeing your old age,
I therefore show you kindness."
Sǒu recognized his voice with his ears and said, "This sounds exactly like the voice of my son Shùnzi!"
Shùn said, "It is I."
He then stepped forward and embraced his father's head,
crying loudly without restraint.
Shùnzi wiped his father's tears,
and licked his eyes with his tongue,
whereupon both eyes immediately regained sight.
His mother also became intelligent,
and his brother could speak again.
The people in the market, seeing this,
could not help but sigh with sorrow.
At that time, Shùnzi brought his parents back to their home.
Gǔsǒu (wept and said), "My son is filial."
Without considering the consequences,
he gathered neighbors and relatives,
and took a knife to kill his stepmother.
Shùnzi clasped his hands and pleaded with the elder, "If you kill Āniáng,
Shùn will truly be without filial piety.
Please consider this, elder."
The neighbors were saddened,
for such a thing had never been heard of in the world.
After his father spared his mother's life,
his heart and mind were completely joyful,
and his name spread throughout the land.
Emperor Yáo heard of this
and gave him his two daughters in marriage:
the elder, Éhuáng,
and the younger, Nǚyīng.
Yáo then abdicated his position to Emperor Shùn.
Yīng gave birth to Shāngjūn,
who was unworthy.
Shùn therefore abdicated his position to King Xià Yǔ.
The poem says:
Gǔsǒu filled the well and became blind,
Shùnzi always cultivated the fields on Lìshān.
He took rice to Jìdū and met his parents,
and by licking their eyes with his tongue, restored their sight.
Another poem says:
Filial piety to parents touched Heaven,
Shùnzi dug a well and obtained silver money.
His parents crushed Shùnzi with stones,
which moved the well-digger to connect to the eastern house.
*Shùnzi Zhìxiào Biànwén* (Transformation Text of Shùnzi's Extreme Filial Piety), one scroll.
It is found that *Bǎisuì Shī* (Poem of One Hundred Years) says: "Shùn at twenty studied.
At thirty,
Yáo promoted him.
At fifty,
he extensively managed the affairs of the world.
At sixty-one,
he replaced Yáo and ascended the imperial throne.
He reigned for thirty-nine years.
He went on a southern inspection tour
and died in the wilds of Cāngwú
at the age of one hundred.
He was buried in Jiǔyí (Mount Jiǔyí) south of the [Jiāng] River.
This is Línglíng.
Shùnzi's surname was Yáo,
his courtesy name Chónghuá."
It is also found that *Lìdì Jì* (Records of Successive Emperors) says: "Shùn's appellation was Yǒuyúshì,
his surname Yáo,
and he had double pupils in his eyes.
His father's name was Gǔsǒu,
his mother's appellation Wòdēng,
a descendant of Zhuānxù,
and a ninth-generation grandson of Huángdì.
His capital was Píngyáng,
later Púbǎn.
Xià Yǔ succeeded him.
Kǒng Ānguó says: "Shùn reigned for fifty years,
and was one hundred twelve years old.
He died
and was buried on Mount Jiǔyí in the wilds of Cāngwú.
The first year of Emperor Shùn was Wùyín."
Recorded on the fourteenth leaf of *míngshēng* in the month of Zhūmíng Ruìbīn, in the *jǐyǒu* year, the fifteenth year of Tiānfú, when the year was *jǐyǒu*.
Once there was a virtuous scholar,
named Hán Péng.
He was an orphan from a young age,
suffering the loss of his father.
He alone supported his aged mother,
carefully practicing filial piety.
His mother's desire was for him to serve in distant offices.
Remembering his mother lived alone,
he therefore married a virtuous wife,
Chénggōng Sùnǚ,
who was seventeen years old at the beginning of their marriage,
her name being Zhēnfū.
She was already virtuous to the point of being sagely,
obviously outstanding and splendid,
her appearance graceful and charming,
without equal in the world.
Although she was a woman,
she clearly understood the classics and books;
all her actions
accorded with heavenly principles.
Three days after entering his home,
their intentions aligned in cohabitation.
They made a vow together,
each guarding their body.
You, my lord, need not marry another wife,
like fish and water;
I, your concubine, will also not remarry,
serving one husband until death.
This 3227 is Scroll B.
The original text has a complete beginning but an incomplete end.
Hán Péng (韓朋) went out traveling,
serving as an official in the state of Sòng (宋國).
It was agreed he would be gone for three years,
but six autumns passed and he did not return.
Péng's (朋) mother missed him,
her heart filled with vexation and resentment.
His wife thought of him,
and from her innermost being, she was moved,
suddenly taking up her brush,
and composing a letter word by word.
Its writing was vivid,
the words like fragmented gold,
like pearls and jade.
She wished to send the letter with a person,
but feared people would gossip;
she wished to send the letter with a bird,
but birds always fly high;
she wished to send the letter with the wind,
but the wind is in the empty void.
If the letter were sensitive,
it would reach Péng (朋);
if the letter were not sensitive,
it would fall and scatter among the grass.
The letter was sensitive,
and reached Péng (朋).
Hán Péng (韓朋) received the letter
and deciphered its words.
The letter said: "Vast, vast white waters,
flowing with swirling waves.
Bright, bright moon,
obscured by floating clouds.
Lush, lush waters,
with their seasons in winter and summer.
If not sown at the right time,
grain and beans will not grow.
All things sprout and transform,
not violating the heavenly timing.
Long have we not seen each other,
my heart is deep in thought.
A hundred years together,
was only good for a moment.
You do not remember your kin,
your aged mother's heart is sorrowful.
Your wife is alone and frail,
often sleeping solitary at night,
constantly filled with great sorrow.
I have heard that when a hundred birds lose their mates,
their cries are mournful;
sleeping alone at dusk,
the night is long and distressing.
Mount Tài (太山) at its birth,
is high and low, rugged and towering.
Above it are a pair of birds,
below it are divine turtles,
playing day and night,
always returning together.
What sin have I committed now,
to be solely without splendor?
The ocean waters surge,
waving without wind.
Those who fulfill are few,
those who destroy are many.
There are birds on the South Mountain,
a net is spread on the North Mountain;
the birds fly high by themselves,
what can the net do?
May you just be safe,
and I will have no other concern."
Hán Péng (韓朋) received the letter,
his heart moved with sorrow,
he did not eat for three days,
nor did he feel hunger.
Hán Péng (韓朋) wished to return home,
but there were no circumstances for it.
He held the letter carelessly,
and lost it before the palace hall.
The King of Sòng (宋王) found it,
and greatly admired its words.
He immediately summoned his ministers,
and also the Grand Astrologer: "Whoever can bring Hán Péng's (韓朋) wife,
will be granted a thousand *jīn* (斤) of gold,
and an estate of ten thousand households."
Liáng Bó (梁伯) addressed the King, saying: "Your subject can bring her."
The King of Sòng (宋王) was greatly pleased,
and immediately dispatched an eight-wheeled carriage,
and dappled horses with white forelegs,
with officials attending before and after,
totaling more than three thousand people.
They set off on the road,
as swift as wind and rain.
Three days and three nights,
they arrived at Péng's (朋) house.
The envoy dismounted,
knocking and calling at the gate.
Péng's (朋) mother came out to see,
her heart filled with fright.
She immediately asked the caller: "Whose envoy are you?"
The envoy replied: "I am an envoy sent by the state of Sòng (宋國),
a companion and friend of Péng (朋).
Péng (朋) is a *gōngcáo* (功曹),
I am a *zhǔbù* (主簿).
Péng (朋) has a private letter,
sent for his new wife."
The old woman turned and said to the new wife: "According to this guest's words,
Péng (朋) is now an official,
and has found a successful path."
Zhēnfū (貞夫) said: "The new wife had a bad dream last night,
confused and unclear.
I saw a yellow snake,
coiling around the leg of my bed.
Three birds flew together,
two birds fought each other.
One bird's head was broken and its teeth fallen out,
its feathers falling profusely,
blood flowing abundantly.
Horse hooves clattered,
the ministers were mighty.
Up and down I saw no neighbors,
let alone a guest from a thousand *lǐ* (里) away.
A guest from afar,
can ultimately not be trusted.
With clever and articulate words,
he fraudulently presents Péng's (朋) letter.
If Péng (朋) were truly outside,
his new wife would go out to see him.
Old woman, tell the guest,
just say that the new wife is ill in bed,
and cannot bear any medicine."
She then declined the guest's offer,
acknowledging his arduous journey.
The envoy replied: "The wife hears her husband's letter,
why is she not happy?
There must be some other affair,
involving the neighbors."
Péng's (朋) mother was old,
and could not discern the true intention.
When the new wife heard the guest's words,
her face turned green and then yellow: "If this guest's words
mean there is some other affair,
then I would want to question his intention,
and lose my reason.
Sending me to see the guest,
would be to lose my mother's virtuous son.
From now on, the mother-in-law will also lose her daughter-in-law,
and the daughter-in-law will also lose her mother-in-law."
Thereupon she descended from the golden loom,
bidding farewell to her royal duty,
saying: "For a thousand autumns and ten thousand years,
I will weave you no more.
Clear, clear well water,
when will I draw you?
Pot and stove,
when will I cook on you?
Bed and boudoir,
when will I sleep on you?
Vast, vast courtyard,
when will I sweep you?
Green, green garden vegetables,
when will I pick you?"
She went in and out weeping bitterly,
the neighbors felt sorrow.
Lowering her head, she walked backward,
tears falling like rain.
She ascended the hall to bow to the guest,
and the envoy helped her into the carriage.
Zhēnfū (貞夫) got into the carriage,
swift as wind and rain.
Péng's (朋) mother behind,
cried out to heaven and earth,
wailing loudly,
and the neighbors gathered in alarm.
Zhēnfū (貞夫) said: "What good is crying out to heaven,
what escape is there in calling to earth?
A four-horse carriage once gone,
how can it ever return!"
Liáng Bó was swift,
daily moving further away.
Upon first arriving in the State of Sòng,
over nine thousand lǐ,
light shone into the palace.
King Sòng found this strange,
and immediately summoned his ministers,
and also the Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐ).
They opened books and sought divinations,
wondering about its meaning.
The Erudite (Bóshì) replied: "Today is jiǎzǐ,
tomorrow is yǐchǒu.
With all the ministers gathered,
the king will gain a good wife."
Before his words were finished,
Zhēnfū arrived.
Her face was like congealed cream,
her waist like bound silk,
possessing beautiful patterns.
Of the palace women and beauties,
none could compare to her.
King Sòng saw her
and was greatly pleased.
For three days and three nights,
the joy was endless.
He immediately appointed Zhēnfū,
making her his empress.
Attendants before and after
entered her palace.
When Zhēnfū entered the palace,
she was haggard and unhappy,
sick in bed and unable to rise.
King Sòng said: "You were the wife of a commoner,
now you are the mother of a nation.
What is there to be unhappy about?
Your clothes are brocade and fine silk,
your food is whatever you desire.
The Imperial Secretary (Huángmén Shìláng)
is always at your side.
What is there to be unhappy about,
or not joyful?"
Zhēnfū replied: "Leaving home and parting with kin,
to serve Hán Péng in separation,
life and death have their place,
nobility and lowliness have their distinction.
Reeds have their land,
thorns have their clumps,
jackals and wolves have companions,
pheasants and rabbits have pairs.
Fish and turtles have water,
they do not enjoy high halls.
Swallows and sparrows fly in flocks,
they do not enjoy phoenixes.
I am the wife of a commoner,
I do not enjoy being the wife of King Sòng."
The lady was worried and unhappy,
the King said: "The lady is distressed,
who can admonish her?"
Liáng Bó replied: "I can admonish her.
Péng is not yet thirty years old,
he is over twenty,
his appearance is graceful,
with black hair and fair skin,
teeth like jade pendants,
ears like hanging pearls.
Therefore, she misses him,
and her feelings are unhappy.
One must quickly harm Péng's person,
and make him a prisoner."
King Sòng then adopted his words,
and immediately struck Hán Péng, knocking out both his front teeth.
He was also dressed in old, torn clothes,
and made to build the Qīnglíng Terrace.
When Zhēnfū heard of this,
it pained her liver and intestines deeply,
her heart was vexed with resentment,
thinking of him constantly.
Zhēnfū petitioned King Sòng, saying: "Once the Qīnglíng Terrace is built,
I beg to be allowed to go and see it briefly."
King Sòng granted it.
He then bestowed an eight-wheeled carriage,
claw-colored (or red-maned) horses,
with attendants before and after,
over three thousand people,
who went to the foot of the terrace.
There she saw Hán Péng,
cutting grass to feed the horses.
Seeing his wife, he felt shame,
and covered his face with grass.
Zhēnfū saw him,
and her tears fell like rain.
Zhēnfū said: "King Sòng has clothes,
but I do not wear them;
if the King has food,
I do not taste it.
I miss and long for you,
like the thirsty long for water.
Seeing your suffering,
cuts my heart and intestines.
My appearance is haggard,
I am determined to repay King Sòng.
Why the shame,
covering your face with grass,
avoiding and hiding from me?"
Hán Péng replied: "On the southern mountain there is a tree,
named Thornbush.
One branch, two stems,
small leaves and flat heart.
My appearance is haggard,
I have no heart.
I have heard of water flowing east,
and fish of the Western Sea.
Leaving the lowly and going for the noble,
what do you think of that?"
When Zhēnfū heard these words,
she lowered her head and turned back,
tears falling like rain.
She immediately tore off three inches of silk from the front of her skirt,
bit her tooth to draw blood,
and then wrote a private letter,
attached it to an arrowhead,
and shot it to Hán Péng.
Péng received this letter,
and then immediately died by himself.
When King Sòng heard of it,
his heart was shocked,
and he immediately asked his ministers: "Did he die by himself,
or was he killed by someone?"
Liáng Bó replied: "When Hán Péng died,
there were no injuries,
only a three-inch plain letter,
tied beneath Péng's head."
King Sòng immediately took it and read it.
Zhēnfū's letter said: "The sky rains continuously,
fish swim in the pond,
the large drum is silent,
the small drum has no sound."
King Sòng said: "Who can interpret this?"
Liáng Bó replied: "I can interpret it.
The sky rains continuously are her tears,
fish swimming in the pond is her intention,
the large drum being silent is her breath,
the small drum having no sound is her thoughts.
Her words are for all under heaven,
their meaning is truly profound!"
Zhēnfū said: "Hán Péng is already dead,
why speak further?
I only wish for Your Majesty's kindness,
to bury him with proper rites,
can this not benefit future generations?"
King Sòng immediately sent people to the east of the city,
to dig a hundred-zhang deep tomb pit,
which was the burial rite for the Three Dukes (Sān Gōng).
Zhēnfū begged to go and see it,
not daring to linger long.
King Sòng granted it.
He ordered her to ride in a plain carriage,
with attendants before and after,
over three thousand people,
who went to the burial site.
Zhēnfū got out of the carriage,
circled the tomb three times,
howling and weeping mournfully,
her voice reaching the clouds,
approaching the pit and calling out to her lord,
but her lord did not hear.
She turned her head and bade farewell to the officials: "Heaven will repay this kindness.
I have heard that one horse is not fitted with two saddles,
and one woman does not serve two husbands."
Before her words were finished,
she immediately entered the chamber,
her clothes soaked in bitter wine,
then brittle like green onions,
she pulled left and pulled right,
and with her hands, she disappeared.
The officials were terrified and flustered,
all beating their chests.
They immediately dispatched an envoy,
to run and report to King Sòng.
The Wáng heard these words,
and was greatly enraged.
He grabbed a sword from beside his bed,
and killed four or five of his ministers.
Flying wheels came and went,
and all the officials gathered.
There was a great rain across the land,
and water flowed into the pit,
making it difficult to retrieve.
Liáng Bó admonished the Wáng, saying: “There is only certain death,
no chance of life.”
The Sòng Wáng immediately sent someone to retrieve him.
Zhēn Fū was not found,
only two stones were obtained,
one green and one white.
The Sòng Wáng saw them,
buried the green stone to the east of the road,
and the white stone to the west of the road.
A guìshù grew to the east of the road,
and a wútóng grew to the west of the road.
Their branches met,
their leaves intertwined,
their roots connected below,
and beneath them flowed a spring,
blocking passage completely.
The Sòng Wáng went out on an excursion and saw them,
asking: “What kind of trees are these?”
Liáng Bó replied: “These are Hán Péng’s trees.”
“Who can explain this?”
Liáng Bó replied: “Your minister can explain it.
The branches meeting signify his intent,
the leaves intertwining signify her thoughts.
The roots connecting below signify their vital energy,
and the flowing spring beneath signifies their tears.”
The Sòng Wáng immediately sent people to cut them down.
For three days and three nights,
blood flowed profusely.
Two scrolls fell into the water,
transforming into a pair of yuānyāng,
who raised their wings and flew high,
returning to their homeland.
Only one feather remained,
most beautiful and upright.
The Sòng Wáng obtained it,
and immediately stroked and caressed its body,
which emitted a brilliant radiance.
Only the neck remained unpolished,
so he immediately stroked and caressed the neck,
and its head immediately fell off.
He forcibly took the common man’s wife,
and unjustly killed the virtuous.
Before three years had passed,
the Sòng kingdom perished.
Liáng Bó and his son,
were exiled to the frontier.
Those who do good receive blessings,
those who do evil incur calamity.
One scroll of the "Hán Péng Fù."
Written by Zhāng Dào on the eighth day of the third month in the Guǐsì year.
(The previous section is missing) ) Where do the Sān Gōng come from?
Square and round feet,
where is there no gold?
I see that those noble officials in court,
all come from diligent study □□□□□□□.
After three or two years of distant study,
if I do not ride in a carriage and wear a seal,
I swear I will not return to my hometown.
If I do not follow this □□□□□, I shall become mere dirt.”
Having said this,
he straightened his attire and manner,
walked to the front of the hall,
clasped his hands, and addressed his Niáng, saying: “Your son has heard that in ancient times there was Sīmǎ Xiāngrú,
who studied at □□ (Zǐtóng) Mountain,
and was known and renowned.
Sū Qín did not study at Guǐgǔ,
but did not return without wearing the seals of the six states.
Your son has heard: learners are like ox hair,
those who succeed are like unicorn horns.
The ancient texts and edicts,
cannot be mastered in a single reading;
returning home,
cannot be achieved in one step.
Your son now bids farewell to Niáng,
to study afar for three [or two] years,
may Niáng please grant permission!”
His mother heard her son’s words,
and tears involuntarily flowed from her eyes.
She called out to Qiū Hú: “You, come closer,
and listen to your Niángniáng’s words.
The outer writings say: when parents are present in the hall,
children should not travel far,
if they travel, they must have a fixed direction.
Furthermore, you lost your Ā Yé when you were young,
I raised you alone,
and helped you establish yourself.
Now you want to leave me to pursue study,
you must reconsider carefully.
If you wander astray outside,
how will you regret it then? It will be too late.”
Qiū Hú respectfully replied to his Ā Niáng: “Your son has heard that Zēng Shēn was extremely filial,
yet left his parents to serve Zhòngní,
without idleness or weariness,
searching through the Three Histories all day long,
thoroughly understanding the Nine Classics,
to bring honor to his ancestors,
and leave his name for ten thousand generations.
I have also heard that Tài Gōng □ was poor and loved learning,
eventually meeting Wén Wáng,
later attaining the position of Sān Gōng,
how much his former wife regretted it then? It was too late.
Now I intend to pursue study,
diligently emulating the ancients,
in three or two years,
I will surely return home!”
His mother heard her son’s words,
and weeping, she replied again to her son: “You and I, mother and son,
have deep grace and heavy righteousness.
I do not refuse to let you travel and study,
but if you study at home now,
why worry that you won’t master skills and arts?
Even if I let you seek a teacher,
will you immediately become an official?
It is better for you to suppress your desire and stay at home,
deep plowing and shallow sowing,
widely engaging in sericulture,
reading in your leisure time,
will you not achieve success?
It is good to be reunited with your Niáng,
and to constantly see your young new wife,
sharing good things,
knowing bad things yourselves,
laughing and rejoicing together,
expressing shy affection,
rather than separating your Niángniáng,
leaving her lonely and solitary,
weeping as she walks alone.
Even if you achieve success outside,
when you return, will you be able to see me?
Now you are repeatedly,
abandoning me to travel and study,
exert yourself diligently,
and return home soon,
do not let me worry.”
Qiū Hú bid farewell to his mother,
and went to his wife’s chamber.
Her brows were furrowed and unpainted,
her appearance had suddenly changed,
her disheveled hair hung long,
and tears flowed from her eyes.
Qiū Hú addressed his Niángzi, saying: “Husband and wife are of utmost importance,
their union aligns with heaven and earth,
connecting above like golden orchids,
and sharing a coffin below.
Two forms combine into one,
bare bodies in harmony,
attached to bones and buried in the earth,
becoming dust together with Niángzi.
Now I have received Niáng’s instruction,
permitting me to travel and study,
I wonder if Niángzi has granted permission or not?”
His wife heard her husband’s words,
her heart was sorrowful,
and her words were filled with grief.
She spoke, saying: “Lángjūn!
As a child, I am not a member of your family by birth,
nor will I be a ghost of your family in death.
Although I am the mistress of a prominent household,
I am not someone your Yē Niáng oversees.
I have been fostered for fifteen years,
and always intended to leave.
A girl turns outwards,
following her husband for a thousand li.
Today I am assigned to Lángjūn,
and I will obey your decisions, good or bad.
For Lángjūn to pursue study,
this truly pleases my original heart.
Should you achieve success in learning one day,
please return home as early as possible!”
Having bid farewell to his wife,
he put on ten scrolls of texts,
all of which were the "Xiàojīng," "Lúnyǔ," "Shàngshū," "Zuǒzhuàn," "Gōngyáng," "Gǔliáng," "Máoshī," "Lǐjì," "Zhuāngzi," and "Wénxuǎn,"
and then set out on his journey.
Not a month or so passed,
when he journeyed to Shèngshān,
and entered it.
This mountain was also unlike other mountains: its ridges soared to the clouds,
brushing past the sun and moon,
its cliffs hung ten thousand *rèn* high,
vines dangled a thousand *xún* down,
ravines and valleys wound and met,
deep streams intertwined,
bird paths were impassable,
and human traces completely absent.
Qiūhú arrived at this mountain,
and then ascended a stream and entered a valley,
winding around ravines and patrolling forests,
the paths were rugged,
and springs dripped into channels.
Journeying to the deep ridge,
the terrain was positioned strategically,
the mountain peaks were high and bright,
with countless roots of forest trees,
and flourishing flowers and medicinal plants,
all were white sandalwood and black poplar,
camphor and sappanwood,
catalpa and *téngnǚ*,
dissipating fragrant breezes,
peaches, plums, and olives,
holding beauty and longing,
their aroma was not that of *yìzhì* or betel nut.
Qiūhú walked to the foot of the forest,
and saw a stone hall.
Within a *xún* of the entrance,
dwelt an ancient immortal of several thousand years,
who was thoroughly versed in the Nine Classics,
and clearly understood the *Qīlüè*.
Qiūhú immediately paid his respects,
and then diligently served for three years,
mastering the Nine Classics.
When his studies were complete,
he bade farewell to his teacher and left the mountain,
but did not return home,
instead heading to the state of Wèi,
intending to seek office.
With disheveled hair, he wandered aimlessly,
feigning madness and foolishness,
and presented a memorial to Chén Wáng,
vowing not to serve,
to demonstrate his loyalty.
The memorial stated: “Your servant has heard that when the tiger’s stripes are not yet fully revealed,
its strength to devour oxen is already present;
when a swan stretches its wings,
how can it be limited by the effort of parting the clouds?
Dù Zhōuyóu visited Lǔ,
and the Marquis of Lǔ summoned and enlightened him.
Tàigōng fished at eighty,
and King Wén enfeoffed him as prime minister.
Your servant was born in the city of Lǔ,
and grew up in the lands of Wèi,
not having practiced the merits of Cháofù,
but roughly knowing the intentions of Xǔyóu.
Your servant now leaves his home and country,
to serve Your Majesty’s dragon court,
Your Majesty’s benevolence nourishes the court,
why begrudge a single position?
I kowtow and deserve death.”
When the King of Wèi received the memorial,
he was exceedingly pleased.
He declared: “I have heard that since the beginning of heaven and earth,
it has been necessary to have ministers to assist [the ruler].
I am the head,
and ministers are my limbs.
Seeing this worthy minister from the state of Lǔ,
now come to assist the state,
I immediately appoint him Left Chancellor,
and bestow three thousand households upon him.
Silks and brocades,
another one hundred thousand are granted,
singing and lute-playing maidens,
choose as many as you wish,
and servants, both young and strong,
as many as you desire.”
After Qiūhú arrived in the state of Wèi,
several years passed,
he annihilated border forces,
crushed the violent and pacified rebels,
no grievances were left unresolved,
no missions were left unaddressed,
people on the roads sang praises,
all extolling the emperor’s grace.
As for Qiūhú’s wife,
ever since her husband left to study,
six years had passed,
letters were not exchanged,
and communication was cut off.
His wife did not know if her husband was still alive or not.
During this time, she diligently practiced filial piety,
working as a slave when going out,
and as a maid when coming in,
enduring the cold in winter,
and the heat in summer,
raising silkworms and weaving,
to serve her mother-in-law,
diligently day and night,
never ceasing for a moment.
Qiūhú’s mother,
ashamed to see her daughter-in-law alone in an empty room,
without any other thoughts,
then called her daughter-in-law and said: “My son left,
originally planning for three years,
why has he not returned after six years?
I wonder if his life has withered away?
I am ashamed that my daughter-in-law is without a husband,
and shares poverty and hardship with this old woman,
I cannot bear this!
You should not sleep alone in an empty bed,
you should not forever guard an empty room.
You are free to remarry another,
this old woman would never dare to keep you.
I wonder what is in my daughter-in-law’s heart?”
When the daughter-in-law heard her mother-in-law’s words,
she felt a sudden pang in her heart,
and immediately burst into tears,
stepping forward to address her mother-in-law: “My parents arranged my marriage,
originally intending for me to serve my mother-in-law diligently;
my mother-in-law’s son left to study and has not returned,
your daughter-in-law is only fit to serve you for the rest of her life,
why speak of remarrying,
which cuts at your daughter-in-law’s heart?
If my mother-in-law instructs me,
I dare not disobey;
but if by chance your son suddenly returns later,
what shall your concubine say to him?
”When the mother-in-law suddenly heard these words,
she could not help but cry aloud,
tears flowing in streams,
both of them were heartbroken.
Another three years passed,
making a total of six autumns,
then suddenly it became nine years.
Qīu Hú arrived at the morning court on the third day of the third month of the ninth year.
Recalling his mother, he wept tears of sorrow,
clasped his hands before the palace hall,
knelt before the king, bowing four times,
and spoke a single plea: "Your Majesty, your servant has heard that the burdens of the vast heavens
are like seven days without water;
the toil without limit
is like three years of weeping blood.
Dǒng Yǒng sold himself to bury his parents,
and a celestial maiden came to repay his kindness;
Guō Jù buried his child and was granted gold,
for which August Heaven took notice.
A child who shares his clothing
does not complain of frost and cold;
a child of Cháo Fù
would not refuse to guard [his parents] even unto death.
Your servant’s kind father passed away early,
leaving only his mother living alone,
who suckled and raised your servant
until he is now established.
Your servant has also heard that the filial crow has the grace of regurgitating food to its parents,
the lamb kneels to repay its mother,
the ox holds the affection of licking its calf—
how can a mother and child not be fond of each other?
Your servant has been away from his homeland
for nine years now,
and knows nothing of his kind mother's life or death.
Your servant now serves the king with loyalty and zeal,
but his family at home has no way of knowing the details.
Your Majesty's benevolent cloud
spreads sweet dew widely,
nourishing all people,
and the common folk are all without resentment.
Although your servant has received great rewards,
it is like walking in embroidered robes at night.
I earnestly hope for your heavenly grace,
to be permitted to return to my country,
and go back to my old village.
Is this not Your Majesty's gracious kindness?
Only when your servant can see and repay his kind mother
will he truly know himself to be a son.
I humbly await your imperial decree.
What punishment do I deserve?"
When King Wèi heard these words,
he wept tears and assembled his officials,
expressing to his subject: "I have heard that with heaven and earth,
all things are born,
and a ruler is established,
with his ministers lending their aid.
I am the head,
and you are my arms and legs.
In this kingdom of mine,
Qīu Hú has made a name for himself with his talent and aided the state.
Since being appointed prime minister,
he has shown filial piety and loyalty.
Lǐ Jīnshí,
whose prestigious name has spread for ten thousand *lǐ*,
his countenance is uniquely outstanding,
his talent and virtue are exemplary.
This subject remembers his kind mother,
and now wishes to return.
I have feelings of attachment,
so I shall grant him one hundred ingots of gold,
and one thousand lengths of patterned silk.
I shall temporarily allow him to return
to show respect to his esteemed mother.
Once your mission, my lord, is accomplished,
and you have seen your mother, return early."
Qīu Hú, having received the king's command,
was at once joyful and sorrowful.
Sorrowful at leaving the royal court,
joyful at being able to see his kind mother.
He bowed to the king and departed,
then immediately set out on his journey.
By the time of mulberry leaf gathering,
he arrived at his home country.
He rode in a carriage, dressed in purple robes,
with a golden belt around his waist,
and accompanied by an escort.
As he passed through the mulberry grove,
he changed his clothes and proceeded forward.
The trees spread their branches, covering the ground,
their boughs intertwined.
He wished to find someone
to inquire about the news at home.
Looking up, he suddenly saw his chaste wife
alone in the mulberry grove, gathering leaves.
Her appearance had changed,
her face was unadorned,
her dishevelled hair hung long,
her heart heavy as she gathered mulberries.
Qīu Hú suddenly saw his chaste wife,
and gazed at her for a long time.
Her manner was graceful and beautiful,
her face like white jade,
her cheeks touched with red lotus,
her waist like a willow branch,
her delicate eyebrows distinct.
He temporarily stopped his horse,
approached and looked closely.
Because he did not recognize his wife,
he presented a poem:
A jade face reflects a rosy blush,
a golden hairpin is worn while gathering mulberries.
Eyebrows like dark ink appear amidst the branches,
a silk robe is hidden among the leaves.
Cheeks surpass spring peaches and plums,
a body like white snow and frost.
Qīu Hú called out: "My lady!
Have you not heard: 'Gathering mulberries is not as good as seeing a young man,
toiling in the fields is not as good as a bountiful harvest!'
I would graciously bestow upon you two ounces of gold,
and a bundle of patterned silk.
Might I temporarily request my lady to stay in my embrace for a moment?
Would my lady kindly permit this or not?"
The woman came down from the tree,
composed her features.
Not recognizing her husband,
she called out, "My lord!
My husband went away to study
nine years ago now,
and there has been no news, no messages.
My old mother-in-law is elderly,
sitting alone in the hall.
I would rather endure the cold in winter,
and the heat in summer,
rearing silkworms and weaving,
to serve my mother-in-law.
A single horse cannot wear two saddles;
how can a single ox pull two chariots together?
My family is poor and humble;
I would rather starve to death
than value gold.
If my husband were to suddenly arrive one day,
what could this concubine say to him?
Even if gold were piled halfway to heaven,
and patterned silk stacked like hills,
this concubine would still not have such affections;
I would rather hold to my poverty and die."
When Qīu Hú heard these words,
his face showed shame.
He then drove his carriage past.
After traveling a few steps,
he sighed inwardly: "I have heard of chaste men and virtuous women
from ancient times to the present,
but now I see one before my very eyes.
Whose wife is worthy of being recorded in the historical annals,
her name passed down for ten thousand generations!"
Before he had finished speaking,
he arrived home.
He saw his kind mother sitting alone in the empty hall,
unaware of her son's return.
She sighed and said: "Qīu Hú,
when you went away to study,
the original term was three years,
why is it now nine years since you left?
Has your fate perhaps withered and fallen?
Has your body perhaps turned to the Yellow Springs,
your life scattered by the wind?
Or have you perhaps pursued pleasure and not returned?"
Before she finished speaking,
she saw her son,
dressed in purple robes,
standing before her.
Fearing his mother would not recognize him,
he rushed into the hall,
and knelt before his mother: "Do you recognize your son?
I am Qīu Hú.
I have now achieved my mission
and have returned to repay my mother's grace of suckling and raising me."
When his mother heard her son's words,
she called out: "Qīu Hú!
I thought of you not with words,
but as separated by a lifetime—how could I have expected to speak with you face to face?
I am pleased with your gold and silks, my son,
not because I covet your official glory,
but I am ashamed for your wife who has slept alone for nine years.
That you are now esteemed
is not due to your diligent study,
but to the merit of my filial wife."
She sent someone to the mulberry grove
to call her daughter-in-law.
Before the messenger even reached the roadside,
she saw her returning from gathering mulberries.
A villager reported: "Your husband has arrived!
Obeying your mother-in-law's instructions,
I was sent to call you."
Smiling, she immediately returned,
and at home, met her husband.
Suddenly, she heard her husband had arrived.
She could not contain her joy;
joy was in her heart,
and her face was wreathed in smiles.
She went home
and sought her husband in the northern hall,
and met her kind mother-in-law.
The new wife wished to bow in thanks to her mother-in-law,
so she entered her room
to take out her dressing table and adorn herself
to meet her husband.
She drew her emerald eyebrows,
and then applied the hibiscus-like makeup.
She put on her wedding clothes,
and covered her face with a silk fan,
wishing to appear as she did on her wedding day.
She went to the front of the hall and performed the proper courtesies,
to make her mother-in-law happy.
Seeing the new wife arrive,
her mother-in-law humbly thanked her for her nine years of filial devotion and effort,
and then descended the steps,
weeping and calling out: "New wife!
My son has returned!
His studies are complete,
the imperial carriage and seal are with him;
he is a prime minister of the state.
With gold and colorful silks,
he humbly thanks you for your filial kindness.
May the new wife accept them."
Having heard her mother-in-law's words, she turned her face to bow to her husband,
and looked closely at him.
It was none other than the dignitary who had given her gold in the mulberry grove.
Her heart was displeased,
and tears streamed down her face,
she choked and said nothing.
Her mother-in-law was very puzzled,
and repeatedly asked the new wife: "My son has been away for nine years,
and the new wife has now earned a reputation for filial piety.
Why, upon seeing my son return today,
are you suddenly unhappy this morning?
The new wife must have a secret affair
with someone in the neighborhood.
Why don't you quickly tell the truth?
If there is no other reason,
you shouldn't be like this!"
The new wife heard her mother-in-law's words,
and tears streamed down her face.
She then asked her mother-in-law to listen to the reason for her unhappiness.
"The new wife truly has no secret affair.
I only regret two things about your son: firstly, he is unfilial at home,
secondly, he is disloyal to the state."
Her mother-in-law called out to the new wife: "If my son were disloyal to the state,
how could he return home with official honors?
If he were unfilial at home,
the gold and silks would not be suitable for me to see.
If there is no other reason,
why are you making up such words?"
The new wife replied to her mother-in-law: "If your son were filial and kind at home,
heaven's grace would bestow gold,
instructing him to return home
to repay his mother's nurturing kindness.
But before he even saw his mother,
he already gave it to someone in the mulberry grove.
That is why he is disloyal to the state
and unfilial at home.
My parents,
I was matched to him,
and I have served for nine years,
but there have been many shortcomings in my offerings.
This humble gesture,
mother-in-law, I hope you will approve of this filial and kind new wife (
continued below).
On the day Emperor Huìchāng
ascended the throne, he abolished the Three Treasures,
demolishing monasteries,
which caused all monks and nuns across the land
to return to lay life and flee.
It is said that among them was a monk named Fǎhuá Héshàng
who lived in Xíngzhōu.
Knowing that the emperor was without the Way,
he wrapped up the Sūtra and carried it
all the way to the mountains of Suízhōu to hide,
temporarily dwelling in a thatched hut.
He chanted daily
and read sūtras every day.
This moved eight people,
who did not reveal their names,
to come and listen daily.
One morning,
seven people arrived first,
and one arrived later.
Fǎhuá Héshàng felt doubt in his heart,
and spoke to ask: "May I ask, venerable elder,
where do you reside?
What is your name?
Every day eight people come together,
why did you, sir, arrive late today?"
The elder replied: "We
are none other than the eight great dragon kings of the sea.
We know that the Venerable Master is reading a volume of the *Fǎhuá Jīng Yì*
and dedicating its merits to us, the aquatic family,
so that all may share in the blessings.
Our family has nothing to repay you with.
Fearing that the Venerable Master may encounter difficulties,
we specially came to protect and assist you.
Please do not blame us for arriving late just now.
It is because Yáng Jiān of Suízhōu
is destined by heaven
to within a hundred days
have his skull replaced
because his crown of "pacifying heaven" is unstable.
If the Venerable Master does not believe this,
the prefect is currently suffering from a brain ailment,
and no one can cure him.
We eight brothers have nothing else to repay you with,
but we have a dragon paste to give to the Venerable Master.
If you go before the prefect of Suízhōu,
apply the paste,
and he will surely recover.
If you succeed in this,
you must remember our earnest request:
within a hundred days,
an imperial envoy will arrive with an edict.
Advancing one day means death,
retreating one day means injury.
If he later becomes emperor,
he must revive the Buddhadharma.
Then our wishes will be fulfilled.
Now, we bid farewell to the Venerable Master and depart."
Having spoken these words,
they suddenly disappeared.
After Fǎhuá Héshàng saw the dragon kings depart,
he went straight to the yamen of Suízhōu.
The gatekeeper went in to report:
"There is a monk outside
who is skilled in marvelous techniques.
He claims he can heal,
and I dared not not report it."
The prefect heard this,
and immediately invited the monk to ascend to the hall and sit.
He spoke to ask: "I am
suddenly afflicted with a brain ailment.
All prescriptions have been tried,
but no cure has been found.
I know the Venerable Master possesses marvelous techniques.
If you can cure me,
I will certainly not let you down."
Fǎhuá Héshàng heard this,
and took a small box from his sleeve.
He then applied the dragon immortal paste directly to the crown of his head.
It is said that before the paste reached the crown of his head,
there was nothing,
but as soon as it touched the skull,
it was as if a Buddha's hand had plucked it out.
The prefect, being cured,
bowed repeatedly to him
and said to the Venerable Master: "Although the imperial court has issued a clear decree
that no monks or teachers are to be hidden,
it would be a good thing if you were to temporarily stay and hide in my yamen."
Fǎhuá Héshàng heard this,
remembered the dragon kings' earnest request,
and dared not stay long.
He said to the prefect: "Within a hundred days,
you are destined by heaven
to receive an imperial edict from an envoy.
Advancing one day means death,
retreating one day means injury.
If you later become emperor,
you must revive the Buddhadharma.
Then my humble wish will be fulfilled.
Now, I bid farewell to the prefect and return to the mountains."
After the prefect saw the monk depart,
he still had doubts in his heart,
so he wrote on the wall as a record.
Before and after, not many tens of days passed,
when sure enough, the Supervisor of the Astronomical Bureau observed the celestial phenomena at night,
and knew that Yáng Jiān of Suízhōu, within a hundred days,
was destined to receive the Mandate of Heaven.
He presented a memorial to this effect.
When the Emperor read the memorial,
it was as if a great pestle struck his heart.
He immediately dispatched a high-ranking palace official directly to Suízhōu to proclaim the edict.
Upon receiving the edict, the Duke
dared not stay long.
So he set out on the journey with the envoy,
traveling with great speed without stopping,
until they settled down at Chánglè Post Station, more than ten *lǐ* from Cháng'ān.
No sooner had they rested,
the Duke suddenly remembered the instructions of the Fǎhuá Monk: "Within a hundred days,
you are destined to receive the Mandate of Heaven.
Advance one day, and you will perish;
retreat one day, and you will be harmed."
"If I have an audience this [day] morning,
I will certainly meet his poisonous hand."
Having thought this,
he then ordered the imperial envoy to consult with him,
and to have the audience on the following day.
The imperial envoy assented
and presented a memorial to report this.
When the Emperor read the memorial,
his dragon countenance was greatly pleased.
Only Consort Yáng was in tears.
Upon seeing this, the Emperor
declared and asked the Empress: "This crime only concerns Yáng Jiān alone,
it has nothing to do with the Empress."
Consort Yáng bowed in thanks
and went to the inner palace,
thinking to herself: "My father will have an audience tomorrow,
and he will surely meet his poisonous hand.
What good is it for me to be an Empress, to enjoy this glory?
It would be better to take poison and die first,
to avoid seeing the Duke suffer."
Having thought this,
she bathed in perfumed water,
changed her clothes,
and filled a cup of medicinal wine, placing it in front of her dressing table.
The Empress re-combed her cicada-wing hair,
and redrew her moth-like eyebrows.
Just as she was dressing,
she suddenly saw a person in the mirror,
who looked back and stared.
It was the Saint (Emperor) himself.
She rose from her seat.
The Emperor asked: "Empress, you are dressing as usual,
what is the wine for?"
Upon being asked, Consort Yáng's
plan descended from heaven.
She replied to the Saint: "When this concubine dresses,
she must drink this cup of wine.
Firstly, to soften the hair;
secondly, to preserve youth.
It is merely to serve Your Majesty,
nothing else."
When the Emperor heard this,
he was overjoyed:
"The Empress still preserves her youth;
will not I, the lonely one, become handsome after drinking it?"
Upon hearing this, Consort Yáng
quickly offered the cup,
and said to His Majesty: "When this concubine drinks it,
it is called 'dressing wine'.
If the Saint drinks it,
we should change the name of the wine.
What should it be called?
It should be called 'Myriad Years Cup'.
May the Saint live for myriad years, myriad myriad years!"
The Emperor, not knowing it was medicinal wine,
took it and drank it.
It is said that before the wine was drunk, there was nothing amiss;
as soon as it reached his mouth,
his brain split, and his body died.
Upon seeing this, Consort Yáng
dragged the coffin
