under the dragon bed.
She temporarily covered it with a screen.
Then she went to the front hall,
and dispatched an inner palace attendant
directly to summon Yáng Jiān.
Upon receiving the edict, the Duke
felt as if a great pestle had struck his heart.
He dared not disobey the imperial command.
He immediately went for an audience,
proceeding directly to the palace gate.
The official reported his arrival.
When Consort Yáng heard the report,
she ordered him to be granted an audience.
Upon being granted an audience, the Duke
hastened past the palace screen,
bowing and shouting "Long live the Emperor!"
Upon seeing him, Consort Yáng
commanded her attendants: "Help the Duke up,
and grant him ascent to the hall."
Yáng Jiān raised his eyes and suddenly saw the Empress,
thinking to himself: "Will I not escape this calamity today?"
Having thought this,
he then ascended to the hall.
Consort Yáng asked: "Father, do not be afraid.
The Lord has returned to the vast sea (died),
and today you shall become the sovereign of myriad chariots."
When Yáng Jiān heard this,
he was still doubtful.
"If you do not believe it,
go to the dragon bed,
see his coffin,
and then you will believe."
Yáng Jiān replied to the Empress: "I am of humble power,
how can this be?"
The Empress asked: "Father, with whom are you on good terms at court?"
"I have a connection with the Left and Right Jīnwǔ."
When the Empress heard this,
since the power of these two was entirely in her hands,
why worry that a great matter would not succeed?
So she went to the front hall,
and dispatched someone to summon General Hú and Lǎng, the Left and Right Jīnwǔ.
Upon receiving the edict, the two
went directly to the front of the hall.
Suddenly seeing Yáng Jiān,
they felt doubt in their hearts.
The Empress asked the generals: "I know you have a connection with the Duke.
The Lord has already returned to the vast sea,
and now I intend to enthrone the Duke as ruler.
What are your thoughts?"
Lǎng replied to the Empress: "Enthronement is possible,
but what about the assembled court officials?
What should be done?"
The Empress asked: "General, tonight you shall inspect five hundred imperial guards.
They must be equipped with broad-bladed *mòdāo*,
and lie in ambush under the armored screens.
Tomorrow morning, when my father comes to court,
I will personally ask them.
If they agree to enthrone the Duke as ruler,
let nothing be said;
if there is a single dissent,
kill them all in front of the hall,
and enthrone another as minister.
Would that not be a good thing?"
The generals assented,
and then inspected five hundred imperial guards,
who were then ambushed under the armored screens.
The next day, when they came to court,
all the civil and military officials were indeed in front of the hall.
The Empress announced: "The Lord has already returned to the vast sea,
and now I intend to enthrone Duke Yáng of Suízhōu as the master of the universe.
What are your thoughts?"
Upon hearing this, Dàoyóu flicked his sleeve and left.
All the civil and military officials, unable to fathom the situation,
were doubtful in their hearts.
They looked towards the hall
and saw a white sheep, twelve *chǐ* long,
with bared fangs and sharp mouth.
It came down from the hall,
roaring like thunder,
intending to devour all the assembled court officials.
Upon seeing this, everyone
knew that Yáng Jiān was destined to receive the Mandate of Heaven.
They all
bowed and shouted "Long live the Emperor!"
Thus, he was enthroned,
and proclaimed himself Emperor Wén of Suí.
This brought about the submission of the four barbarians
and the surrender of the eight barbarian tribes.
At that time, Chén Wáng of Jīnlíng,
knowing that Yáng Jiān was the ruler,
felt discontent.
He issued an imperial edict to all the ministers of the court,
who gathered before the palace hall.
He then asked: “I, Ānú, now intend to raise an army
to subdue the arrogant Qín.
What are your thoughts, sirs?”
At that time, Zhèn-Guó Shàng-Jiāng-Jūn Rèn Mánnú stepped out from the ranks
and reported, saying: “Your Majesty,
I wish to be appointed as a general
to lead an army to cut them down.
Once Xī-Qín is subdued,
Your Majesty can then proceed.”
Chén Wáng heard this and said: “It shall be as you propose.”
He then appointed Xiāo Móhē and Zhōu Luóhóu as generals
to subdue the arrogant Qín.
The two received the imperial edict,
bowed and danced in thanks for the grace,
and led an army of over forty myriad men,
setting off on their journey.
Within less than ten days,
they reached Guōkǒu and established a camp for rest.
The two generals discussed
marching in two columns,
each with over twenty myriad men.
Xiāo Móhē would attack Sòng, Biàn, Chén, and Xǔ,
while Zhōu Luóhóu would subdue Ān, Fù, Táng, and Dèng.
Upon entering the border regions,
the local villagers and common people submitted memorials to report to heaven.
The Emperor reviewed the memorials,
feeling as if struck in the heart (dà chǔ zhōng xīn).
He then hammered gongs and beat drums,
gathering all civil and military officials and ministers,
who assembled before the palace hall.
The Emperor asked: “I, Ānú, am without virtue,
and have presumptuously ascended to rule.
Now, Chén Shūbǎo of Jīnlíng has become rebellious,
disobeying me, Ānú.
I now intend to appoint a general
to lead an army to cut them down.
Who can go?”
At that time, Zuǒ Lè-Jiāng Hèruò Bì stepped out from the ranks and said: “Your Majesty, I request to lead the army.”
Just as Hèruò Bì requested to lead the army,
one person disagreed.
Who was it?
It was the renowned general Hán Xióngnán (Hán Qínhǔ),
who had lost his father in childhood,
and had personally adopted the alias Qínhǔ.
Feeling discontent,
he stepped out from the ranks, saying: “Your Majesty,
how can a small puddle (tí gōng xiǎo shuǐ)
compete with the vast waves of the great sea?
Even if ants gather in heaps,
how can they become a threat to heaven?
I volunteer to lead the army,
to capture Chén Wáng alive on a specified day and present him.
How dare I not perform this report?”
The Emperor heard this,
and seeing Qínhǔ, who was thirteen years old (nián dēng yī shí sān suì),
still wet behind the ears (nǎi xīng wèi luò),
and yet possessed such great aspirations (yǒu rì dà jīn),
thought, “What worries do I, Ānú, have for the state!”
He intended to appoint Hán Qínhǔ as general,
but feared that Hèruò Bì would be obstructed.
He considered appointing both of them as generals,
but if such a situation existed even before the palace hall,
when leading troops outside,
they would surely quarrel amongst themselves.
“You two may return to your private residences for now.
Come to court another day,
and there will be another edict.”
Later, when they came to court again,
all the ministers of the court were gathered before the palace hall.
He then cast a golden seal,
and first appointed Yáng Sù as Dū Zhāo-Tǎo-Shǐ.
Secondly, he appointed Hèruò Bì as Fù Zhī-Jié.
Thirdly, Hán Qínhǔ was appointed Xíng-Yíng Mǎ-Bù-Shǐ.
The three received the imperial edict,
bowed and danced in thanks for the grace,
and exited the court gate,
leading an army of over thirty myriad men,
setting off on their journey.
Without stopping,
they quickly reached Zhèngzhōu.
The vanguard scouts reported that Xiāo Móhē was leading an army of over twenty myriad men,
camped in Chénliú.
They returned with a full report of the situation.
Shàng-Jiāng-Jūn Yáng Sù heard this,
and immediately established a camp there,
ascending to his tent and sitting down.
He then summoned the two generals,
who stood before him.
He then asked the two generals: “Emperor Wén of Suí stated before the palace hall
that you should swiftly subdue Jīnlíng.
Now the enemy army is pressing close.
Who can go?
If you return victorious,
report it with a memorial.”
No sooner had the general asked,
Hán Qínhǔ stepped out from the ranks
and reported to the general: “Qínhǔ can go.”
“How many troops do you need?”
“I need thirty-five thousand cavalry and infantry.”
He immediately ordered them to be provided.
Qín Hǔ obtained troops,
and the army immediately set off,
marching swiftly without stopping.
They arrived at the border of Zhōngmóu,
and the army encamped there.
Qín Hǔ ascended to his tent and sat down,
then summoned an official soldier to stand before him,
and repeatedly instructed: "You are to scout.
First, obtain the general's orders,
then ascertain the enemy's military secrets,
and return quickly.
You will be handsomely rewarded."
The official soldier assented,
changed his clothes,
and disguised himself as a commoner.
He carried a basket of steamed buns,
and went directly into Xiāo Mòhē's camp,
selling them there.
Having gathered military intelligence,
he immediately returned.
He reported to Qín Hǔ's tent with an assent.
Qín Hǔ asked the official soldier: "What is the military intelligence?"
The official soldier replied respectfully: "The cavalry has a black banner with 'Hǎiyǎn' (Sea Eye) written on it,
and the infantry has a red banner,
with the character 'Shèng' (Victory) filling its center.
The camp gates are wide open,
allowing common people to come and go for trade."
Qín Hǔ heard this,
and immediately knew that Xiāo Mòhē was not a skilled general.
It has been said since ancient times: "A slow army will soon perish,
and a slow ruler will bring the nation to ruin."
Having finished speaking,
he ordered his soldiers
to change their banners and insignia.
At dusk that night,
they immediately set out.
After traveling more than twenty *lǐ* from Xiāo Mòhē's camp,
they took a secret path,
marching swiftly without stopping.
They arrived at the banks of the Jīnlíng River,
plundered boats,
and led their army across.
Upon reaching the southern bank,
all the boats
were sunk in the water,
and then they tied their own banners
to display Qín Hǔ's name.
Leading the army to raid,
they reached Shítóudiàn.
The households cried for help,
and submitted a memorial to the throne.
King Chén, upon reading the memorial,
felt as if a great pestle had struck his heart.
He immediately beat the gongs and drums,
gathering all his civil and military officials and ministers,
all of whom assembled before the palace.
King Chén declared and asked: "I, the unworthy one,
have presumptuously claimed the title of ruler.
Now that Suíjiā soldiers have arrived,
who can defeat them?"
When King Chén asked this,

Rèn Mánnú, a famous general of thirty years and Protector of the State Grand General (Zhèn Guó Dà Jiāngjūn), stepped forward: "I humbly report to Your Majesty: I do not know how many Suíjiā soldiers there are.
Since Qín Hǔ commands an army of thirty-five thousand,
I request to lead thirty-five thousand troops.
There will be no need to deploy formations or unfurl banners;
upon hearing Mánnú's name,
they will immediately surrender."
King Chén heard this,
and ordered the inspection,
brooking no delay.
Mánnú then led thirty-five thousand troops
directly to Qín Hǔ's formation,
shouting in unison,
demanding the Suíjiā soldiers to engage in battle.
Qín Hǔ saw this,
and led his army forward,
asking loudly: "What is the name of this senior general,
and what is your official position?"
The general replied respectfully: "My surname is Rèn, my given name is Mánnú,
and my official position is Zhèn Guó Dà Jiāngjūn."
Qín Hǔ heard this,
and tears streamed from his eyes.
He remembered: "My deceased father entrusted me, saying: 'If you ever become a general,
when you arrive in Jīnlíng,
there is a general named Rèn Mánnú who studied with your father in the same hall,
transcribing books.
When you meet him,
you must observe the proper etiquette between father and son.'
Who knew we would meet today!"
Having finished his thoughts,
he then came forward and addressed the general: "Qín Hǔ bears three staff wounds on his body,
and cannot bow,
I beg the general not to mind."
Mánnú heard this,
and it immediately reminded him of Hán Xióngnán,
thinking to himself: "A father must not fight his son."
He asked Qín Hǔ: "Withdraw your troops and return.
Mánnú will report to King Chén,
send envoys for peace,
and establish a nation of propriety and righteousness.
Would this not be an excellent matter?"
Qín Hǔ heard this,
and felt conflicted,
replying to the general: "When I personally bid farewell to Emperor Wén of Suí,
I pledged to capture Jīnlíng.
If this one task remains unfulfilled,
I must return with three items
to present to Emperor Wén of Suí,
then I will retreat."
Mánnú heard this: "What is the first item you require?"
Qín Hǔ replied: "Firstly, I require the geography and rivers of the Chén territory,
and the number of households,
then I will retreat."
Mánnú heard this: "[This is a small] matter;
I will report it to King Chén."
Mánnú asked: "What is the second item you require?"
Qín Hǔ replied: "Secondly, I require the arsenal and treasury,
to reward the three armies,
then I will retreat."
Mánnú asked: "What is the third item you require?"
Qín Hǔ replied: "Thirdly, I require the head of Chén Shúbǎo to present to Emperor Wén of Suí,
then I will retreat."
Mánnú heard this,
knew the son was disrespectful,
and suddenly became furious.
Qín Hǔ saw this,
drew his sword and brandished it,
asking the general: "The sword in Qín Hǔ's hand
was personally bestowed by Emperor Wén of Suí in his palace.
Its blade reflects frost and snow,
and in battle,
it distinguishes neither kin nor stranger."
Mánnú heard this,
turned his horse, and arrayed a 'Left Concealed Right Barbarian' formation,
demanding the Suíjiā soldiers to engage in battle.
Qín Hǔ saw this,
broke into a smile,
and asked his generals: "Do you recognize this formation?"
All the generals uniformly did not recognize it.
"Although Qín Hǔ was young,
he extensively read his late father's military treatises.
This is the 'Left Concealed Right Barbarian' formation.
See the red banner at the ford ahead?
Below it are all obstacles,
and inside are trip ropes with hooks.
Do not touch them;
you must remember this clearly."
He saw that on the 'Right Barbarian' formation,
there were many soldiers,
and at the front were all bows and crossbows.
Qín Hǔ gave the order: "Shout loudly with the banners!
Enter together with the banners.
If anyone retreats,
I will execute all the generals!
Do not say I did not warn you!"
Having spoken,
they shouted loudly with the banners,
and entered all at once.
This Chén formation, upon a single strike,
immediately disintegrated.
Mánnú led the remaining defeated soldiers
and entered the city.
When Chén Wáng heard the news,
he was extremely furious.
He ordered his attendants,
“Bring him in!”
Dragged horizontally and pulled upside down,
he was brought directly before the hall.
Chén Wáng rebuked him, saying: “You abominable thief,
when confronting the enemy in battle,
you recognized your kin,
thereby destroying Ànú's state.
A defeated general,
it is difficult for him to survive;
a minister who causes the downfall of the state,
his crime is unforgivable.
Drag him out of the army gate
and behead him, then report back!”
Rèn Mánnú, undeterred,
raised his head slightly and said: “I deserve death ten thousand times over, Great King.
I beg you to dispatch troops again
to fight the Suí family soldiers.”
When Chén Wáng heard this,
remembering the great achievements of the renowned general,
he ordered his attendants
to let him raise his head.
Mánnú bowed and danced in gratitude,
then reported, saying: “I wish to request troops
to fight the Suí family soldiers again.
If we return victorious,
I will enthrone Your Majesty,
let you face south and assume the title of emperor.
Wouldn't that be a good thing!”
When Chén Wáng heard this,
he immediately ordered a review of the soldiers in the city,
and commanded them to be handed over.
Mánnú led the army,
feeling undaunted.
From the city, he arrayed a ‘Dragon Emerging from Water’ formation,
advancing directly to the front of the Suí family soldiers.
He raised a large banner and shouted,
demanding battle.
Qín Hǔ, upon seeing this,
smiled broadly,
and turned to his generals, saying: “Mánnú is indeed a renowned general.
Despite his recent defeat, he remains undaunted.
He has arrayed a grand formation from the city.
Do you recognize it or not?”
The generals replied, “General,
though we know how to exert ourselves,
we are not versed in military texts.
What do you say, General?”
Qín Hǔ heard this and said: “Though I am still young,
I have studied my late father’s military texts.
If one encounters the ‘Dragon Emerging from Water’ formation,
one must array the ‘Five Tigers Mimicking Mountains’ formation.”
After he finished speaking, this formation was completed.
Because no generals came forward,
he felt doubt in his heart.
He looked back at this formation,
thinking, if a tiger has no claws or teeth,
how can it be fierce and formidable?
So he drew five hundred archers from the rear guard
to serve as claws and teeth.
When was this formation arrayed?
It was in the year, month, day, and hour of Yín.
Once this formation was complete,
it corresponded to heaven and earth.
Mánnú, upon seeing it,
lost sight of the Suí family soldiers.
He saw the entire field filled with large tigers,
baring their fangs and sharp mouths,
coming to devour Jīnlíng.
Mánnú pondered in his heart: “If one encounters the ‘Five Tigers Mimicking Mountains’ formation,
one must array the ‘Thirty-six Myriad Human Spear’ formation.
Even fighting for ten days and ten nights,
victory or defeat would still be unknown.
My handful of soldiers
are like a piece of meat
entering the tiger’s jaws.
Without being gnawed and chewed,
in the space of a bite,
they will all be utterly destroyed.
I have heard that those who achieve success depart,
and those who have no future cease.
It is better to reverse our weapons
and lay down our armor to surrender.”
Having finished pondering,
he tied himself with straw ropes
and bound his elbows with hemp,
going directly before the general’s horse.
Qín Hǔ, upon seeing this,
ordered his attendants
to lift Mánnú up, saying:
“Those who resist are killed,
but those who surrender are family.
Allow me to report this to Suí Wén Huángdì,
and request that you be adopted and cared for as an uncle.
That would satisfy Qín Hǔ’s wish.”
Having said this,
he led his army into the city.
Chénwáng saw the Suí family soldiers arrive,
and then, fleeing in panic, entered a dry well.
The deities did not assist him,
and it became a flat plain.
When the generals and soldiers saw this,
they immediately captured him,
and brought him before the general's horse.
They rebuked him, saying: "You despicable thief, who harbored disloyal intentions,
and disturbed Zhōngyuán.
Now that you've been caught,
what explanation do you have?"
Chénwáng, being rebuked,
remained silent, speechless.
He was then loaded onto a cart
and taken to the court of Suí Wén Huángdì.
Without stopping, they hastened
until they reached the border of Xīn'ān.
A vanguard commander had learned that Zhōu Luóhóu was leading an army of over two hundred thousand,
intending to intercept their lord.
Qínhǔ heard this,
and then ordered Chénwáng to be brought forth and rebuked, saying: "To betray one's lord
is not blessed by Heaven.
First, I will execute your head,
and then return to the main camp
to await Zhōu Luóhóu in battle."
Chénwáng heard these words
and spoke to the general: "Please allow me to write a letter to Zhōu Luóhóu asking him to surrender.
Wouldn't that be a good thing?"
Qínhǔ heard this
and immediately ordered him to write the letter.
Chénwáng's letter said: "Ānú, when I was in charge of Jīnlíng,
I governed over fifty prefectures,
and over three hundred counties.
I held vast territories,
and commanded an army of a million.
I intended to sweep across the world,
and proclaim myself supreme.
Little did I know that Qínhǔ's soldiers would arrive with a single blow,
causing immediate collapse,
and I was captured on the spot.
Even if you, my lord, command an army,
you must not engage the Suí family in battle.
If you harbor doubts in your heart,
Heaven will not bless you.
Now, Chénwáng's letter has reached Zhōu Luóhóu's hands, open it and read."
After the letter was finished,
a young general was dispatched directly to Zhōu Luóhóu's camp to deliver the letter.
Luóhóu received the letter,
his eyes filled with tears,
and he thought to himself: "My lord has already been captured.
Even if I were to win and turn back the army,
where would the credit go?"
After reflecting, he said: "Generally, a man
should adapt to circumstances;
it is better to surrender to him."
First, he sent twenty myriad sets of military clothing and armor,
then he bound himself with straw ropes
and went directly before the general's horse,
speaking respectfully: "I am a defeated general,
facing a choice between life and death.
I humbly beg the general to accept my surrender."
Qínhǔ heard this,
and said to the general: "Those who resist will be slain,
those who surrender become family."
Having gained the two principal generals,
they set off on their journey,
traveling day and night without stopping,
to the court of Suí Wén Huángdì.
The emperor reviewed the memorial,
and his dragon countenance was greatly pleased.
He immediately ordered an audience.
Qínhǔ was granted an audience,
first presenting the two principal generals,
then he respectfully approached the screen,
bowing and shouting "Long live!"
The emperor saw this,
and his dragon countenance was greatly pleased: "I grant you leave to return to your private residence to rest.
When Yáng Sù arrives,
there will be another imperial decree."
Qínhǔ bowed and thanked him for the grace,
then exited the palace gate
to rest at his private residence.
Not even ten days later,
Yáng Sù returned victorious from his battle with Xiāo Móhē,
and went directly to the palace gate.
The official in charge reported this to the emperor.
The emperor heard the report
and immediately ordered an audience.
Yáng Sù was granted an audience,
respectfully approached the screen,
bowing and shouting "Long live!"
The emperor saw this,
and then summoned all the ministers of the court,
gathered them before the palace hall,
and cast golden seals.
He then appointed Hán Qínhǔ as Kāiguó Gōng,
remotely commanding Yángzhōu as Jiedushi.
Second, he appointed Yáng Sù as Dōngjīng Liúshǒu.
Third, he bestowed upon Hè Ruòbì brocade, silk, and gold and silver artifacts.
The three generals received the decrees,
bowed and thanked him for the grace,
exited the palace gate,
and each returned to their private residences.
Not even ten days later,
the Dàxià Chányú of Běifān sent a Tūjué chieftain as an envoy,
who arrived in Cháng'ān,
and challenged Suí Wén Huángdì to battle.
The emperor heard this
and gathered all the civil and military officials and ministers,
all before the palace hall.
The emperor asked: "The Chányú challenges me to battle,
what is your opinion?"
As soon as the emperor asked,
the barbarian envoy, unfamiliar with court etiquette,
stepped out of his rank and said: "I respectfully report to Your Majesty: the barbarians excel at archery,
and propose a shooting contest right here in the palace hall.
If you can counter my humble arrow,
we will send tribute annually,
and declare ourselves your subjects for years to come.
If you cannot counter my arrow,
then right here in the palace hall,
the fate of your state will be decided."
The emperor heard the report,
and immediately, in the palace hall,
set up a target,
drew two deer,
and instructed them to begin the shooting contest.
The barbarian saw this,
and was overjoyed.
He bowed to the emperor
and shot immediately.
The arrow left the string
with the force of splitting bamboo,
neither east nor west,
hitting the exact center of the deer.
The emperor saw this,
and asked the ministers: "Who can counter it?"
At that time, the Left General Hè Ruòbì said: "I am willing to counter the arrow."
The emperor heard this,
and said: "As you have proposed."
Hè Ruòbì then took his bow,
drew an arrow,
placed the nock on the string,
and shot immediately.
The arrow flew from the string,
neither east nor west,
hitting the same hole.
The emperor saw this,
and his dragon countenance was greatly pleased.
All the ministers of the court,
bowed in unison,
shouting "Long live!"
At that time, Hán Qínhǔ saw that the arrow was not truly countered,
and refused to bow,
standing alone in the palace hall.
The emperor asked: "What is your opinion?"
Qínhǔ reported: "I am willing to counter the arrow."
The emperor heard this,
and said: "As you have proposed."
Qínhǔ bowed and thanked him,
then took his bow,
drew an arrow,
placed the nock on the string,
and shot immediately.
As the arrow left the string,
its force was like a thunderous roar,
neither east nor west,
hitting the barbarian's arrow nock directly,
passing completely through from shaft to arrowhead,
and flying suddenly past,
beyond the target by more than ten paces,
burying itself three feet deep in the earth.
The barbarian saw this,
and was extremely frightened.
He quickly came forward
and bowed deeply.
Qínhǔ saw this
and rebuked him, saying: "You despicable little beast,
harboring presumptuous intentions,
disturbing Zhōngyuán.
Now before the palace hall,
what explanation do you have?"
The barbarian general heard this,
and was extremely frightened.
He immediately took his leave
and set off on his journey.
Suí Wén Huángdì saw this,
and then dispatched Hán Qínhǔ as an envoy to make peace with the barbarians.
Qínhǔ received the decree,
bowed and thanked him for the grace,
then bid farewell to the emperor
and set off on his journey with the barbarian general.
Before and after, not even ten days passed,
when they arrived at the border of the Fān family's territory.
The Chányú received the imperial envoy,
ascended his tent and sat down.
He then summoned his thirty-six eagle-shooting princes,
and instructed them all in his presence: "Since the imperial envoy is here,
and there is no music or entertainment,
and the Fān people excel at archery,
shoot down eagles and geese
to entertain the imperial envoy."
The princes bowed,
and at once mounted their horses.
Suddenly, they saw an eagle approaching from the north.
As soon as a prince saw it,
he immediately shot.
The arrow, once released from the string,
went neither east nor west,
but flew past the eagle's front wing.
When the Chányú saw this,
he suddenly became furious,
and commanded his attendants
to seize the prince,
tear open his belly and take out his heart,
saying, "You have disgraced our Fān ancestors!"
When the imperial envoy saw this,
he promptly came to intercede,
and spoke to the Fān King: "Let this prince be spared this time.
I, however, wish to request a bow and arrows,
to shoot an eagle to entertain the Chányú."
When the Chányú heard this,
he handed a bow and arrows to the imperial envoy.
Qín Hǔ received them,
and while contemplating,
suddenly two eagles
flew by, fighting over food.
When Qín Hǔ saw them,
he was overjoyed,
bowed to the Fān King,
and immediately prepared to shoot.
Qín Hǔ galloped ten paces,
grasped the bow with his arm at twenty paces,
took an arrow at thirty paces,
nocked the arrow to the string at forty paces,
drew the bow into a full circle while shouting,
and at fifty paces, turned his body and shot backward.
The arrow, once released from the string,
had the force of splitting bamboo,
going neither east nor west.
It pierced the throat of the front eagle,
passing straight through,
and then hit the heart of the rear eagle,
causing both eagles to fall before the horses.
When the Fān King saw this,
they all acclaimed, "Good!"
The imperial envoy then took the opportunity to say with a slight threat: "Qín Hǔ is only slightly skilled in archery;
Emperor Wén of Suí has one hundred and twenty commanders who shoot geese,
all of them highly skilled."
When the Fān King heard this,
he quickly dismounted,
bowed and danced facing the south,
shouting "Long live!"
After the bowing and dancing,
he selected one hundred fine horses,
a thousand camels,
various offerings such as *gǔduō* (rams), deer, and musk,
to present to the imperial envoy.
Qín Hǔ then took his leave
and set off on his journey.
Not even ten days passed,
when he reached Cháng'ān,
and proceeded directly to the palace gate.
The officials reported his arrival.
When the Emperor heard the news,
he ordered him to be granted an audience.
Qín Hǔ was granted an audience,
hurried past the screen wall,
bowed and danced, shouting "Long live!"
When the Emperor saw him,
he was overjoyed,
and bestowed upon Qín Hǔ brocade, silk, and gauze,
gold and silver vessels,
and a pair of beauties.
He was told to return to his private residence to rest,
and that there would be further instructions after a month.
Qín Hǔ bowed and danced in thanks,
then went to his private residence to rest.
Not even two ten-day periods passed,
when he suddenly felt unwell,
his eyes twitching and ears burning.
He pondered in his heart,
then ascended the hall and sat down.
Before he had even settled,
suddenly the ground split open in a cross shape,
and a person emerged,
clad in golden chainmail,
wearing a phoenix-winged helmet,
holding three weapons,
bowed his head and loudly saluted.
When Qín Hǔ saw him,
he immediately asked: "Who are you?"
The divine person replied: "I am General Wǔdào."
"Why have you come?"
"Last night, at the third watch, I received a celestial decree
that the General is to become the lord of the underworld."
When Qín Hǔ heard this,
he replied to the Great God Wǔdào: "May I request leave for three days?
Is this possible?"
The Great God Wǔdào reported to the General: "Because the ghosts and spirits of the underworld
have no one to manage them,
not even a moment can be spared."
When Qín Hǔ heard this,
he suddenly became furious,
and asked: "By whom are you managed?"
"I am managed by the Great King."
Qín Hǔ retorted: "Because you have not yet taken leave of your primary lord,
I will give you a hundred iron rods to your left side."
When General Wǔdào heard this,
he was so terrified that sweat streamed down his back: "Your subject reports to the Great King: never mind three days,
you may have leave for a full month."
Qín Hǔ then commanded General Wǔdào: "Go quickly to the underworld to inspect the ghosts and spirits,
and wait for me on the third day."
General Wǔdào bowed,
and his form vanished like a shadow.
After Qín Hǔ saw General Wǔdào leave,
he wrote a memorial to report to Heaven,
detailing the matter to Emperor Wén of Suí.
The Emperor read the memorial,
and was greatly astonished.
He summoned Qín Hǔ
directly to the front of the palace hall.
"Because of my lack of virtue,
I have presumptuously claimed the title of尊 (Exalted One),
unaware that the General is to become the lord of the underworld.
What will become of my humble country?"
Qín Hǔ replied: "Your subject reports to Your Majesty,
should there be any great calamity,
just report it,
and your humble subject will surely lead the armies of the underworld to assist."
When the Emperor heard this,
he commanded all the court officials to a three-day feast,
bidding farewell to Qín Hǔ right in front of the palace hall.
On the third day,
in the midst of joyous singing,
suddenly one person dressed in purple,
and another person dressed in scarlet,
riding a black cloud,
stood before the palace hall,
and loudly saluted.
When Qín Hǔ saw them,
he asked: "Who are those standing before the hall?
Answer immediately."
"We two are from the Celestial Bureau and the Earthly Bureau,
come to take the Great King,
for no other reason."
Qín Hǔ said: "First be given wine and food to consume,
and wait aside for now."
The two bowed,
and each went to one side.
Qín Hǔ then bade farewell to the Emperor,
personally took leave of all the court officials,
returned to his residence,
entrusted his wife, children, and all the good and bad servants of the household,
and then left.
Having finished his instructions,
he went to his bed and lay down.
No sooner had he been covered with a brocade quilt,
he immediately mounted his horse and grasped the saddle,
then ascended the cloud path,
arrived before Emperor Wén of Suí's palace hall,
and then bade farewell to His Majesty and departed.
When the Emperor saw this,
tears filled his eyes,
and he held a cup, poured out wine as an offering, and spoke.
The painting book ends here,
with no further transcription.

and furthermore followed the teachings of Tàishàng Lǎojūn.
Yè Jìngnéng, upon seeing her, admired her,
and immediately took notice,
staying in the abbey
as a Dàoshì.
Day and night she diligently cultivated herself,
learning with great effort and hardship.
At the age of twenty,
she entered the Daoist path.
She dressed in a simple cap and yellow cloak,

Her sincere devotion moved the spirits,
and so she was met by a divine being.
Yè Jìngnéng did not know whence it came.

and devoted her heart entirely to the Daoist path,
moving Dàluó Gōng Dìshì,

the names of all spiritual beings

fearing that people might know celestial secrets.

we shall meet in Dàluó Tiān
at an appointed time."

with no thought of turning back.

but if she suddenly wished to uproot the earth and move mountains,
she could immediately use a divine talisman.
Yè Jìngnéng then refined her practices within Huìjīshān.
She could respond to the celestial gates above,
and communicate with the earthly veins below.
All ghosts and spirits under heaven
were summoned by Yè Jìngnéng,
and no deities refused to obey her commands.
Yè Jìngnéng then, within Huìjīshān,
commanded divine beings and demons to rush about,
and nothing failed to suit her will.
She could summon when she wished to summon,
and command when she needed to command.
In terms of mastery of the Dao,
her talismans and registers were unparalleled.
Within the universe,
there was no one superior to Yè Jìngnéng.
Moreover, this Dàoshì was beautiful and lucid in appearance,
with a broad and tranquil disposition.
When she reached a certain point,
her nature could adapt to urgency or slowness;
if she suddenly wished to travel,
her mind could accomplish it in an instant,
traveling thirty to fifty thousand *lǐ* a day.
If she did not eat,
she could go for thirty to fifty days;
if she wished to eat,
she could instantly consume sixty or seventy portions and still not be full.
Sometimes she would conceal herself and vanish without a trace,
or immediately transform into a hundred people.
Now, she encountered the Son of Heaven of the Táng dynasty.
Since the creation by the Sānhuáng and Wǔdì,
none have been as sagely and enlightened as our Xuánzōng Huángdì.
The court ministers
spoke without flattery or deceit.
The emperor's reign title was Kāiyuán.
Since the emperor himself cultivated the Dao,
he ordered the construction of venerable images throughout the realm,
as well as abbeys and halls,
thereby re-exalting Daoism.
Yè Jìngnéng went from Huìjīshān to Cháng'ān,
leaving her name.
After traveling for several days,
Dàluó Wáng transformed into a river,
which was about five *lǐ* wide,
and had no bridges or boats to cross it,
thus testing Yè Jìngnéng.
She then wrote a talisman
and threw it into the water.
The river dried up,
and Yè Jìngnéng immediately crossed.
After several days,
he arrived about five lǐ east of Huá Zhōu's Huá Yīn Xiàn.
In the fourth month of that year, the selections were made,
and all were dispatched to their posts.
There was a magistrate from Cháng Zhōu's Wú Xī Xiàn, Zhāng Lìng, who was passing by the shrine of Mount Huà Yuè with his wife and children.
Zhāng Lìng, with his wife,
offered wine, dried meat, camels, and horses,
and sacrificed to the mountain deity, seeking blessings.
It happened that on this day, the mountain deity, lacking a third夫人 (fū rén) in the temple,
sent her down to the inn.
At the third watch of the night,
he sent someone to fetch her.
At three points into the third watch,
she suddenly died.
The magistrate did not know that the mountain deity had come to marry (take) her,
and cried out to heaven loudly,
his emotions entangled.
Jìng Néng was staying in a nearby inn,
and suddenly heard the very sharp sound of weeping.
Jìng Néng then asked, "Why are you weeping?"
Zhāng Lìng replied, "My wife suddenly died tonight."
Jìng Néng said, "She must have been taken by the mountain deity!"
He wished to revive Zhāng Lìng's wife.
Zhāng Lìng said, "Venerable Master, if you can revive her,
I would not dare to disobey you even if it meant sacrificing my life,
I will obey your command."
Jìng Néng asked the magistrate, "Did your wife not have any prior illness?"
Zhāng Lìng replied, "She had no illness before;
she only died upon arriving here.
Jìng Néng, if you save her,
I swear not to be ungrateful."
Jìng Néng then took a brush and wrote a black talisman,
blew it into the air,
and it transformed into a black-clothed divine figure,
swift as a cloud,
who immediately arrived before the mountain deity's temple.
As soon as the doorkeeper saw him,
he ran to report to the mountain deity, saying, "An envoy from Tài Yī has arrived."
The mountain deity immediately bowed,
and allowed the envoy to enter directly into the main hall,
who said, "Tài Yī sends word:
Why did you arbitrarily take another living person's wife,
separating husband and wife,
and causing them to lose their affection?"
The mountain deity replied to the envoy, "This was all arranged by the celestial bureaucracy
for her to be my third fū rén.
It is not Tài Yī's business.
Therefore, please return,
and report this accordingly."
The envoy bowed in acknowledgment,
and immediately returned,
fully relaying the mountain deity's words.
Jìng Néng's expression changed to one of indignation.
He again took a vermilion brush and wrote a talisman,
blew it into the air,
and it transformed into an envoy
dressed in vermilion robes.
In an instant, the envoy arrived.
The mountain deity hurried down from the hall
to face the envoy respectfully.
The envoy said, "You should not take another living person's wife.
Tài Yī is extremely angry.
Where is Zhāng Lìng's wife now?"
The mountain deity replied to the envoy, "How dare I presumptuously take another living person's wife?
This was all arranged by the celestial bureaucracy.
I humbly request the envoy to clarify this,
and I shall be greatly fortunate."
The envoy said, "Do not let this woman cost you your life, my lord,
and implicate the celestial bureaucracy!"
The mountain deity said, "I humbly request the Great Envoy
to kindly mediate,
I will certainly not let you down."
The envoy returned to the inn to see Jìng Néng,
and fully relayed the mountain deity's words,
saying that it was all arranged by the celestial bureaucracy
for her to be the third fū rén,
and not a presumptuous act.
Upon hearing this, Jìng Néng
changed his expression and countenance,
and angrily said to the envoy, "This is a serious matter!"
He then dismissed him to the side.
He again took realgar and two feet of white silk,
drew a talisman, blew it into the air,
and it transformed into a great general.
He wore golden armor
and a helmet,
was ten feet tall,
and had a waist several spans wide.
He then drew a sword,
roared like thunder,
his eyes blazing
like streaks of lightning.
In a flash,
he arrived before the mountain deity's temple.
At that moment, Zhāng Lìng's wife was bowing in the hall.
The envoy, with a stern expression, cried out, "Hah!
Why did this lord take another living person's wife?
Tài Yī is extremely angry
and orders me to bring your head!"
He did not allow the mountain deity to explain,
drew his sword, ascended the hall,
and prepared to strike down the mountain deity.
Seeing the envoy ascend the hall, the mountain deity
was filled with fear and panic,
not knowing what to do,
and immediately fled.
His relatives stepped forward,
pleading and bowing,
asking the envoy to just take Zhāng Lìng's wife away.
The relatives reported back to the lord,
saying there was no need to keep this woman,
lest Tài Yī be further angered.
The mountain deity himself hurried down from the hall,
knelt and bowed,
pleading with the envoy.
Immediately, Zhāng Lìng's wife was led back to the inn.
Before long,
Zhāng Lìng's wife regained consciousness.
She reported to her husband, "While I was bowing in the hall before the mountain deity,
suddenly a general appeared,
wearing golden armor
and a helmet.
He drew his sword, ascended the hall,
and was about to strike down the mountain deity.
The mountain deity feared him,
and thus released me to return."
Zhāng Lìng, hearing his wife's account,
was overjoyed,
and he and his wife together saluted and thanked Jìng Néng,
saying, "Venerable Master, you have saved my wife's life,
your kindness is as heavy as Mount Yuè.
We do not know how to repay you?"
Zhāng Lìng then took twenty bolts of silk from a basket and presented them to the Venerable Master.
Zhāng Lìng said, "We only have this silk;
it is insufficient for a poor child or an orphan.
My wife and I
should forever be your servants
to repay your personal kindness.
We humbly hope, Venerable Master,
that you will accept our humble gift."
Jìng Néng said, "The dharma gate of the Dao
does not concern itself with worldly possessions,
does not seek carnal desires,
does not covet honor or wealth,
but only saves the sick people of the world,
that is the dharma gate.
Because of the deep affection between you, the magistrate, and your wife,
Jìng Néng then saved her life.
You should simply proceed to your post
and use the silk to cover your travel expenses.
Do not press me again.
When Jìng Néng arrives in Cháng'ān,
he will have his own money and silk."
The husband and wife then bowed and took their leave of Jìng Néng.
Jìng Néng immediately took his staff and set off on his journey.
Within ten days,
he arrived in Cháng'ān,
and settled in the Xuán Dū Guàn.
For a full month,
he did not leave the courtyard,
only playing the qín and singing long,
to express his feelings.
The servants of the guàn
often secretly watched,
seeing no kitchen,
nor any place for eating.
Three to five of his peers
came to visit and inquire about his Daoist arts.
Jìng Néng fully explained the power of talismans
and how to cure diseases caused by spirits and demons.
There was nothing he could not speak of.
Thus, word spread from one person's mouth
into the ears of ten thousand.
Within a few days,
the common people of the two markets of Cháng'ān
all knew that there was a Daoist guest in the Xuán Dū Guàn
who could heal illnesses caused by demons
and possessed the power of talismans.
At that time, in Chóngxiánfāng, there was a girl of sixteen or seventeen named Kāng Tàiqīng,
who was possessed by a wild fox spirit.
She would laugh or cry,
walk or sit,
or run wildly into the streets,
and then curse and swear at people with foul language.
At that time, a neighbor reported to Kāng Tàiqīng, saying: “There is an itinerant Daoist in Xuándūguàn,
who can cure the illness caused by wild foxes.”
Kāng Tàiqīng heard this,
and accompanied by his wife,
they both went to the inner courtyard of the abbey,
bowed to Jìngnéng,
and explained the symptoms: “We beg the Venerable Master to provide healing,
and we would not be ungrateful even unto death.”
Jìngnéng said: “This illness is caused by a wild fox.
If you wish for it to be cured,
just bring a felt rug,
and four large nails.
I will heal it immediately.”
Kāng Tàiqīng then returned home,
fetched a felt rug and the nails,
and brought the girl to the abbey.
When Jìngnéng saw the girl,
he immediately knew it was an illness caused by a wild fox.
Jìngnéng then held a sword in his left hand,
grabbed the girl with his right hand,
and cut her into three sections,
blood flowing all over the ground.
Everyone in the courtyard
was astonished.
Kāng Tàiqīng and his wife cried out to heaven and earth,
shouting loudly and running,
and went to the county office to report that the Daoist from Xuándūguàn had killed someone with a sword.
Jìngnéng was not flustered or afraid at all.
He covered the girl’s body with the felt rug,
and put the nails at its four inner corners.
Blood flowed from under the felt.
Countless people watched,
all saying: “Within the imperial city,
how dare such a thing happen?
Who would not cry out?”
Jìngnéng, however, stayed in his room,
playing the zither and singing loudly,
unconcerned by the events.
After a short while,
the chief of the捕賊官 (bǔzéiguān, 'bandit-catching official') and the officers in charge of the matter,
all arrived at Jìngnéng’s courtyard,
and asked: “Where is the Daoist who killed someone?”
Jìngnéng replied from his room: “Here!
Why are the officials in such a hurry?
Jìngnéng is curing the illness caused by a wild fox.
Ignorant idlers
are mistakenly saying I killed someone.”
The officials turned and asked,
and Kāng Tàiqīng reported to the officials, saying: “There is a person under the felt.”
The officials saw the blood flowing copiously from under the felt,
and said to Jìngnéng: “The murder scene is clearly visible,
yet you dare to resist!”
Jìngnéng said to the officials: “Why don’t you lift the felt and examine it?
Why do you enforce such crude and negligent laws!”
The chief of the bǔzéiguān then ordered his subordinates
to lift the felt and examine it.
They said: “Kāng Tàiqīng’s daughter is lying with a wild fox.
The girl is perfectly unharmed,
and the wild fox is cut into three sections.”
The chief of the bǔzéiguān and his men
were utterly astonished.
Kāng Tàiqīng and his wife prostrated themselves in gratitude.
The girl’s possession illness
was immediately cured.
The chief of the bǔzéiguān fully reported the incident.
The Yǐn personally visited the abbey to pay his respects,
then asked for his name,
and greatly admired him.
The Yǐn spoke of this extraordinary and sacred matter,
and recorded it in a memorial to the throne.
Emperor Kāiyuán favored Daoism,
and did not revere Buddhism.
So he dispatched a palace envoy to Xuándūguàn to proclaim an imperial edict for Jìngnéng to report to the court.
Upon receiving the edict, he traveled
directly to the front of the palace hall.
As soon as the Emperor saw him,
Jìngnéng expounded the Daoist teachings,
which were pure, ethereal, subtle, and profound,
greatly pleasing the Emperor.
The Emperor desired the art of eternal life.
Jìngnéng reported: “There are Daoist talismans that can ascend to heaven and earth,
and eliminate the illnesses caused by spirits, demons, goblins, and evil entities;
also, divine elixirs can be refined,
without obstruction.
If Your Majesty seeks the ultimate truth of the method of eternal life,
it will also be easy.”
Xuánzōng heard Jìngnéng’s report,
and was greatly pleased.
He said to Jìngnéng: “I wish to become your disciple.
Venerable Master, be my teacher,
and for now, reside in the abbey.”
The abbey selected a courtyard,
and arranged for people to attend to him daily.
Every day, the Emperor personally drove to Jìngnéng’s courtyard,
to discuss Daoist teachings.
And court officials,
all wished to go there.
The common people, too,
all revered Daoism.
Suddenly, one day,
the Emperor desired to seek immortality,
and summoned Jìngnéng to the inner palace for consultation.
Jìngnéng reported: “Your subject and Your Majesty shall go to gather immortal herbs from afar.”
While Jìngnéng’s original body remained in the abbey,
he transformed into another body to gather immortal herbs with His Majesty.
They traveled to Qiántángjiāng,
where they saw the water was vast and deep,
its breadth immeasurable.
There were evil sea monsters in the river,
so boats dared not cross.
Jìngnéng then wrote a talisman,
threw it into the river,
and the river water became clear for three days,
drifting the evil sea monsters onto the sandbanks.
As soon as Jìngnéng saw them,
he immediately cut them into three sections.
Then they crossed the river,
obtained the immortal herbs,
and presented them to the Emperor.
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
Only Gāo Lìshì did not believe they were immortal herbs,
and so he reported: “Your subject fears that these herbs
are not true immortal herbs.
Your subject proposes to test them!”
The Emperor said: “By what method shall we test them?”
Lìshì reported: “Your subject proposes, within the inner palace,
to dig an underground tunnel and beat five hundred drums inside.
Your Majesty shall summon Jìngnéng,
and say that a demon has arisen in the inner palace,
and ask how the Venerable Master will eliminate it.”
The Emperor agreed to the suggestion,
and Lìshì immediately dispatched men to dig the tunnel,
and beat five hundred drums inside.
The Emperor then summoned Jìngnéng,
who, receiving the edict, came to the front of the palace hall.
The Emperor granted him entry to the hall,
and spoke of the sound of demon drums in the inner palace.
Jìngnéng, obeying the command to eliminate the sound of demon drums,
asked for a bowl of water,
and in front of the Emperor,
sprinkled it while performing a ritual.
As soon as the water left his mouth,
clouds and mists darkened the sky,
and it transformed into a great snake,
which entered the underground tunnel.
Its eyes were like hanging mirrors,
its mouth like a basin of blood,
and its venomous breath formed clouds.
All five hundred men let out sounds of extreme fear,
and dared not beat the drums.
Once Jìngnéng heard the sounds cease,
he reported: “Your subject informs Your Majesty,
it was not the sound of demon drums.”
The Emperor said: “If it was not the sound of demon drums,
what was it?”
Jìngnéng reported: “Your Majesty was testing your subject’s power with talismans.
Order the men to beat the drums.”
When the Emperor heard this,
he felt ashamed before Jìngnéng,
and then returned to the abbey.
For three days before and after,
the Huángdì summoned Yè Jìngnéng to a banquet within the Dà'nèi,
where music was played with xiāosháo flutes.
It was the beginning of autumn,
and cool breezes gradually encroached.
At the Dà'nèi banquet,
he enjoyed himself with his pínfēi,
drank several rounds together,
and there was a profusion of singing and playing.
The Huángdì's heart was not joyful;
he said to Yè Jìngnéng: "When Zhèn holds a banquet now,
it's not like this at all;
does Tiānshī have a zhānglìng [method]
to make the banquet joyful and entertaining?"
Yè Jìngnéng received the emperor's command,
rose immediately,
and faced a Cùnánmán painted jar in the western corner of the hall,
which could hold about one dàn [stone].
Yè Jìngnéng concentrated his mind and performed a ritual,
secretly seeking joy,
to gladden the Huángdì's heart,
and entertain him with a roast.
Thereupon, Yè Jìngnéng took a brush from his bosom,
and painted a Dàoshì on the jar,
holding a wine cup and drinking,
then affixed it to the jar.
The jar then transformed into a Dàoshì,
three chǐ tall,
wearing a chūguān and huángpèi,
standing in the western corner of the hall.
Yè Jìngnéng memorialized: "Your Majesty seems unhappy at this banquet;
your subject has invited a drinker for Your Majesty,
and this feast will surely be joyful."
The Huángdì heard this
and said to Yè Jìngnéng: "What kind of drinker is this,
who understands Zhèn's mind?"
Yè Jìngnéng memorialized: "It is a Dàoshì,
who profoundly understands zhānglìng,
is skilled at banquets,
can discuss the present and recount the past,
knows everything,
is widely learned and capable,
and known to all in the human world."
His Majesty summoned the Dàoshì;
the Dàoshì received the summons
and hurried directly from the western corner of the hall to the front of the hall,
repeatedly addressing himself as "your subject."
When Xuánzōng saw him,
his lóngyán brightened greatly;
the fēihòu and cǎinǚ
all laughed joyfully.
The Dàoshì did not miss a single court formality,
so the Huángdì granted him ascent to the hall,
saying, "Sit opposite Zhèn and answer questions."
The Emperor then asked: "Honorable Master, how big is your capacity for drink?"
Yè Jìngnéng memorialized: "This honored one has a great capacity;
he is truly a heavy drinker,
able to add thirty to fifty points each round,
and is difficult to get drunk suddenly."
The Dàoshì drank whenever a round came,
without any refusal.
The Huángdì was extremely joyful,
and their sitting together was harmonious;
the fēihòu and cǎinǚ all
encouraged him to drink three shēng.
The Dàoshì was encouraged to drink quite a lot,
not missing a single round.
From sìshí to shēnshí,
the Dàoshì drank about one dàn,
and the wine jar was completely full.
There were five shēng of wine left in the zūn;
Yè Jìngnéng, wanting to display the Dàoshì's power,
memorialized: "Your Majesty, the banquet is about to end;
your subject suggests offering the remaining wine to the honored master;
I humbly hope Your Majesty will grant your subject's request."
The Huángdì said: "Granted!"
The wine was then bestowed upon the honored master;
the Dàoshì firmly refused,
memorializing: "Your subject fears losing court decorum and failing in etiquette."
Yè Jìngnéng said: "Knowing that the exalted one is a heavy drinker,
why refuse?"
The Dàoshì memorialized: "My wine [capacity] is already full;
I truly cannot drink more!"
Yè Jìngnéng, seeing his firm refusal,
faced the Huángdì and angrily said: "This Dàoshì must eventually be sentenced to decapitation!"
The Huángdì said: "What crime has he committed,
that he should be suddenly beheaded?"
Yè Jìngnéng memorialized: "It is because he has greatly offended me."
The Huángdì assented to the memorial,
and ordered Gāo Lìshì to take a sword and behead the Dàoshì.
The head fell with the sword,
and was tossed aside.
The head was originally the lid of the wine jar,
the body was the painted body of the jar,
on which a Dàoshì had been drawn,
with a talisman affixed.
The wine jar was full and thus drunk.
The Huángdì burst into laughter upon seeing this,
the fēihòu celebrated the emperor's pleasure together,
and all the palace women cried out in amazed laughter.
Gāo Lìshì gazed repeatedly, unable to distinguish [the illusion],
and sighed with wonder upon re-observing it.
Huángdì Xuánzōng and the court ministers
praised Yè Jìngnéng as surpassing the ancients and excelling the present,
his transformations boundless,
his talismans revealed,
his sacred mysteries profound,
rare in the human world,
his manifestations unfathomable,
no different from Tàishàng Lǎojūn.
Xuánzōng wholeheartedly loved the Dao,
and earnestly sought immortality,
exposing his innermost thoughts,
hoping for longevity.
He also coveted the wonders of talismans.
The Huángdì also dreamt one night of a spirit-man,
who brought dragon liver.
The Emperor asked the spirit-man: "From where does this liver come?"
The spirit-man replied: "The Upper Realm ordered the spirits to bring it."
The Huángdì obtained dragon liver in his dream;
its taste was very delicious.
Suddenly he awoke with a start,
and there was nothing at all.
The Huángdì pondered the dream,
then summoned Yè Jìngnéng to question him.
Yè Jìngnéng memorialized: "Your Majesty is destined to eat dragon meat."
The Huángdì said: "How can it be obtained?"
Yè Jìngnéng memorialized: "Fetch a basin of water."
He placed a sword across it,
performed a ritual, drew a talisman,
and threw it into the basin,
where clouds and mist suddenly darkened.
After a long while,
the mist receded and the clouds dispersed;
a spirit-man appeared in the air,
delivering a dragon leg,
weighing over thirty jīn.
Yè Jìngnéng received it,
and presented it to the Huángdì.
The Huángdì was greatly pleased upon seeing the dragon meat,
and his lóngyán brightened.
The court generals and ministers all said: "Since ancient times, there has been no one like Yè Jìngnéng!"
In Kāiyuán the thirteenth year, there was a great drought throughout the land.
The Emperor then summoned his hundred officials.
The Huángdì said: "There is a severe drought outside the pass,
and no rain within the pass.
What do you, sirs, suggest?"
Prime Ministers Jǐng and Chóng memorialized: "Why does Your Majesty not ask Yè Jìngnéng to pray for rain?"
The Huángdì heard this,
then summoned Yè Jìngnéng to appear,
who received the summons and proceeded directly to the front of the hall.
The Huángdì said: "There is a severe drought throughout the land.
How can Tiānshī pray for rain for Zhèn,
to save the myriad people?"
Yè Jìngnéng memorialized: "Your subject will summon the deities of the Wǔyuè to question them for Your Majesty."
The Huángdì said: "Go and question them immediately."
Yè Jìngnéng, before the Huángdì,
immediately set up an altar,
drew five talismans,
and first summoned the direct officials of the Wǔyuè to ask for rain.
The Wǔyuè said: "It is all up to the Heavenly Bureau."
Yè Jìngnéng then summoned the Heavenly Bureau,
and stated explicitly: "It is urgently due to the common people throwing away their flour and rice cakes,
which has caused this three-year drought."
Yè Jìngnéng said: "Because the Huángdì desires rain,
wherever there is surplus rain,
order it to descend quickly!"
The Heavenly Bureau said: "Rain will come as decreed by Heaven."
Venerable Master Yè then ordered the Wǔyuè and Sìdú to make arrangements,
and quickly bring forth rain together.
After three days, the rain was sufficient,
all grains ripened abundantly,
and the myriad people sang in praise.
By the fourteenth year,
the Emperor granted a great amnesty to all under Heaven,
allowing the common people to light lanterns for offerings.
The palaces viewed the lanterns,
making merry.
There was also an edict: the people in the wards and markets
were allowed to light lanterns,
and no curfew was to be imposed.
After viewing the lanterns, returning to the Dànèi,
the Emperor asked: “Are all the zhōuxiàn like this?”
Yè Jìngnéng reported: “Shǔdū has lanterns,
with offerings to the utmost,
I fear the capital may not compare!”
The Emperor then asked: “How far is Jiànnán from here?”
Yè Jìngnéng reported: “It is three thousand lǐ from here.”
The Emperor asked: “How do you know about that place?”
Yè Jìngnéng reported: “Your subject has just returned from viewing it there.
If Your Majesty does not believe what your subject has reported,
it would be difficult for you to go by yourself;
if you go with your subject,
we will arrive in an instant.”
The Emperor said: “If you take朕 with you,
what attendants will follow,
how many people will go together?”
Yè Jìngnéng reported: “It can be one person and I.”
The Emperor said: “What color clothes will we wear?”
Yè Jìngnéng reported: “Those attending
all wear plain clothes.”
The Emperor said: “Then order Gāo Lìshì and others to quickly prepare,
and swiftly go with you to Jiànnán to view the lanterns.”
Gāo Lìshì and others received the imperial command in person,
and immediately arranged their attire.
Thereupon, he performed a ritual,
and brought the Emperor and his accompanying retinue,
to Jiànnán to view the lanterns.
It was as swift as flying clouds,
like a flash of lightning.
The Emperor and his attendants arrived in Jiànnán in a short while,
toured the streets,
and visited various places together.
They also saw lanterns displayed in the wards and markets,
offerings crisscrossing,
and music to the utmost,
which greatly pleased the Emperor.
Yè Jìngnéng then brought the Emperor to the Shǔwáng Diàndiàn,
where the retinue watched together,
and he ordered several pieces of music to be played.
The Emperor said to Yè Jìngnéng: “Tiānshī,
the night is deep,
朕 intends to return to Cháng’ān.”
Yè Jìngnéng reported: “Your Majesty has toured Shǔchuān today,
but has not yet seen everything;
if you wish to return to the capital,
we can go now.”
Yè Jìngnéng reported again: “When Your Majesty visits this commandery,
you must let the people of Shǔjùn know that you have seen the lanterns,
and music was played in the Shǔwáng Diàndiàn.”
The Emperor said: “How can I let the people know that 朕 came to view the lanterns?”
Yè Jìngnéng reported: “Your Majesty must leave an article of clothing worn on your body in the Shǔwáng Diàndiàn.
Later, the Jiédùshǐ will surely send someone to search the hall,
and when they see this undershirt,
they will surely send someone to present it.
Your Majesty can then say that 朕 personally came to view the lanterns and enjoy the music,
hence leaving the undershirt,
to prove it is not false.
Then the people of Shǔ and the officials and common folk
will all know that Your Majesty viewed the lanterns,
wouldn't that be excellent?”
The Emperor then left a small undershirt,
in the Shǔwáng Diàndiàn.
Yè Jìngnéng saw the Emperor leave the clothing,
then performed a ritual,
and in a moment,
they returned to Cháng’ān together.
Yè Jìngnéng reported: “This is the Dànèi.”
The Emperor turned over with shame and regret,
seeking the Dao immortals,
sighing that Yè Jìngnéng's deeds were unfathomable,
and his talismans in the world were incomparable.
The Emperor wholeheartedly sought the art of eternal life,
when suddenly he heard the Dànèi strike the fourth drum,
the clepsydra's divisions clear,
the Emperor replied to Yè Jìngnéng: “Tiānshī, please return to your Daoist temple for now,
and Yè Jìngnéng will see 朕 tomorrow morning.”
Yè Jìngnéng bowed,
and returned to his Daoist temple.
The Emperor said to Gāo Lìshì: “The road to Shǔ is far,
obstructed by mountains and rivers,
yet in a blink of an eye,
we reached the various zhōujùn.”
That night, the Jiédùshǐ and the officials and common folk,
again heard music played in the Shǔwáng Diàndiàn,
until daybreak.
The people of Shǔjùn were deeply surprised,
and intensified their search,
suspecting it to be extraordinary people.
Pursuits were tumultuous,
fearing it was spirits or monsters.
They also found an undershirt.
After searching for several days,
there was no trace.
The Jiànnán Jiédùshǐ dared not conceal it,
and immediately wrote a memorial to report it,
stating it was a strange event,
respectfully sending Zhai Cháng, a staff member and Censor-in-chief, to present the memorial.
Less than ten days later,
he arrived in Cháng’ān.
The Emperor read the memorial,
spread it on the jade desk,
and read it through once.
He also saw the undershirt,
and his imperial face showed great pleasure,
knowing it was not false.
The Emperor personally inquired about the matter,
and the envoy fully explained: “On the night of the fifteenth day of the first month, at the second watch,
carriages and horses with attendants,
all dressed in white,
numbered over a hundred people,
went to the Shǔwáng Diàndiàn to play music,
and left when the music ended.
They left behind an undershirt,
and after searching, no trace was found.
This is a strange omen,
and your humble servant was ordered by the regional commander to report it.”
The Emperor said to Zhai Cháng: “Last night, on the fifteenth day of the first month,
朕, Yè Jìngnéng, and the accompanying retinue rested in the Shǔwáng Diàndiàn,
hence I ordered music to be played.
After the performance concluded
and we returned,
fearing that Shǔjùn would not know of 朕's visit,
I purposely left the undershirt.
You quickly report to your regional commander,
朕 will issue a separate edict of special reward.”
Zhai Cháng bowed and bid farewell to the Emperor,
then immediately set off on his journey.
His heart was full of joy,
feeling the dew and rain on his body,
his relatives were honored,
and all his kinsmen celebrated.
Less than ten days later,
he arrived in Shǔ,
and fully conveyed the imperial edict.
The officials and common people of Jiànnán
all said that the Emperor communicated with gods in the universe,
traveling throughout the world,
not to mention the borders of Shǔchuān,
and the various prefectures dared not arbitrarily enforce laws.
The Emperor daily personally inquired of Yè Jìngnéng about Daoist methods,
and Yè Jìngnéng often presented them,
the Emperor never forgot anything.
Suddenly one day,
the Empress, having no son,
intended to ask Yè Jìngnéng: “Your concubine hears that Yè Jìngnéng's magic is connected to the gods,
your concubine wishes to have a son,
and dares not but report it.”
The Emperor then summoned Yè Jìngnéng and asked: “Before 朕 ascended the throne,
I already had an Empress;
but since ascending the throne,
I have had no children at all.
Tiānshī, a Daoist priest,
please seek a son for 朕,
which is important for the state.
朕 and the Empress
dare not fail Tiānshī.”
Yè Jìngnéng reported: “Sons and daughters are due to predestined fate,
how can Jìngnéng seek them?”
Yè Jìngnéng then inquired of Tiāncáo,
and presented a petition to Dìfǔ.
Yè Jìngnéng then wrote a talisman before the Emperor,
blew it into the air,
and it immediately transformed into a spirit,
then ascended to heaven.
He also wrote a talisman and petitioned Dìfǔ.
In a short while, Tiāncáo and Dìfǔ both reported: “The Empress is not destined to have a son in this life.”
Yè Jìngnéng fully reported.
On the fifteenth night of the eighth month,
the Huángdì and Jìngnéng, along with their attendant retinue,
admired the moon from a high place.
The Huángdì said to Jìngnéng: "The affairs within the moon,
can they be fathomed?"
Jìngnéng replied: "My words, too, I fear would be of no avail.
I wish to take Your Majesty to the Moon Palace for a visit, would that be acceptable?"
The Huángdì said: "How can one go?"
Jìngnéng replied: "Your Majesty cannot go alone.
If you go with your servant,
what difficulty could there be!"
The Huángdì was greatly pleased.
The Huángdì said: "Can the attendants accompany us?"
Jìngnéng replied: "Watching lanterns in Jiànnán
is a place for ordinary people;
the Moon Palace is in the upper realm,
different from the human world.
Because Your Majesty has a share of immortality,
you may temporarily go."
The Huángdì asked again: "What color clothes should I wear?"
Jìngnéng replied: "You may wear white brocade cotton clothes."
The Huángdì said: "Why wear white brocade cotton clothes?"
Jìngnéng replied: "Because it is a crystal palace,
and the cold air is piercing."
The Huángdì dressed and immediately set off.
Jìngnéng performed his magic,
and in an instant they arrived inside the Moon Palace.
They saw buildings, halls, and pavilions,
unlike those of the human world;
the gates, doors, and windows
were entirely different from this world.
The Huángdì carefully observed the buildings and halls,
and upon entering the double gate,
he saw more palaces outside the buildings,
leading all the way to the Grand Hall.
Everything was made of crystal, lapis lazuli, and agate,
its vastness unfathomable.
Crystal was used for windows,
and crystal for towers and platforms.
He also saw several beautiful women,
dressed in clothes weighing three *zhū*,
each holding a crystal plate in her hand,
and within the plates were vessels,
all made of crystal and seven precious treasures combined.
Upon seeing the Huángdì, they all observed proper decorum.
Jìngnéng led the Huángdì directly to a sāluó tree to look at it.
The Huángdì saw that the tree's
height was unfathomable,
its branches directly covering three thousand great thousand worlds.
The color of its leaves
was no different from white silver,
and its flowers were like the color of clouds.
As the Huángdì slowly walked beneath the tree,
he paused and stood for a moment,
the cold air piercing him,
the snow freezing him to the bone.
The Huángdì said to Jìngnéng: "The cold air is very chilling,
I wish to return to the palace."
Jìngnéng replied: "Accompanying Your Majesty for this excursion
is truly a wondrous immortal experience,
unlike the lower realm.
Your Majesty need not rush.
Please leisurely admire the moon and observe.
Then, when you return,
would it not be excellent?"
The Huángdì leaned against the tree,
feeling the cold deepen,
and asked Jìngnéng again: "I can no longer endure this cold.
I wish to return now.
If we stay for another moment,
I fear it may become impossible."
When Jìngnéng heard the Huángdì's words again,
he could not help but smile.
He immediately performed his magic,
and in an instant they were back in Cháng'ān.
The Huángdì wholeheartedly sought the Dharma,
clasped his hands before him,
and addressed the Heavenly Master: "Show me the Daoist methods,
and I will dedicate my entire life,
eternally receiving heavenly blessings,
and you shall be my teacher."
Jìngnéng replied: "My humble Daoist methods
are all through the power of talismans and incantations.
How can they be transmitted?"
The next morning,
when the officials attended court,
the Huángdì said: "Last night, at the third watch,
I went with Heavenly Master Yè to the Moon Palace to observe.
I saw that inside and out, the clear sky was vast,
the buildings, halls, and pavilions were all different,
all decorated with seven precious treasures."
The officials all congratulated the Huángdì: "Since the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, Zhōu, and Qín,
there has been no one like Your Majesty!
If the Daoist teachings can communicate with spirits,
and the talismans and incantations are supremely marvelous,
then no one in the world surpasses Heavenly Master Yè!"
The Huángdì then commanded the Grand Astrologer
to record it in the Táng Lù.
Several days later,
Jìngnéng saw a palace woman in the inner palace,
of exceptional beauty,
always favored by the Huángdì.
Jìngnéng then returned to his Daoist temple,
wrote a talisman,
and transformed it into a spirit.
Every night at the third watch, the divine being
would bring the palace woman to sleep in the temple,
and just at dawn,
would send her back to the palace.
Days and months passed,
already half a year had gone by,
and the beautiful woman, dizzy as if drunk,
noticed nothing.
Suddenly she reported to the Huángdì: "I am now pregnant.
Only awaiting the difficult birth,
I dared not not report it."
When the Huángdì heard the report,
he immediately knew it was Jìngnéng's magic
and sent someone to fetch him.
He then ordered the beautiful woman not to tell anyone,
and the Huángdì summoned Gāo Lìshì to deliberate,
planning to kill Jìngnéng in the Grand Hall.
Jìngnéng, in his temple, knew this early on.
The Huángdì said to Gāo Lìshì: "Yè Jìngnéng can move mountains and overturn seas,
change the cosmos,
control the universe,
ascend into the void at will,
and transform without difficulty.
I plan to kill him,
but I fear it will be difficult.
What plan do you have
to kill him for me?"
Lìshì replied: "Yè Jìngnéng's coming and going on clouds
all relies on the power of talismans and incantations.
If we now scheme to kill him in the Grand Hall,
how can Jìngnéng know?
Your Majesty simply summons Jìngnéng to the hall and grants him a seat.
Behind the hall, secretly arrange five hundred swords.
Your Majesty will grandly question him about his methods.
While Jìngnéng is explaining his Daoist methods,
Your Majesty will grandly display your imperial majesty,
and your servant will secretly give the signal.
The five hundred men will simultaneously rush into the hall with their swords,
and he will surely be killed."
The Huángdì said: "That plan is excellent."
Having received the command, Lìshì
then took five hundred men from the Jīnwú guard.
Their swords were as bright as snow and frost.
They lay in ambush behind the hall,
without letting anyone know.
The Huángdì then summoned Jìngnéng.
Jìngnéng already knew about the ambush behind the hall,
but he was not concerned.
When he arrived before the hall,
the Huángdì granted him a seat
and spoke of his Daoist methods.
The Huángdì said: "What other methods are there?"
Jìngnéng knew the Huángdì was pressing him about his magical arts: "Their number is extremely vast.
If Your Majesty intends to ask about all of them,
there will be no end to it.
What your servant has seen can only be as much as this!"
When the Huángdì heard Jìngnéng's reply,
he suddenly changed color in anger
and displayed great imperial wrath.
Gāo Lìshì immediately dispatched five hundred men,
who simultaneously entered the hall,
intending to decapitate Jìngnéng.
Jìngnéng saw the five hundred men draw their swords and enter the hall,
but he was not flustered or afraid.
Before the Huángdì, he slowly walked at a leisurely pace: "I will not rush either!"
The five hundred men simultaneously raised their swords,
looming over Jìngnéng.
Jìngnéng concentrated and performed his magic,
and immediately transformed his body and entered into a palace pillar,
his traces unseen.
The Huángdì was startled and alarmed,
walking several circles around the pillar to look.
He repeatedly called out: "Heavenly Master!
Heavenly Master!
I had no such intention!
Gāo Lìshì instigated this evil thought!
I earnestly wish that Heavenly Master would perceive my sincerity!"
Jìngnéng replied from inside the pillar: "My original wish was to serve Your Majesty for your entire life,
who knew that Your Majesty would harbor such evil intentions midway!"
The Huángdì then ordered Gāo Lìshì to cut and chop at the pillar to see.
Gāo Lìshì complied and chopped at the pillar.
When about half of the pillar and above was cut away,
it clearly became apparent
that there was no trace of Jìngnéng at all.
Jìngnéng replied again from inside the pillar: "Your servant shall now return to Dàluó Tiān!"
The Huángdì and Gāo Lìshì saw a stream of purple qi
ascend into the sky and depart.
The Huángdì regretted it, but it was too late.
The imperial court's generals and ministers
all said that the Huángdì hastily accepted Lìshì's plan,
causing the Heavenly Master to no longer dwell in the human world,
but to return to the upper realm.
Indeed, it was not Jìngnéng's fault.
From this time onward, the Emperor
longed for Yè Jìngnéng day and night,
unable to rest or eat.
Within ten days,
a court envoy, having traveled over a hundred *lǐ* into Shǔchuān,
suddenly saw Yè Jìngnéng slowly walking along.
Yè Jìngnéng saw the envoy
and called out loudly, "Envoy, stop for a moment!"
The envoy heard the call,
dismounted from his horse,
stepped forward to bow and ask after the Celestial Master,
and said, "May Your Majesty enjoy ten thousand blessings on the coming day."
The envoy asked, "How did you come to be here?"
Yè Jìngnéng replied, "I am going to return to Dàluó Gōng.
Tomorrow was too sudden,
and I did not have time to bid farewell to the Emperor.
Envoy, please convey a message to His Majesty from Yè Jìngnéng:
Yè Jìngnéng is on his way,
and did not have time to compose a memorial.
I humbly request His Majesty's understanding and scrutiny.
If you wish to see this minister again,
you must wait until the seas dry up and the rivers run barren,
and mountains shift and the earth collapses."
Having said this,
in an instant,
he was gone.
The envoy then returned to the imperial court,
and first reported the events in Shǔchuān to the Emperor,
then reported: "When your servant returned from Jiànnán,
about a hundred *lǐ* from Shǔchuān,
I met Yè Jìngnéng walking slowly along,
who asked me to convey to Your Majesty: tomorrow was too sudden,
and he did not have time to bid Your Majesty farewell.
Furthermore, being on the road,
he did not have time to compose a memorial.
If Your Majesty wishes to see him,
you must wait until mountains shift and the earth collapses,
and the seas dry up and the rivers run barren.
He ordered your servant to report this verbally,
and I dared not fail to report it."
When the Emperor heard Yè Jìngnéng's message conveyed by the envoy,
he stood before the palace and gazed towards Shǔchuān,
his eyes filled with tears as he cried loudly, saying:
"My Yè Jìngnéng,
there is no equal in this world.
He diligently cultivated the Daoist teachings,
with a pure, empty, and profound will.
He refined the nine-cycle divine elixir,
and achieved eternal life and immortality.
Taking just one pill,
its efficacy is incomparable.
The divine talismans of Yuánshǐ Tàiyī
could move heaven and earth.
He could summon the five departments to converse with them,
and command the Five Peaks to be driven by his hand.
If creation needed to shift, it shifted;
if heaven and earth needed to stop, they stopped.
He could also take me to view the Moon Palace,
and then return to play in Shǔchuān.
When I harbored different intentions,
the conflict was imminent.
Summoned to the palace,
he had no fear or apprehension.
When asked about his Daoist arts,
his replies were unparalleled.
With swords all over his body,
he cast his form into a pillar.
There was no place to find him,
how could one know his intentions?
The envoy returned from Jiànnán,
but he had already arrived there.
He ordered a verbal message to be conveyed,
able to preserve beginning and end.
I have truly failed you, my dear,
I wish you knew my feelings.
Gazing afar at Shǔchuān,
my tears flow in vain.
Since the dawn of creation,
he is the one and only.
Let his name be inscribed for me,
and listed in the green histories."
《Yè Jìngnéng Shī》 (Poem by Yè Jìngnéng).
Once, the Master (Kǒngzǐ) traveled east,
and came to the foot of Jīngshān.
On the road, he met three young children.
Two children were playing,
one child was not playing.
The Master found it strange and asked, "Why are you not playing?"
The child replied, "Big games kill each other,
small games hurt each other.
Playing yields no merit,
clothes are torn and insides empty.
Following each other to throw stones
is not as good as going home to pound grain.
Up to parents,
down to siblings,
I only wish not to report them,
fearing disrespect.
I contemplate this matter carefully,
therefore I do not play.
Why do you find it strange?"
Xiàng Tuō was also following along, building a city of earth,
sitting inside.
The Master said to the child, "Why don't you get out of the way of the carriage?"
The child replied, "I have heard that the sages said: they know astronomy above,
geography below,
and human nature in between.
From ancient times until now,
I have only heard of carriages avoiding cities,
how could I hear of cities avoiding carriages?"
The Master was speechless at that moment,
and so ordered the carriage to avoid the city and take the lower road.
He sent someone to ask, "Whose child is this?
What is his surname and given name?"
The child replied, "My surname is Xiàng and my given name is Tuō."
The Master said, "Though you are young,
you know very profound matters."
The child replied, "I have heard that a fish, three days after birth,
swims in rivers and seas;
a rabbit, three days after birth,
can circle three *mǔ* of land;
a horse, three days after birth,
can chase after its mother;
a human, three months after birth,
knows its parents.
Heaven creates naturally,
why speak of young or old!"
The Master asked the child, "Do you know what mountain has no stones?
What water has no fish?
What gate has no barrier?
What carriage has no wheels?
What ox has no calf?
What horse has no colt?
What knife has no ring?
What fire has no smoke?
What person has no wife?
What woman has no husband?
What day is insufficient?
What day has surplus?
What male has no female?
What tree has no branches?
What city has no envoy?
What person has no courtesy name?"
The child replied, "An earth mountain has no stones.
Well water has no fish.
An empty gate has no barrier.
A funeral carriage has no wheels.
A mud ox has no calf.
A wooden horse has no colt.
A chopping knife has no ring.
Fireflies have no smoke.
Immortals have no wives.
Jade maidens have no husbands.
Winter days are insufficient.
Summer days have surplus.
A solitary male has no female.
A dead tree has no branches.
An empty city has no envoy.
A young child has no courtesy name."
The Master said, "Excellent!
Excellent!
If I were to travel the world with you,
would that be permissible?"
The child replied, "I will not travel.
I have a strict father,
whom I must attend to;
I have a kind mother,
whom I must support;
I have an elder brother,
whom I must obey;
I have a younger brother,
whom I must teach.
Therefore, I cannot accompany you."
The Master said, "I have a *shuānglù* board in my carriage,
how about we play a game together?"
The child replied, "I do not play games.
If the Son of Heaven is fond of gambling,
the winds and rains will be irregular;
if the feudal lords are fond of gambling,
state affairs will not be governed;
if officials are fond of gambling,
documents will be delayed;
if farmers are fond of gambling,
planting will miss its season;
if students are fond of gambling,
they will forget to read books and poems;
if children are fond of gambling,
they will be whipped.
These are useless matters,
why learn them!"
The Master said: “Shall I, with you, pacify all under Heaven,
is this possible or not?”
The boy replied: “All under Heaven cannot be pacified.
