There are high mountains,
there are rivers and seas,
there are dukes and ministers,
there are slaves and servants.
Therefore, it cannot be pacified.”
The Master said: “If I, with you, level the high mountains,
fill up the rivers and seas,
eliminate the dukes and ministers,
and discard the slaves and servants,
all under Heaven will be vast and open.
How could it not be pacified?”
The boy replied: “If the high mountains are leveled,
beasts will have nowhere to rely;
if the rivers and seas are filled up,
fish will have nowhere to return;
if the dukes and ministers are eliminated,
people will create right and wrong;
if slaves and servants are discarded,
whom will the noble people employ?”
The Master said: “Excellent!
Excellent!
You know that on the roof grow pines,
before the door grow reeds,
on the bed grow cattails,
dogs bark at their masters,
wives sit and make mothers-in-law serve them,
chickens turn into pheasants,
dogs turn into foxes.
What is this?”
The boy replied: “The pines growing on the roof are its rafters.
The reeds growing before the door are its blinds.
The cattails growing on the bed are its mats.
Dogs bark at their masters
because there are guests nearby.
Wives sit and make mothers-in-law serve them,
it is because they are newly married.
Chickens turn into pheasants
when they are in the mountains and marshes.
Dogs turn into foxes
when they are in the hills and mounds.”
The Master spoke to the boy, saying: “Do you know whether husband and wife are close,
or parents are close?”
The boy said: “Parents are close.”
The Master said: “Husband and wife are close.
Alive, they share a bed and pillow;
dead, they share a coffin.
Their love and affection are extremely deep.
How can they not be close?”
The boy replied: “What kind of talk is this!
What kind of talk is this!
A person having a mother
is like a tree having roots;
a person having a wife
is like a cart having wheels.
If a cart is broken, one can build a new one,
and will surely get a new one.
If a wife dies, one can marry again,
and will surely get one from a virtuous family.
If one tree dies,
a hundred branches wither.
If one mother dies,
all children are orphaned.
To compare a wife to a mother,
how can it not be perverse?”
The boy then asked the Master: “Why can geese and ducks float?
Why can swans and cranes sing?
Why are pines and cypresses evergreen in winter and summer?”
The Master replied: “Geese and ducks can float because their feet are flat.
Swans and cranes can sing because their throats and necks are long.
Pines and cypresses are evergreen in winter and summer because their hearts are strong.”
The boy replied: “Not so!
Shrimp can sing,
is it because their throats and necks are long?
Turtles and soft-shelled turtles can float,
is it because their feet are flat?
Bamboo from Hú is evergreen in winter and summer,
is it because its heart is strong?”
The Master asked the boy: “Do you know how high Heaven is?
How thick the Earth is?
How many beams Heaven has?
How many pillars Earth has?
Where does the wind come from?
Where does the rain originate?
Where does frost come out?
Where does dew emerge?”
The boy replied: “Heaven and Earth are separated by ninety-nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine *lǐ*.
The thickness of the Earth
is equal to Heaven.
Wind comes from Cāngwú.
Rain comes from high places.
Frost comes from Heaven.
Dew emerges on all grasses.
Heaven has no beams,
Earth has no pillars.
It is supported by clouds from the four directions,
thus they are considered pillars.
What is so strange about that?”
The Master sighed and said: “Excellent!
Excellent!
Only now do I realize that the youth are truly formidable.”
When the Master and Xiàng Tuō debated,
the Master was inferior to Xiàng Tuō in every respect.
The Master harbored a desire to kill Xiàng Tuō,
and so composed a poem, saying:
Sūn Jìng hung his head and pricked his thigh,
Kuāng Héng chiseled a hole in the wall to steal light at night.
Zǐlù was by nature fond of valor,
fond of reading poetry and books was Zǐzhāng.
Xiàng Tuō, at seven years old, could speak,
and answered Kǒng Qiū very powerfully.
Xiàng Tuō went into the mountains to study,
and crossed his hands before the hall, addressing his mother.
“Son studies beneath a hundred-foot tree,
no need to accept a caretaker, what method is there?”
His parents, old and confused,
entrusted the Master with two cartloads of straw.
The Master left, and years passed,
Xiàng Tuō's parents had no expectations.
He took a hundred bundles and burned them,
the rest he would feed to cattle and sheep another day.
The Master immediately demanded the straw back,
the parents' faces turned pale.
At once they wanted to pay double the price,
three ingots of gold or more for each bundle.
“Gold and silver are all useless,
where is young Xiàng Tuō?”
“My son left years ago,
studying literature beneath a hundred-foot tree.”
When the Master heard these words,
his heart was happier than usual.
The Master rode his horse into the mountains,
climbing mountains and crossing ridges with great determination.
Every tree measured less than a hundred feet,
vines intertwined, very long.
The Master made someone take a pickaxe,
and dug underground, where there was a stone hall.
Inside the first gate were stone lions,
outside the second gate were stone *Jīngāng*.
Entering the middle gate, he listened carefully,
two companions studying like a line of geese.
The Master drew his sword and chopped at them,
but the two people were not harmed.
They turned into silent stone figures,
but the iron knife cutting them made blood gush out.
Xiàng Tuō's last breath was not yet extinguished,
he turned his head and looked far away, addressing his mother:
“Collect my crimson blood,
and keep it at home for more than seven days.”
His mother could not bear to see her son's blood,
and poured it by the dung heap.
On the first and second day, bamboo roots grew.
On the third and fourth day, the bamboo was lush and green.
The bamboo stalks grew tall and straight, a hundred feet high,
each segment like an army of divine kings.
Bows, knives, and weapons were carried on their bodies,
the treasured sword at their waist was white as frost.
The two immediately sought victory,
who knew Xiàng Tuō had died first?
The Master was then greatly frightened,
and clearly established a temple in the prefecture and county.
One scroll of the *Kǒngzǐ Xiàng Tuō Xiāngwèn Shū*.
In mid-spring, the second month,
swallows soar in pairs.
Wishing to build a dwelling,
husband and wife deliberate.
Measuring east and west,
examining north and south,
only avoiding the general and the Grand Duke (Tàisuì),
will naturally bring blessings without calamity.
Take the high head of the beam,
build a mud cave,
climb up to the beams and ridges,
use grass for a bed.
At peace, not worrying about danger,
not nesting in verdant curtains.
Choosing a fortunate place,
thus relying on grand beams.
As soon as the arrangements are made,
temporarily go to the embankment.
Then there was a
Huángquè,
with a sharp head,
leaning against the streets and byways,
bullying the weak with strength.
Seeing that Yàn was not present,
it came in to plunder.
Seeing its house clean and tidy,
it immediately occupied it itself.
Its wife, children, and servants,
all joyfully celebrated,
and boasted like a strongman: "By its efforts,
a field worker gets rabbits,
and a sandal maker gets stew.
The ancient saying is clear,
it truly is not wrong.
Force a fist,
and the arm will come off.
If Yàn comes in,
we'll use a stick to trip its feet.
It is merely single and alone,
let me, Āmǎng, hack it.
Moreover, with its lips chattering,
we'll make you wet yourself in the end."
Before the words were settled,
Yànzi immediately returned,
landing and calling out.
Què'ér came out,
not asking good or bad,
but immediately punched and grabbed.
Pushing left and shoving right,
pulling ears and slapping cheeks.
The children twisted its legs,
the wife bit down.
Yànzi was beaten,
its corpse was pitiful.
Its head could not be lifted,
its eyes could not open.
Husband and wife faced each other,
their breath choked, their voices sorrowful:
"We never offended the leopard's tail,
why did we suffer this bird disaster?"
So it went to Fènghuáng,
and presented a petition to explain:
"Yànzi is poor and alone,
and built a house,
but was forcibly seized by Què'ér,
and moreover threatened.
It said: 'I will explicitly order a search for guests,
and mark them as regular.
You, a runaway who lost your registration,
I have never seen you perform royal service.
I will eventually send officials to beat your back,
and exile you to Dān, Yá, Xiàng, Bái!'
It said: 'The wild magpie is my maternal uncle,
the dove is my paternal uncle,
the provincial and county officials
are my closely related kin.
If you submit a petition against me,
I fear it will be of no benefit to you in the end.
Quickly leave my doorstep,
otherwise you will soon be slapped.'
Yànzi did not understand,
and sought justice through reason.
Then it was seized by the head and dragged,
its clothes grabbed and torn.
Confused honorable fists,
crosswise bald scratches.
Several father and sons
all beat it together.
Yànzi was beaten,
its feathers injured and falling,
unable to move,
its life hanging by a thread.
We humbly request an inspection,
as there are visible bruises.
We cannot bear this injustice,
and ask the King to hold it accountable."
Fènghuáng said: "Yànzi's petition
is sincere in its words and reasoning,
Què'ér's arrogance
is beyond description.
Eventually, both parties
must face each other to clarify,
only then, knowing right from wrong,
can a judgment be made."
It specifically dispatched Liáo to apprehend it.
Liáo received the command,
not daring to delay.
Half running, half trotting,
swift as a shooting star.
Arriving outside the door,
it stood listening for a long time.
It distinctly heard Què'ér's
voice from inside the nest.
Què'ér said: "Last night I had a bad dream,
and this morning my eyes twitched.
If we don't fight privately,
we might incur official anger.
Lately, corvée duties
have been levied frequently.
Most likely, Yànzi
has submitted a petition.
Instruct the men and women
not to open the door.
If anyone asks for me,
say I went to the east village."
Liáo called out from beyond the door: "Don't hide so foolishly!
I have just heard what you said,
come out quickly and discuss it with me.
Why did you seize its house,
and moreover beat and injure it?
Fènghuáng has ordered your apprehension,
you must bear the consequences yourself.
You cannot escape even by entering a hole,
no matter how many ways you think."
Què'ér was frightened,
terrified and panicking;
the whole family, big and small,
was also alarmed and flustered.
So it came out and knelt before Liáo,
calling it Dàláng and Èrláng:
"Sir, you have traveled far in the heat,
please come into the nest for coolness.
There are no sudden guests without sudden hosts,
please sit for a moment and chat about household matters."
Liáo said: "This fellow is very foolish,
and utterly unaware,
just seeing leniency,
you try to pass the time.
Talk about food,
I am not hungry.
You must go quickly,
lest the King be displeased by the delay."
Què'ér was already distressed,
valuing delay,
procrastinating, hoping to escape.
It spoke dry, forced words,
pleading a thousand times: "Please be lenient and let me go until tomorrow,
I will still have some small gift."
Liáo became angry,
and immediately grabbed its waist.
Què'ér was troubled,
but its eyebrows did not furrow.
It was seized and taken away,
and soon arrived at the province.
Fènghuáng saw it from afar,
and asked who it was.
It immediately bowed its head and knelt,
saying: "I am a commoner, Què'ér,
falsely accused by Yànzi of seizing its house,
and yesterday received the King's order to be apprehended.
I crawled and ran,
not daring to be late.
Yànzi's petition
is entirely false,
blinding eyes, high and low,
I ask the King to investigate it face to face."
Fènghuáng said: "This rogue is scoundrelly,
envious and malicious,
how can it be tolerated?
It tries to manipulate me and control me.
Pull out its spine,
pluck off its left leg,
and expose its brain."
Què'ér was terrified out of its wits,
and repeatedly pleaded 'death penalty,'
asking for Yànzi to be called to confront it.
A Yànzi 燕子 suddenly poked its head out,
bowed, and explained: “The Què'ér 雀兒 seized the dwelling,
but now that it is peacefully settled,
the injuries it inflicted
will not be added.
I witnessed it firsthand;
how can you claim it’s false?”
The Què'ér 雀兒, knowing it had cheated and bullied,
its face remained shriveled.
It begged to make an oath,
with many words: “If I truly seized the Yànzi’s 燕子 dwelling,
then I wish for a generation of poverty.
In the morning, I’ll be seized by hawks;
in the evening, by owls.
Walking, I’ll be caught in a net;
sitting, I’ll be struck by a pellet.
My enterprises will not advance;
my dwelling will be unstable.
Every day, one mouth will be buried,
and my whole family will not survive.”
Though a hundred kinds of curses were uttered,
the Fènghuáng 鳳凰 was still hard to deceive.
The Yànzi 燕子 said: “When a person is desperate, they burn incense;
when a dog is desperate, it jumps over a wall.
It's just like you, full of boils and leprosy,
burying your own corpse!
These are all roundabout curses,
vainly trying to deceive the great king.”
The Fènghuáng 鳳凰 was greatly angered,
and immediately ruled after the statement: “The Què'ér’s 雀兒罪 crime
cannot be denied.
When the root cause was investigated,
it still resisted.
Its offense is to be punished with five strokes,
and its neck put in a cangue, its body imprisoned for judgment.”
The Yànzi 燕子 sang with joy,
immensely pleased: “You seized my dwelling,
caught and destroyed my dwelling.
You thought it would bring you good fortune to the end,
how could you expect Heaven to repay you!
Now it is your turn, Àmǎng 阿莽,
five strokes are just the beginning.”
At that time, a Jígē 鵙鴿 (Jílíng 鶺鴒) was nearby,
who was the Què'ér’s 雀兒昆季 brother.
He had a strong sense of urgency and distress,
and did not leave his side to attend him.
When he saw the Yànzi 燕子 singing with joy,
he immediately stepped forward to intervene: “My elder brother offended Your Honor,
and I, your humble servant, am truly ashamed.
I have heard that when a fox dies, a rabbit grieves,
as evil harms its own kind.
All within the four seas are brothers,
how much more so those of the same foul taste.
Today, he can argue his own case,
let the officials handle it as they will.
Why must you further peck at a dead sparrow,
and curse him afterward?”
The wife, hearing that the Què'ér 雀兒 had been flogged,
could not help but feel dejected.
She merely pounded her chest and slapped her bosom,
shaking her head, thinking of Àmǎng 阿莽.
Taking two steps as one,
she rushed to the prison to see him.
She saw the Què'ér 雀兒 lying on the ground,
his face ashen as dust.
A dressing was sewn on his back,
appearing about one and a half feet high.
Seeing the Què'ér 雀兒 in distress,
tears fell from her eyes like rain.
She immediately poured urine into his mouth,
and pasted old paper onto his wounds.
At that time, (she) advised,
“Why are you so stubborn and refuse to listen?
Why idly stir up trouble like a broken gong?
Indeed, you have seen the officials preside over the court.
Further subjected to endless cangue and imprisonment,
what good will it do your body?
This is self-inflicted misfortune,
you cannot blame others (for being) your ancestors.”
The Què'ér 雀兒, though stubborn,
still spoke wildly in his desperation: “As a man,
there are mistakes in affairs.
My back has been broken open,
what more is there to fear?
I live only once,
and die only once.
As the proverb says: it is better to encounter ten wolves and nine tigers,
than to face the rage of one fool.
Now I have met this Yèmǎng 夜莾 (Zhěmǎng 者莽) with his red breath,
it’s all because of this black fellow who is the ancestor.
I am now in prison,
I would rather die than be disgraced.
You should go quickly,
and summon the Qúyù 鸜鵒.
His head is pointed,
rely on him to seek a tune,
to bite and gnaw at the powerful,
and tell him to mediate with the Fènghuáng 鳳凰.
If I can just avoid another beating,
I will give him a bundle of Qímó 祁摩.”
After the Què'ér 雀兒 had been imprisoned for several days,
he asked the jailer to remove his cangue.
The jailer repeatedly refused,
so the Què'ér 雀兒 tried to persuade him with sweet words: “Officials cannot tolerate a needle, but privately they can tolerate a cart.
I beg you to remove it until evening court,
there’s no need to insist so stubbornly,
the food bringer will surely have hairpins.”
The jailer said: “You have not yet been cleared,
that is why you remain in this yellow sand.
I am merely a humble official,
how can I accept bribes?
If by chance it reaches the king’s ears,
I will be crushed like sesame seeds.
I would rather make you angry,
than let me remove your cangue.”
The Què'ér 雀兒 sighed: “In ancient times, the Three Dukes were oppressed by jailers;
I see it for myself today.
I must only recite Buddha’s name in my mouth,
and make vows in my heart:
if this official matter is resolved,
I will copy one scroll of the Duōxīnjīng 《多心經》.”
Then he persuaded the warden,
hoping for less interrogation: “All the officials, high and low,
say you are upright and capable.
Under today’s circumstances,
I beg you for a little convenience.
There is paper and brush ready,
don’t say I come empty-handed and cold-faced.”
The warden said: “Do you wish to be released,
or to retreat and repent?
You seized his dwelling,
and did not know how to be humble,
but acted violently and crudely,
beating him when he was already in distress.
You are a criminal under the king’s law,
the Fènghuáng 鳳凰 ordered me to interrogate you.
Tomorrow morning, when you go to court,
you will surely receive another beating.
Ten strokes have already passed the heavenly gate,
death is but half an inch away.
Just prepare your back to receive it,
what use are secret words to (persuade)?”
The Què'ér 雀兒 was questioned,
and became even more choked with anger.
Receiving the questions,
he felt even more distressed.
“Question: The Yànzi 燕子 built its dwelling,
intending to sustain itself,
how could you be so rude and tyrannical,
daring to forcibly seize it?
Answer!”
“The Què'ér’s 雀兒兒 name is Nǎozi 腦子,
and he was chased urgently by the old crow,
running without choosing his path,
entering any hole he found.
He temporarily sought refuge in the Yànzi’s 燕子 dwelling,
to avoid being captured.
It was truly to escape danger,
a matter of urgency.
It was not a forceful seizure,
I beg the King to understand.”
“Further question: Since you claim to be escaping danger,
why did you threaten,
and even trip and beat him,
causing him to lose his feathers?
The state has its regular punishments,
you should be lashed a hundred times.
Do you have any other reason,
to clarify yourself?
Answer!”
“The Què'ér 雀兒 merely sought refuge,
and temporarily stayed in the Yànzi’s 燕子 dwelling.
Seeing it empty,
he temporarily rested and relieved himself.
When the Yànzi 燕子 arrived,
he was about to step forward to apologize.
But without understanding the situation,
the Yànzi 燕子 cursed him angrily at first sight.
Father and son gathered together,
implicating everyone.
In anger, he did not consider the difficulty,
and immediately started fighting.
The Yànzi 燕子 claims to have lost feathers,
but the Què'ér 雀兒 is now also limping.
The injuries to both families
are comparable.
If you wish to precisely argue about occupying the dwelling,
I beg to pay its price.
If you wish to proceed according to the law,
I truly dare not object.
Seeing that I have the merit of an Upper Pillar of State,
I beg you to accept it as payment for my crime.”
“Again asked: Forcible seizure of a dwelling with intimidation,
a crime beyond tolerance.
Given your high achievements,
where did you first establish merit?
Please answer!
” “However, Xuè'ér went in Zhēnguān nineteen,
when the Grand General campaigned against Liáodōng.
Xuè'ér volunteered to serve as a retainer,
and was then assigned to the vanguard.
Not riding a horse,
not bending a bow,
holding moxa fire in his mouth,
sending it upwind.
Gāolì was consequently vanquished,
and thus merit was established.
In a similar case, he was awarded Shàng Zhùguó,
and there are several declarations of merit to be seen.
If there is a desire for investigation,
please check in the Shānhǎijīng.
Fènghuáng judged, saying: “Xuè'ér is bald,
forcibly seized the Yàn's nest,
upon questioning the root cause,
there was originally no submission.
Since there is the merit of Shàng Zhùguó for redemption,
he should not be kept long in prison.
He should be released immediately,
without further administrative bother.
Xuè'ér was released,
joyful beyond measure.
He then called Yànzi,
and they drank two sheng.
“Recently I offended you,
I beg your compassion.
From now on,
I will serve you differently.
Before others, hide it,
do not bother again.
When Yàn and Xuè had reconciled,
they travelled to a neighboring village,
where there was a meddlesome Hónghè,
who asked the two: “In your recent dispute,
Xuè'ér could not retreat to quiet,
opened his eyes and wet the bed,
violating his regulations.
It was due to Fènghuáng's grace,
that your humble lives were spared.
If the Yàozi had caught you,
your lives would have ended right then and there.
” Then he scolded Yànzi: “Why are you so stubborn and foolish,
over such a small matter,
why the dispute,
you almost endangered his life,
acting so inhumane.
Both of you are ignorant,
it is right that I do not associate with you.
Yàn and Xuè replied with one voice: “Who knew Fènghuáng would not be angry,
but instead be criticized for being superficial by the meddlesome Hónghè.
You cannot even judge affairs,
and in the end have few words.
If you indeed possess high talent,
please compose a poem or rhapsody.
Hónghè, though well-intentioned,
was ridiculed,
and so composed a poem,
to present to the two:
Hónghè's inherent heart has lofty aspirations,
Yàn and Xuè have always been ignorant of it.
One morning I will reach the blue clouds,
for three years I will fly and sing at that time.
Yàn and Xuè replied with one voice:
The great Péng truly plans to journey south,
the tiny Jiāoliáo nests in a single branch.
Each finds contentment in their own freedom,
what does it matter if these two insects know?
Yànzi Fù, one scroll.
This song is truly fitting for itself,
nowhere else in the world is there its superior.
Xuè'ér and Yànzi,
together composed the Kāiyuán Gē.
Yànzi is truly difficult to match,
able to speak and also verbose.
His whole life, his heart is vigorous and healthy,
among birds, there is none superior.
Dwelling on the hall's beam,
carrying mud to build a nest.
Pursuing friends and relatives,
not associating with inferior birds.
In autumn and winter he hides in stone caves,
in spring and summer he is among humans.
In the second month he comes to the thicket,
in the eighth month he returns to the mountains.
Holding the herb of longevity in his mouth,
other matters are leisurely.
If he does not die through winter,
he will return again this year.
Soaring and playing in the clouds,
twisting and turning in flight.
Returning to his old dwelling,
each settling in their original nest.
In the thicket, he met a bird,
who called himself Xuè'ér.
Shaking his head, he spoke directly and wildly,
his words were full of deceit.
Xuè'ér truly harbored ill intentions,
changing and manipulating, now up, now down.
Knowing his nest was good,
he came horizontally to invade.
He asked Yàn, “What mountain bird are you?”
Yàn landed and made a sound: “It's futile to come asking for my nest,
I'll let you go, but settle down your heart.
Yànzi said to Xuè'ér: “How dare you act so wrongly!
Hearing your previous words,
we originally did not know each other.
Living here for one winter,
warmly raising my wife and children.
You should be ashamed,
yet you blame and argue!
Xuè'ér said to Yànzi: “Do not speak boastfully of grace.
Loud words certainly lack reason,
no need for a quarrelsome beak.
The authorities have reason,
it will be clearly proclaimed.
I am indeed entitled to sit in this empty space,
how can Xuè'ér act arbitrarily?
Yànzi said to Xuè'ér: “How dare you act like a stubborn fool.
Sitting in my house,
yet trying to deceive the owner.
Now that I demand it,
you speak wild words about the authorities.
Raising a toad leads to illness,
I tell you, there is no doubt!
Xuè'ér said to Yànzi: “It's not about your quarrelsome beak.
I ask where you live and reside,
in which prefecture did you originally live?
The government is now requisitioning guest residents,
specifically to capture vagrants.
Sly boy, set aside your taunts,
change your mind and withdraw.
Yàn heard this, clapped his hands and laughed: “It's not about your wild words.
My large dwelling is in the mountains,
this is my manor.
My ancestral home is in Jīngzhào,
my birth origin is in the imperial capital.
Just return to his nest,
your wild words are inappropriate.
Even if I have no household registration,
it ultimately doesn't concern you.
I obtained eternal blessings,
and can settle anywhere.
These words are all true,
the whole world knows it.
If you don't believe my words,
please ask a scholar.
Xuè'ér said to Yànzi: “Why bother with such elaborate explanations?
How did you obtain eternal blessings?
Your words are all empty.
My spirit and eyes bear witness,
when alive, I can be at ease.
Where did you get your skills?
Your wild words deceive the villagers.
Your head is like a solitary pounding bird,
your body like a large (lacquer) shape.
Your body is stained with bean juice,
your feet and hands are like nails.
Always handling a smelly large (black bag),
directly wanting to cover a Hu-bottle.
What way do you govern the country,
to usurp my name of eternal blessing?
"In the past, it was originally Wú Wáng's palace,
where swallows built their nests.
Palace maids played games at night,
and then caught the nests and burned them.
At that time, there was no place to live,
so we lodged on the hall beams for a night.
That king saw us with pity,
and his compassion was also generous.
Do not despise our small bodies,
our spirits are exceedingly heroic.
One hundred places on the hall beams,
we soar and float in the clouds.
On the water, we swallow floating insects,
in the air, we catch flying insects.
Truly, there is no comparison,
we once married into the Hǎi Lóng Gōng.
The third daughter of the Hǎi Lóng Wáng,
her hair was more than seven *chǐ* long.
She carried us in her mouth and laid us beneath her belly,
how could swallows be merely praised?
Please read the *Lúnyǔ* to verify,
ask Gōngyě Cháng,
who was then in chains,
and because of a swallow, escaped calamity.
The sparrow said to the swallow: "Bend your ear and listen carefully!
If you wish to return to your nest,
first settle your beak's voice.
Red sparrows are anciently called auspicious,
my brothers are in the Tiān Tíng.
Princes and kings hold hands with them,
the court and the countryside all know their names.
We are of one kind, dwelling between heaven and earth,
but our destinies are not equal.
When wheat ripens, I eat first,
when grain ripens, I taste it first.
When winter comes and summer goes,
how have I ever left the Dìxiāng?
My descendants fill the world,
my fathers and uncles are throughout the villages.
Ever since I could distinguish,
my kind mother's heart was truly at peace.
Always pondering the ten good deeds,
realizing the desire for impermanence.
When hungry, I always eat the five grains,
never killing a single living creature.
I pity you as a distant guest,
for this reason, I do not contend with you."
The swallow sighed to himself: "I do not boast to the sparrow.
When hungry, I always eat the nine elixirs,
when thirsty, I drink cinnabar.
I cannot distinguish the four seas,
my heart yearns for Hóng Yá.
Do not wonder why I hide through winter,
it is only because I enjoy the mountain home.
Dwelling long makes people despise us,
rare visits make them pleased to see us.
For this reason, I hide through winter,
not because I fear hunger or cold.
The secluded cliffs are truly joyful,
I ramble and play in the mountains and wilds.
Originally I intended to be observed,
but instead, I was observed by observers.
A tiger, although fierce,
is not as strong as many dogs.
My nest has been taken away,
intimidating me into official action.
Empty contention is of no benefit,
there is nothing better than seeing the Fènghuáng."
Since the sparrow was taken by the swallow,
they directly went to see the King of Birds.
The Fènghuáng sat on its platform,
with a hundred birds surrounding it on all sides.
It paced and looked around,
and saw the swallow holding words in its mouth.
"My nest was violently seized,
I name the sparrow.
Bearing grievances, I come to plead and appeal,
to inform Your Majesty, the Dàwáng."
The sparrow and the swallow,
both stood before the Wáng.
The Fènghuáng personally issued its judgment,
"He who has reason shall speak first."
The swallow spoke first: "Listen to my words.
I will truthfully state the facts,
and reveal the original cause and circumstances.
Suffering from the invasion of my dwelling,
how dare I speak if I am in the wrong?
Not discerning, the yellow-headed sparrow,
banded together with ruffians to commit acts of power.
A swallow had a dwelling,
and it was violently seized.
It is hard to remain silent when wronged,
I humbly beg for your deliberation.
Though the sun and moon shine brightly,
they cannot illuminate what is covered by a basin.
Empty words are originally powerless,
who would be willing to enter the Wáng's gate!"
The Fènghuáng angrily said to the sparrow: "Why do you seize and bully it!
Both of you have nests,
why suddenly commit such wrong?
"The sparrow stepped forward and addressed the Fènghuáng: "How can Your Majesty not know!
Thoroughly investigate and ask all the details,
how can you believe empty words!
The sparrow is merely a bird,
each living in villages.
Neither of us has fixed dwellings,
we settle ourselves wherever we go.
Seeing an empty nest,
it was old and ruined, not new.
After long investigation, it originally had no owner,
so I conveniently settled myself there.
A deed accomplished cannot be destroyed,
it cannot be moved or altered.
I sat comfortably within it,
cherishing and keeping it safe."
The swallow addressed the Dàwáng: "The sparrow is speaking wildly.
It is also a Qióngqí bird,
crafting elaborate words and phrases.
It brings mud to build a nest,
and its mouth is full of sores;
If Your Majesty does not believe my words,
I beg you to ask the master of the house."
The Fènghuáng then pronounced judgment: "Two birds, come forward.
Without speaking, I already understand everything,
the facts are clearly apparent.
You despicable yellow-headed bird,
you speak so glibly about the circumstances.
Quickly return its nest to it,
and do not delay any further."
The sparrow addressed the Fènghuáng: "I am willing to follow your judgment.
Your Majesty orders me to return its nest,
I beg for some flexibility.
The sparrow is a tax-paying household,
how can it be treated the same as an outsider?
The swallow comes and goes seasonally,
it occupies the nest but does not stay through winter."
The Fènghuáng said to the sparrow: "Quickly return the swallow's nest!
I have now made my judgment,
the sparrow is not in the right.
I am the lord of a hundred birds,
my laws are not to be trifled with.
Justice demands it to be so,
there can be no partiality."
The swallow gained its dwelling back by reason,
it was joyful and happy again;
The sparrow was so ashamed it wished to die,
with no place to settle itself.
The swallow does not seek favors from others,
sparrow, do not be angry.
Formerly, I heard the ancients say,
three disputes lead to becoming kin.
In the past, the sage Yáo Wáng,
held the throne for twenty years.
Zhèng Qiáo served the four seas,
and married immediately upon meeting.
Yuán Bó was ill at home,
Chén Xiāng (Jù Qīng) promised a thousand *lǐ*.
The Yān Wáng resented the Qín Guó,
his weeping horse transformed into a *lín*.
He held his grain and sat, awaiting death,
for ten thousand generations he received acclaim.
Bǎi Yáo (Bó Táo) remembered the court,
choking with sobs and tears streaming.
Wáng Yì had the virtue of breaking a horse,
yet he still could not share.
Wǔ Zǐxū attacked Chǔ,
and the two cities also had nothing to say.
Unable to emulate ancient virtues,
the two of them were just birds.
Because of arguing over a ruined nest,
they merely wasted their energy.
Wealth is like dirt,
benevolence and righteousness are heavier than mountains.
The swallow is truly at fault now,
sparrow, do not be angry.
The sparrow said to the swallow: "After this separation, there is no need to discuss.
The dwelling is your family's dwelling,
it is reasonable and not empty talk.
I repaired it for a whole winter,
all that was ruined and fallen, it was all true.
You should be ashamed,
yet you dragged me to see the Wáng.
The Fènghuáng abides by the Buddhist Dharma,
it does not intend to kill or harm anyone;
if suddenly it blames and strikes with emotion,
how much shame upon its golden body!"
The swallow spoke to the sparrow: "These words are not meant in anger.
Since you mend the roof,
there is no need for rent.
Twelve months a year,
five hundred cash per month,
if we were to calculate the rent,
it would surely cost you your life."
A poem from The Rhyme-prose on the Swallow.
Written by the local tribute scholar Wáng Fū.
I have furtively observed that Shénnóng once tasted a hundred herbs,
and from this the five grains were distinguished.
Xuānyuán created clothing for them,
and passed it down to teach later generations.
Cāng Jié created their characters,
Kǒng Qiū expounded and transformed the Confucian doctrine.
It is impossible to recount every detail from the beginning,
so I will gather the essential points.
May I briefly ask about tea and wine,
which of the two has the greater merit?
Which one should be considered humble and small,
and which one should be honored?
Today, each must present its case,
the stronger will bring glory to its lineage.
Then Tea came out and said: "Everyone, calm down,
listen to a few words.
The chief of a hundred herbs,
the flower of ten thousand trees.
Valued for its pistil,
prized for its sprouts.
Called 'míng cǎo' (tea herb),
named 'chá' (tea).
Presented to the residences of the five marquises,
offered to the imperial household.
Timely fresh offerings are brought in,
bringing a lifetime of glory.
Naturally noble and revered,
why is there a need for boasting?"
Then Wine came out and said: "What laughable words!
From ancient times to the present,
tea is cheap and wine is quý.
A single cup of wine thrown into the river,
the three armies proclaim themselves drunk.
When the monarch drinks it,
they shout 'Wànsuì!'
When the ministers drink it,
they are granted 'fearlessness' by the emperor.
It harmonizes death and establishes life,
the gods savor its essence.
Wine and food are friendly to people,
never having ill intentions.
With wine, there are commands,
benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom.
It naturally deserves to be honored,
why bother comparing it to others?"
Tea said to Wine: "Do you not hear it said: Fúliáng, Shèzhōu,
sought by all nations.
Shǔshān, Méngdǐng,
scaling mountains and crossing ridges.
Shūchéng, Tàihú,
buying maids and buying slaves.
Yuèjùn, Yúháng,
gold and silk as bags.
The emperor's purple and white,
rarely seen among people.
Merchants come seeking it,
boats and carts fill the channels.
Based on these traces,
which one should be considered small?"
Wine said to Tea: "Do you not hear it said: Qíjiǔ Gānhé,
for which one bets brocade and gauze.
Pútáo Jiǔyùn,
nourishing to the body.
Yùjiǔ Qióngjiāng,
the cups of immortals.
Júhuā Zhúyè,
exchanged between monarchs.
Zhōngshān Zhà Mǔ,
sweet and beautiful.
One becomes drunk for three years,
a tale passed down through ages.
It fosters humility in villages,
and harmonizes the military commanderies.
Oh, your understanding,
there is no need for futile effort."
Tea said to Wine: "My tea herb,
the essence of ten thousand trees.
Sometimes white as jade,
sometimes like gold.
Famous monks and great virtuous ones,
hidden in Zen forests.
Drinking it while conversing,
can dispel drowsiness.
Offered to Mílè,
presented to Guānyīn.
For a thousand kalpas, ten thousand kalpas,
all Buddhas admire it.
Wine can break up families and scatter households,
leading to widespread debauchery.
After three cups are drunk,
it only causes people to sink deeper into sin."
Wine said to Tea: "Three cash for one bowl,
when will you get rich?
Wine connects with noble people,
desired by dukes and ministers.
It once made Lord Zhào play the qín,
and King Qín strike the fǒu.
You cannot invite singing with tea,
you cannot teach dancing for tea.
Drinking tea only causes back pain,
drinking too much causes stomach illness.
If one drinks ten cups a day,
the intestines swell like a yá gǔ (official drum).
If one consumes it for three years,
one will develop dropsy as if raising shrimp."
Tea said to Wine: "I achieve fame at thirty,
donning belt, headscarf, and comb.
Crossing seas and riding rivers,
to present myself at the golden court.
Brought to the marketplace,
before fully arranged.
People come to buy it,
wealth overflows.
Instantaneously one becomes rich,
not waiting until tomorrow or the day after.
Oh, your wine can cause confusion and disorder,
drinking it leads to much chatter and fuss.
In the streets, innocent people are ensnared,
receiving no less than seventeen lashes on their backs.
Wine said to Tea: "Do you not see that ancient talents and scholars,
in their poems, all say: 'When thirsty, a cup
can nourish life.'
And also: 'Wine is a medicine to dispel sorrow.'
And again: 'Wine can nurture the worthy.'
The dregs of the ancients,
are now passed down.
Tea is cheap, three cash for five bowls,
wine is cheap, seven cash for half a cup.
Offering wine to express gratitude for presence,
showing courtesy.
National music,
originated from Jiǔquán.
Eating your tea-water all day long,
how could one dare to move a single string or pipe?"
Tea said to Wine: "Do you not see it said: 'A boy of fourteen or fifteen,
should not associate with wine houses.'
Do you not see the xīngxīng bird,
losing its life for wine?
You say: 'Eating tea causes illness,
drinking wine nurtures the worthy.'
Yet we see 'wine yellow' (jaundice) and 'wine sickness' (alcoholism),
but never 'tea madness' or 'tea frenzy.'
King Āshìshì killed his father and harmed his mother for wine,
Liú Líng 'died' for wine for three years.
After drinking, people scowl and glare,
fighting with angry fists.
The reports only mention 'crude and violent drunkenness,'
never 'tea drunkenness.'
Inevitably, they are imprisoned and flogged,
the local official demands money.
A large cangue around the neck,
and rafters thrown onto their backs.
Then they burn incense and swear off wine,
chanting Buddhist prayers and seeking heaven,
never drinking again for the rest of their lives,
hoping to avoid misfortune."
The two debated their respective merits,
unaware that Water was standing by their side.
Shuǐ, on behalf of Chá and Jiǔ, said: "Oh, you two,
what's the rush?
Who allowed you
to each attempt to claim credit?
Your words slander each other,
speaking of west and east.
Life's Four Great Elements are
earth, water, fire, and wind.
If tea doesn't have water,
what kind of appearance does it make?
If wine doesn't have water,
what kind of form does it take?
Eating rice and yeast dry
harms people's intestines and stomach.
Eating tea leaves dry
only chafes and breaks the throat.
All things require water,
it is the ancestor of the five grains.
Above, it responds to the heavenly phenomena;
below, it accords with good and ill fortune.
The Jiāng, Hé, Huái, and Jì rivers –
where I am, there is passage.
I can also flood and devastate heaven and earth,
and I can also dry up and kill fish and dragons.
The nine-year disaster during Yáo's reign
was only because I was involved.
Thus, all under heaven respect and worship me,
and the myriad people follow me.
Yet I don't claim to be a sage;
why do you two need to compete for credit?
From now on,
you must be harmonious.
Then wine shops will prosper,
and tea houses will not be poor.
Remain brothers forever,
and you must persevere from beginning to end.
If a person reads this volume,
they will never suffer from wine madness or tea sickness for all eternity.
《Chájiǔlùn》, one scroll.
Written by Yán Hǎizhēn, disciple of the Zhīshùyuàn, on the fourteenth day of the first month in the Rénshēn year of the third year of Kāibǎo (970 CE).
《Jiàngmóbiàn》 Yāzuòwén.
Years come and years go, subtly shifting,
yet no one takes it to heart or comprehends it.
Just yesterday, the temples were rosy and vibrant,
but now the head is covered in white threads.
Though one is honored and thousands assent,
all urgent matters become like a dream.
And further, seeing old people with stooped backs,
still busily toiling for wives and children.
Do you not see that coming to life and going to death
is like ants endlessly circulating;
toiling for clothes and food
is like silkworms spinning cocoons?
Even if there are heroes who can lift mountains and tripods,
they ultimately lie buried in three feet of earth.
Even if there are those with jade plaques and golden embroidery,
they cannot escape becoming a handful of ashes.
Do not cling to a long stay;
observe the moment of departure.
Though one speaks of the highest heavens,
all ultimately reach the land of impermanence.
The deep affection of a young wife
cannot provide a gate to escape death;
the profound love of a cherished son
will ultimately not suffer hardship in your stead.
In this bustling, turbid world,
why cling to a long dwelling?
In this vast, confused state,
how can one plan to leave?
If one does not cultivate the ever-blooming wisdom tree,
the awakened flower will soon wither.
Places of joy in heavenly palaces
must lead to rebirth in the depths of hell.
Alas, do not lament death;
once gone, one is born again.
It is truly lamentable and grievous
that you do not reflect:
a lifetime is like a lamp in the wind, fleetingly extinguished,
a hundred years are like a spring dream, busy with suffering.
Place your hand over your heart and ponder carefully;
worldly affairs have never lasted long.
No matter if gold and silver fill the treasury,
how can you take them with you when you die?
Rosy cheeks gradually wrinkle like chicken skin,
green hair soon turns white like a crane's feathers.
And those acquaintances from before
are all, from beginning to end, subject to old age, sickness, and impermanence.
Spring, summer, autumn, and winter, the four seasons urge on,
causing human life to undergo transmigration.
A thousand mountains clearly bear white snow,
ten thousand trees are secretly about to bloom with red flowers.
Swallows come and go, time is pressing,
flowers bloom and wither, competing to push and fall.
Upon hearing of health, one must awaken to understanding,
then in the future, one will surely be spared transmigration.
If you wish to ask if such things exist,
chant the title of the sutra and bring it forth.
With this, we recite and praise the merits born of the Mahāyāna,
reverently offering them to adorn the noble position of our current emperor.
May the sun of Shùn shine eternally,
and the years of Yáo be forever preserved.
May the Phoenix State be extended for a thousand autumns,
and the Dragon Map be protected for ten thousand years.
We humbly consider our prefect, the Púshè:
his divine endowment is upright and righteous,
he descends from a mountain, an heroic spirit.
He harbors profound benevolence for benefiting beings,
and possesses the grand achievement of bringing order to the world.
His family is renowned for its distinguished lineage,
he nurtures and cares for the common people.
He oversees the pure regulations of the state's governance,
and holds the important position of balancing land and water.
Since his arrival in this district,
every household feels like spring.
Everyone spreads songs of his good governance,
and together celebrates the transformation of peace and prosperity.
Thus, the harvests are abundant year after year,
and the jurisdiction is tranquil and peaceful.
Grain stores are piled high like mountains, flowing like rivers,
and the sounds of commerce spread throughout the district.
We reverently offer these praises of merit,
to adorn our prefect, the Sītú.
May the Great River flow again,
and its waters forever encircle the universe;
may his purple ribbon last a thousand years,
and his achievements forever support the altars of earth and grain.
Next, we offer praises of merit,
reverently offered to adorn the Holy Princess, the Empress Mother.
May the crimson osmanthus south of the mountains
remain unchanged through the four seasons;
and the cold plum north of the ridge
stand out uniquely with a single branch.
Again, we offer praises of merit,
to adorn the noble positions of all the young ladies and gentlemen of the household.
May the sons serve the nation with distinction,
assisting the sacred court;
may the young ladies' eyebrows reach the Dragon Palace,
and their persons grace the Imperial Gates.
May the gate have many beautiful jades,
and the residence embrace good fortune.
May a thousand disasters not descend upon the household,
and ten thousand blessings all arrive at your noble dwelling.
Then, may the great generals before the yamen
be utterly filial and loyal;
and the accompanying officials
be solely pure and upright.
May the city and local temples,
and the altars of the local deities,
preserve their high peaks for a thousand autumns,
and all within the seas proclaim peace.
[Again, we offer praises of merit,
reverently offered to adorn our Dū Sēngtǒng Héshàng.
May he forever receive imperial grace,
to be the Guàndǐng Guóshī.
May he forever guard the platform,
assisting the enlightened king in governing and transforming.
The golden immortal's birth
was originally in the Zhōu dynasty;
the propagation of the counterfeit Dharma
began in the Hàn dynasty.
In the time of King Zhāo,
he had an auspicious dream for a thousand autumns;
in the Rénwǔ year,
he abandoned the imperial palace for the snowy peaks.
Six years of ascetic practice,
the Four Wisdoms perfectly complete.
He defeated ninety million demonic armies,
and achieved the eighty glorious auspicious marks.
Thus, he became honored above and below heaven,
Buddha alone being supreme,
and among the Three Realms,
there was ultimately none to compare.
It is now the auspicious season of Qīngyáng,
the midst of springtime,
the day when the Buddha renounced the imperial palace,
and the day when the whole household gathers auspicious blessings.
Seeing the Buddha's white hair-mark,
what blessing will not arrive?
Seeing the golden man's supreme form,
what disaster will not cease?
With firm vows from three kalpas,
and the Six Pāramitās perfectly fulfilled.
His body nearly filled with countless merits,
the eighty subsidiary marks about to be complete.
If not coming here to save and deliver,
then where else will he await the opportune moment?
At that time, he was not in other countries,
but manifested provisionally dwelling in Tuṣita Heaven.
On that day, our Buddha, to deliver all sentient beings,
abandoned the royal palace,
and practiced the Dao in the snowy mountains.
After six years of ascetic practice,
His four wisdoms were perfectly complete.
On the morning of the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month,
He descended the mountain to bathe in the Xīlián Hé,
washing away years of grime from His body,
and attaining a golden body of purple-gold.
Emerging from the pure river of love,
He met the elder Jíxiáng.
A vast grass mat was spread out,
and offerings were diligently presented.
The cowherd girl offered milk at this time,
and the Four Heavenly Kings presented their bowls on this day.
As soon as He ascended the seat,
the demonic palace was shaken.
At that moment, the demon king
spoke these words:
“Six years in the mountains, undergoing ascetic practice,
His four wisdoms are perfectly complete, and His Dao-fruit firm.
He descends the mountain, desiring to save sentient beings from suffering,
washing off grime in the Xīlián Hé.
As soon as He emerged from the river, He met an elder,
who spread a vast grass mat, forming a good緣 (yuán).
The cowherd girl personally offered milk in devotion,
and the Four Heavenly Kings brought their bowls to the riverbank.
As soon as He was seated,
the heavenly palace shook,
thus knowing His sacred power is boundless.
The demon king immediately observed the lower realm,
and then knew that the Tathāgata had appeared in the world.”
Thereupon, the demon king, having observed the lower realm,
saw neither men committing the five heinous crimes,
nor filial sons.
He only saw our Prince Xīdá, son of Jìngfàn Dàwáng in Nán Yánfú Tí, about to attain perfect enlightenment.
The demon king pondered and said: “If I allow Him to convert and deliver sentient beings,
our disciples
will take refuge in the Buddha.
It is better to seize the opportunity, gather our followers first,
inspect the demonic palace,
trouble Qú tán,
and prevent Him from appearing in the world.”
At that moment, the demon king spoke these words:
“The demon king raged, circling swiftly,
summoning countless demonic spirits and ghost gods.
Beholding the Tathāgata now appearing in the world,
his heroic spirit could not endure, and anger arose.
He knew not that his own evil spirits
could hold mountains and overturn seas to destroy the golden man.
He commanded the ghost gods to exert their full strength,
to capture the Tathāgata and satisfy my desire.”
Thereupon, the demon king struck a golden bell,
gathering a million followers.
He immediately dispatched Mǎtóu Luóchà to temporarily serve as the Yóuyì Jiāngjūn,
and the swift Yèchā to be the vanguard general.
Jiūpánzhà guǐ lined up with spears and halberds to advance,
while Píshèshē shén led armored soldiers to follow.
He summoned the Āxiūluó army as assault troops,
their eyes shining brightly;
He ordered Pílìduō shén to follow behind,
who then appeared sometimes angry, sometimes joyful.
Moreover, there were Yèchā Yúhòu,
Luóchà Dūxún,
all with sword-like teeth and spear-like fangs,
sharp fur and copper claws,
holding iron clubs in their hands,
and carrying red snakes.
They drove goblins and sprites to advance,
with Wǎngliǎng ghost gods behind.
Yánluó Wáng was the supreme commander,
managing all the armies.
The Wǔdào Dàshén also served as Yāyá Dàjiàng,
and knew how to execute and cleave.
He summoned Fēng Bó and Yǔ Shī to form one camp,
and called upon the Xíngbìng Guǐwáng to form another troop.
There were ten thousand kinds of妖婆 (yāopó),
but with ears, one could not hear;
a thousand kinds of weapons,
yet one had never seen them.
Then they arrayed in two formations,
divided into four flanks,
circling left and blocking right,
advancing front and cutting off rear.
They used thunder as war drums,
and lightning flashes as vermilion banners,
unleashing fierce winds to sweep forward,
and urging venomous dragons to the rear.
Vipers and snakes coiled and knotted,
filling the ground and streams.
Gods and ghosts crossed over,
shaking their spirits and moving their eyes.
Moreover, there were flying ghosts,
whose forms were unknown.
Some had five eyes and six teeth,
three bodies and eight arms,
four shoulders and seven ears,
nine mouths and ten heads,
yellow hair and red beards,
pointed heads and broad foreheads.
Some had thick wrists and thin arms,
small heads and long legs.
They unfurled their banners (flags) in the mountains and rivers,
and exhaled clouds and mist with their breath.
They shook the sun and moon,
and trembled heaven and earth.
They made chirping sounds,
and transmitted the Pōzhà roar.
The demon king personally led his army,
and arrived in the forest.
First, dense clouds spread out,
then ink-like rain poured down.
Huge logs and beams
blocked the void.
They held stones and carried mountains,
obscuring the sun and moon.
A strong wind suddenly arose,
uprooting trees and blowing sand,
so that heaven and earth could not distinguish east from west,
and in the darkness, one knew not north from south.
With a unified command,
they descended from the sky.
In an instant,
they reached directly beneath the Bodhi tree.
“A million kinds of demons are gathered,
intending to capture the Tathāgata as if it were easy.
The army commander commands all ghost gods,
‘Do not return until Qú tán is dead!’”
The demon king himself was the grand marshal,
managing all armies according to his command.
Dense clouds spread in the sky,
pouring down black mist like an ink pond.
Raindrops, if they struck, were like arrows,
hailstones, if they met a person, were like repeated hammers.
Mountains were carried in their palms,
rivers were twisted and poured directly down.
A commotion in the sky,
the world startled,
only the sound of killing was heard in the commands.
Where red flags unfurled, residual rosy clouds arose,
where black banners hung, jade-green clouds flew.
Ghost gods in the clouds were all fierce,
and the demon king continuously displayed his might.
They surrounded the Buddha's body thousands of times,
intending to capture the Tathāgata and satisfy their vile desires.
At this, our Buddha beneath the Bodhi tree,
meditated with right mindfulness, saying: “All these external paths have come,
how shall I deal with them?”
Then He arose with the power of compassionate good roots,
skillfully subduing the evil followers,
without needing weapons,
nor troubling soldiers and horses.
The weapons held by the Tathāgata
were entirely different from theirs.
He donned the armor of patience,
wielded the sword of wisdom,
bent the bow of meditation,
and aimed the arrow of compassion,
rode the horse of ten powers,
and applied the whip of diligence.
Before the sword of shame was raised,
the demon generals were alarmed;
before the sword of wisdom was swung,
Pōxún was terrified.
Those who emitted smoke and spat flames
were instead burned by themselves;
those who carried stones and lifted mountains
sank and fell by themselves.
The external paths’ bows, as they were about to be drawn, their strings broke;
their arrows, as they were about to be shot, flowers spontaneously grew;
their spears, before being whirled, broke by themselves;
their swords, before being swung, their blades fell off;
thunder turned into Brahma sounds,
hailstones became pearls.
Red flags appeared and disappeared,
fragrant winds arose by themselves,
fierce fires and black smoke
were replaced by sandalwood mist.
Our Buddha manifested His meditative power,
and Pōxún and the external paths were terrified beyond measure.
The large ones sought escape in the mist,
the small ones fought shaking in the clouds.
Seeing this, the demon king
then withdrew his army.
The Luóchà kowtowed,
proclaiming their mortal sins.
Turning their weapons, they departed,
returning to the demonic palace,
their venomous anger not yet gone,
still raging and so forth.
The demon king had displayed all his divine transformations,
yet could not shake our Tathāgata.
As soon as the precious sword was wielded, its blade was gone;
the bow, as it was about to be drawn, its string broke.
Carrying mountains and snatching seas, displaying their divine powers,
huge logs and beams filled the void.
Attempting to harm the Tathāgata, the Lord of the Three Realms,
was just like falling leaves meeting the autumn wind.
The demon king, himself the grand marshal,
terrified, hid himself with nowhere to go.
Then he personally issued orders before the army,
urgently withdrawing his troops to return to his palace.
He did not consider that he himself belonged to the category of evil deities,
but compared himself to the Great World-Honored One in Heaven.
Although Arhats are lesser sages,
their power can withstand myriad layers of heavenly demons.
The host of ghosts and spirits,
in myriad forms,
are like a shallow pool compared to the power of the Tathāgata.
No matter how many transformations you display before him,
the Tathāgata does not stir a single hair.
Seeing that this formation seemed to be losing, the Māwáng
withdrew his army,
and returned to heaven.
Not realizing his own weak power,
he rashly intended to vex and harm the Tathāgata.
His feelings of anger
had not yet subsided.
Then, sitting upright in the main hall,
he reclined on a fragrant couch,
wringing his wrists and raising his eyebrows,
pursing his lips in unbearable frustration.
The Māwáng had three daughters,
who, suddenly seeing their royal father unhappy,
stepped forward and reported to the Great King:
“Recently, your appearance seems to have changed;
why are you troubled and unhappy?
Is it because various devas are vexing and disturbing you?
Or is there unrest in the palace?
Or are you worried about matters of your kingdom’s territory?
Or are you concerned about your daughters’ well-being?
We only wish our royal father, with compassion,
would now tell your daughters the reason.”
The royal father said:
“It is not concern for my daughters’ well-being;
you have naturally already grown up.
Nor am I worried about matters of the kingdom’s territory;
what more is there to worry about in the joyful heavenly palace!
It is because of Śuddhodana’s Siddhārtha,
who has recently attained perfect enlightenment.
I cannot bear to see him now appearing in the world,
as I fear he will convert all my followers.
If I allow him to teach and convert,
he will convert all my followers and disciples.
What scheme should I now devise
to eliminate him and prevent him from appearing in the world?”
Thereupon, the three daughters advanced and stepped forward,
advising their royal father:
“Gautama, since childhood, has been in deep palaces,
how could he possibly sever enjoyment of sights and desires?
Moreover, as a young man with a beautiful appearance,
it is precisely the time to covet joy and pursue pleasure.
We now all wish to descend to Jambudvīpa
to disturb him and prevent him from attaining the fruit of enlightenment.
We will surely make him lose heart
and fail to achieve the unsurpassed great Bodhi.”
The Māwáng heard this plan and
was extraordinarily joyful.
He allowed his servants to adorn them
with brocades and silks from the treasury.
They swept their cicada-like hair to the side,
and inserted phoenix hairpins diagonally,
their bodies adorned with brocades and silks,
their arms entwined with necklaces.
The beautiful women of the eastern neighbor
were truly inferior;
the enchanting women of the southern land
were clearly no match.
Their jade-like complexions were like snow,
making the beauty of Luòpǔ seem a mere boast;
their vermilion faces like flowers,
making the appearance of Wūshān seem an idle tale.
They moved like flowing clouds and falling rain,
overthrowing states and cities.
People floated in five-colored robes,
the sun shone on clothes of three *zhū*.
Immortal maidens followed behind,
holding jeweled canopies in their wake;
celestial weavers led the way,
wafting fragrant breezes that filled the path.
He summoned the colorful women of the six palaces,
and positioned them on the left;
he ordered the ladies of the entire country,
to be divided and situated on the right.
They came directly from the upper realm
to before the Buddha.
Songs and dances were performed simultaneously,
pipes and strings competed in their melodies.
In terms of charm, they were truly women of brocade and silk,
and in terms of appearance, they uniquely surpassed spring.
Their bodies were adorned with robes of three *zhū* from the heavenly palace,
their feet trod on a patch of cloud from Wūshān.
The first daughter said: “World-Honored One!
World-Honored One!
How long does a person live in this world?
If one does not live in glory and splendor,
one wastes one’s days in vain.
My beauty
is truly unparalleled.
I should not boast,
but it is rare in the human world.
Therefore I have come to serve you,
vowing for a thousand years.
Do not reject my lowliness,
I will forever be your companion like a zither and a se.”
(The daughter said): “I urge you not to attain great Bodhi;
why must your mind be so stubbornly deluded?
I have left my kind parents to descend to the lower realm,
willingly taking myself as your wife and husband.”
(The Buddha said): “I now wish to attain great Bodhi,
to preach the Dharma and convert the deluded masses.”
The second daughter said: “World-Honored One!
World-Honored One!
A descendant of the Golden Wheel King’s lineage,
an imperial prince and royal grandson,
you abandoned your royal position
to be alone and solitary in the mountains.
My intention in coming now
is no other;
I wish to accompany you in the mountains,
to sweep the ground, burn incense, and fetch water.
When the World-Honored One is not present,
I can look after the home and guard the dwelling.”
(The daughter said): “I love wearing brocade robes,
which are naturally fragrant without burning aloeswood or musk.
I have left my kind parents to descend to the lower realm,
vowing to sweep your golden couch with my slender hands.”
(The Buddha said): “My every thought is on impermanence;
where is there little need for burning incense?”
The third daughter said: “World-Honored One!
World-Honored One!
I am young,
and my parents particularly dote on me.
I am uniquely beautiful,
and rarely intelligent.
Indra and Brahmā
frequently came to inquire,
but my parents disliked their humble status
and did not allow me to become their wife.
I see the World-Honored One is handsome,
and also the prince of Śuddhodana.
You are complete in the three virtues and six arts,
and perfectly skilled in both civil and martial arts.
Therefore, I abandoned my parents,
and purposefully came down to Jambudvīpa,
not daring to be the Buddha’s wife,
but willingly to forever hold your seat cushion.”
(The daughter said): “I am fifteen springs old,
just like a lotus emerging from the water’s edge.
Seeing you complete in both civil and martial arts,
and excelling in the six arts and three virtues.
I have left my kind parents to descend to the lower realm,
I do not wish to become a monk or nun.”
(The Buddha said): “You should have long ago abandoned your female body,
only because of your past obstructions to the Buddha’s cause.”
The demonesses did not believe the World-Honored One’s words,
and defiantly uttered strong words,
lightly annoying the Buddha.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One extended his golden arm
and pointed at the bodies of the demonesses;
all three instantly transformed into old hags.
Their eyes were like vermilion bowls,
their faces like burning embers,
their foreheads broad and heads pointed,
chests high and noses crooked.
Their hair was yellow and teeth black,
eyebrows white and mouths green.
Their faces were wrinkled like skin covering skulls,
their necks long like chopsticks.
Their whole bodies adorned in brocade and embroidery
transformed into two pieces of plain cloth skirts;
the combs and hairpins on their heads
transformed into a tangled mess of snakes.
Their bodies were hunched and necks shrunken,
just like old owls suffering from the cold;
their waists bent and legs long,
like stalks of grain after autumn.
Their entire bodies were a laughingstock,
like mere corpses.
The three looked at each other,
their faces pale.
Confused in their hearts,
they looked into a mirror,
only to see a hundred ugly forms remaining,
not a trace of their thousand charming features.
The three sisters
said: “This is not
the work of heaven,
but all due to our own self-created calamity.
Where has our charming beauty gone?
Ugliness has arrived at this moment.
Our eyes' pupils are like fire,
the goiters on our chests are like dippers.”
I have heard that when the Rúlái expounds the Dharma,
it encompasses millions of Ganges sands;
when the Púsà transmit the Sūtras,
it reaches thousands of worlds.
Initially, at Lùyuàn,
he converted the five Jùlún;
finally, arriving at Shuānglín,
he subdued the ten Fànzhì.
He expounded profound words, and the waves of the river of love ceased;
he spoke of Bōrě, and the mountains of vexation collapsed.
He gathered the three points into the true origin,
and purified the six dusts in the human realm.
Therefore, within the great city of Shèwèi,
he aroused compassionate thoughts to deliver all sentient beings;
in the garden of the elder Jǐgū,
he held the lamp of wisdom to transmit the Dharma seal.
The Rúlái, putting on his robe and holding his bowl,
walked majestically in the clear morning,
and at mealtime,
returned to his original place.
Begging for food prolonged the work of blessings and virtues,
and in sequence showed the compassion of equality.
Washing his feet manifested the merit of upholding precepts,
and spreading his seat was to quietly contemplate in meditation.
Thereafter, humans and gods looked up and surrounded him,
dragons and spirits respectfully and joyfully listened.
Xūpútí, possessing dignity, came forth from the assembly,
arranging his Dharma robe and raising his sincerity.
Wishing to initiate a discourse on non-form,
he then raised a question with doubts.
Thus, he was called "rare" by the disciples,
and praised with "excellent" by the Buddha.
Consequently, the profound gate was widely opened,
and the treasury of meaning greatly revealed.
Those who heard the Sūtra had their four minds not overturned,
their five eyes brightly shining,
and attained the four fruits.
They dispatched the three worthies of self and others,
and were able to wander in the eight right paths;
the four characteristics of self and others,
they understood their essence to be all empty,
and the six classes of sentient beings,
all returned to Nirvāṇa.
The giving in the beginning, middle, and end is not considered much,
the emptiness of the ten directions is immeasurable.
All forms are non-forms,
thus one sees the Rúlái's Dharmakāya;
birth is equal to no-birth,
thus one attains the equality of truth and illusion.
Thus, the seven treasures filling the great chiliocosm,
compared to the four lines, are entirely light;
sentient beings in the latter five defilements,
by a single hearing, surpass to a superior realm.
Thereafter, even the Dharma should be relinquished,
attachment to the raft would instead lead to sinking.
It merges self and other into emptiness of emptiness,
and obliterates right and wrong into wondrous existence.
Not stained by the realm of the six dusts,
one accords with Bódí.
Then, by searching within the six consciousnesses,
all phenomena are contained within Bōrě.
All Buddhas of the three ages,
are born from this Sūtra;
the most wondrous Bódí,
comes forth from this Sūtra.
Furthermore, it encompasses all teachings,
and is recognized as the essential guide among all Sūtras.
Its transmission and translation to Zhōngxià,
has been over several hundred years.
Although it has been recited and circulated,
and commentaries are numerous and varied,
there is still fear that its meaning might not accord with the sage's mind,
or its principle might deviate from the Middle Way.
I humbly consider our great Táng Hàn Holy Ruler, the Emperor Kāiyuán Tiānbǎo Shèngwén Shénwǔ Yìngdào Bìxià,
whose transforming influence surpasses a thousand ages,
and whose renown transcends a hundred kings.
His literary achievements encompass the subtleties of the five classics,
his military might breaks the spirits of the nine Yi tribes.
The eight directions are governed by his non-action transformation,
the four quarters sing praises of his Yáo and Shùn-like reign.
Furthermore, after the spread of his transforming influence,
he always greatly promoted the three teachings.
Sometimes he delved into Confucianism and Daoism,
exhausting their nature and exploring their origins;
he annotated and explained the Buddhist school,
making its phrases profound and its meaning far-reaching.
His sacred grace surges with the sea springs,
and his celestial palace shines as brightly as the sun and moon.
Daoism was thus revived,
and the Buddhist sun again radiated its light.
Above the precious groves,
the palm leaves joyfully bloomed in profusion;
in the garden of total retention,
the Dharma clouds generously moistened.
Now, regarding the title "Jīngāng Bōrě Bōluómì Jīng":
"Jīngāng" is used as a metaphor for firmness and sharpness,
"Bōrě" is named for wisdom,
"Bōluó" refers to the other shore,
reaching the vast name "Mìduō",
"Jīng" means to string together.
It is a model of good governance,
hence it is called "Jīngāng Bōrě Bōluómì Jīng".
The Great Awakened World Honored One, in the country of Shèwèi, in the garden of Jīshù Jǐgū,
proclaimed this Sūtra,
opening our secret treasury.
The four assemblies surrounded him,
immortals and spirits protected and supported him,
heaven rained four kinds of flowers,
and clouds cleared the eight realms.
This is indeed the wondrous power of the Rúlái,
which is difficult to express in words!
Xūdá was benevolent and kind,
fond of assisting the orphaned and poor,
hence he was named Jǐgū after his deeds.
He spread gold to buy land,
built a monastery,
invited the Buddha and welcomed monks,
hence his name is listed in the Sūtra.
Jītuó, seeing his reverence for the Dharma,
contributed trees for the shared construction,
and because the ruler is revered and the minister is less so,
their names are marked with a sequence.
The detailed account of these events
is narrated in the text below.
In the past, there was a great kingdom in Southern Tianzhú,
named Shèwèi Chéng.
Its king's might shook the nine heavens,
his fame spread across the eight directions.
Along its three borders, the waves of conflict subsided;
within its four frontiers, the dust of strife settled.
The wise prime minister, who assisted the state, was named Xūdáduō.
He was skilled in strategy,
and profoundly grasped the opportune moments of his era.
People called him a pillar of the state,
his virtue as weighty as salt and plums.
However, he always harbored heretical views,
and had not yet revered the Three Jewels.
He did not crave glory or position,
but delighted in diligent cultivation.
He had several children at home,
the youngest of whom was not yet married.
One day, during a festival,
he suddenly thought to himself: "My family lacks nothing now,
and is esteemed within the country.
My youngest son is not yet married,
it is fitting that he should marry in due course.
If there is no suitable match in our own country,
I will send envoys to seek one in a foreign land."
That day, he made arrangements at home,
and then ordered his treasury to be opened,
from which a thousand taels of gold were taken,
several jade rings,
soft brocade and light silk,
thousands of sheets and tens of thousands of bolts,
and a hundred strong elephants.
That day, they set out on their journey.
"You must proceed diligently and swiftly,
it is not advisable to delay even for a star-lit night.
Success is the limit,
do not begrudge resources.
As long as it pleases my son,
I will heavily reward you upon your return!"
After bidding farewell,
they acknowledged and departed immediately.
They traveled day and night,
and soon reached their destination.
As they walked through streets and alleys,
they listened attentively.
During their travels,
they happened upon Ānáan begging for food.
Having never seen such a sight in their lives,
they were extraordinarily astonished.
Holding his staff and alms-bowl,
he proclaimed his request for food in a clear voice.
Hùmí's family had long practiced the Ten Virtues,
and always personally welcomed Buddhist monks;
young and old alike,
all revered the Three Jewels.
Though the young lady lived in the inner chambers,
she suddenly heard the sound of begging for food.
With profound reverence,
she rushed out of the door,
prostrated herself with five limbs to the ground,
and gazed upon and saluted Ānáan.
She inquired about the diligent efforts of his path of transformation,
and requested the compassionate one's acceptance of her blessings.
The envoy saw her figure (as if) against a wall,
her appearance was peerless.
Xīshī could not compare to her divine grace,
and the beauty of the Luò Pǔ goddess could not equal her enchanting splendor.
He stared directly and carefully,
fearing to violate propriety;
then he slowly withdrew,
and gently asked a neighbor: "Whose house is this?
The trees are verdant and sparse,
in front stands a gate of valor,
and outside are long spears.
With its jeweled towers and precious pavilions,
it resembles a royal palace;
its singing-girls and ponds with terraces,
are quite different from an ordinary person's residence."
The neighbor replied: "Have you not heard of the Prime Minister who assists the state,
named Hùmí?
He assists in governing the court,
and receives a daily stipend of ten thousand coins.
Apart from the king,
he is the second most honored,
and in matters of state policy,
not an inch is discussed without his counsel."
Upon hearing this, the envoy
was startled and awed in his heart.
He again asked the neighbor: "I am very fortunate
to meet such a virtuous person.
I wonder how many children the Prime Minister has?
I am a guest from a distant land,
sent here on a mission;
you too must not refuse a brief stay,
and please tell me about the Prime Minister's family, even if briefly."
The neighbor replied: "The Prime Minister has three daughters in total:
two are already married to imperial grandsons,
and one is currently unmarried.
Her beautiful appearance
is unparalleled in the country;
her demeanor and pure conduct
are unique in all ages.
Upon hearing these words, the envoy
was overcome with joy and comfort.
He immediately sought an audience,
and presented a written letter.
After the envoy was granted an audience,
he bowed in salutation.
He had not yet expressed his innermost feelings,
but first exchanged pleasantries about the weather.
The host and guest observed courtesies,
holding gatherings for several mornings;
but the proposal of marriage
had not yet been accepted.
One night, the elder (Hùmí's father),
young and old alike, were in a flurry,
sweeping and cleaning the halls,
and repairing the courtyards,
adorning them with fragrant mud,
and exquisite, rare ornaments.
Banners hung around every courtyard wall,
and every room was covered with felt carpets.
The elder (Xūdá) saw him rise early,
unable to sleep;
and also saw the exquisite furnishings.
He asked in surprise: "Is it for a family gathering?
Or are you inviting an emperor?
Why are young and old in such a hurry,
making such beautiful arrangements?"
The elder replied: "I am not preparing for a gathering,
nor am I inviting an emperor.
I intend to invite the Buddha and monks,
to offer them devotedly."
Xūdáduō, having good habits from birth,
had once been close to Buddhist monks.
Suddenly hearing the name of the Buddha,
sweat poured from his body.
Xūdá said: "What divine wonder does the Buddha possess?
What virtue and ability do the monks have?
That upon hearing their name,
I am covered in sweat and tremble.
Where do they reside?
Please tell me the details.
I regret having followed a false path for so long,
and not knowing the true way.
Now I deeply thirst for knowledge,
I wish you to explain the origin."
Hùmí said: "The Buddha is not an ordinary person,
he is the prince of King Jìngfàn from Kāpíluó Chéng.
His ancestors successively
ruled with the golden wheel for a thousand generations;
his lineage is honored through generations,
a true descendant of the phoenix.
" Hearing this, Xūdá
was astonished and awed in his heart.
His fervent longing
remained deep within him.
He wished to visit the place,
to behold the revered countenance.
Hùmí replied to the elder: "The Buddha is not far now,
he is right here in Qíshéjué Shān,
commanding the eight classes of nāgas and devas,
expounding the principles of the three vehicles.
Tonight is already late,
it will not be too late to go tomorrow morning."
The elder, hearing of the Buddha's virtues and abilities,
could not sleep.
With sincere longing and reverence,
he focused his thoughts on the compassionate revered one.
The Tathāgata, observing this deep devotion,
then emitted a brilliant light that illuminated everything,
the heavens and earth became clearly visible,
like the overflowing radiance of a thousand suns.
Xūdá suddenly saw the bright light,
and thought it was dawn.
He followed the light directly to the city gate,
but the gate was not yet open.
Xūdá then knew of the power,
and his reverence increased greatly.
Thinking of the Tathāgata,
he sighed and lamented:
"High towers and lofty double gates,
the path is blocked on this clear night, preventing passage.
I long to see the revered countenance but cannot,
I hesitate and gaze, unable to reach.
I always regret living in a land of heretical views,
not yet touched by the wisdom-pestle to crush the mountain of evil.
May the compassionate revered one guide me,
I sincerely gaze and salute the revered countenance."
Sudá’s lamentation was complete.
The Tathāgata’s divine ear heard it from afar,
and He knew his thoughts immediately.
Ten thousand *lǐ* offered no obstruction.
He again emitted divine light, shining brightly,
and the city gate suddenly opened by itself.
When Sudá saw the gate open,
he followed the light directly to the Buddha’s abode.
He circumambulated dozens of times,
exhausting his utmost sincerity,
focusing his gaze on the Venerable Face.
How can the mixture of sorrow and joy he felt be described?
Sudá, enlightened by the Buddha,
shed thousands of lines of tears from his eyes.
“Your disciple has lived in the land of wrong views,
accumulating sins all day, serving the demon king.
I humbly pray, Heavenly Master, accept my invitation,
and bestow blessings upon Śāyé for a bridge.”
The Buddha knew that his good roots were ripe,
making him capable of transformation and easy to guide.
So, He immediately agreed to his request and complied,
accepting his earnest invitation.
He called out, “Elder!
I am the Lord of the Three Realms,
the most supreme and most honored.
My movements are calm and dignified,
attended by *tiānlóng*.
Brahmā is on my left,
and Indrā leads the way.
Heavenly *xiān* fill the sky,
and the four assemblies rush like clouds to the roads.
It is necessary to extensively build halls and stupas,
and erect many *tángfáng*.
My disciples are numerous now,
and their living space is cramped.
You, too, have long been a teacher of external paths,
unfamiliar with the rules and rituals.
Let my Śarìfú accompany you,
and ask him about the methods one by one.”
Having received the invitation,
and moreover having the saint accompany him,
Sudá immediately selected two strong elephants,
on which he placed pavilions.
Not many days passed before
they arrived at the city of Śāyé.
He then accompanied the saint,
inspecting the land for a *jiālán*.
First, they went east of the city,
where he saw a garden from afar,
with abundant flowers and fruits, and very fine ponds and pavilions.
Sudá brandished his whip forward,
and said to the *Héshang*, “Is this garden suitable?”
Śarìfú said, “Elder,
although the garden is good,
there is too much garlic;
its stench permeates the sky,
making it unsuitable for saints and sages to reside.”
Sudá turned the elephant around,
returning to the west of the city.
He suddenly saw a garden,
whose woods were far superior to the previous one.
Sudá composed himself, clasped his hands,
and said to the *Héshang*, “Since you said the previous one was unsuitable,
is this garden suitable for habitation?”
Śarìfú said, “Elder,
this place was once a horse market,
where living beings were slaughtered.
The foul smell and blood make it truly unsuitable for habitation.”
He reined in the carriage and traveled to the north of the city.
He saw another garden,
with lush and vigorous woods.
He said to the *Héshang*, “Is this garden suitable?”
Śarìfú said, “Elder,
although the garden is good,
and the woods are sprawling,
there are many wine shops and rooms for prostitution,
which foster the dullness of living beings
and nourish the root source of the sea of suffering.
