This place is unsuitable;
you must choose another.”
The Elder inspected three places,
and the Venerable one all said they were unsuitable.
Did the Buddha have no connection with this place,
or were there many karmic obstructions from past lives?
Sudá became embarrassed and fidgety,
pacing aimlessly beyond his usual manner.
Annoyed and resentful, he turned the carriage around
and went out to inspect the south of the city.
Not too close, nor too far from the city,
prominently situated on the thoroughfare,
he suddenly saw a garden,
whose bamboo and trees were extraordinarily luxuriant.
In the three springs and nine summers,
the scenery was fresh and fragrant;
in winter and early autumn,
the remaining flowers were luxuriant.
The grass was verdant and sprouted green,
and the flowers glowed and opened red.
There were a thousand kinds of ponds and pavilions,
and ten thousand varieties of fruits and medicines.
Fragrances wafted to the nose,
and birds chirped in harmony.
The trees swayed, proclaiming the name of the Three Jewels,
and the divine bell vibrated with the sound of ending suffering.
Auspicious *luán* and propitious *fèng* vied to display the splendor of their brocade feathers;
jade maidens and immortal youths competed to play the music of eternal life.
When the Elder saw this garden,
it deeply pleased his heart.
So, he composed himself,
and said to the *Héshang*, “The previous three places,
you all said were unsuitable.
Is this garden now
to your liking?”
Śarìfú said, “Elder,
I have achieved a small fruit,
and my spiritual power is humble.
I must enter *dìng* to observe it,
then I can know its good or bad qualities.”
Śarìfú collected his mind and entered *dìng*,
concentrating for a moment.
He observed this garden,
finding it to be entirely without fault.
Past Buddhas, hundreds of thousands of them,
had all resided therein,
expounding the Dharma and saving people,
their numbers like dust and sand.
When Śarìfú saw this,
his body and mind rejoiced.
He smiled and relaxed his countenance,
and reported to the Elder, “This garden is not only suitable for my Teacher to reside in this life,
but also the thousand Tathāgatas of the Auspicious Kalpa
have all resided here.
It is the most auspicious and supreme,
with none superior.
To build a *jiālán*,
only this land is needed.”
Śarìfú and the Elder discussed the place:
The Elder, having received the saint’s protection,
had all his deluded thoughts enlightened.
Śarìfú accompanied him to build the *dàocháng*,
intending to invite the Tathāgata to expound the four sentences.
He surveyed three sides of the city, finding them unsuitable for habitation,
and the Elder was annoyed and hesitant.
Riding the elephant, he pondered and moved forward,
suddenly seeing a garden with luxuriant flowers and fruits.
Sudá and Śarìfú rode white elephants,
heading towards the south of the city to look around.
Suddenly, they saw thousands of precious trees,
whose flowers bloomed in extraordinary colors, unequalled.
Auspicious clouds and propitious canopies filled the sky,
and white *fèng* and green *luán* soared in the air.
Sudá sighed in admiration at its rarity,
gazing at the venerable face and asking the *Héshang*.
Śarìfú turned his head and reported to Sudá, “This garden is wonderfully beautiful and rarely encountered.
A sacred bell appears among the trees,
and heavenly *xiān* in the air hold offerings.
Past Buddhas first dwelt here,
extensively saving countless sentient beings.
It is clear that the saint’s power is inconceivable;
this is the place where the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma.”
Sudá was very surprised and doubtful to hear this: “This garden is rare in the country.
I do not know who its original owner is,
how can I buy it with a hundred schemes?
Everyone loves good things in the world,
and it is very difficult to find someone who will not sell.”
For a long time, he was lost in thought and unhappy,
his heart anxious and embarrassed.
He called a gardener and asked, “Who is the current owner of this garden?
I have urgent business and must see him;
tell me quickly, do not delay.”
The gardener clasped his hands and explained in detail, “The garden owner is rich and noble, not to be treated lightly.
He is currently the Crown Prince of the Eastern Palace,
coming daily to oversee it himself.
He hasn't been to the garden for three or four days,
so it has been extensively adorned, more splendid than usual.
Elder, if you wish to know the garden owner,
he is the son of the King of Bōsī!”
Sū-Dá (須達) asked the Heshàng (和尚): "Is this park suitable?"
Shè-Lì-Fú (舍利弗) said to the zhǎngzhě (長者): "This park is not only loved by my original teacher, Shì-Jiā-Móu-Ní (釋迦牟尼),
but also by countless Buddhas of the past,
who resided here.
People with heavy defilements,
when treading this ground, become pure.
Divine bells and celestial music,
ring constantly without being struck;
exotic fragrances and celestial flowers,
compete in a chaotic shower.
Heshàng (和尚) should return to your place,
while this disciple will temporarily go to the Eastern Palace,
to inquire with due禮儀 (lǐyí) and investigate,
to see if it can be acquired.
If they are willing to sell,
we will not dispute the price, high or low;
if there's a stubborn refusal,
we must ingeniously break it down.
With a thousand stratagems and ten thousand schemes,
we must not rest until it is done."
Sū-Dá (須達) bid farewell and immediately set off,
heading straight to the gate of the Eastern Palace.
He entered at an unusual hour,
and went directly to see the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince, seeing the important minister from afar,
immediately descended the steps to greet him.
The Crown Prince said: "You are an important minister who aids the nation,
always serving my monarch.
For what urgent matter,
do you suddenly appear before this solitary one at an unusual hour?"
Sū-Dá (須達) wished to speak plainly,
but found it a little difficult to begin.
So he temporarily devised a cunning speech,
and replied to the Crown Prince: "Yesterday, while on my way,
I happened to pass by the Crown Prince's park.
From afar, I saw strange disasters arising,
and flocks of strange birds crying.
I reined in my horse to observe,
and suddenly felt my heart and spirit tremble.
The ponds and pavilions were parched,
and the flowers and fruits withered and sparse.
If the Crown Prince does not believe my words,
send an envoy to observe the truth."
The Crown Prince heard these words,
but was not greatly alarmed.
"This solitary one bought this park myself,
and it has been many years.
In the three springs, the soft willows
are verdant and their branches droop;
in the nine summers, famous flowers
illuminate the ponds and pavilions.
It is fully capable of dispelling sorrow and releasing闷 (mèn),
gladdening the heart and spirit.
Now you suddenly utter such words,
are you not speaking falsely?"
Sū-Dá (須達) straightened his attire,
and addressed the Crown Prince: "The Crown Prince is supremely noble and revered,
the heir apparent of the nation.
Your humble servant attends the imperial steps,
a pillar of the royal house.
How can one be so slanderous,
or speak such falsehoods?
If there is the slightest discrepancy,
can your servant survive?
If the Crown Prince does not believe,
come personally to observe,
verify the truth,
and demonstrate your foolish servant's loyalty."
The Crown Prince said: "You are a loyal minister,
you should not speak falsely;
if this matter is truly so,
how can we ward off the evil?"
Sū-Dá (須達) replied to the Crown Prince: "If things are acting strangely,
they must be resold to another person.
The Crown Prince should post notices at the four gates,
stating that the park is for sale.
The mouths of the multitude can melt metal,
and disaster and good fortune will naturally dissipate.
If someone intends to buy,
ask a high price: let the ground be covered with gold,
and the tree branches be full of silver coins.
People in the world value treasures,
so there will surely be no one willing to buy."
The Crown Prince heard these words,
agreed and assented,
and on that day, notices were posted,
at the four gates of the city.
Sū-Dá's (須達) secret plan accomplished,
he then bid farewell to the Crown Prince.
He then took down the notices
from the four gates,
and went straight into the Eastern Palace,
to see the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince was displeased by this matter,
mounted his horse and left the city,
to observe it personally.
Accompanied by Sū-Dá (須達),
he went directly to the park.
He looked around,
and it was no different from before;
he observed from all four sides,
and there was no abnormality.
He inquired of the park overseers,
and there were no changes at all.
The Crown Prince then became angry,
and sternly reprimanded Minister Sū-Dá (須達): "You should now be planning for the state,
or intending to conspire with foreign nations,
instigating discord between ruler and minister,
estranging father and son,
bringing ruin to home and nation—
this too must be due to you!
A gentleman,
at home, fulfills filial piety;
serving the nation, fulfills loyalty;
establishes himself with respect and caution;
and abides by laws and regulations.
Thus he preserves his emolument and position,
and finishes his rich and noble life.
How can a minister be disloyal,
speak with loss of integrity,
not only bringing disaster upon himself,
but also disgracing his ancestors?
I will report to His Majesty for his grace,
and make it so you have no place to hide your body.
Rise or fall, honor or disgrace,
are merely a matter of a breath.
Though face to face, it is like a thousand li,
occupying an honorable position,
yet eating the emoluments in vain—
you are now such a one!
I must report to the Heavenly Court,
and your body shall suffer ten thousand executions!"
At that time, acting for the Dharma against his feelings,
not fearing the loss of his body and life,
the ruler and minister both contended,
each intending to see the King.
The Shǒu-Tuó Heavenly King (首陀天王), hearing their words from the sky,
thought to himself: "If I do not advise these people,
this good deed will surely encounter obstacles."
Concealing his celestial form,
he transformed into an old man,
with crane-white beard and eyebrows,
leaning on a frail staff in his hand,
and directly rushed before the Crown Prince's horse,
raising his voice and shouting: "Stop,
young master!
Good and evil have their reasons,
why the clamor and dispute?
Superior and inferior have their etiquette,
noble and humble must maintain their decorum.
How can you block streets and intercept alleys,
puffed up with anger and shouting loudly!
Each state your original intention,
and the matter must be judged according to truth.
The Son of Heaven still served the Three Elders;
in ancient times, the elders were supported and their words sought.
Do not falsely concoct empty words,
disturbing the public office.
I, this old man, will judge fairly,
and hope for a decision free of bias."
The Crown Prince dismounted,
angered by the deception,
and fully recounted the origin,
complaining to the old man;
The old man heard his account,
and sternly reprimanded Minister Sū-Dá (須達),
listing a thousand kinds of wrongs,
and hundreds of kinds of faults.
With glaring eyes and angry gaze,
he shouted at Minister Sū-Dá (須達),
to appease the Crown Prince's anger,
and remove the obstacles for the good deed. As for the situation:
The Crown Prince, seeing no disaster or怪 (guài) in the park,
immediately knew Sū-Dá (須達) had spoken falsely.
"You are a loyal minister who speaks falsehoods,
cleverly maneuvering to take my park.
I will submit a memorial to the King for action,
and you will be cut in half instantly, your life incomplete."
While the two were disputing and their words unfinished,
Shǒu-Tuó Heaven (首陀天) suddenly appeared midway.
On his face were a thousand wrinkles of red,
and cold tears like springs in his eyes.
Supporting himself with a thousand-year-old靈壽 (língshòu) staff,
he tottered forward to meet the Crown Prince.
"This is the Crown Prince's banquet place,
close by, near the imperial countenance.
Gentlemen should truly unite and contend in virtue,
the wise do not need to make loud noises.
Tell all your affairs to this old man,
and I will judge fairly, without bias."
The Crown Prince cupped his hands and addressed the elder: "Please listen for a moment, no need to be angry.
This solitary one holds the position of Crown Prince,
and half a retinue always accompanies me.
Minister Sū-Dá (須達) is short-sighted and foolish,
not upholding the righteousness between superior and inferior, ruler and minister.
Baselessly devising deceitful schemes and secret plots,
he cleverly intends to usurp the nation."
“I humbly wish that you, elder, would observe and examine!
Who does not idly speak of calamities and good omens?”
The elder heard this and, suppressing his voice, glared: “Recently I heard that you are a loyal minister,
but your words are inconsistent and unreliable.
You idly hold the position of a state minister, governing ordinary people.
Why bother to speak vaguely of calamities and omens arising?
Your fraudulent intentions are impure.
According to this, your crime is hard to forgive;
the king will know and have you cut in half and reduced to dust.”
The elder, with a gentle expression, said to the Crown Prince: “The lord of men should not utter two different statements.
It is better to set a high price that is hard to meet,
than to say it will be sold and then not sell, going against people’s wishes.
I, an elder, have seen many things,
and I give straightforward advice to ensure fairness.
From now on, let us be harmonious and not argue,
that lord and minister may serve each other well.”
Sūdá said to the elder: “Can one hand clap alone?
Two hands striking each other produce sound.
One word can destroy a nation;
the error lies within a hair’s breadth.
In ancient times, a promise given by a single word
was held dearer than a thousand pieces of gold and would not be changed.
Uttering words is easier than turning one’s palm,
but retracting them is harder than pulling up a mountain.
How can one’s initial words not match one’s later words!
The Crown Prince put out a notice,
saying he would sell the garden,
but when the notice was taken down and discussed,
he immediately said he would not sell it.”
The elder’s original intention was
to favor Sūdá, the great minister.
However, to accommodate the Crown Prince’s wishes,
he gnashed his teeth and feigned anger at Sūdá.
Sūdá felt flustered and anxious,
and withdrew several steps.
Then he bowed to the Emperor’s son and stepped forward: “Although I, an old man, am a subject,
I am not yet at the age of 'smooth hearing' (age sixty).
A gentleman serves diligently from the fifth watch of the night,
and the Master inquired at the Grand Ancestral Temple.
A family depends on its eldest son,
and a nation relies on loyal ministers.
A boat travels because of water,
and lips and teeth depend on each other.
If the lips are parted and the teeth exposed,
and the water dries up, the boat stops.
If there is a lord without ministers,
on what can the nation depend to stand firm?
Knowing that I might inadvertently cause offense,
it is best to comply and resolve things privately.
A harmonious family can raise silkworms in winter;
all actions, whether advancing or retreating, must be done with propriety.
The Crown Prince’s garden must be vast
with dense trees.
To cover the ground with gold,
and to have tree branches laden with silver coins,
even if one emptied all granaries and treasuries,
there would surely be no time when someone would be willing to buy it.
If the transaction does not go through,
the garden will remain his.”
The Crown Prince heard these words,
and immediately followed the instructions.
He then turned to Sūdá, the great minister,
and demanded this high price.
Sūdá promptly complied,
without any hesitation regarding the price.
They discussed the matter face-to-face on the spot,
and immediately drew up a contract.
Many guarantors were added,
and heavy penalties for breach were set.
Fearing that the Crown Prince might change his mind,
and that his initial desire would not be fulfilled.
Immediately, he opened the treasury
and brought out purple-gold.
One hundred strong elephants were selected,
to carry and transport it immediately.
Blessed by the power of the sages,
it quickly spread everywhere.
Only a few remaining steps
were left to be completely covered.
See how the gold was spread:
Sūdá, having received the elder’s judgment,
knew he was speaking from his true heart with a gentle expression.
He immediately selected strong elephants from the herd,
opened the treasury, and purely loaded purple-gold.
Steep peaks and high mountains were all covered,
exactly spread so no needle could penetrate.
All family members, noble and humble,
chanted the sound of Mahāprajñā.
In an instant, it was all spread;
the power of the sages is indeed profound.
As Sūdá was about to finish spreading the gold,
the remaining work was not much.
He pondered anxiously in his heart,
considering which treasury to open next.
While he hesitated,
the Crown Prince became suspicious,
and said to the elder: “You are hesitant;
it is not too late to regret.
Why do you pause
after beginning the work?”
Sūdá replied: “Even if my flesh and body were spread on the ground,
I would not shirk the labor;
how much less would I begrudge
a small amount of wealth before the Buddha!
The era of the Buddha is hard to encounter,
appearing once in many eons.
If I do not earnestly and sincerely exert myself,
what good will regret do later?”
The Crown Prince said: “You now treat wealth as dirt,
and value virtue as a treasure.
With such determination to buy the garden,
what do you intend to use it for?”
Sūdá replied: “What I am buying now
has another purpose.
Yesterday, through the fortuitous occasion of a marriage,
I met the Great Sage.
His father is named Śuddhodana,
his mother, Māyā.
He awakened by himself,
without a teacher among humans or gods,
excellently known as a Pratyekabuddha.
His body is sixteen feet tall,
with a halo around his head and back,
like the radiance of a thousand suns,
difficult to compare.
He can also shake heaven and earth,
making all beings peaceful.
He can move mountains and rivers,
without the appearance of movement;
he can swallow wind and inhale fire,
without harming a single hair.
When danger approaches,
invoking his name makes it dissipate immediately.
I have only roughly described his virtues,
speaking briefly.
To extensively praise the Great Sage’s abilities
would be impossible even over countless eons.”
The Crown Prince heard this,
and sweat streamed down.
“If there are such magnificent virtues,
I, the lonely one, deeply wish to prostrate myself.
For the remaining uncovered area,
please stop the work;
the silver coins on the trees,
I, the lonely one, will also offer.”
The lord sang and the minister harmonized,
elegantly conforming to the principle of propriety;
seeing worthiness, one aspires to emulate it,
which aligns with the teachings of the ancient sages.
With one heart and one mind,
they jointly built a monastery (saṅghārāma).
Is this not like boats depending on water,
and neighboring boats helping each other across?
Having finished pondering,
they immediately accompanied Śāriputra,
walking east and west,
and surveying north and south.
Suddenly, they saw a nest of ants,
crawling all over the ground in countless numbers.
Their number was unknown.
Śāriputra saw these ants,
smiled and brightened his countenance,
and to Sūdá and Jìtuó, explained the past cause:
Sūdá bought the Crown Prince’s garden,
his body and mind overjoyed beyond measure.
He immediately invited Śāriputra into the garden,
to measure and survey the land.
As they had not fully completed their circuit east and west,
they suddenly encountered a nest of ants.
Śāriputra turned and said to Sūdá: “Observe these beings of evil karma!
When Vipassī Buddha appeared,
they were already born here in ant bodies.
Today they again meet Śākyamuni;
this time, their evil karma should be discarded.
Grant them the Ten Precepts and the Three Refuges,
and bestow upon them the sweet dew water of Bodhi.
From this point forward, they will depart forever,
and be reborn among the multitudes of devas.”
The elder resolved to build a monastery,
with lecture halls and courtyards all fully equipped.
The joyous sounds boomed in the Tuṣita Heaven,
as he saw his body being born there from afar.
Having finished spreading the gold, he looked up with devotion,
and urgently needed to construct the monastery’s design.
Not sparing treasures, gold, and silver,
he issued a proclamation inviting all skilled artisans in the country.
Beneath the three-gate tower, Vajra guardians were sculpted,
and in every courtyard, paintings were commissioned.
The side halls, hermitages, and corridors,
when seen, could also remove calamities and obstacles.
Zithers and lutes were hung in the four corners,
the wind blowing through them produced myriad bright sounds.
There were also flutes, vertical flutes, and konghous,
with copper cymbals and pipa responding in harmony.
The high seat for expounding the Dharma was splendidly adorned with jewels,
and incense made from sandalwood was burned as an offering.
Nine grades of rebirth according to vows,
with Kālaviṅkas soaring in the sky.
The elder, with devout heart, built the pure dwelling,
while all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas watched from the sky.
Prince Jìtuó made a grand vow,
wishing for the Bodhi sprout to gradually grow.
Once Sūdá had finished purchasing the garden,
he and the Prince then returned.
Suddenly, along the way,
they encountered the six heterodox teachers.
Before asking for details,
they angrily retorted at first sight: "The Prince, as the heir apparent of a nation,
should have a retinue of half an army when traveling;
the elder, honored as prime minister,
is a minister who supports the nation and aids in governance.
How can you disgrace the nation and debase yourselves,
with no more than ten attendants on horseback?
Though Yáo's rafters were unhewn,
it was to proclaim a name for frugality;
though Shùn's pots lacked a meaty smell,
it was to curb the affliction of extravagance.
Moreover, long sashes and wide sleeves
still form the prestige of a strong nation;
golden pillars and jade steps
display the nobility of former kings.
This is recorded in the *Shī Jīng* and *Shū Jīng*,
not something I claim from my own mind.
Why are you traveling so hastily,
lightly, with only one rider?
Is it perhaps to conspire against the state?
Or do you have other intentions?
This matter must be recorded in a memorial and presented to the King,
for him to decide and understand its meaning."
Let's see how the reasons for the interrogation were put forth:
"The Prince is the second noblest in the nation;
his comings and goings must be regulated by all officials.
Why do you have no more than ten attendants,
spurring your reins to arrive here on the road?
Tell me honestly and clearly,
do not hide or refuse anything, good or bad."
The Prince dismounted and reported to the respected teachers: "You do not know that Sūdá bought a garden.
We intend to invite the Tathāgata here to preach the Dharma,
as I, your humble servant, sincerely admire and wish to take refuge.
We have just finished the act of 'spreading gold,'
and that is why we are now returning.
Every word of this is true,
I reveal my heart and liver, hoping you will understand."
The six teachers heard these words and laughed incessantly,
"Gū Tán's illusions are hard to compare!
He uses sweet words and honeyed tongues to deceive people,
and his mother died seven days after his birth.
He could not bear to sit in a jade palace or a pearl tower,
and abandoned his father to flee into the deep mountains.
The words he utters are called sūtras,
and he boasts that his body is golden and exceptionally unique.
If he comes to this country, he will harm ordinary people;
we must not open our eyes and step (stab) heedlessly.
Tomorrow morning, we shall prepare a memorial to the ruler,
and both gains and losses must be tested before His Majesty.
How can the trivial stream from a cow's nose
be compared to our ocean waters!"
When the six teachers heard the Buddha was invited to reside there,
anger arose in their hearts,
their cheeks swelled high,
their brows furrowed fiercely,
their teeth gnashed and clamped,
utterly grim and bitter.
"I would rather die once
than live a second time in vain.
All my disciples have been led astray,
leaving me no path to survival.
Everywhere I go, I am bullied,
all day long, he is made the ancestor.
Even emperors lower themselves to him,
let alone common folk and the lower classes.
How can I voice my present grievances?
I must go to the King and lay out my case."
The six teachers hurried,
striding roughly and swiftly,
rushing to the dragon court,
beating their drum of grievance.
The King sent his officials
to inquire into the origin.
The six teachers choked, their voices hoarse,
and for a long time they were silent, deep in thought.
They then spoke to the Great King: "Your servant has heard that since the creation of heaven and earth,
there have been rulers and ministers.
The sun and moon shine brightly,
relying on the transforming influence of the sagely ruler.
Now, the eight directions are earnestly respectful,
and guests from the four seas arrive.
But there are disloyal sons and treacherous ministers
who seek to conspire against the King's governance,
harboring wickedness and embracing flattery,
disregarding public opinion.
They shamelessly enjoy the honor of prime minister,
and consume a salary of ten thousand *zhōng* in vain.
Your servant has heard that treacherous ministers destroyed six states,
and treacherous women caused strife among six relatives;
Sūdá and Jìtuó
are exactly such today.
How can it be that without even being heard in the Heavenly Court,
they entice a 'Hu god' from a foreign land?
They delude ordinary people,
calling themselves 'Buddha.'
They are unfilial to their parents,
constantly violating the grace of caring for them.
They are disrespectful to the King,
contravening the etiquette of ministers.
They are not diligent in their livelihood,
and shave people's heads whenever they meet them.
They falsely speak of hell and heaven,
but when sought, no one has seen them.
If they come here,
we fear they will harm the nation and ruin families.
Your servant now reveals his heart and liver,
humbly hoping for Your Sacred Grace to examine and understand."
Let's see how the accusations against the Tathāgata were put forth:
"The King's Prince is the most honored in the nation;
how can he bring in a 'Hu god' from a foreign land?
The treacherous minister Sūdá is the ringleader,
inciting evil and falsehood to disturb what is upright and true.
It is precisely because Gū Tán has many illusions,
that he is disloyal and unfilial to the ruler.
He does not pay homage to the King or bow to his parents,
but instead belittles the noble and reveres the foolish.
I humbly pray, Great King, to open your precious mirror,
and let its light shine upon your servant today for examination."
The six teachers pleaded their case again,
hunching their backs, bowing low, and lowering their heads:
"The supernatural powers we have acquired
have accumulated over many years and long seasons.
Our spiritual manifestations are myriad;
the whole nation knows our skill.
Remembering my achievements,
each one learned from my teacher.
Your humble servant now reports to the King,
especially hoping for heavenly grace and protection."
The six teachers again presented to the King, saying: "Your servant now has something to state truthfully.
The treacherous minister and rebellious son are plotting an insidious scheme;
I fear the nation will be destroyed and its people perish.
Sūdá's original intention was to invite a 'Hu god,'
planning to extensively spread evil (calamity) in the city.
They destroy our righteous Dharma in an inconceivable way,
inviting extremely base and wicked outsiders from afar.
This is vulgar and despicable, not to be relied upon;
humbly hoping the enlightened ruler will examine it."
The King said: "Reverend masters,
please listen carefully and consider,
there is no need to be hasty.
I will inquire into the origins
and investigate the facts of the matter.
If there is any error or neglect,
both of you will together suffer ten thousand punishments."
The King's officials
arrested Sūdá
and Prince Jìtuó,
and encircled them with a living staff.
Let's see how the questioning about the reasons at the execution ground proceeded:
The King asked: "Sūdá, for what reason
did you arbitrarily buy a garden to make it into a temple?
You plan to invite Gū Tán here,
but the six teachers say it will bring disaster.
I am in the deep palace and know nothing of this;
you must explain fully without any concealment.
How does Gū Tán compare to (my) six teachers?
Choosing the good and acting upon it should be a good thing."
The Emperor sat in the Lílī hall,
his hands folded, facing south, guarding the center.
Eloquent literati discussed yin and yang,
while valiant warriors held precious fans.
Sūdá was captured and asked about the origin: "Why have I not seen you for several days?
I also heard you brought a 'Hu god' from a foreign land;
I reckon your crimes are unforgivable."
Sūdá pleaded his case and reported: "Your servant has served at the jade steps for many years.
I have always been cautious, pouring out my heart and liver,
never committing even an inch of falsehood.
If you compare the heterodox teachers with the Tathāgata,
it is like comparing good grain to weeds.
The Buddha's body is magnificent, sixteen feet tall,
while the heterodox teachers are like tiny fireflies.
The four great oceans can be contained in a hair's tip,
and five-colored divine light issues from his mouth.
Brahmā and Śakra always lead the way,
and the eight divisions of dragon spirits all follow behind.
How can a mere sweating shrimp
dare to contend with the great sage Qílín in battle!"
The king heard the praise,
but had not yet ascertained its origin.
He then called Sū-dá forward: "You must investigate thoroughly,
and not make any mistake.
Honor and disgrace, ascent and decline,
all hang in the balance at this very moment.
I am the lord of a nation,
governing myriad states.
You must exhaust your loyalty and devotion;
you must not be complacent and change your mind.
When the Son of Heaven is enraged,
a million corpses can be laid low,
and blood can flow for a thousand *lǐ*.
What lineage does this Fó belong to?
Did he have any family in previous generations?
Who did he consult and learn the Dao from?
What virtues and morals does he possess?
Do not conceal anything,
tell me the full truth.
If there is even a slight discrepancy,
you will be dealt with according to the law by my hand."
Sū-dá respectfully replied to His Majesty: "In the past lives of the Rú-lái,
he has appeared as a thousand Wheel-Turning Kings.
His lineage has been continuously passed down,
with honor and glory never ceasing.
From his ancestors to his father,
all held the esteemed position of a myriad-chariot ruler.
His noble sons and distant descendants
are all renowned as true scions of the phoenix.
His father is known as Jìng-fàn,
the most revered among the eight nations.
His mother is named Mó-yé,
peerless in the [five] heavens.
The Rú-lái was born in the Southern Tiān-zhú Kingdom,
and grew up in Jiā-pí-luó City.
From birth to death,
from death to rebirth,
there was nothing he did not do,
nothing he did not accomplish,
nothing he did not experience,
nothing he did not pass through.
He grew up in Jìng-fàn-wáng's palace,
known by the name Xī-dá.
When he was past nineteen,
he understood life and death.
Before he was twenty,
he leaped over the palace walls.
Beneath the Pú-tí tree,
he remained untainted by worldly affections,
diligently toiled for years,
and wasted away his form.
He ate sesame and wheat daily,
barely sustaining his life.
Birds nested on his head,
and successfully raised their young.
His head was like a messy nest,
his neck like a needle.
His ribs were like the rafters of a decaying house,
his eyes like stars at the bottom of a well.
His body was emaciated and weak,
resembling a hungry ghost.
Through accumulated merit and virtue,
he achieved the Pú-tí Dao.
His body was one *zhàng* and six *chǐ* tall,
with a radiant halo around his head and back.
A myriad-character symbol was on his chest,
clearly visible.
He had a broad and long tongue,
and a broad and flat forehead.
He had the chest of a lion king,
and hair that curled clockwise.
The Rú-lái attains Ní-pán but does not die,
and attains Pán but is not born.
Stirred, he is not turbid;
clarified, he is pure.
Obscured, he is not dark;
darkened, he is bright.
Looked at, his form cannot be seen;
listened to, his voice cannot be heard.
He is high but not perilous,
low but not unstable.
He can transform rivers and seas into *sū-lào* (ghee and cream),
and turn the great earth into crystal and glass.
He can pick up Mount Xū-mí and know its weight,
and chop the four seas into dry pits.
With eyes closed, he travels ten thousand *lǐ*;
with eyes open, he stops instantly.
He can manifest a great body that pervades the world,
or manifest a small body,
hiding his form within a speck of dust.
The Rú-lái, when cut with a knife, does not bear resentment;
when medicine is applied, he does not fuss.
He does not rejoice when he finds something,
nor does he weep when he loses something.
He does not feel disturbance in a crowd,
nor does he feel lonely when sitting alone.
His two minds are one and the same,
equal and indistinguishable.
He can manifest a hundred billion *fēn-shēn* (manifested bodies),
and partake in meals everywhere.
His first name is Xī-dá,
his second title is Rú-lái.
He is the teacher of gods and humans,
possessing all wisdom.
Among the four births and three realms,
he is the most excellent and most revered.
I have only briefly described his abilities;
even after countless eons of praise, they would not be exhausted.
Your Majesty!"
The king heard these words
and was overwhelmed with joy.
"Although you have praised these abilities,
you have not yet proven their truthfulness.
It is necessary to test them face-to-face,
then their right and wrong can be determined.
Can your teacher
compete with my Ho-shàng or not?"
Sū-dá respectfully replied to His Majesty: "A crossbow of a thousand *jūn*
[should not] be triggered for a tiny mouse.
A hundred-foot blazing furnace
should not be used to ignite a single hair.
There is no need for our great Sànt-tiān-shī;
even the smallest disciple
can easily compete."
The king asked: "Who is this disciple
who can compete with my Ho-shàng?"
Sū-dá respectfully replied to the Great King: "The Fó's disciple
is none other than
Shè-lì-fú."
The king said: "Shè-lì-fú
is my Ho-shàng's nephew.
He only recently left home to become a monk,
and his study of the dharma is still shallow.
Calculating his accumulated practice,
not much time has passed.
The old and young cannot stand shoulder to shoulder;
how can he compete with my Ho-shàng!"
"Although Yàn Yīng was small,
he could scheme against ministers like tigers and wolves.
Virtue does not depend on old age;
without wisdom, a hundred years are spent in vain.
Rather than fabricating falsehoods,
it is better to verify them for the truth.
Gold, refined a hundred times,
becomes even more radiant;
*qiān-xī* (lead and tin), put into a furnace,
instantly turns into ashes.
I humbly hope for your clear declaration,
issuing an edict for a grand assembly.
Announce it to all officials,
and let a great contest be observed,
then the victor can be determined.
If the Six Teachers win,
your servant shall be executed a myriad times,
and my family confiscated."
The king then ordered all departments: "You must prepare quickly.
On the eighth day of next month,
establish a Dao-chǎng south of the city.
If the Fó school is strong,
I and all the people of this country
will all take refuge in the Fó.
If there is the slightest error,
both of you shall be executed."
When Sū-dá received the decree,
he was not overly anxious in his heart.
He immediately returned home,
frowning and looking distressed.
Shè-lì-fú saw his worry and fear,
and his altered appearance.
He then exclaimed in surprise,
and asked with wonder: "Why are you worried and fearful, Eldest One,
and your countenance altered?" Sū-dá said: "This disciple went to court today,
and personally received a clear decree,
ordering that on the eighth day of next month,
a Dao-chǎng be established south of the city,
where each will display their supernatural powers
to determine superiority.
If the Fó school wins,
the king and his ministers will all vow allegiance.
If the Six Teachers are strong,
the Crown Prince and this humble one will both suffer execution.
I am now a common person of shallow wisdom,
and cannot fathom the greatness of the sànts.
I sincerely wish for your compassion;
may you reveal the truth about how to proceed!" Shè-lì-fú, to relieve his anxiety,
spoke boastfully:
Sū-dá replied to Shè-lì-fú: " [The king] has ordered that on the eighth day of next month,
a great Dao-chǎng be established south of the city,
where various supernatural powers will be displayed by each."
The king himself drives to supervise their abilities;
all the officials consult in detail to discern gains and losses.
I earnestly wish the Heshang would explain his thoughts,
for his advance and retreat must be clearly stated.
Shèlì fú (Śāriputra) smiled and replied to Xūdá (Sudatta): "All delusive phenomena must be cut away.
When externalists contend with me in spiritual powers,
it is like offering a fish to an otter.
The bright moon has not been seen to compare with firefly glow;
the sea water cannot be discussed in terms of a peck or a spoonful.
It is like the summer sun melting spring ice,
or refined gold compared to a splinter of wood.
The followers of external paths are all chaff;
once a strong wind rises, there is nothing to gather.
I will now subdue demons and seize strength,
dispatching them all to be converted into Púsàs (Bodhisattvas)."
Shèlì fú (Śāriputra) smiled and relaxed his countenance,
saying to Xūdá (Sudatta): "Although I am now a Minor Sage,
I do not consult those of high status.
Simply put, rectifying government and destroying evil
is but a minor task.
Even if there were tens of millions of celestial māras (demons),
filling the void,
they could not move a single hair;
much less could mosquito-like six teachers
possibly contend!
I have now sharpened my sword and fed my horses,
only awaiting the opportunity for trial.
There is no need for delay;
speed is essential.
For the Elder to remonstrate again,
saying eight days is too late—
when a rabbit enters (a dog) rushes out,
who can long endure waiting for cooked food?
It must be displayed tomorrow;
please shorten the eight-day period." Xūdá (Sudatta) then reported to the king again.
The king, according to his request,
issued a proclamation to all officials: "This very night, until dawn,
all arrangements must be completed.
For the Buddha's dharma hall,
you must make preparations;
for what the six teachers require,
I myself will provide.
Tomorrow morning, at first light,
the contest must begin."
After the clear proclamation was issued,
Xūdá (Sudatta) immediately returned home.
Arriving at his house,
he could not find Shèlì fú (Śāriputra).
Xūdá (Sudatta) clapped his hands in shock and dismay,
crying out: "Disaster!
A great anomaly has occurred!
Tomorrow is the promised date for the holy contest,
yet today my assistant has secretly fled.
Even if the plan were unfeasible,
he should not have failed to inform me.
I, your disciple, for the sake of the Dharma,
am willing to sacrifice my body;
how can the Prince's person
be innocently subjected to slaughter!"
Anxiously he searched,
unaware of his whereabouts;
he inquired throughout the streets,
but no one knew where he had gone.
Then he met a young cowherd and questioned him about his loitering: "When you were in the fields,
did you meet my Heshang?"
The boy bowed and replied to the elder: "Yesterday, driving cows and chasing grass,
I happened to reach the edge of Qīlǐjiàn (Seven-Li Gully).
I saw a bald-headed boy,
wearing a red robe,
sitting peacefully asleep under a tree.
I don't know what kind of being he is.
Elder, you should go and see for yourself."
Hearing this, the Elder
immediately knew it was Shèlì fú (Śāriputra) himself.
Within this country,
there was no other shaven-headed person.
The Elder rushed his chariot and drove swiftly
to the edge of Qīlǐjiàn (Seven-Li Gully).
Directly beneath the Nígū (Nyagrodha) tree,
with those to his left and right,
he clasped his hands together and came forward,
addressing the Heshang: "Your disciple personally heard the imperial decree,
the injunctions are extremely strict.
Heshang, you yourself urged for haste,
promising to contest tomorrow.
How can you be unaware of the urgency,
coming to this place,
disregarding business,
and coming here to sit and sleep?
The slightest oversight
means both our lives will be lost.
Even if your disciple is to blame,
Heshang, how can you bear to see it!"
How did he present his plea?
The Elder clasped his hands and addressed the Shé Lí (Acarya): "Your disciple is foolish and unaware.
Spreading gold and buying the garden, I did not shrink from the task;
the externalists seized me and tortured me.
Your disciple personally received the instruction;
Láodùchā (Purāṇa Kāśyapa) wishes to contend in divine power.
Fearing wavering in the midst of the contest,
it is for this reason that I frequently furrow my brow with worry."
When Shèlì fú (Śāriputra) heard Xūdá (Sudatta)'s words,
he entered samādhi to contemplate.
Calming his spirit and purifying his thoughts, he rested his mind,
subduing delusive thoughts and ceasing all wrongdoing.
The six defilements, though rampant, could not taint him,
knowing that the power of concentration is inconceivable.
Constantly fearing that the power of a Śrāvakā's (hearer's) path is weak,
he earnestly wished for the Rúlái (Tathāgata) to protect and uphold him.
Shèlì fú (Śāriputra) did not move from his original seat,
but wielded his divine powers,
immediately arriving at the summit of Jízhǒufēngshān (Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain).
He wept sorrowfully, shedding tears,
choking and his voice hoarse,
circumambulating the Shìzūn (World-Honored One)
more than ten times.
How did he beseech the great sage's powerful blessing?
Shèlì fú (Śāriputra) cried sadly and addressed the Fǎwáng (Dharma King): "The Rúlái (Tathāgata) commanded me to establish a monastery.
Before I could sincerely complete its construction,
the multitude of six teachers became somewhat formidable.
I, your humble disciple, have weak divine power;
I hope for your protection and the lending of your mighty light.
If they can be subdued all at once,
I will convert them all to join the monastic order."
The Buddha told Shèlì fú (Śāriputra): "There is no need to be sad;
it is because your Śrāvakā (hearer)'s path power is weak."
Then he called Ānán (Ānanda) to approach,
saying, "Take my Saṅghāṭī (outer robe) from the rack.
You have always been used to subdue demons throughout kalpas;
no need to exert spiritual powers or wisdom."
"Take my golden Kāṣāya (robe);
countless benevolent deities will protect it.
The māra kings, upon seeing it, will all be subdued,
and the purity of the Dharma nature will attest to unconditionedness."
Shèlì fú (Śāriputra) suddenly arose from his meditation;
to his left and right, he saw no other people,
only Minister Xūdá (Sudatta),
accompanied by the eight classes of dragons and deities,
surrounding and supporting him from front to back,
and on all four sides.
Āxiūluó (Asuras) held the sun and moon to lead the way;
Jǐnnàluó (Kinnaras) grasped swords and spears to follow behind.
At that time, the wind master made wind,
the rain master brought rain,
dampening the dusty clamor
and leveling the roads.
Divine kings held staves;
Vajras (Diamond-wielding deities) held pestles,
selecting the valiant and mighty,
arranging the ranks.
Then they blew the dharma conch,
struck the dharma drum,
brandished swords and spears,
displaying their majestic wrath.
Their movement was like rushing thunder;
their advance like spreading clouds.
There were also the Snow Mountain Elephant Kings,
and golden-maned lions,
eyes wide with shock, brows raised,
gnashing their teeth,
shaking their furry coats,
wagging their heads and tails.
The procession's banners reached to the heavens;
spears and halberds covered the ground.
Each contended to display their awe-inspiring divine power,
bestowing it upon our Rúlái's (Tathāgata's) great disciple. What was it like?
Shèlì fú (Śāriputra) bid farewell to the assembly,
and on that day, set out on the journey.
Pílóu Tiānwáng (Virūḍhaka-devarāja) held a golden banner;
Títóulàizhā (Dhṛtarāṣṭra) held a jade scepter.
Their armor covered their entire bodies, all of gold;
their swords and arrows were entirely made of iron.
The blue-faced Jīngāng (Vajra) was dark in color;
the fire-headed Jīngāng (Vajra)'s rage did not cease.
Bells and drums boomed, shaking the heavens;
auspicious light shone brightly and purely.
Celestial immortals scattered fragrant flowers from the sky;
sounds of praise followed one after another.
Firelight emerged from the demon-subduing pestle;
frost and snow arose from the blade of wisdom.
May all Buddhas arise with compassion,
so that the banners of evil will soon all be shattered.
The divine power, in less than a snap of the fingers,
in an instant reached the imperial palace gates.
King Bōsīní saw Shèlìfú,
and then addressed his assembled officials,
saying, "Each of you must pay attention.
The Buddhists are on the east side,
the six teachers are on the west.
I am on the north,
and the officials and common people are on the south.
Victory and defeat are two paths;
each must be clearly remembered.
If the Ho shang is victorious,
strike the golden drums and lower the golden tallies.
If the Buddhists are strong,
strike the golden bell and mark the 'shàng' character."
Each returned to their position,
then allowed the display to proceed.
Shèlìfú slowly and gracefully walked,
ascending the lion's throne.
Láodùchā was positioned within a jeweled tent,
held and supported on all four sides.
Shèlìfú immediately ascended the precious throne,
like a king among lions,
and uttered a refined and marvelous sound,
addressing the four assemblies, saying: "Within my Buddhadharma,
we do not establish the notion of self and other.
We manifest righteousness and crush heterodoxy,
using expedient means for these displays.
What transformations does Láodùchā have?
Let them be displayed!"
The six teachers heard these words
and suddenly conjured a treasure mountain,
several yóujūn high.
Steep and emerald green jade,
towering with white silver.
Its summit touched the Milky Way,
with clusters of fresh, fragrant bamboo.
The sun and moon were to its east and west,
the constellations Cān and Chén to its north and south.
There were also pine trees reaching the sky,
and ten thousand sections of wisteria.
On its peak, hermits lived in peace,
and various immortals wandered and observed.
Riding cranes and mounting dragons,
immortal songs intertwined.
Who among the four assemblies did not exclaim in admiration?
All who saw it praised it.
Although Shèlìfú saw this mountain,
his heart felt no fear or difficulty.
In a moment,
he suddenly conjured a Vajra.
What form did this Vajra take?
The Vajra's head was round like the sky;
the sky's roundness merely served as its cover.
Its feet were square, ten thousand lǐ wide;
the great earth was barely enough for its anvil.
Its brows were verdant like two layers of green mountains,
its mouth was as vast as rivers and seas.
It held a precious pestle in its hand,
and flames shot skyward from the pestle.
With one strike at the heterodox mountain,
it was instantly pulverized.
Mountain flowers withered and scattered,
and the bamboo and trees were nowhere to be found.
All the officials together exclaimed at its marvel,
and the four assemblies all shouted with joy.
Hence it is said, how did the Vajra's wisdom-pestle shatter the heterodox mountain?
The six teachers' wrath was hard to contain,
they conjured an incomparable treasure mountain.
Steep and craggy for several yóujūn,
covered with purple kudzu and golden vines.
Mountain flowers were verdant, forming brocade patterns,
gold and rock towered, and emerald clouds arose.
Above were Wáng Qiáo and Dīng Lìngwēi,
fragrant water flowed within the treasure mountain.
Flying immortals often scattered famous flowers,
the great king saw it from afar and rejoiced.
Shèlìfú saw the mountain enter the assembly,
calmly remained still in samādhi.
Instantly, he conjured a great Vajra,
with high brows, broad forehead, and a vast body.
Holding a golden pestle with flames reaching the sky,
one strike at the heterodox mountain pulverized it.
The outsiders choked, their voices hoarse,
the four assemblies all shouted with joy simultaneously.
At that moment, the emperor was astonished,
and the four assemblies were delighted.
Since this round was not as good as his,
what other divine transformation would there be?
At that time, the elder Xūdá struck the great bell,
holding a golden plaque,
and reported to the king to mark his "shàng" character.
The six teachers saw the treasure mountain collapse,
their anger soared to the sky,
they became even more enraged,
and again reported to the king, saying: "Our divine transformations
are without end.
Although one round was not as good,
we are sure to win in the next display."
Láodùchā suddenly, amidst the crowd,
conjured a water buffalo.
The buffalo had shining horns piercing the sky,
its four hooves were like the swords of Lóngquán;
its dewlap dragged on the ground,
its two eyes were as bright as the sun and moon.
With one roar,
it sounded like thunder and lightning.
The four assemblies sighed in admiration,
all saying the outsiders had become strong.
Although Shèlìfú saw this buffalo,
his demeanor remained perfectly calm.
Suddenly, he conjured a lion,
fierce and irresistible.
This lion's mouth was like a canyon,
its body like a snow mountain,
its eyes like shooting stars,
its fangs like frosty swords.
It roared and roared furiously,
advancing directly into the arena.
When the water buffalo saw it,
its soul fled, and it knelt on the ground.
The lion first broke its neck bones,
then snapped its spine,
before it could even chew,
its form was pulverized.
The emperor exclaimed in astonishment,
the officials and common people were bewildered.
The six teachers were terrified and panic-stricken;
how could the crown prince not rejoice greatly?
The six teachers were enraged before the king,
conjuring a pitiable water buffalo.
It went straight into the arena, startling the four assemblies,
grinding its horns and digging the ground, roaring up to the sky.
The outsiders all shouted "Good!"
My Dharma is transmitted by the people of the country.
Shèlì sitting on his throne was not alarmed,
entirely because his wisdom was immeasurable.
He adjusted his clothes and calmed his mind,
and conjured a majestic lion king.
Its roaring eyes were like stars and lightning,
its slender fangs and swift claws were sharp as frost.
With heroic spirit, it flicked its tail,
advancing directly to harm the water buffalo.
It was instantly broken and digested,
bones and all were chewed and vanished completely.
Twice the Buddhists had been victorious,
the outsiders were at their wit's end, with no strategy.
Since the six teachers had been inferior twice,
their expressions gradually showed shame and embarrassment.
Forcing a stubborn face,
they conjured a pond amidst the crowd.
Its four banks were adorned with seven treasures,
and golden sand covered its bottom.
Duckweed and water caltrops
grew lushly across the green water;
soft willows and lotuses
encircled the spiritual pool with their fragrance.
Shèlì saw the wondrous pond,
but did not exclaim in surprise.
He conjured a white elephant king,
its body vast,
its eyes like the sun and moon.
It had six tusks in its mouth,
each tusk spouting seven lotus flowers.
On each flower were seven celestial maidens,
playing stringed instruments,
and singing stringed songs.
Their voices were refined, wonderful, and fresh,
their postures graceful and beautiful.
The elephant slowly moved its steps,
going directly into the pond,
kicking east and west,
circling north and south.
With its trunk it sucked the water,
and the water dried up.
The banks collapsed, dust flew,
turning into dry land.
At that moment, the six teachers lost color,
the four assemblies exclaimed in admiration,
all the officials of the country
together cried out in wonder; how was it so?
The pond's banks were made of seven treasures,
agate and coral competing in brilliance.
Fish in the pond leaped, adorned with crowns,
turtles and soft-shelled turtles scrambled to hide.
Lotuses in the water shone brightly,
all who saw them were amazed.
The outsiders exclaimed in wonder,
saying, "Watch me contend for strength this time!"
Shèlì looked south,
and conjured a great six-tusked fragrant elephant.
Its gait was like a moving snow mountain,
its body vast and immeasurable.
From its mouth protruded six towering tusks,
each tusk a hundred zhàng high.
On each tusk were seven lotus flowers,
and within the flowers, peerless jade maidens.
They played qín and sè, singing stringed songs,
their refined, wonderful, and fresh voices harmonizing.
Together they praised Amituó's Land of Ultimate Bliss,
hand in hand, encouraging each other to go there.
The elephant then moved its steps and entered the pond,
kicking and trampling both east and west, and onto the banks.
With its trunk, it sucked up all the water until it was dry,
causing the six masters (Liù Shī) to choke with sorrow and melancholy.
The six masters (Liù Shī) frequently suffered defeats,
their hearts growing increasingly vexed.
"This morning, strangely, we are no match for him;
last night's dream was upside down.
Our faces are rough, red, and yellowish,
our lips and mouths unusually dry (zào).
Our bellies are hot, feeling as if boiled in soup,
and our intestines ache as if stirred by a knife.
Though Qú Tán (Gautama) is like a wicked wolf,
he cannot withstand the bites of a pack of dogs.
Shè Lì Fú (Śāriputra) has little wisdom and clumsy strategies,
yet he shows his cleverness before Lǔ Bān (Lu Ban).
If this time he suddenly gains strength,
he will shatter all that came before.
Unwilling to suffer humiliation,
they suddenly transformed a poisonous dragon.
Its mouth spewed smoke and clouds,
darkening the sky and obscuring the sun.
It raised its eyebrows and darted its eyes,
shaking the earth with thunderous roars.
Lightning flashed, now dark, now bright,
auspicious clouds sometimes spread, sometimes rolled up.
It terrified the four assemblies,
and startled ordinary people.
The whole nation saw it,
marveling at its spiritual strangeness.
Shè Lì Fú (Śāriputra) sat calmly on his precious throne,
completely without fear.
He transformed a golden-winged bird king (Jīn Chì Niǎo Wáng),
with wondrous feathers and extraordinary bones.
It flapped its double wings,
obscuring the light of the sun and moon.
Its claws and talons were slender and long,
no different from the swords of Fēng Chéng.
It swooped down from the sky,
like a shooting star from heaven.
From afar, it saw the poisonous dragon,
and engaged it in combat several times.
"Though it won't satisfy my hunger for a full meal,
it will at least help to stave off starvation."
The bird first pecked its eyes,
then greedily devoured its four limbs.
With two movements of its beak,
not even bones remained.
The six masters (Liù Shī) trembled with fear and exclaimed in astonishment,
their minds in a daze:
On this day, the six masters (Liù Shī) gradually became distraught,
their resentment knew no bounds, no [ ] to control it.
Although they fought hard and resisted,
they ultimately knew they would fall.
Again, they transformed a poisonous dragon,
spewing smoke and clouds from its mouth with violent intent.
Thunder roared and lightning flashed, mist obscured the sky,
gravel and stones flew, sounding like firecrackers.
The crowd in the arena was terrified and exclaimed in astonishment,
looking at each other and all saying, "Good!"
When Shè Lì (Śāriputra) saw the poisonous dragon arrive,
he immediately manifested the wondrous-feathered golden-winged bird.
It tore off its head and tail without difficulty,
and when it opened its mouth, it first pecked its brain.
Its ribs were crushed into fine dust,
and the six masters (Liù Shī) knew not what to say.
The awesome power of the Three Jewels (Sān Bǎo) is immeasurable,
and the demon king (Mó Wáng) trembled with vexation.
The King said: "Monk (Héshàng), you boast wildly,
with a thousand kinds of skills;
but when tested before people,
you can do nothing.
What other divine power do you have?
Quickly manifest it!"
The six masters (Liù Shī) summoned their strength,
and reported to the King, saying: "Within our dharma,
spiritual transformations are endlessly inexhaustible."
Suddenly, among the multitude,
they transformed two ghosts.
Their appearance was ugly and evil,
their bodies rugged and monstrous.
Their faces were bluer than northern indigo (biàn),
their eyes like cinnabar and fiery red.
Fire issued from their mouths,
and smoke arose from their noses.
They moved like streaking lightning,
and darted like flying whirlwinds.
They raised their eyebrows and blinked their eyes,
terrifying all around.
Those who saw them felt their hair stand on end,
but Shè Lì Fú (Śāriputra) remained calm by himself.
Shè Lì Fú (Śāriputra) hesitated and pondered,
when Pí Shā Mén (Vaiśravaṇa) appeared before the King.
His awesome power was brilliant,
his armor and weapons gleaming.
Earth gods supported his feet,
and a precious sword hung at his waist.
The two ghosts, upon seeing him,
begged for their lives repeatedly, how could they respond:
The six masters (Liù Shī) themselves claimed to be incomparable,
and transformed two yellow-headed ghosts.
Their heads were of a strange species, ugly corpses,
terrifying all around and causing dread.
Shè Lì Fú (Śāriputra) had a thought, a brief contemplation,
and Pí Shā Tiān Wáng (Vaiśravaṇa Deva-King) arrived by himself.
The Deva-King looked back and stared with quivering eyes,
and the two ghosts became confused, fainted, and fell to the ground.
On this day, the outsiders (wàidào) (Shè Lì Fú) broke the demon army,
the six masters (Liù Shī) were terrified and lost their souls.
Thanks to the compassionate Shè Lì Fú (Śāriputra),
who endured and bore it with all his divine power.
Just as donkeys and mules carrying heavy loads climb a long road,
only then did they know they could be compared to dragons and qílín.
Merely because their hearts were deluded by evil small paths,
he guided them to take refuge in the great Dharma gate.
Although the six masters (Liù Shī) had lost five times,
they still did not surrender.
"Let's try one more time and see;
the later achievement will compensate for the previous faults.
If by chance we lose again,
then we will willingly bow our heads and submit to him."
Having finished pondering,
suddenly, among the multitude, they transformed a large tree.
Its branches and leaves were luxuriant,
obscuring the sun and reaching the clouds,
its trunk soaring with fragrant branches,
reaching ten thousand ren high.
Auspicious birds and propitious phoenixes,
sang harmoniously throughout its branches and leaves;
emerald leaves and fragrant flowers,
covered several li, creating a shadowy darkness.
At that time, those who saw it,
all exclaimed in astonishment.
Shè Lì Fú (Śāriputra) suddenly, from among the multitude, transformed a Wind God (Fēng Shén).
He clasped his hands forward,
and reported to the Monk (Héshàng): "To blow away the three-thousand great-thousand worlds (sānqiān dàqiān shìjiè)
in an instant is not difficult;
much less this small tree, a mere trifle,
how dare it stand against my wind power!"
Having spoken,
he opened his bag and immediately blew.
At that moment, the earth rolled up like cotton,
stones shattered like dust,
branches scattered to other regions,
and the trunk's whereabouts were unknown.
The outsiders (wàidào) had no place to hide,
and the four assemblies all cheered at once, how was it:
The six masters (Liù Shī) frequently lost five times,
and again before the King, transformed a tree.
Its height could be several yóuxún,
its branches luxuriant and flourishing.
Shè Lì Fú's (Śāriputra's) spiritual power is inconceivable,
his divine transformations exceedingly rare and wondrous.
He came from the Buddha (Fó) to subdue the outsiders (wàidào),
sequentially having the great wind blow them all away.
The divine king (Shén Wáng) roared like thunder,
a long snake uprooted the tree, leaving no branches intact.
In a flash, it all disappeared,
the outsiders (wàidào) were blown about, having nowhere to cling.
The six masters (Liù Shī) were blown off their feet,
their incense burner and precious vessels flew with the wind.
Their precious throne swayed precariously, about to fall,
and the outsiders (wàidào), in their fear and urgency, all supported it.
Both sides discussed the weakness of the six masters (Liù Shī),
"Can a mustard seed be compared to Mount Xū Mí (Sumeru)!"
At that time, the King reported to the Monk (Héshàng): "For many days now,
I have vainly offered reverence,
extensively bestowed jade and silk,
and wrongly wasted national reserves.
Only now do I know that true gold is mixed with brass (tóu),
distinguished by visual inspection;
dragons and snakes are mixed together,
only then can their abilities be discerned.
Monk (Héshàng), your power is exhausted, your influence at its end,
in every matter you are weak.
You must humble yourself and bend your will,
be defeated and submit to him.
Do not vainly praise our people (wǒ rén) further,
discussing heaven and earth."
The six masters (Liù Shī) heard these words,
and assented obediently.
Their faces flushed with shame,
they had nowhere to hide.
Shè Lì Fú (Śāriputra) saw the evil followers subdued,
and his heart and spirit rejoiced.
"It is not by my own strong power,
but all by the Buddha's (Rúlái) blessing."
Thereupon, he soared straight up,
leaping into the empty sky,
as high as seven tārā trees (duō luó shù).
Fire issued from his head,
and water from his feet.
Sometimes he manifested a large body,
filling the empty sky,
sometimes he manifested a small body,
like a mustard seed.
He performed divine transformations,
manifesting eighteen kinds,
and the people of the entire nation,
all looked up in awe, how was it:
Shèlìfú 倏忽現神通，
踊身直上在虚空。
或現大身遍法界，
小身藏形芥子中。
Láodùchā 愕然合掌立，
我法豈得與他同。
共汝捨邪歸正路，
相將慚謝盡卑恭。
鬬聖已來極下劣，
迴心豈敢不依從。
各擬悔謝歸三寶，
更亦無心事火龍。
累歷歲年枉氣力，
終日從空復至空。
各自抽身奉事佛，
免被當來鐵碓舂。
《Jiàngmó biànwén》一卷。
或見不是處，
有人讀者，
即與正著。
《Chíshì (Púsà)》第二
經云：時魔 Bōxún 從萬二千天女，
狀 Dìshì 鼓樂弦歌，
來詣我所。
是時也，
Bōxún 設計，
多排婇女嬪妃；
欲惱聖人，
剩列奢華艷質。
希奇魔女，
一万二千；
最異珍珠，
千般結果。
出塵菩薩，
不易惱他；
Chíshì 上人，
如何得退。
莫不盛裝美貌，
無非多着嬋娟。
若見時教巧出言詞，
税調着必生退敗。
其魔女者，
一个个如花菡萏，
一人人似玉無殊。
身柔軟兮新下 Wūshān，
貌娉婷兮纔離仙洞。
盡帶桃花之臉，
皆分柳葉之眉。
徐行時若風颯芙蓉，
緩步處似水摇蓮亞。
朱脣旖旎，
能赤能紅；
雪齒齊平，
能白能浄。
輕羅拭體，
吐異種之馨香；
薄（縠）掛身，
曳殊常之翠彩。
排於坐右，
立在宫中。
青天之五色雲舒，
碧沼之千般花發。
罕有罕有，
奇哉奇哉。
空將魔女嬈他，
亦恐不能驚動。
更請分爲數隊，
各逞逶迤。
擎鮮花者慇懃獻上，
焚異香者備切虔心。
合玉指而禮拜重重，
出巧語而詐言切切。
或擎樂器，
或即吟哦；
或施窈窕，
或即唱歌。
休誇 Yuènǚ，
莫説 Cáozhì.
任伊 Chíshì 堅心，
見了也須退敗。
大好大好，
希哉希哉。
如此麗質嬋娟，
争不妄生動念。
自家見了，
尚自魂迷；
他人覩之，
定當亂意。
任伊修行緊切，
税調着必見迴頭；
任伊鐵作心肝，
見了也須粉碎。
魔王道： “我只（没）去，
定是菩薩識我。
不如作 Dìshì 隊仗，
問誶伊 Chíshì Púsà.”
於是魔王大作奢華，
欲出宫城，
從天降下。
周迴捧擁，
百匝千遭。
樂韻弦歌，
分爲二十四隊。
步步出天門之界，
遥遥别本住宫中。
Bōxún 自乃前行，
魔女一時從後。
擎樂器者喧喧奏曲，
響聒青霄；
爇香火者灑灑（澹澹）煙飛，
氤氲碧落。
競作奢華美貌，
各申窈窕儀容。
擎鮮花者共花色無殊，
捧珠珍者共珠珍不異。
琵琶弦上，
韻合春鶯；
簫笛管中，
聲吟鳴鳳。
杖敲羯鼓，
如抛碎玉於盤中；
手弄秦筝，
似排雁行於弦上。
輕輕絲竹，
Tàicháng 之美韻莫偕；
浩浩唱歌，
Húbù 之豈能比對。
妖容轉盛，
艷質更豐。
一群群若四色花敷，
一隊隊似五雲秀麗。
盤旋碧落，
宛轉青霄。
遠看時意散心驚，
近覩者魂飛目斷。
從天降下，
若天花亂雨於乾坤；
初出魔宫，
似仙娥芬霏於宇宙。
天女咸生喜躍，
魔王自己（已自）欣歡。
此時計較得成，
Chíshì 修行必退。
容貌恰如 Dìshì，
威儀一似 Fànwáng。
聖人必定無疑，
Chíshì 多應不怪。
天女各施於六律，
人人調弄〔於〕五音。
唱歌者詐作道心，
供養者假爲虔敬。
莫遣聖人省悟，
莫教菩薩覺知。
發言時直要停騰，
税調處直須穩審。
各請擎鮮花於掌内，
爲吾燒沉麝於爐中。
呈珠顔而剩逞妖容，
展玉貌而更添艷麗。
浩浩簫韶前引，
喧喧樂韻齊聲。
一時皆下於雲中，
盡入修禪之室内。
(吟)：魔王隊仗離天宫，
欲惱聖人來下界。
廣設香花申供養，
更將音樂及弦歌。
清泠空界韻嘈嘈，
潦亂雲中聲響亮。
Húbù 莫能相比並，
Kūcí 不易對量他。
遥遥樂引出魔宫，
隱隱排於霄漢内。
香爇煙飛和瑞氣，
花擎繚亂動祥雲。
琵琶弦上弄春鶯，
簫笛管中鳴錦鳳。
羯鼓杖頭敲碎玉，
秦筝絲上落珠珍。
各裝美貌逞逶迤，
盡出玉顔誇艷態。
个个盡如花亂發，
人人皆似月娥飛。
從天降下閉乾坤，
出彼宫中遮宇宙。
乍見人人魂膽碎，
初觀个个盡心驚。
(韻)：Bōxún 是日出天來，
樂部 青霄碧落排。
玉女貌如花艷坼，
仙娥體似月空開。
妖桃强逞魔 Púsà，
美質徒〔誇〕惱聖懷。
鼓樂弦歌千万隊，
相隨捧擁競徘徊。
誇艷質，
逞身材，
窈窕如花向日開。
十指纖纖如削玉，
雙眉隱隱似刀裁。
Holding musical instruments,
also blowing and playing,
they gracefully descended from the cloud tops.
From the sounds of the xiāo and dí, voices were heard from afar;
on the strings of the pípa, the melody was mournful.
Songs trickled forth,
laughter echoed,
surrounding Bōxún in a circular array.
Their procession was just like that of Dìshì descending,
their solemn presence precisely like Fànwáng arriving.
They must act covertly,
so as not to arouse suspicion,
feigning piety to bow before the Dharma Platform.
When asked, they must not show any alarm,
and their eagerness must not reveal any incongruity.
Agarwood and musk,
held in their hands,
were offered as temporary tribute with full intention.
Truly, they awaited the sànt-rén's mind to be disturbed,
then, wherever he moved, they would tempt him.
They must remember,
and keep in mind,
not to let the practitioner's Dharma-eye open.
If Chíshì were to achieve enlightenment,
the Mā family and their retinue would surely be destroyed.
Cleverly they enticed,
well they arranged,
forcefully using words to express their intentions.
When they appeared, his mind would fall,
and they would lead him astray by indulging his desires.
Songs and music,
competitively blowing and playing,
a confused clamor overflowing the path in array.
The demonesses and demon king entered the chamber,
chanting and bringing forth vexations from every place.
(The sūtra says): "With his retinue, he bowed at my feet,
joined palms reverently,
and even practiced the firm Dharma."
At that time, Bōxún had a verse:
(Poem): "For the sake of deep meditation, you dwell here;
I now intentionally descend from the sky-path.
I revere your observance of precepts, pure as the moon;
I recall your lofty eminence, like an isolated peak.
Engaged in samādhi, I know not how long your practice has been;
seated in meditation, I have not yet discerned what the Dharma is like.
Today, I come with my retinue to pay homage,
may I ask, Śīxiōng, do you possess myriad blessings?"
(Prose): At that time, Bōxún spoke to Chíshì, saying: "Venerable sir, you have practiced for a long time,
spending much time in meditation.
You uphold the firm Dharma-virtue,
binding your mind and spirit to maintain your resolve.
Your thatched hut is utterly silent,
your stone chamber deep and serene.
I imagine the mornings and nights are solitary,
and presume your daily routine is laborious.
The gate of Chan is profound and distant,
the Dharma of emptiness is difficult to understand.
I know not the depth or shallowness of what you have attained,
nor what merits you possess.
I have left the heavenly realm,
descending from the heavenly palace.
Because I ponder your unparalleled virtuous conduct,
because I recall your unique lofty solitude.
Today, I am delighted to meet you,
I humbly hope, Great Sage, in your compassion,
you will grant me a small talk about the taste of Dharma."
(Plain Poem): "Temporarily abandoning the five desires, I descended from heaven,
to pay homage at Śīxiōng's meditation platform.
Drums, music, strings, and songs express my offerings,
incense, flowers, and precious fruits convey my heart's intent.
I rejoice in beholding the Great Being a thousand times,
I delight in bowing to the eminent person a hundred times.
I humbly hope for your compassion to proclaim the wondrous Dharma,
I now entirely hope to extinguish all dust and defilement."
At that time, Chíshì did not recognize the demon king,
mistaking him for Jiāoshījiā,
and incorrectly identifying him as Dìshì.
Therefore,
(the sūtra says): "I said he was Dìshì,
and spoke to him, saying: 'Welcome,
Jiāoshījiā!'
And even practiced the firm Dharma with him."
(Prose): On that day, Chíshì Púsà addressed Dìshì, saying: "The lifespan and blessings in the heavenly palace have a limit;
do not mistake wealth, nobility, and extravagance
for something eternally long-lasting.
When you rise and sit, there is natural music,
and sheng and songs to your liking.
Therefore, there are many different kinds of fragrant flowers,
freely at your will.
Heavenly males and heavenly females
attend without cease;
treasure trees and treasure groves
are visited without rest.
Wherever your mind wishes to go,
that becomes a pavilion;
whenever you walk according to your desires,
it naturally forms precious fragrance.
When flowers open, it is daytime;
when flowers close, it is twilight.
If you think of clothes, silks and satins appear in thousands of layers;
if you want food, a hundred flavors of delicacies appear.
Such wealth and nobility are truly extravagant.
Yet, all these are causes and conditions that do not last,
all are unstable blessings.
Dìshì,
Dìshì!
You must know,
you must know!
Do not cling to the five desires,
do not indulge your will in the heavenly palace.
Although your lifespan is long,
it is not ultimately endless;
although you are wealthy, noble, and extravagant,
how can there be any permanent security?
When lifespan and power are exhausted,
you will ultimately fall into the three lower realms of hell;
when merits and virtues are gone,
you will re-enter the path of saṃsāra.
Like a blazing fire,
when the wood is consumed, it turns to dust;
like an arrow shot into the sky,
when its force is spent, it ultimately falls to the ground.
You cannot escape birth and death,
you cannot escape impermanence.
Quickly relinquish internal and external treasures,
and attain the wondrous fruit of unconditioned being.
Be diligent in the Buddha-Dharma,
and realize true suchness.
Lesser cling to worldly glory,
and know that it is suffering.
I deeply trouble Dìshì,
and will now bid farewell to your retinue.
I have briefly expounded something profound to you,
so you may awaken to transcending birth and death."
(Ancient Chant, upper and lower sections): The heavenly palace cannot escape impermanence,
when merits and virtues are slightly diminished, one falls.
Wealth, nobility, and extravagance are ultimately not long-lasting,
indulging in sheng and songs is not enduring.
Though you boast of beautiful jade maidens,
though you flaunt the captivating charms of the moon goddess,
though you are extravagant and free,
ultimately you cannot escape impermanence.
Though you boast of thousands of layers of brocade,
though you feast on a hundred flavors of delicacies,
though all your desires are met,
ultimately you cannot escape impermanence.
Though merits and virtues adorn your body,
though your retinue surrounds you always,
though you enjoy pleasure according to your desires,
ultimately you cannot escape impermanence.
Though clear music plays stringed songs,
though pavilions are everywhere,
though concubines attend you,
ultimately you cannot escape impermanence.
Though her beauty is most rare,
though the heavenly palace is rich and noble,
though flowers bloom filling the path with fragrance,
ultimately you cannot escape impermanence.
Do not indulge your body and mind in the upper realm,
do not delve deep into the five desires in heaven,
do not take extravagance as the ultimate goal,
do not indulge in wealth and nobility without cultivating.
You should know that there is decline in that place,
like an arrow shot into the sky, it eventually falls to the ground;
if one can realize this regarding body, life, and wealth,
then cultivation will lead one beyond impermanence.
(Chant): "I thank Dìshì for descending from heaven,
and deeply appreciate the array of strings, songs, drums, and music.
May all the jade maidens awaken,
may the beautiful ones all emerge from the dust and defilement.
When will the wealth of the heavenly palace end?
How many tens of thousands of times have you suffered in the hells?
If one can comprehend this regarding body, life, and wealth,
then one can truly escape the three calamities for a long time.
You must remember,
and bear in mind,
to return to the upper heavenly palace.
May the mountain of the five desires' karma diminish daily,
may the obstructing peaks of delusion be destroyed at every moment.
May a firm and secure treasury be found within the body,
may the defiling ailment of the womb be removed from the mind.
Dìshì, touched by Śīxiōng's Dharma teaching power,
asked how he could repay him, and sang thus:
(Sūtra): He then said to me,
'Righteous one, accept these twelve thousand heavenly maidens,
who can be prepared for sweeping and sprinkling.'"
All heroes,
all resisted,
their distinguished divine countenances made the demons lose heart.
Outwardly awe-inspiring (formidable) yet inwardly compassionate,
at that time all wished to hasten to the abbot's residence.
Myriad upon myriad were all distinguished,
their momentum like the vast ocean pushing aside huge waves.
Throngs surged forward, all willing to go,
group after group, all distinct.
Bodhisattva monks,
young or old,
all declared their wish to follow the compassionate Zūn.
Good men and good women also accompanied them,
every one like a Tathāgata, encountering no obstacles.
Arranged in order,
how splendid and clear,
the sounds of xiāo, sè, kōnghóu, zhēng, and dí resonated.
Incense burners burned chéndán and various precious spices,
myriad upon myriad clasped their palms together.
Wénshū was humble,
the Shìzūn praised him,
Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas, young and old.
He must then lead the multitude,
not to hesitate or delay.
Wénshū bowed out,
all gazed in admiration,
accepting the mission to discuss the Dharma extensively in Píyé.
To witness Wéimó's success in expounding the Dharma,
all together bowed in farewell to the golden image.
Arriving there,
they saw the Dharma master,
who honed and polished them to be clear and bright,
universally enabling humans and devas to awaken to true reality,
all together bowed in thanks to the golden image.
Bathed in the Zūn's compassion,
all were permitted to go,
to enter Píyé, as per a past cause,
to meet the two eminent persons who discoursed on emptiness,
all together bowed in thanks to the golden image.
Scattering fragrant flowers,
riding precious elephants,
the lion with golden fur was supreme,
to send Wénshū to inquire about the source of illness,
all temporarily bade farewell to the golden image.
Voices clamored,
music resounded,
his wondrous virtue and majestic presence were top-tier,
eight thousand Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas,
all temporarily bade farewell to the golden image.
(The sūtra says) At this time, devas and humans, Bodhisattvas, arranged themselves,
surrounding Wénshū in millions of koṭis.
Some held precious flowers and scattered them in the air,
some presented wondrous melodies, their sounds lingering.
Dragon spirits raced through the mist, leading the way,
ghost soldiers flew on clouds, urging from behind.
Having departed the Shìzūn's Dharma assembly,
who knows what splendor and majesty will be proclaimed next.
(The sūtra says): "Thereupon Wénshū" to "entered the city."
(Spoken) Wénshū accepted,
leading the multitude forward.
Five hundred Śrāvakas accompanied him,
eight thousand Bodhisattvas were his companions.
Thereupon, at the Ānyuán assembly,
the listeners were countless.
They accompanied the great beings all the way to Píyé,
following Wénshū and passing through the abbot's residence.
It was springtime,
a thousand flowers vied in laughter in the gardens and forests;
the season was in its verdant prime,
myriad trees all flourished in the mountains and fields.
Thus, Wénshūshīlì
personally went to the abbot's residence.
He then assumed a majestic bearing,
arranging his retinue and belongings.
Thereupon, a jeweled crown covered his head,
and necklaces adorned his body.
He bade farewell to the Shìzūn on the platform of a thousand flowers,
and inquired about the lay practitioner in the one-zhàng room.
Dragon spirits led the way,
Bodhisattvas welcomed him from the front.
Auspicious qi filled the sky,
heavenly flowers shimmered in the sun.
Banners and pennants were arrayed in pairs along the road,
dragon-shaped ceremonial standards advanced in ranks.
The brilliant light vied with the dazzling sun,
elegant music mingled with梵音.
Eight thousand Bodhisattvas attended,
five hundred Śrāvakas accompanied him.
At once they bowed in farewell to the compassionate Zūn,
all heading to Wéimó to inquire about his illness.
At this time,
people were numerous,
voices clamored.
Throngs in the clouds,
cheers beneath the sun.
Auspicious qi stopped at the emerald peaks,
propitious iridescent clouds spread far and wide.
His ushṇīṣa stood tall,
his jeweled robe sparkled.
He wore a marvelous robe of six zhū,
and a seven-jeweled crown.
Gold threads were pressed into layers,
fragrant breezes stirred, wafting gracefully.
Leading magnificent lions,
each step could summon the wind.
Sitting on a thousand-petaled lotus,
it contained the emerald hue of watery mist.
Leading the multitude of heavenly followers,
departing from the Buddha's assembly at Ānyuán.
Heavenly maidens and heavenly youths,
welcomed from the front and circled from behind.
Transformed beings in the sky,
gazed from afar in the clouds.
He arranged his majestic bearing,
and directed his followers.
Everyone in Píyé city saw him,
all saying his divine power was immense.
Wénshū's retinue was truly commendable,
temporarily bidding farewell to Múnní, the sacred master's home.
Tens of thousands of teams of immortal youths led the way,
Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges accompanied him.
Golden crowns and jade pendants shone with azure (clear sun) light,
cloud robes and pearl necklaces caught the emerald haze.
Lions, mighty and roaring, led in front and behind,
turning to sit upon precious lotus flowers.
(Interruption) The retinue, high and low, lined the road,
layer upon layer reflecting the golden platform.
Golden censers and jade tables appeared in the sky,
dragon-shaped ceremonial standards and banners unfurled in the mist.
Bodhisattvas following were all joyous,
Śrāvakas behind them laughed heartily.
Before one could clearly open one's eyes to see,
they had already arrived at Wéimó's assembly.
Truly rare,
King among the Dharma,
manifesting traces provisionally as Miàojíxiáng.
Golden-purple light shone from the jewels within his robe,
from between his eyebrows, a white hair-light occasionally radiated.
Auspicious signs on the flower platform appeared from time to time,
the wondrous lotus seat had a special name.
In an instant, they passed through the abbot's room,
all eagerly wishing to bow to the King among the Dharma.
(Interruption) Śrāvakas filled the empty sky in vast numbers,
Bodhisattvas clamored as they entered the room.
Umbrellas and canopies filled the path beneath the cloud-heads,
banners and flowers in the mist echoed with clear sounds.
Dragon spirits, vigorous and strong, all snapped their fingers,
praising Wénshū's purplish-gold countenance.
They filled Wéimó's abbot's room,
whether ordinary or sagely, thousands upon thousands of layers.
(Interruption) The accompanying listeners were countless,
all stood before Wénshū's precious seat.
The Eight Legions ceased their chanting of fish-梵曲,
the Four Kings' retinue encircled the golden lotus.
In the sky, only heavenly flowers were seen falling,
in the clouds, only the smoke of dragon's brain incense was heard.
Myriad millions of listeners were vast and numerous,
a thousand groups of sagely beings were bustling and clamoring.
(Sūtra) Wénshū's retinue was truly marvelous,
ordinary and sagely beings accompanied him in millions of koṭis.
Bodhisattvas surrounded the precious seat on both sides,
Śrāvakas encircled the flower platform on all four sides.
From the Ānyuán assembly, they gazed and bowed from afar,
