in the abbot's feast, auspicious splendor unfolded.
The householder saw Wénshū enter the room,
how he arranged himself will also be proclaimed.
Volume One of "Wénshū Wèn Jí" (Mañjuśrī's Inquiry into Illness).
Now, as for the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
the gates of heaven open,
the doors of hell are flung wide,
the karma of the three evil realms is extinguished,
and the ten good deeds increase.
For all the monks, this is the day of *Pravāraṇā* [at the end of] the summer retreat.
On this day, blessings gather,
and all the deities, the eight divisions of *Nāga*s and *Deva*s,
all come to seek blessings.
Those who provide offerings receive present-life blessings and resources,
and for the deceased, it secures rebirth in a superior realm.
Thus, the *Yúlánpén* with a hundred flavors
is formally offered to the Three Jewels.
Relying on the radiant grace of the great assembly,
it rescues those in dire straits, as if hanging upside down.
In ancient times, when the Buddha was alive,
there was a disciple named Mùlián.
Before he left home and became a monk,
his name was Luóbǔ.
He deeply believed in the Three Jewels,
and revered the Mahāyāna.
At one time, he wished to travel to another country for trade,
so he divided his wealth and treasures,
instructing his mother to prepare a vegetarian feast in his absence,
to make offerings to all Buddhas, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, and all beggars.
After Luóbǔ departed,
his mother developed a mind of stinginess and avarice,
and all the wealth and resources he had entrusted
she secretly concealed.
Her son returned home not many days or months later,
having completed his business.
His mother said to her son: "According to your instructions,
I prepared a feast and created blessings."
Because of this deception of both ordinary people and saints,
when her life ended, she consequently fell into the Avīci Hell,
suffering all manner of intense torments.
After Luóbǔ completed three weeks of mourning rituals,
he immediately went to the Buddha and became a monk.
Following the karmic habits of his past lives,
he heard the Dharma and attained the fruit of an Arhat.
He then used his spiritual eye to search for his kind mother,
but throughout the six paths of transmigration,
he could not find her.
Mùlián arose from his meditation,
and with sorrow, consulted the World-Honored One: "Where is my kind mother enjoying happiness?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Mùlián: "Your mother has already fallen into Avīci,
and is suffering all kinds of torments.
Although you have attained the holy fruit,
what can you do?
If it is not the day of the summer retreat's victorious release for the monastics of the ten directions,
only with their collective power can she be saved."
Therefore, the Buddha, out of compassion,
opened this expedient means,
to establish the *Yúlánpén* festival,
which is precisely this matter.
Ever since Luóbǔ's parents passed away,
he performed mourning rituals and observed abstinence for three weeks.
Hearing joyous music brought him no joy, harming his countenance;
eating delicious food held no sweetness, hurting his sinews and bones.
He heard that the Tathāgata was in the Deer Park,
and had compassion for all humans and *Deva*s.
Now I follow the path and seek the Tathāgata,
going to the Twin Grove to ask the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha slowly approached,
and bowed his head to the *Héshàng*, the two-legged honored one.
To his left and right were the great multitude of *Śakra* and *Brahmā*,
to the east and west were the great generals *Sànzhīshén*.
On his chest, the *svastika* symbol was of crystal color,
and behind his head, the circular halo was like the moon's disk.
If you wish to know about the hundred treasures and thousand flowers above,
they are exactly like the five-colored clouds in the sky.
This disciple is foolish, dwelling in the five desires,
unable to abandon greed and hatred.
It is directly because of my heavy karma accumulated throughout life,
that calamity has reached my kind mother, causing her to enter the gate of springs.
I only fear that impermanence will press upon me,
and I will sink in the sea of suffering, the ford of birth and death.
I pray the Buddha, out of compassion, will deliver this disciple,
so I may single-mindedly follow the path and repay my two parents.
The World-Honored One, upon hearing Luóbǔ's words,
knew his uprightness and lack of evil intent.
He counted on his fingers, first discussing the Four Noble Truths,
then explaining that one should destroy the seven defilements.
Even if one accumulates treasures as high as the clouds,
it is not as good as teaching someone to become a monk for a short time.
It is exactly like a blind turtle encountering a floating log,
or like a great fire producing a lotus flower.
The raging fiery house is hard to escape,
the vast sea of suffering is boundless.
It is directly for the sake of sentient beings' discriminations
that the Tathāgata thus established the three vehicles.
The Buddha called Ānán to shave his head,
and his clothes transformed into a *kāṣāya*.
Immediately he attained the fruit of an Arhat,
and afterwards received the *Prātimokṣa*.
Luóbǔ was then before the Buddha,
and from the golden censer, fragrant smoke gently rose.
The six kinds of jade trees shook the great earth,
and the four flowers displayed their forms against the clear sky.
A thousand kinds of brocade adorned the bedding,
and ten thousand pearl banners hung in the air.
The Buddha himself proclaimed, "My disciple,
is named the great Mùlián, who possesses divine powers."
At that time, Mùlián, under the Twin Grove trees,
attained the fruit of an Arhat.
Why was this so?
According to the *Fǎhuājīng*, it is said: "The poor son first received his wages,
and then removed dung";
this is precisely that.
First attaining the fruit of an Arhat,
then afterward learning the Way.
Look at Mùlián's place of meditation in the deep mountains:
Mùlián, having shaved his beard and hair,
then entered the deep mountains.
In a secluded, pure, uninhabited place,
he then meditated, contemplating emptiness.
Meditating, contemplating emptiness, knowing good and evil,
subduing the mind and dwelling the mind without attachment.
Facing objects, still and unwavering,
the left foot must still press the right foot.
He sat upright on a large rock,
with his tongue touching his upper palate.
All the white bones were empty,
and the breath was without entanglement.
At that time, herds of deer ceased their cries in the forest,
approaching the clear pond to gaze towards the sea.
Under the bright moon in the courtyard, he listened with his Dharma eye,
under the green pines on the mountain, he sat only in meditation.
The sea mists on the horizon glowed like rosy clouds,
beyond the ridges, green mountains gazed at the watchtowers.
The autumn wind rustled through the forest,
yellow leaves drifted and floated on the water.
Mùlián peacefully sat in the realm of emptiness,
calming his mind both internally and externally, gradually cultivating.
He attained the *Śrāvaka* status, dwelling in the holy land,
entering and exiting the mountains with freedom.
Mùlián arose from his meditation,
swiftly performing supernatural powers.
He came like urgent thunderbolts,
and left like a gust of wind.
Sea geese cried at their snares,
and ospreys escaped their nets and cages.
The mists and clouds in the pond were emerald,
the sky was clear, and the distant path was red.
With divine powers, he gained freedom,
tossing his begging bowl, he soared into the sky.
At that moment, in an instant,
he ascended to the Brahma Heaven palace.
Mùlián arrived at the celestial court,
hearing only the sound of drums and music.
Red towers half-reflected golden palaces,
and emerald windows were entirely made of white jade.
He knocked on the door three or five times with his staff,
and tears involuntarily welled up on his chest.
An elder came out and spoke with him,
first discussing loyalty and filial piety with palms joined.
He began: "Elder, do you recognize me?
This humble monk is from Nányánfú Tí,
I lost my parents when I was young.
My family was very wealthy but had few children and grandchildren,
and I was all alone with no companions.
My kind mother was named Qīngtí,
and my father was named Fǔxiàng.
Throughout their lives, they performed many deeds creating fields of merit,
after their passing, they should have been reborn in this heaven.
What a pitiful, rich, noble, and extravagant place,
just seeing it makes one's heart joyful.
Bells and drums clanged in harmony with elegant sounds,
and the *se* zithers also played with bright, distant sounds.
Their sorrowful, laborious efforts never ceased,
the grace of breastfeeding is hard to forget.
Are they well and at peace after our separation?
I have come here to seek them out."
The elder heard his words, and his expression seemed sad,
his heart was bewildered, and he spoke slowly:
"This disciple has one son in Yánfú,
but I do not recall having a son who became a monk.
Do not blame this *Héshàng* for questioning you closely,
there are many types of human relationships in the world.
At first glance, your words seem simple,
but when holding one's breath, it becomes a bit difficult.
In the mundane world, there are many with the same names and surnames,
and hundreds of similar appearances.
I don't recall ever knowing such a countenance,
I just keep thinking, but there's nowhere to place it.
O *Shālì*, you have come to recognize me with such bitter earnestness,
please tell me more about the affairs of our home."
Mùlián 到 tiāngōng 尋父,
至一門見長者,
白言長者: "貧道小時,
名字 Luóbo.
父母亡没已後,
投佛出家,
剃除鬚髮,
號曰 Dàmùqiánlián,
神通第一."
長者見說小時名字,
即知是兒: "別久,
好在已否?"
Luóbo Mùlián 認得慈父,
起居問訊已了: "慈母今在何方受於快樂?"
長者報言 Luóbo: "汝母生存在日,
與我行業不同.
我修十善五戒,
死後神識得生天上.
汝母平生在日,
廣造諸罪.
命終之後,
遂墮地獄.
汝向 Yánfú Tí mínglù 之中,
尋問阿孃,
即知去處."
Mùlián 聞語,
便辭長者,
頓身下降南 Yánfú Tí,
向冥路之中,
尋覓阿孃不見,
且見八九個男子女人,
閒閒無事,
Mùlián 向前問其事由之處:
但且莫禮拜.
賢者是何人,
此間都集會.
閒閒無一事,
來遊城郭外.
貧道今朝至此間,
心中只手深相怪."
諸人答言啟和尚:
"只為同名復同姓,
名字交錯被追來.
勘當恰經三五日,
無事得放卻歸迴.
早被妻兒送墳墓,
獨自拋我在荒郊.
四邊更無親伴侶,
狐狼鴉鵲競分張.
宅舍破壞無投處,
王邊披訴語聲哀.
判放作鬼閒無事,
受其餘報更何災.
而今死生路已隔,
一掩泉門不再開.
塚上縱有千般食,
何曾濟得腹中飢.
號咷大哭終無益,
徒煩攪紙作錢財.
寄語家中男女道,
勸令修福救冥災."
Mùlián 良久而言: "識一 Qīngtí Fūrén 已否?"
諸人答言: "盡皆不識."
Mùlián 又問: "Yánluó Dàwáng 住在何處?"
諸人答言: "和尚,
向北更行數步,
遙見三重門樓,
有千萬個壯士皆持刀棒,
即是 Yánluó Dàwáng 門."
Mùlián 聞語,
向北更行數步,
即見三重門樓,
有壯士驅無量罪人入來.
Mùlián 向前尋問阿孃不見,
路旁大哭,
哭了前行,
被所由將見於王.
門官引入見大王,
問 Mùlián 事〔由〕之處:
大王既見 Mùlián 入,
合掌逡巡而欲立.
"和尚有沒事由來?"
連忙案後相挹:
"慚愧闍梨至此間,
弟子處在冥途間,
拷定罪人生死.
雖然不識和尚,
早個知其名字.
為當佛使至此間?
別有家私事意?
Tàishān 定罪卒難移,
總是天曹地筆批.
罪人業報隨緣起,
造次何人救得伊.
腥血凝脂長夜臭,
惡染闍梨清淨衣.
冥途不可多時住,
伏願闍梨早去歸."
Mùlián 啟言: "不得說,
大王照知否?
貧道生年有父母,
日夜持齋常斷午.
據其行事在人間,
亡過合生於淨土.
天堂獨有阿耶居,
慈母諸天覓總無.
計亦不應過地獄,
只恐皇天橫被誅.
追訪蹤由天地遍,
悲嗟悔恨乃長噓.
業報若來過此界,
大王曾亦得知否?"
Mùlián 言訖,
大王便喚上殿,
乃見 Dìzàng Púsà,
便即禮拜.
"汝覓阿孃來?"
Mùlián 啟言: "是覓阿孃來."
"汝母生存在日,
廣造諸罪,
無量無邊,
當墮地獄.
汝且向前,
吾當即至."
大王便喚業官、伺命、司錄,
應時即至.
"是和尚阿孃名 Qīngtí Fūrén,
亡後多少時?"
業官啟言大王: "Qīngtí Fūrén 亡來已經三載,
配罪案總在天曹錄事司 Tàishān Dūwèi 一本."
王喚善惡二童子,
向 Tàishān 檢 Qīngtí Fūrén 在何地獄,
大王啟言和尚: "共童子相隨,
問 Wǔdào Jiāngjūn,
應知去處."
Mùlián 聞語,
便辭大王即出.
行經數步,
即至 Nàihé 之上,
見無數罪人,
脫衣掛在樹上,
大哭數聲,
欲過不過,
迴迴惶惶,
五五三三,
抱頭啼哭.
Mùlián 問其事由之處:
Nàihé 之水西流急,
碎石巉巖行路澀.
衣裳脫掛樹枝傍,
被趁不教時向立.
河畔聞他點名字,
胸前不覺沾衣濕.
今日方知身死來,
雙雙傍樹長悲泣.
生時我捨事吾珍,
金軒駟馬駕朱輪.
為言萬古無遷改,
誰知早個化為塵.
嗚呼哀哉心裡痛,
徒埋白骨為高塚.
南槽龍馬子孫乘,
北牖香車妻妾用.
異口咸言不可論,
長噓嘆息更何怨.
造罪之人落地獄,
作善之者必生天.
如今各自隨緣業,
定是相逢後迴難.
握手叮嚀須努力,
回頭拭淚飽相看.
耳裡唯聞唱道急,
萬眾千群驅向前.
牛頭把棒河南岸,
獄卒擎叉水北邊.
水裡之人眼盼盼,
岸頭之者淚涓涓.
早知別後（到沒）艱辛地,
悔不生時作福田.
Mùlián 問言 Nàihé 樹下人曰: "天堂地獄乃非虛,
行惡不論天所罪,
應是冥靈亦共誅.
貧道慈親不積善,
亡魂亦復落三塗.
聞道將來入地獄,
但曰知其消息否?"
罪人總見 Mùlián Shī,
一切啼哭損雙眉:
"弟子死來年月近,
和尚慈親實不知.
我等生時多造罪,
今日受苦方始悔.
Even if wives and concubines fill the mountains and rivers,
who would be willing to die and take their place?
When will I ever again depart the gate of the underworld [Quánmén],
to report to my children and grandchildren at home:
'There is no need for white jade coffins,
nor to toil with gold to bury the tomb mound.
Long sorrowful laments are ultimately useless;
I will not hear drums, music, or stringed songs.
If you wish for the deceased to be free from suffering,
there is nothing better than cultivating merit to save the souls of the departed.'
The Monk then returned,
and conveyed the message to all the people,
instructing them to accumulate blessings [zàofú]
to save the departed.
Except for the Buddha [Fó] alone,
there is no way to achieve salvation.
May the Monk's Bodhi [Pútí] and Nirvāṇa [Nièpán]
remain ever-present and never perish.
Carrying all sentient beings,
diligently sharpening the sword of wisdom [zhìhuì jiàn],
sweeping away the forest of afflictions and eradicating them,
extending universal compassion throughout the world,
such are the great vows of all Buddhas [Zhūfó].
Should one escape from Avīci Hell [Nílí],
it is due to the Monk's universal compassion as a kind parent.
After Mùlián [Mùlián] had asked,
he continued to walk forward.
At that moment, in the middle,
he arrived at the seat of the General of the Five Paths [Wǔdào Jiāngjūn],
where he would ask for news of his mother [āniáng].
The General of the Five Paths [Wǔdào Jiāngjūn] had a fierce and evil nature;
his golden armor shone brightly, and sword lights intertwined.
To his left and right were over a million people,
all with swift flying hands and feet.
Their shouts were like thunder, startling and shaking;
their angry eyes shone like lightning, dazzling the cranes.
Some had their bellies split open and hearts exposed;
others had their faces peeled raw.
Even though Mùlián [Mùlián] was a saint,
his soul was startled and his胆 [dǎn] dropped.
Mùlián [Mùlián] wept, thinking of his kind mother [cípīn],
his divine powers swift as wind and clouds.
If one heard of a crucial place in the underworld [Míngtú],
none surpassed this great general.
Spears were gathered on both sides, blocking the main road;
on the east and west, staffs stood with over ten thousand people.
Even if one raised one's eyes to look southwest,
one would see the imposing God of the Five Paths [Wǔdào Shén].
guarding this path for how many eons.
A thousand armies and ten thousand multitudes decide their punishments and names,
each from the start following their own karma [yuányè].
"My humble mother [címǔ bàngxíng tán],
her soul drifts between the paths of the underworld.
If one asks where the three evil paths [sāntú] are most painful,
all say it is the Ghost Gate Pass [Guǐmén Guān] of the Five Paths [Wǔdào].
The path of beasts [chùshēng èdào] is especially abundant with people;
the good path of heaven [hǎodào tiāntáng] is idle morning and night.
All sinners pass through here;
I pray, General, for your inspection."
The General clasped his hands and addressed the Saṃghā [Shélí]: "There is no need to weep and damage your countenance.
This path always has sands as numerous as the Ganges;
if suddenly asked who Qīngtí [Qīngtí] is, who would know?
Mount Tai [Tàishān] has many important registers,
inspected by the Heavenly Office [Tiāncáo] and the Underworld Bureau [Dìfǔ] simultaneously.
All officials know their names from the documents,
and warrants come down passing through here.
Today, this disciple is an official of the underworld [míngguān],
and will (briefly) search and inspect for the Saṃghā [Shélí].
If by chance her name is found,
it will not be difficult to trace her whereabouts."
The General asked his subordinates: "Have you seen a Lady Qīngtí [Qīngtí Fūrén]?"
A Dūguān [Dūguān] on the left replied to the General: "Three years ago,
there was a Lady Qīngtí [Qīngtí Fūrén]
who was summoned by a warrant from Avīci Hell [Ābí Dìyù];
she is currently suffering in Avīci Hell [Ābí Dìyù]."
When Mùlián [Mùlián] heard this,
he addressed the General: "General, you reported to the Monk [Héshang]
that all sinners are judged by the King [Wáng],
and only then do they descend.
Why did my humble mother [āniáng] not see the King [Wáng]?"
The General reported to the Monk [Héshang]: "There are two kinds of people in the world who do not see the King's [Wáng] face: the first kind,
who in their lifetime [píngshēng zài rì]
cultivated the Ten Virtuous Deeds [shíshàn] and Five Precepts [wǔjiè],
their consciousness [shénshí] after death is born in heaven,
〔and they do not see the King's face〕.
The second kind,
who in their lifetime [shēngcún zài rì]
did not cultivate good karma [shànyè]
and committed many sins,
after their death,
immediately enter hell,
and also do not see the King's [Wáng] face.
Only those who are half evil and half good [bàn'è bànshàn zhī rén]
will see the King's [Wáng] face for judgment,
and only then will they be reborn [tuōshēng],
receiving retribution according to their karma [yuányè].
" When Mùlián [Mùlián] heard this,
he immediately went to the various hells to search for his mother's [āniáng] whereabouts:
Mùlián's [Mùlián] tears fell as he remembered his carefree mother [yì xiāoyáo];
the karma [yèbào] of sentient beings drifts like the wind.
His kind mother [cípīn] reached a place of extreme hardship;
her soul [húnpò] had already vanished at that time.
Iron wheels often descended from the sky;
fierce flames constantly burned beneath her feet.
Her heart and intestines were scattered everywhere;
her bones at times seemed like rotten charcoal.
Ten thousand bronze birds pecked at her heart;
boiling iron liquid poured over her head a thousand times.
May I ask, is the suffering of the sword-tree [jiànshù] ahead
like being ground and chopped at the waist?
It cannot be spoken of;
congealed fat and shattered blood [níngzhī suì xuè] like brine.
Vast and circuitous for hundreds of miles,
towering down for one yojana [yǒuxún].
Ten thousand iron spears were placed beneath it, and a thousand layers of smoke and fire blocked the four gates.
May I ask what kind of sins are punished here?
It is only the sin of murder in Jambudvīpa [Yánfú].
After Mùlián [Mùlián] spoke, he continued to walk forward,
and in a moment,
reached a hell.
Mùlián [Mùlián] addressed the Lord of Hell [Yùzhǔ]: "Is Lady Qīngtí [Qīngtí Fūrén] in this hell?
She is my humble mother [āniáng],
so I have come to search for her."
The Lord of Hell [Yùzhǔ] reported to the Monk [Héshang]: "This hell is full of men;
there are no women.
Go forward and ask in the Sword Mountain Hell [Dāoshān Dìyù];
you will surely find her there."
Mùlián [Mùlián] walked forward and reached another hell,
named Sword Mountain [Dāoshān] on the left,
and Sword Tree [Jiànshù] on the right.
In this hell,
sharp swords faced each other,
and blood flowed in trickles.
He saw the Lord of Hell [Yùzhǔ] driving countless sinners into this hell.
Mùlián [Mùlián] asked: "What is this hell called?"
A Rākṣasa [Luóchà] replied: "This is the Sword Mountain and Sword Tree Hell [Dāoshān Jiànshù Dìyù]."
Mùlián [Mùlián] asked: "What sins did the sinners in this hell commit [zuò hé zuìyè]
to fall into this hell?"
The Lord of Hell [Yùzhǔ] reported: "The sinners in this hell,
in their lifetime,
damaged the permanent property of the monastery [qīn sǔn chángzhù],
defiled the monastery [yúní qiélán],
liked to use the monastery's [chángzhù] water and fruit,
and stole the monastery's [chángzhù] firewood.
Today, they are made to climb the sword-tree [jiànshù] with their hands,
where every limb and joint is severed:
white bones lie scattered horizontally and vertically on Sword Mountain [Dāoshān],
and there are tens of thousands of human heads on the Sword Tree [Jiànshù].
If one wishes not to climb Sword Mountain [Dāoshān],
nothing surpasses filling the monastery grounds [sìjiā] with good soil.
Planting fruit trees in the monastery [qiélán],
and donating seeds, doubling the permanent property [chángzhù].
Ah, these sinners are unspeakable;
they have suffered countless eons [léi jié shòuzuì dù héngshā]
and have not yet escaped since the Buddha's Nirvāṇa [Fó Nièpán].
This prison is hundreds of miles east and west,
sinners run chaotically, shoulders jostling.
The wind of karma [yèfēng] blows fire to burn them from the front,
and jailers thrust pitchforks from behind.
Their bodies and heads are shattered like tiles instantly,
their hands and feet immediately turn to powder.
Boiling iron with rising light scorches their mouths;
those it hits are pierced through the left and hollowed through the right.
Bronze arrows fly sideways, shooting into their eyes;
sword-wheels cut vertically from the sky.
It is said that for a thousand years they will not be human again,
the iron rakes gather them, and they are made alive again."
Mùlián heard the words,
wept and sighed,
and stepped forward to ask the Jail Master: "Is there a Fūren Qīngtí
in this hell?
" The Jail Master replied to the monk: "What relative
is she?" Mùlián replied: "She is this humble monk's loving mother."
The Jail Master reported to the monk: "There is no Fūren Qīngtí in this hell.
In the hells ahead,
all are women;
you might find her there."
Mùlián heard this,
and proceeded further.
He reached a hell
about one yóuxún in height,
where black smoke billowed,
and a foul stench filled the sky.
He saw a horse-headed luóchà
holding an iron fork,
standing proudly.
Mùlián asked: "What is the name of this hell?"
The luóchà replied: "This is the Bronze Pillar and Iron Bed Hell."
Mùlián asked: "What sins
did the sinners in this hell commit
during their lives
to be condemned to this hell?"
The Jail Master replied: "During their lives,
women with men,
and men with women,
who engaged in sexual misconduct on their parents' beds,
disciples on their teachers' beds,
or servants on their masters' beds,
shall fall into this hell.
East and west are impassable,
men and women
are mingled half and half."
Women lie on iron beds, nailed through their bodies;
men embrace bronze pillars, their chests rotting away.
Iron drills are always kept with sharp blades,
their greedy teeth are as quick as an auger.
When their intestines are empty, they are filled with iron balls;
when they cry out for thirst, they are灌 (irrigated) with molten iron.
Thorns pierce their bellies like knives splitting them apart;
swords and halberds in the air leap and scatter like stars.
Knives gouge their flesh and bones, tearing them to pieces;
swords cut their livers and intestines, severing them inch by inch.
It cannot be described;
hell and heaven are counterparts.
Heaven is filled with joy day and night,
but in hell, no one comes to rescue them.
If one's parents are still alive and one performs good deeds for them,
they receive one-seventh of the merit.
Even if the East Sea turns into mulberry fields,
those suffering will still not be released.
Mùlián finished speaking,
and proceeded further.
After a moment,
he arrived at another hell,
and asked the Jail Master: "Is there a Fūren Qīngtí in this hell?"
The Jail Master replied: "Fūren Qīngtí,
is she your mother, reverend?"
Mùlián replied: "She is my loving mother."
The Jail Master reported to the monk: "Three years ago,
there was a Fūren Qīngtí who
also came to this hell.
She was summoned by a dispatch from Ābí Dìyù,
and is now in Ābí Dìyù."
Mùlián fainted and fell to the ground,
but after a long while, his breath returned,
and he gradually moved forward.
He then met a luóchà guarding the path and asked:
Mùlián walks with much sorrow and distress,
swords and blades by the roadside are like wild grass.
He turns sideways and hears from afar the realm of hell,
wind and fire roar at once.
Remembering his loving mother, his intestines almost break;
the path ahead is not far, he will arrive soon.
Suddenly he meets the Yèchā King,
who sits on the great road with his sword drawn.
He said: "This humble monk is a disciple of Shìjiā Rúlái Fó,
who has attained the Three Insights and transcended birth and death.
My sorrowful loving mother, named Qīngtí,
passed away and her soul fell here.
Just now I toured other hells,
and those I asked all said she was not there.
Recently it was said that my mother was taken to Ābí Dìyù,
and the General should also know about this matter.
Tell me truly whether she is there or not, do not hesitate,
the milk nourishment in the human world is the deepest kindness.
Hearing of my loving mother, my bones and marrow ache,
who can quickly know the heart of this humble monk?"
The yèchā heard the words, his heart trembling,
and he spoke directly, without further hesitation:
"Your filial piety, reverend, is rare in ancient and modern times;
you do not fear the netherworld to personally tour and search.
Fūren Qīngtí seems to be there,
[(missing characters)]
Iron is poured to form the city, copper makes the walls.
Karmic winds roar and blow at once;
those who arrive have their bodies scattered like wreckage.
I advise you, Zhélí, to return early to your abode;
it is a futile effort to search here.
It is better to go quickly to see Rúlái;
what good is it to beat your chest in regret?"
Mùlián, hearing of the difficulty of hell,
immediately turned around.
He threw his bowl into the air,
and in an instant,
he arrived at the Suōluólín.
He circled the Fó three times,
then sat to one side,
gazing at the Venerable Countenance,
his eyes not leaving it for a moment.
He spoke to the Shìzūn:
"It has been a long time since I left Rúlái,
seeking her traces throughout heaven and earth.
Although my father was born in heaven,
I have never met my loving mother again.
I heard she is suffering in Ābí Dìyù,
thinking of it, my liver and intestines break.
Fierce fires, dragons, and serpents make it difficult to approach;
I have no means to quickly find a way.
Rúlái's divine power can move mountains and seas,
all sentient beings cherish and adore you.
A distressed minister naturally knows how to report to his lord;
how can I see my loving mother again?"
The Shìzūn called out: "Dà Mùlián,
do not weep in sorrow.
The sins of the world are like a rope;
they are not brought upon by others.
Quickly bring me my tin staff,
which can remove the Eight Difficulties and Three Disasters.
Just diligently chant my name,
and hell will open for you at that time."
Mùlián, relying on the Fó's divine power,
launched himself downward,
as swift as a wind-arrow.
In an instant,
he arrived at Ābí Dìyù.
In the sky, he saw fifty ox-headed and horse-faced beings,
luóchà and yèchā,
with teeth like sword trees,
mouths like blood basins,
voices like thunder,
eyes like lightning,
on duty for the Heavenly Court.
Upon seeing Mùlián,
they called out from afar: "Reverend, do not come!
This is not a good path;
this is the road to hell.
In the black smoke to the west
is all the poisonous qi of hell;
if it touches you, Reverend, you will turn to dust:
Reverend, have you not heard that in Ābí Dìyù,
even iron and stone suffer calamity?
Where is hell, you ask?
It is in the furious black smoke to the west!"
Mùlián chanted the Fó's name countless times,
thinking, "Hell is originally my home."
He wiped away tears in the air and shook his tin staff;
the ghosts and spirits immediately fell like flax.
White sweat flowed like pouring rain,
he was dazed and unconsciously sighed.
They dropped their three-edged clubs from their hands,
and threw their six-pronged forks far from their arms.
Rúlái sent me to see my loving mother,
to save Pōzhā from Ābí Dìyù.
Mùlián passed through without hindrance,
the jailers looked at each other, not daring to stop him.
Mùlián (目連) walked forward,
arriving at a hell.
A hundred or so paces away,
he was drawn in by the fiery氣,
and almost fell backward.
This Ābí (阿鼻) hell
had iron cities towering high,
vast and reaching to the clouds,
a forest of swords and halberds,
and layers of knives and spears.
Sword trees, a thousand *xún* (尋) high, were sharp and pointed,
needles rubbing against each other.
Myriad knife mountains stretched horizontally,
rugged and falling chaotically.
Fierce fires surged and roared like thunder,
leaping and filling the sky.
Clusters of sword-wheels shone like stars,
dust spreading across the ground.
Iron serpents spat fire,
scales spread on all sides.
Bronze dogs sucked in smoke,
barking loudly from three directions.
Caltrops rained down from the sky,
piercing the chests of men.
Awls and drills flew sideways from above,
gouging and stabbing the backs of women.
Iron rakes gouged eyes,
crimson blood flowing westward.
Bronze forks cut into waists,
white fat drawn eastward.
On the knife mountains,
entering the charcoal furnace,
skulls were shattered,
flesh and bone rotted,
sinews and skin broke,
arms were severed.
Splintered flesh splattered outside the four gates,
congealed blood profusely covered the sides of the prison walls.
Cries of anguish reached the heavens,
precarious and trembling.
[Sound of] thunder on the ground,
rumbling and distant.
Upward, clouds and smoke scattered diffusely,
downward, iron clanged chaotically.
Arrow-haired demons scurried about,
bronze-mouthed birds cried out noisily.
Tens of thousands of jailers,
all with ox heads and horse faces.
Even if one had a heart of iron and stone,
their soul would tremble with fear.
Mùlián (目連) held his staff and listened intently,
his thoughts on Ābí (阿鼻) surging.
All other hells had a respite,
but this Ābí (阿鼻) hell saw no stopping.
Multitudes like the sands of the Ganges entered simultaneously,
their bodies transforming into a single form.
If one person were to enter alone,
their body would still fill the iron-encircled city.
[Sound of] clanging, difficult, difficult to shake the iron,
precarious in the cloudy sky,
rumbling and clanging, encompassing the earth grandly.
Long serpents, glistening, thrice black,
large birds, rugged, with two green wings.
Ten thousand red furnaces fanned broad charcoal,
a thousand layers of crimson flames spewed meteors.
East and west, iron drills pierced cruel tendons,
left and right, bronze pincers shot into eyeballs.
Golden chains rained down like wind and rain,
molten iron poured from the sky.
Alas, how painful, unbearable!
Long nails were driven into their backs and bellies.
When Mùlián (目連) saw this, he cried out, "Wondrous!"
He focused his mind on chanting Buddha's name thousands of times.
The wind blew poisonous gas, which he breathed in from afar,
watching his body turn into a pile of ash.
With one shake, the black city gates and locks fell.
With another shake, the two doors of the underworld opened.
Mùlián (目連) had not yet called out when
jailers, holding forks, came out:
"Monk, whose news do you seek?
This city is vast, ten thousand *yóuxún* (由旬) wide.
No one can close it in a hurry.
Swords and blades gleam, each a tiny point.
Those suffering are full of sorrow and regret.
Great fires blaze, illuminating the ground,
thick smoke and mist darken the sky.
Suddenly we see a *shélí* (闍梨) standing here,
someone we have never met before.
By all accounts, there should be no one else here.
This must be the compassionate power of the Three Jewels."
The hell-master said, "Monk, why did you open the gates of hell?"
[Mùlián (目連)] replied, "If I, the poor monk, did not open them, who would?
The World-Honored One sent something to open them."
The hell-master asked, "What did he send to open them?"
Mùlián (目連) replied to the hell-master, "He sent a twelve-ringed staff to open them."
The hell-master then asked, "Monk, why have you come here?"
Mùlián (目連) replied, "My mother is named Qīngtí Fūrén (青提夫人),
so I have come to look for her."
When the hell-master heard this,
he went back into the hell, to the top of a high tower.
He waved a white banner,
beat an iron drum,
asking, "Is Qīngtí Fūrén (青提夫人) in the first compartment?"
Qīngtí Fūrén (青提夫人) was not in the first compartment.
He proceeded to the second compartment,
waved a black banner,
beat an iron drum,
asking, "Is Qīngtí Fūrén (青提夫人) in the second compartment?"
She was not in the second compartment either.
He proceeded to the third compartment,
waved a yellow banner,
beat an iron drum,
asking, "Is Qīngtí Fūrén (青提夫人) in the third compartment?"
She was not there either.
He proceeded to the fourth compartment, and she was not there either.
He then went to the fifth compartment and asked,
and was also told no.
He proceeded to the sixth compartment,
and was also told Qīngtí Fūrén (青提夫人) was not there.
The hell-master went to the seventh compartment,
waved a green banner,
beat an iron drum,
asking, "Is Qīngtí Fūrén (青提夫人) in the seventh compartment?"
At that time, Qīngtí Fūrén (青提夫人) was in the seventh compartment.
Forty-nine long nails were driven into her body,
pinning her to an iron bed.
She dared not answer the hell-master.
The hell-master asked again, "Is Qīngtí Fūrén (青提夫人) in the seventh compartment?"
[Qīngtí Fūrén (青提夫人) replied,] "If you are looking for Qīngtí Fūrén (青提夫人),
this sinner is she."
"Why didn't you answer earlier?"
"I feared the hell-master would take me elsewhere to suffer more,
so I dared not answer."
The hell-master reported, "Outside the gate is a member of the Three Jewels,
with shaven beard and hair,
clothed in Dharma robes,
who claims to be your son,
and has come to visit you."
When Qīngtí Fūrén (青提夫人) heard this,
she thought for a long time,
and then reported to the hell-master, "I have no son who has become a monk.
Is this not a mistake?"
When the hell-master heard this,
he returned to the high tower,
and reported to the monk, "What is the matter,
that you falsely claim a sinner in hell is your mother?
Why do you lie without cause?"
When Mùlián (目連) heard this,
he wept tears like rain,
and replied to the hell-master, "The poor monk conveyed the message incorrectly just now.
When I was young, my name was Luóbo (羅卜).
After my parents passed away,
I became a monk under the Buddha,
shaved my beard and hair,
and was named Dà Mùqiánlián (大目乾連).
Hell-master, please do not be angry.
Please ask one more time."
When the hell-master heard this,
he returned to the seventh compartment,
and reported to the sinner, "The member of the Three Jewels outside, whose childhood name was Luóbo (羅卜),
after his parents passed away,
became a monk under the Buddha,
shaved his beard and hair,
and was named Dà Mùqiánlián (大目乾連)."
When Qīngtí Fūrén (青提夫人) heard this,
[she said,] "If the member of the Three Jewels outside,
whose childhood name was Luóbo (羅卜),
then he is indeed my son! This sinner's fragile heart aches for her child!"
When the hell-master heard this,
he helped Qīngtí Fūrén (青提夫人) up,
pulled out the forty-nine long nails,
unchained the iron锁 from her waist,
and with living staffs surrounding her,
drove her outside the gate,
where mother and son met.
[Sound of many footsteps],
living staffs like fish scales gathered like clouds.
Her thousand years of sin were not to be known,
blood and fluid flowed from her seven orifices.
Fierce flames erupted from her mother's mouth,
caltrops entered from the air with every step.
Like the sound of five hundred broken chariots,
how could her broken waist and spine be picked up?
Jailers held forks, blocking left and right,
ox-heads held chains, standing east and west.
She fell with every step, coming forward,
and Mùlián (目連) embraced his mother, wailing and weeping.
He cried, "Because of this unfilial son,
my compassionate mother fell into the three lower realms.
A family that accumulates good deeds will have abundant blessings,
but august Heaven would not kill the innocent.
My mother was once more beautiful than Pān Ān (潘安),
but now she is withered and utterly ruined.
I once heard that hell was full of suffering,
but only today do I know how difficult the path is.
Ever since the calamity, when my father and mother died,
I have always offered sacrifices at their graves daily."
“Nángnáng, have you eaten yet?
Your appearance is utterly haggard.”
As Ānáng heard Mùlián’s words,
she cried out, slapping her chest, tears streaming down.
“Yesterday, my son and I were separated by life and death;
who knew we would reunite today?
When Ānáng was alive, I did not cultivate blessings,
and all the ten evils were fully present in me.
At that time, I did not heed my son’s words,
and thus I suffer in this great Ābí Dìyù.
Ānáng was once extremely prosperous,
entering and exiting in embroidered curtains and brocade screens.
How can I endure this suffering of Nílí,
transformed into a hungry ghost for a thousand years?
My tongue is pulled out a thousand times in my mouth,
my chest is plowed a hundred times by an iron plow.
My bones, joints, muscles, and skin are severed everywhere,
without knives or swords, they wither away on their own.
In an instant, I die a thousand times,
then I am sung back to life.
Entering this prison, we all suffer together,
regardless of noble or humble, or even dukes and ministers.
If you diligently offer sacrifices at home,
you will only gain a reputation for filial piety in the village.
Even if you pour wine on graves,
it is not as good as transcribing a single line of sūtra.”
Mùlián sobbed, his tears falling like rain,
then immediately turned to consult the jailer:
“Although this poor monk is a renunciant,
my strength is too little to save my compassionate mother.
Mutual concealment among the five degrees of kinship
is a saying of ancient sages.
I only wish the jailer would release my mother,
and I will suffer perpetually in her place.”
The jailer was a man of stern temperament,
his face darkening with anger.
“Although this disciple serves as jailer,
all judgments are made by Píngděng Wáng.
If Ānáng has committed sins, Ānáng must bear them;
if Āshī has committed sins, Āshī must endure them.
The golden tablets and jade slips cannot be erased,
and no one will ever alter them.
The time for suffering has now arrived;
she must be brought to the hall of punishment, upon the knives and spears.
If the monk wishes for Ānáng to be released,
it is better to go home and burn precious incense.”
Mùlián’s compassionate mother’s voice was sorrowful,
as jailers with pitchforks urged her on from both sides.
As she was about to reach the prison entrance and fall,
she burst into a long lament: “Farewell!”
Qīngtí Fūrén, with one hand,
held the prison gate, looking back.
She said: “Farewell,
my sinful body’s precious child!
Nángnáng once practiced stinginess and jealousy,
not fearing the karmic retribution of future lives.
She said there was a heaven but no hell,
and slaughtered many pigs and sheep to sacrifice to ghosts and gods.
She only delighted in the immediate pleasures of her body,
unaware of the torment of deceased souls on the path to the underworld.
Now that I suffer the pains of Nílí,
only now do I know to regret my own actions.
When I regret, what path can I know?
Spilt water cannot be retrieved, as the common saying goes.
When will I escape the suffering of bōzhà?
How dare I hope to be reborn as a human again?
Āshī is a disciple of Rúlái Fó,
and truly understands the kindness of parents.
If one day you attain enlightenment,
do not forget Nángnáng’s hardships in hell.”
When Mùlián saw his mother depart,
he wished he could destroy himself.
He threw himself down as if Mount Tài collapsed,
blood splattering from all seven orifices.
He cried: “Nángnáng, please do not enter yet;
turn back and listen to your son’s words again.
The affection between mother and child is of heavenly nature,
and the grace of nurturing is natural.
When your son and Nángnáng part today,
when will we ever meet again?
How can I bear to hear this bōzhà suffering?
My heart is deeply pained and constantly anxious.
Hell does not permit substitution,
I can only wail and cry out in great resentment.
Since I cannot save you from separation,
your son will also die at the prison gate with Nángnáng.”
Mùlián saw his mother returning to hell,
heart-broken to the bone,
his voice hoarse with sobs.
Then he threw himself down,
like the collapse of the Five Great Mountains,
blood spurting from all seven orifices.
After a long while, he died,
then revived again,
pressing his hands on the ground, he stood up,
tidied his clothes,
and flew up into the air to the presence of Shìzūn:
Mùlián’s mind was utterly clouded,
people’s words seemed indistinct and unheard.
After a long period of contemplation, he awoke,
threw his bowl, and ascended into the air to question Shìzūn.
Mùlián complained to Fó about his bitter suffering,
fully describing the mountain of knives and forest of swords:
“By the Fó’s divine power and borrowed might,
I was able to see my compassionate mother in Ābí.
The iron city was filled with billowing smoke and fire,
the forest of sword blades had tens of thousands of layers.
Human fat and minced meat mixed with molten copper,
spurting flesh, containing fat, congealed in blood.
How can my kind parent’s appearance endure this,
suffering invasion by knives and swords through long nights?
Her white bones ascend the sword tree ten thousand times,
her fair face climbs the knife forest a hundred times.
Among all under heaven, what is most important?
The affection of parents, their grace is deepest.
Rúlái is the compassionate parent of all sentient beings,
may you illuminate this foolish and confused heart.”
Rúlái was inherently greatly compassionate,
hearing these words, he sadly furrowed his brows:
“Sentient beings rise and fall in the net of transmigration,
just like a rabbit caught in a net.
Your mother committed many sins in the past,
her soul fell directly into Ābí.
This sin will not be exhausted even after kalpas,
neither Fó nor ordinary mortals can know its extent.”
Fó called Ānán and the other disciples,
“I will go to the underworld myself to save her.”
Rúlái led the eight divisions of dragons and devas,
surrounded front and back,
emitting light and shaking the earth,
to save the suffering in hell:
Rúlái’s sacred wisdom is inherently balanced and fair,
with compassion, he saves sentient beings in hell.
Innumerable dragon gods and the eight divisions,
followed in a procession, moving forward.
Faintly, obscurely,
in heaven and on earth, none compare.
On the left, sinking;
on the right, disappearing;
like a towering mountain emerging from clouds.
Lofty and majestic,
heaven and hell opened at once.
Moving like rain,
stirring like thunder,
like the moon, round and rising from the sea.
Alone, majestically, with the gait of a lion,
the tiger walked proudly, the elephant king turned.
Heavenly music in the clouds played “Yángliǔ”,
fragrant “Luòméi” fell from the sky.
Dìshì came forward holding a jade treasure,
Fànwáng followed, presenting a golden tablet.
Beyond description, beyond discussion,
Rúlái’s divine power saves the Underworld.
Heavenly beings and the eight divisions on left and right,
four directions of gods serving as escorts east and west.
Between his brows, the white tuft of hair glowed with a thousand colors,
behind his neck, a circular halo of five-colored clouds.
Hell, touched by the light, completely dissipated,
the sword trees and knife forests were like shattered dust.
The jailers, touched by the light, all knelt,
joining their palms and bowing with sincere hearts.
Rúlái today rose with compassion,
hell was devastated and completely destroyed.
Iron pellets transformed into maṇi jewels,
knife mountains transformed into lapis lazuli ground.
molten copper transformed into water of merit.
Cool and winding, it flowed around the pond,
geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks paddled, their tears flowing.
Red waves generated green smoke night after night,
green trees produced purple clouds morning after morning.
All sinners ascended to heaven,
only Mùlián’s mother remained a hungry ghost.
Everything in hell transformed,
all by the sacred power of Shìjiā Fó.
Mùlián, by the power of the Buddha,
was able to see his compassionate mother.
Her roots of sin were deeply entangled,
her karmic power difficult to dispel.
Though she avoided the anguish of hell,
she fell into the path of hungry ghosts.
Her sorrows and sufferings were unequal,
her pains and joys vastly disparate.
Compared to her former life,
this was reduced by a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand times.
Her throat was like a needle's eye,
not even a drop of water could pass.
Her belly was like Mount Tài,
three rivers could not fill it.
She had never heard the name of broth or water,
for months and years,
she suffered the pain of starvation and emaciation.
From afar, she saw clear, cool water,
but close up, it turned into a river of pus.
Even if she obtained delicious, fragrant food,
it immediately transformed into raging fire.
"Mother, you are now starving and distressed,
your life hanging by a thread.
If you do not arouse compassion,
how can I be called a filial son?
The paths of life and death are separated,
a reunion is hard to anticipate.
To save you from this perilous state,
the matter should not be delayed."
"The monastic life
depends on the generosity of believers for its sustenance.
Even if there is communal food,
I fear it would be difficult to digest.
Your son will take leave of you, Mother, and go to the city of Wángshè
to fetch rice to meet you."
Mùlián bade farewell to his mother,
threw his bowl into the air,
and in an instant,
arrived in the city of Wángshè.
He begged for rice in order,
and came to the gate of a prominent elder.
The elder saw Mùlián begging for food at an untimely hour,
and questioned him about his whereabouts: "Monk, the mealtime
has already passed,
for what purpose will you use this begged rice?"
Mùlián replied to the elder:
"After my mother passed away,
her soul plunged into the Avīci Hell.
Recently, she was rescued by the Tathāgata,
her body like withered bones, her breath like a thread.
My heart is breaking inch by inch,
how can others know this cutting pain?
It is indeed not right to beg at an untimely hour,
but it is for my compassionate mother's food."
The elder was greatly astonished upon hearing these words,
and pondered the impermanence of life with unease.
Golden saddles forever sever the heart's attachment to jewels,
a jade-like face has no way to enter the dressing room.
Just sing,
just be joyful,
human life is as fleeting as a flickering candle.
Why seek happiness in paradise?
We only hear that the wicked in hell are many.
Sometimes eat,
sometimes wear,
do not learn from foolish people who hoard much.
It is better to extensively cultivate future causes,
who can guarantee life from morning till night?
Seeing each other, we do not perceive death,
money and possessions must not be cherished more than life.
One day, with hands clasped, entering a long coffin,
what good is empty watering over the tomb?
The wise use money to create many blessings,
the foolish use gold to buy fields and houses.
They toil their whole lives seeking wealth,
after death, it is all divided by others.
The elder suddenly became alarmed and doubtful upon hearing these words,
the auspicious fields of the Three Jewels are hard to encounter.
He urgently urged his attendants not to delay,
to bring rice from home for the ācārya.
Hell suddenly vanished completely,
clearly knowing the Buddhas are inconceivable.
The elder, holding the rice in his hand,
passed it to the ācārya and made a great vow:
"May not only the monk serve his compassionate mother,
but may all sinners in hell be satiated."
Mùlián obtained the fine rice,
and carried the bowl to offer to his compassionate mother.
At that time, he arrived at a vast wilderness,
holding a golden spoon and feeding her himself.
Though Lady Qīngtí suffered the pains of hell,
her avarice and stinginess had not yet been thoroughly removed.
Seeing her son bring the rice bowl,
she immediately felt possessive and parsimonious.
"The one who comes from the Three Jewels
is my son.
He fetched rice for me from the human world.
You all calm your minds.
I will help myself now,
how much more so will I be assisted!"
Mùlián presented the rice and bowl.
His mother, fearing it would be snatched away,
looked around at her companions,
shielding the bowl with her left hand,
and forming a ball of food with her right.
Before the food reached her mouth,
it turned into raging fire.
Though the elder's vow was profound,
it could not overcome her deeply ingrained avarice and obstruction.
Mùlián, seeing his mother like this,
felt his heart and liver torn as if by knives.
"My power as a Hearer is weak now,
my wisdom small, my person insignificant.
I can only appeal to the World-Honored One,
who must know the path to salvation."
Let's see where he fed his mother:
The lady saw the rice and went forward to meet it,
her avarice, not yet eating, merely contended empty-handed.
"My son brought human rice from afar,
he brought it himself, intending to cure my hungry abyss."
"Eating alone is still not enough,
all of you calm your intentions and slowly wait."
Qīngtí's avarice and karmic power were heavy,
raging fire arose in her throat upon entry.
Mùlián saw his mother eat the rice, which became raging fire,
he threw himself down in a heap, like a collapsing mountain,
blood flowed from his ears and nose,
crying, "O Heaven, my mother!"
This rice was offered in Jambudvīpa,
and on the rice was seven feet of divine light.
It was considered fragrant and delicious food,
yet before it entered her mouth, it became fire.
It was solely because her greedy heart had not changed,
thus she suffered this sin year after year.
Now the pain is severe and there is no way,
karmic retribution cannot be replaced.
People of the world, you must not harbor jealousy,
once fallen into the three evil paths, the sin is not yet finished.
Before the fragrant rice could enter her throat,
raging fire came out of Mother's mouth.
All sins in the mundane world fill this Sahā world,
but avarice and greed are the most numerous sins.
Since fire arose from her mouth for no reason,
it is clear that karmic retribution is not controlled by others.
Always practice equality,
and also single-mindedly chant Amitābha.
If only one can abandon the greedy mind,
the Pure Land and paradise will be reached at will.
Qīngtí called out: "Filial son,
this sinful body does not perish by itself.
Without the ācārya performing filial piety,
who would endure hardship to save a mother?
I saw the rice but could not scoop it into my mouth,
a great fire unexpectedly injured me.
How can avarice be cultivated with such thoughts?
It must be residual karma from the past.
The ācārya is my filial son,
give me cold water to relieve my empty intestines."
Mùlián heard his mother ask for water,
his breath choked, his voice hoarse.
While pondering,
he suddenly remembered that south of Wángshèchéng there was a great river,
with boundless wide waves,
named the Hénghé River.
It should also be able to save his mother from the suffering of fire.
When sentient beings in Nányánfútí see this water,
it is cool and refreshing water.
When devas see this water,
it is a jeweled pond of liúlí.
When fish and turtles see this water,
it is a mountain stream.
When Qīngtí saw the water,
it was a river of pus and raging fire.
She walked to the water's edge, and before her son could chant a blessing,
she immediately propped her left hand on the bank, due to stinginess,
and scooped the water with her right hand, due to greed.
Precisely because her heart of stinginess and greed did not stop,
the water turned into fire before it reached her mouth.
Mùlián saw his mother's food turn into raging fire,
and her water turn into raging fire.
He beat his chest and slapped his heart,
weeping and wailing in sorrow.
He came before the Fó,
circumambulated the Fó three times,
then stood to one side,
and said respectfully: “Shìzūn,
this disciple's mother committed various unwholesome deeds,
and fell into the Three Evil Paths.
By your compassionate grace, Shìzūn,
she was saved from her suffering.
But now, eating food turns to fire,
and drinking water turns to fire.
How can she be saved from the suffering of fire?”
Shìzūn called out: “Mùlián,
your mother has not yet been able to eat food.
There is nothing to be done until the fifteenth day of the seventh month, one year from now.
When a great Yúlánpén offering is made,
she will then be able to eat food.”
Mùlián saw his mother was hungry,
and said respectfully: “Shìzūn,
cannot it be done on the thirteenth or fourteenth of each month?
Must we wait until the fifteenth day of the seventh month
in one year to be able to eat food?”
Shìzūn replied: “Not only your mother must make a great Yúlánpén offering on this day,
but it is also the day of Xièxià for those meditating in the mountains,
the day Arhats attain the Way,
the day Dípódádā's sins are extinguished,
the day Yánluówáng rejoices,
and all hungry ghosts universally obtain full satisfaction.”
Mùlián received the Fó's clear teaching,
and immediately went before the stupas and temples on the outskirts of Wángshèchéng,
recited Mahāyāna sūtras,
and extensively cultivated the roots of goodness through the Yúlánpén offering.
His mother then, from this basin,
was able to eat one full meal.
Since obtaining food,
mother and son were not seen again [by each other].
Mùlián searched everywhere for his mother but did not find her.
Tears rained down as he wept sorrowfully.
He came before the Fó,
circumambulated the Fó three times,
then stood to one side,
joined his palms and knelt.
He said respectfully: “Shìzūn,
my mother's food turned to fire,
her water turned to fire.
By your compassionate grace, Shìzūn,
she was saved from the suffering of fire.
Since the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when she obtained one meal,
mother and son have not seen each other again.
Has she fallen into hell,
or has she gone to the path of hungry ghosts?”
Shìzūn replied: “Your mother has neither fallen into hell nor gone to the path of hungry ghosts.
Through your merit of reciting sūtras,
and the roots of goodness from making the Yúlánpén offering,
your mother has transformed her body of a hungry ghost,
and has gone to Wángshèchéng to take the body of a black dog.
If you wish to see your mother,
cultivate an equal mind,
beg for food in order,
without distinction of rich or poor.
When you arrive at the gate of a very wealthy elder's house,
if a black dog comes out,
grabs and holds your jiāshā in its mouth,
and speaks human language,
that is your mother.”
Mùlián, by the Fó's instruction,
then took his alms bowl, held his utensil,
and searched for his mother.
Regardless of poor or rich districts and alleys,
he traveled everywhere,
but did not see his mother at all.
When he arrived at the gate of an elder's house,
he saw a black dog's body
come out from inside the dwelling.
It immediately grabbed Mùlián's jiāshā and held it in its mouth,
and spoke human language,
saying: “My filial son,
you were suddenly able to save your mother from the dark paths of hell,
why can you not save me from the suffering of this dog's body?”
Mùlián responded to his compassionate mother: “It is because your son was unfilial,
bringing calamity upon his compassionate mother,
causing her to fall into the Three Evil Paths.
Would you rather remain in this dog's body?
Or the path of a hungry ghost?”
His mother called out: “Filial son,
receiving this mute retribution in a dog's body,
I am able to exist walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
When hungry, I eat human filth in a pit,
when thirsty, I drink from a flowing stream to quench my emptiness.
In the morning, I hear the elder recite the Three Jewels,
but I don't hear the young lady recite the revered sūtras.
I would rather be in a dog's body,
enduring the filth of the earth,
my ears not hearing the names of hell.”
Mùlián led his mother to the Fó's stupa in Wángshèchéng,
and for seven days and seven nights,
he recited Mahāyāna sūtras,
repented, and kept the precepts.
His mother, by virtue of this merit,
transformed her dog's body,
shed her dog skin,
which hung on a tree,
and regained a woman's body,
fully complete with human form.
Mùlián said to his mother: “A human body is difficult to obtain,
it is difficult to be born in the Middle Kingdom,
the Fó Dharma is difficult to hear,
and a virtuous mind is difficult to arouse.
” He called out: “Mother,
now that you have obtained a human body,
you should immediately cultivate blessings.”
Mùlián led his mother beneath the Sāluóshuāngshù trees,
circumambulated the Fó three times,
then stood to one side,
and said respectfully: “Shìzūn,
since observing the path of karma for this disciple's mother,
and observing her from beginning to end,
what other sins remain?”
Shìzūn did not refuse Mùlián's words,
and observed her through the three karmic paths,
and indeed saw no further personal sins.
Mùlián, seeing his mother's sins extinguished,
was exceedingly joyful,
and said to his mother: “Come, let us return!
The Yánfútí world is not fit to stay in.
Birth and death fundamentally have no dwelling place,
the Western Fó-land is the most excellent.”
Moved, celestial dragons escorted them in front,
and celestial maidens came to welcome them.
They went straight to Dáolìtiān to experience joy.
When the first gāthā was recited to convert Jùlún,
and when this sūtra was being recited,
there were eighty thousand Bodhisattvas, eighty thousand monks, eighty thousand Upāsaka, and eighty thousand Upāsikā,
who bowed in reverence and surrounded them,
joyfully believing, accepting, and practicing.
One scroll of the 《Dàmùjiànlián Biànwén》.
Zhāng Bǎodá Document.
Our Fó, in his causal stages,
cultivated practice for kalpas.
He jumped off a cliff to feed a tiger,
and saved a dove, like Shīpí.
To seek half a gāthā,
his mind remained unshaken.
He cut his body and lit lamps,
making offerings to Pìzhī.
A good friend sought a pearl,
and was lost in poverty.
When his royal father was ill,
he offered his eyes for medicine.
The Great Sage's compassion in his causal stages,
his firm resolve in cultivating practice for kalpas.
He had also made offerings to Pìzhī,
and Dìshìtiān tested him.
He cut flesh to save his royal father,
and remained in the mountains for a long time, holding his breath.
In past lives, he cultivated practice,
thus becoming the Great Master of the Three Realms.
That day, Shìzūn guided Xíngtán,
to save sentient beings entangled by karmic obstacles.
He also knew how to seek pearls in the great ocean,
and Shīpí saved the dove, forming a good affinity.
He went back and forth through the Three Evil Paths,
and served as a boat in the Six Paths of Reincarnation.
To guide his disciples to generate good appearances,
he was graced by the hidden holy power of the Rúlái.
Our Buddha, that day, to save his disciples from the six paths of transmigration,
was like a boat,
transporting all sentient beings
to the other shore.
At this time, one always gets to see the Buddha,
and in this life, one has enough clothes and food.
When the time for cultivation arrives,
one must diligently make vows.
With surplus, make offerings to the Buddha and Saṅgha,
and thus gain the opportunity to meet again.
If one cultivates further at this time,
one will surely see a superior appearance in the next life.
Our Buddha's compassion cannot be overstated;
he saves sentient beings as countless as the sands of the Ganges.
All will reach the state of non-action (nirvāṇa),
and in this life, enjoy abundant wealth and luxury.
Human life is fleeting, like a lamp flame;
worldly affairs are empty, like clouds obscuring the sky.
Making offerings to the Buddha and Saṅgha dispels obstacles;
in the next life, one will surely bow before Longhuā.
The Tathāgata often spoke, enticing and exhorting his disciples:
Burn incense and make vows,
diligently chant Amitābha's name,
practice vegetarianism and perform good deeds,
give alms, for there are many merits;
each one cannot be fully praised.
Setting up a feast brings joy,
and karmic retribution is perfectly fulfilled.
If one frowns even a little,
in the next life, one will surely have an ugly face.
In the days when the Buddha was alive,
there was a virtuous woman
who also made offerings to an Arhat.
Although she had the karma of giving,
she harbored contempt in her heart.
Before three to five days passed,
she died—what efficacy was there in that?
When this woman died at that time,
where did she take rebirth?
She was reborn in the palace of King Prasenajit (Bōsīní Wáng).
This was the karmic cause of giving,
to be reborn into a royal family.
The karma of lightly reviling a sage
resulted in retribution;
it actually fell upon the great king's queen (Mādā-devī).
Just three days after her birth,
she was presented to the great king.
When the great king first saw her,
he was extremely astonished.
The ugly in the world
are born into poverty.
What karma did she cultivate in her previous life
to have an even worse appearance in this life?
The great king said:
"Just thinking about it makes it very strange;
how could my royal lineage be like this?
Ugly people exist in the world,
but I've never seen such a monstrous appearance as today.
She is hunched and shrunken like a tortoise or turtle;
her whole body is like a wild boar's hide.
Even if you are skilled in painting with a clever heart,
a thousand colors cannot depict her.
Her beastly head is utterly repulsive;
there's probably no one comparable in the kingdom.
If one speaks of this girl's appearance,
who will she marry when she grows up?
Thus, the great king was ashamed
and sighed with extreme astonishment.
He then commanded his palace attendants:
"Do not speak of this,"
and sent her to the deep palace,
"Do not bring her forth again;
let me not see her."
The girl's ugliness was rare in the world;
her whole body was like tough black hide.
Her heels were chapped and twisted;
her hair was like a donkey's tail, strand by strand.
When she looked at people, she turned her whole body;
how could she ever walk with grace and etiquette?
Her ten fingers were slender like exposed pillars;
her pair of eyes resembled wooden mallets.
The great king repeatedly pondered her appearance
and sighed several times, "What caused such ugliness to befall her!"
The princess had no grace or charm;
her appearance was extraordinarily terrible.
Her upper lip weighed more than half a catty;
her nostrils were like small bamboo tubes.
She had never known joy since birth;
it was said she smiled once every three years.
Seeking graceful steps from her,
she walked like a sock-footed person from Zhào.
Seeing the girl's ugly form, the great king
often rested his chin in his hand with the queen.
He worried, having no heart to seek a son-in-law;
ashamed, who would he find as a good matchmaker?
Although she resided in a wealthy and noble palace,
her shame was due to lacking beauty that could charm a nation.
He ordered her to be locked away,
the deep palace gates not to be opened.
At that time, King Prasenajit (Bōsīní Wáng) reflected on his daughter's ugliness,
that she was inferior to others.
He therefore sent her to the deep palace,
no longer allowing her to come out often.
Days passed, months went by,
and she gradually grew up.
The queen worried night and day,
fearing that the great king would not consent to her marriage.
Later, during a recreational outing,
the queen composed herself and stepped forward,
addressing the great king thus:
"This humble concubine is often ashamed of her ugly body,
undeservedly residing in the palace and being related to Your Majesty.
Every day before my eyes are riches and nobility,
and morning after morning, only pearls and jewels are used.
Palace women and maids constantly follow;
those who run errands are inner officials.
I am ashamed that this body lacks virtue and wisdom,
yet the great king's favor matches heaven and earth.
This concubine now has a matter to personally report;
may Your Majesty be pleased and not angry:
The Vajra ugly girl has grown up;
how can you bear to let her not marry!
Thereupon, the great king heard the plea
and pondered for a long time.
Before he could speak,
the queen further pleaded:
"The three sisters are all alike,
whether beautiful or ugly depends on karma.
They are all Your Majesty's own flesh and blood;
may Your Majesty bestow your favor and pity equally upon them.
Now that she has grown up in the deep palace,
send her out and let her marry.
Fingers from top to bottom are long and short;
each one, from top to bottom, can be tried by biting.
The great king, seeing the queen's repeated pleas and exhortations,
could not but address the queen thus:
"As the emperor of a nation,
my family members have always been tied by past karma.
How can I bear her greatly flawed appearance
and let her shame me before the court officials?
I know she is my own daughter,
but her ugliness is utterly inhuman.
Just speaking of it frightens everyone;
how can she be married into another family?
The queen then addressed the great king again: "If Your Majesty has no intention of arranging her marriage,
this concubine will not dare to speak again.
If you are inclined to let her marry,
listen to this concubine's plan today.
Secretly summon a prime minister,
instruct him to seek a poor young man,
bestow upon him official rank and treasures,
and arrange for them to be married as husband and wife.
Thereupon, the great king adopted the queen's plan,
immediately summoned a minister,
instructed him to be a matchmaker,
and dispatched him privately.
The minister, upon receiving the decree,
quickly proceeded to the inner hall,
faced the king to receive his instructions,
and accepted the king's orders.
The king said to the minister:
"You now listen to my words,
and consider carefully where they come from:
It concerns the queen of this nation,
who has a biological daughter.
Her natural appearance is not strong;
she just needs to be taken care of.
Seek a young man,
and marry her to him as husband and wife.
The great king then said to his minister:
"You are my minister, I am your sovereign;
today, only the two of us discuss this.
You must carefully and steadily recruit;
sadly, do not let outsiders hear of it.
When suitable, do not dislike lack of talent or skill;
on a rough road, why fear extreme poverty?
By all means, you must make arrangements;
provide some lodging and do not dispute.
Thereupon, the prime minister received the order,
bowed, and left the palace.
He immediately went privately through the markets,
toured various prefectures,
asking people everywhere,
searching every morning.
Later, he suddenly walked through a street
and saw a poor young man whose surname was Wáng.
He inquired repeatedly,
and the young man immediately agreed.
He led him to the inner gate,
first entered to see the king,
and reported that he had found someone.
The emperor's dragon countenance was greatly pleased,
and he immediately summoned the prime minister,
ordering him to quickly bring the young man.
Huángdì 坐相 (zuòyú) Bǎodiàn,
Zǎixiàng qūgōng lái jiàn:

Ménqián yǒu yī érláng,

Dàwáng wénshuō xǐpáihuái,
Juǎn shàng zhūlián yùzhàng kāi.

Qūqǐng [Wáng] Láng.

Yuànhèn qiánshēng hé zuìyè,
Jīnshēng chǒulòu yì xúncháng.
Again and again, she sighed to herself,
〔Sighed〕 without a plan,
so she stopped at her dressing table,
remembering the Buddha in her heart,
begging for protection:
"Distressed that my appearance in this life is not strong,
I tightly pinned up my cloudy bun and gave up red makeup.
How could I have known that I lacked a proper face,
causing bitter deliberation in the dark?
The rouge box I pinched and threw away,
the hairpins, exquisitely carved, fell to one side.
With rain-like tears, I burned incense, contemplating the Dharma assembly,
remotely announcing to the Great Dharma King of Língshān."
Thus, with uncombed eyebrows,
and unbrushed cloud-like hair,
she remotely □ Língshān,
and addressed the Shìzūn:
"Pearls of tears fall continuously, complaining and sighing again,
born a human with a poor face.
A jade leaf does not grow a proper appearance,
a golden vine bears wild field flowers.
It is said that Móuní is sixteen feet tall,
with eighty auspicious marks, known as Shìjiā.
I only wish the Shìzūn would grant me protection,
and bestow upon me some of the thirty-two auspicious marks."
The Buddha, with his mind-penetrating power,
knew remotely that the ugly woman Jīngāng was burning incense and making vows.
So, in front of the steps of the ugly woman's dwelling,
he rose from the ground,
and personally bestowed protection.
The ugly woman suddenly saw the Great Saint Shìzūn (appear) in front of the steps,
her soul collapsed (hún duī) and she threw herself down,
then rose and prostrated,
sobbing sorrowfully.
Just like four birds separating,
she thought of herself,
not hating her diminishment (hèn bù miè) and sinking into the earth.
She addressed the Shìzūn,
begging for protection.
The ugly woman said to the Shìzūn:
"I sigh at the evil karma of my past life,
which caused me to be ugly, not like others.
Slandering saints and sages, I created many sins,
daring to invoke (gǎn zhāo) an appearance like smoke-smudged.
My birth parents disliked me greatly,
my sisters seemed angry every morning.
My husband enters without joy,
my close relatives have never shown affection.
From time to time, I am distressed and shed tears,
often sighing and complaining about this body.
I heard that Língshān is the lord of the Three Realms,
so I burn incense to address the Shìzūn."
The Buddha has the mind-penetrating insight,
and immediately observed it remotely.
He appeared before the princess,
instructing her to repent and make vows.
The ugly woman repented of her transgressions before the Buddha,
her past karma truly self-invoked.
As soon as her repentance ended and vows were made,
the karmic reward was immediately complete and fortunate.
The ugly woman saw the Buddha appear,
her joy was multiplied beyond usual,
so she praised the Rúlái: "May my body be no different from the Buddha's!"
The princess saw the Buddha arrive,
his countenance incomparable in the world,
his hair dark blue, spiraling like a conch,
his eyebrows like the verdant new moon,
his mouth like a Bīnpó fruit,
with forty-two teeth,
his two eyes clear and deep like the sea,
a myriad character (swastika) marked on his chest.
After the ugly woman Jīngāng finished praising the Buddha,
she circled him three times to the right,
and withdrew to one side.
The Buddha, with the power of compassion,
extended his golden arm,
pointing at the ugly woman's body,
and the ugly woman's appearance,
immediately transformed thus:
She praised the Buddha,
sought protection,
bowed her head in worship with a focused heart.
Her countenance instantly changed from its old form,
a hundred uglinesses transformed into a thousand charms.
The ugly woman, having received the Shìzūn's protection,
exchanged her former ugly quality,
for today's elegant manner.
Her ugly physique
transformed into a dignified and auspicious appearance.
She gained a face like a spring flower,
so much so that her husband did not recognize her when he came in.
The princess, light and graceful beyond compare in the world,
was like the woman of Yuè and Cháng'é.
Her face, like a red flower, seemed gently to open,
her jade-like skin, like cotton mixed with white snow.
Previously ugly due to past life's seeds,
today dignified, she met Shìjiā.
Her husband entered and did not recognize her at all,
instead looking for the ugly old woman from before.
The wife said: "Do you recognize me?"
The husband said: "No."
"I am your wife,
how can you not recognize me?"
The husband said: "You're scaring me!
My dear wife, you used to have a beastly face,
making me utterly ashamed in front of people.
Why do you have such a proper appearance today?
Please tell me the reason."
The wife said to her husband: "Since you, before,
were worried about my ugly body,
ashamed to see officials in court.
Your concubine was distressed repeatedly,
and so burned incense and prayed to the Shìzūn of Língshān.
Receiving the Buddha's compassion,
he bestowed protection,
exchanging my ugly physique,
and transforming it into a dignified and auspicious appearance."
The princess said to herself:
"My appearance today is not strong,
deeply ashamed day and night I disgraced Wáng Láng.
I remotely imagined Shìjiā, the lord of the Three Realms,
not abandoning his compassion, descended to this place.
I then prostrated,
and added more incense,
and my appearance was suddenly transformed.
I obtained this dignified appearance today,
and am grateful to the Great Dharma King of Língshān."
Wáng Láng saw his wife's dignified appearance,
clapped his hands with joy,
saying several times: "How delightful!
How delightful!"
He ran inside,
to report to the Great King.
Wáng Láng clapped his hands in joy,
running into the Great King's palace:
"Father-in-law and mother-in-law do not know,
today is a complete transformation!
My little lady has changed now,
she is not the old evil spirit.
If you wish to know the princess's appearance at this moment,
she is just like a Bodhisattva's child before the Buddha."
The Great King heard this with joyful heart,
and hurried to find his daughter.
The Queen's retinue left the palace,
the Great King's imperial carriage arrived at the long street.
As soon as he saw his daughter,
he happily lingered,
her face blooming like radiant peach blossoms.
The Great King and Queen rejoiced greatly,
and therefore specially sent treasures.
Since the princess was made dignified by the Buddha,
she had to gratefully thank the Great Saint,
so she would swiftly go to Qíyuán tomorrow morning,
to prostrate with utmost reverence.
Thereupon, spears and banners shone in the sun,
black banners obscured and reflected,
seven precious treasures,
were offered to the Buddha.
A hundred officials followed the carriage,
a thousand officers followed by decree,
together they went to Qíyuán,
to thank for the daughter's dignified appearance.
After one night,
they arrived at Qíyuán,
to thank the Buddha for his profound grace,
and to ask again and again:
They descended from the imperial carriage,
bowed to the Golden Person,
and further offered precious treasures to the Compassionate Lord.
"What sin did my daughter commit in her past life?
Her ugliness was too difficult to express.
Thanks to the Rúlái's personal protection,
she is like a withered tree reborn in spring.
We only wish the Rúlái, with his compassionate power,
would explain the cause of her cultivation in a past life."
The Buddha said to Bōsīní Wáng: "Listen carefully, listen carefully,
I will enlighten you on a matter,
and explain the past life's causes and conditions."
The Buddha said this woman, in a past life,
once made offerings to a Pìzhīfó,
but even though she made offerings,
she only remarked on his ugly face.
The karmic cause of the offering led her to be born into a royal family,
but the karma of disrespecting the saintly sage,
caused her face to be ugly.
With faithful giving,
one must be joyful.
If a person has a little sour expression (grumpy brows),
then know that the karmic reward will not be fulfilled.
In her past life, she slandered a Pìzhījīa,
which is why her appearance and face were poor.
Because she did not recognize the Āluóhàn,
she mocked and ridiculed him in every way, causing bitter suffering (fēn pā).
If one is about to utter malicious words,
their karmic retribution will surely not be mistaken.
When one encounters the body of Móní and repents,
at that moment, they become like a cluster of flowers.
It is precisely because one uttered malicious words in a previous life
that the karmic retribution today is not in vain.
The karma of slandering an Aróhàn
causes one's appearance to be imperfect.
Two legs emerge like exposed posts,
a pair of arms like coarse rafters.
But as soon as one bows to the Shìzūn three to five times,
at that moment, they become pure white and soft as cotton.
The above describes an ugly transformation.
By Yuánjiàn Dàshī, Left Street Sańglù, bestowed with purple, Yúnbìan narrates:
The blessings and wisdom in the world,
none surpass the Rúlái;
his features are splendid and majestic,
his divine powers are unhindered.
How did the Buddha's noble body come to be?
Its foundation was laid by practicing filial piety.
One must know that the path of filial piety is boundlessly good,
widely praised among the Three Teachings.
If one can be filial to their two parents,
they will attract a thousand Buddhas to protect their conduct.
Mùlián has already saved his mother, Qīngtí;
our Buddha carried Jìngfàn Wáng on his shoulders.
History books for ten thousand generations sing praises of Shùn Zhǔ,
for a thousand years, people laud Wáng Xiáng.
The filial crow returns to feed its parent, still feeling gratitude,
wild geese, as soon as they fly, arrange themselves in formation.
Guō Jù wished to bury his own child,
Lǎolái delighted in wearing colorful clothes.
It is most difficult to deceive or feign sincerity,
not easy to lightly disregard before Heaven.
The name of bamboo shoots growing from crying over them is most revered,
the righteousness of fish leaping from lying on ice is immeasurable.
If one can remove slander from themselves,
they will avoid being harmed by others.
Dogs know how to repay kindness and can [gather] grass,
horses know their master and can drop their reins.
Do not squander wealth on bribery and indulgence in lust,
do not upset kind parents by being wild with drink.
When sons and daughters fall ill, their voices gasp,
their parents weep until tears stream down.
Bearing them on two shoulders is not heavy,
circling Xūmí a thousand times cannot repay it.
Diligently serve them morning and evening, knowing their movements and stillness,
intently watch their countenance and inquire about their well-being.
Swallowing bitterness and spitting out sweetness for three years,
pregnant in the womb for more than ten months.
If they go out far, one's dream pursues them,
if they return late, one stands by the door.
Filial piety and compassion will surely attract heavenly blessings,
the five rebellious acts can bring forth the calamities of hell.
Hardship should be borne as one's own lot,
one should deeply beware of assets entering private quarters.
One must worry about hidden merits being diminished,
do not trust what wives and children say to cause strife.
It is one's own lack of utmost filial feeling,
yet one blames the Gēngjiǎ for obstacles.
Neighbors will angrily spread the word,
the reputation of the five rebellious acts will be known far and wide.
If brothers quarrel in the household,
they will surely cause neighbors to secretly move walls.
Closest kin should share food,
deep friends still share provisions.
When responding in speech, one should be gentle and considerate,
when receiving instructions, one must deliberate carefully.
If one slightly deviates from discretion and lacks kindness and righteousness,
if one slightly delays or makes a mistake, discipline is lost.
It is essential to treat those you employ with kindness,
and even more so to comfort and care for widows and orphans.
Maternal aunts and uncles, and the children of widows and orphans,
take them into your home and bestow favor upon them.
Aid impoverished acquaintances with generosity,
build bridges on difficult and rugged roads.
If one can follow these teachings of the Buddhist path,
it is called a great place of compassion and enlightenment.
Early morning and evening, send your son and wife to rise,
let parents taste the wine and food first.
Living together for not long, there will still be separation,
looking at each other for not long, impermanence will come.
While alive, one is too lazy to offer tea and water,
after death, one fruitlessly toils to offer libations of wine.
To obey and conform with sincerity, believing in the Buddha,
kind words and inquiries are better than burning incense.
Gentle persuasion is needed for kind parents to understand,
ugly reputation must be borne by oneself.
On hot days, one must fan the pillow,
on severely cold months, one must warm the bed.
The remaining years change as swiftly as flowing water,
providing delicacies and comforts is as urgent as fire.
If one can live in harmony like water and milk,
it is better than sacrificing pigs and sheep after death.
How can the sayings not be clearly proclaimed in the neighborhoods?
The spirits will secretly record them.
How can shared roots and branches be divided and cut apart?
How can those from the same womb and milk endure being separated?
The Rúlái expounded five thousand scrolls,
Kǒngshì discussed eighteen chapters.
None of their words failed to proclaim filial piety,
every phrase spoke of gentleness and goodness.
A filial heart is called a true Púsà,
filial conduct is named a great place of enlightenment.
