Filial conduct is the sun and moon in the dim path,
a filial heart is the ladder and boat in the sea of suffering.
A filial heart will forever have a land of purity and coolness,
filial conduct always resides in a land of joy and pleasure.
Filial conduct is no different from the rain in the third month,
a filial heart is no different from the fragrance of a hundred flowers.
A filial heart is as vast as clouds spread,
filial conduct is as clear as sunlight.
Filial conduct can overcome ten thousand calamities,
a filial heart can ward off a thousand misfortunes.
Filial piety is the treasure among all wealth,
filial piety is the king among a thousand kinds of goodness.
In the Buddhist path, filial piety is the root of becoming a Buddha,
one must practice filial piety towards parents.
Contentment in this life avoids reincarnation,
filial piety can eliminate all calamities.
If one can fully practice filial piety towards elderly parents,
it is like opening scriptures all day long.
Kind words should make parents happy,
why wait for parents to urge delicacies?
To be like the Shìzūn's dignified appearance,
it is nothing but having filial piety sung forth.
Hàn Gāo Huángdì commanded Hán Xìn at Péngchéng,
they formed a battle array at Gāixià,
Chǔ was destroyed and Hàn won.
Zhāng Liáng saw that Hán Xìn had killed many people,
Zhāng Liáng played and said: "I shall sing Chǔ songs,
to disperse the Chǔ army."
The song says:
Zhāng Liáng, by order, entered the central camp,
he instructed the young men to listen quickly:
"Tonight, select three to five hundred people,
all who can perform Chǔ songs must present themselves."
Zhāng Liáng's plan was very rare,
that night they surrounded the Chǔ camp.
Just at the third watch, the training was perfected,
Chǔ songs were sung simultaneously from all four sides.
The lyrics say:
"This year we have haphazardly crossed the Háoliáng,
jade dew, fragrant and abundant, fills the valley frost.
A man who has attained high official positions,
how can he forget his father and mother?
Everyone is born from parents,
children are raised by parents,
if not for three years of mother's milk,
from where would a six-foot body grow?
Raising children should only be about knowing the household economy,
offering delicacies at the four seasons and eight festivals.
If delicacies are never offered,
then parents are abandoned, and one lives in vain.
Carrying the burden of war for several years,
a hundred battles, a hundred wounds, life becomes uncertain.
Sometimes in dreams, I lie beneath a spear,
waking up, I am still by the war drums.
Where are the tens of thousands of soldiers withdrawn?
When will letters carried by geese return?
Warhorses are sometimes constantly worn out,
a bow has no night without a strung string.
Urgent, urgent, it makes people old,
swift, swift, it makes people age early.
The roads through mountains and passes are difficult to traverse,
which one is the path to my hometown?
When the Chǔ soldiers heard these words, tears streamed down their faces,
they abandoned all their weapons, spears, and banners,
in groups of three and five, they all fled in disarray,
each eager to return to their camp.
Just past the middle of the third watch,
King Chǔ then became aware,
he drew his sword beneath the stars and came out of the camp,
already seeing five stars intersecting.
I truly rely on my courageous spirit,
but why today am I defeated by Heaven?
Five or six years of bitter warfare,
Péngchéng and Gāixià, a single defeat.
Unlucky at this time, Heaven destroys me,
why does Heaven destroy me?
Since I have the strength to lift mountains and tripods,
if I do not perish now, what is there to do!
A thousand pieces of gold cannot buy back the spring of old age,
drunkenly lying before the steps, forgetting poverty,
if there were no such thing in the world,
three parts of people would be utterly sad, two parts of them.
"Jì Bù" one volume.
Recorded on the fourth day of the fourth month in the fourth year of Tiānfú.
The Crown Prince, Bǐyì, went out for a stroll,
only to invite sorrow.
Upon seeing the plowing and weaving before him,
he could not help but shed tears that filled his eyes,
and his body became covered in dust.
He sighed at the multitude of karmic actions
and pitied the extreme suffering caused by these two [types of work].
When will the strong cease to bully the weak,
ending their mutual enmity?
When will the rich stop exploiting the poor,
ending their toil and hardship?
Therefore, he turned his carriage back onto the road
and returned to the palace with his retinue.
Music he heard as if not hearing it;
dancing sleeves he saw as if not seeing them.
The astonished palace ladies lined the embankment,
in groups of five and three;
the bewildered populace of the whole kingdom,
in countless thousands.
Like clouds rushing by,
like birds flying swiftly.
Just as they were discussing,
he had already returned to the hall.
The gathā says:
Pitying and remembering the karmic deeds of living beings,
sleeves soaking with tears, he turned back, letting them fall.
The passing dancers seemed unseen,
the successive melodies of pipes and songs unheard.
Drums and cymbals shaking the earth resonated across the green fields,
dust filling the sky entangled the red banners.
The whole city, astonished, came out to watch,
people bustling and horses neighing, all returning.
Having returned, he was unhappy.
The King asked, "You went out for a stroll earlier,
why are you unhappy now?"
The Crown Prince replied, "Father King!
When I went out earlier to see the gardens,
I did not know the human world held such hardship.
For the sake of flesh and blood,
they inflict harm for clothing and food.
Plowmen turn up worms for birds to peck,
weavers spin threads while their children toil.
Butchers slaughter oxen and sheep,
hunters set nets and hooks for fish and sparrows.
They mutually cause harm,
ultimately creating enemies.
They live a life of deceit,
the strong bullying the weak.
Therefore, I could not bear to witness it,
and my carriage turned back.
Since all people are tormented by suffering,
why should I alone enjoy happiness?"
The gathā says:
"You only concern yourself with being noble in the imperial palace,
unaware of the myriad hardships beyond its gates.
The boiling and screaming make one hate the butcher,
the netting and catching, the silent sighs, wound the fisherman.
Young women in front of carriages constantly twist threads,
old crows, after the plow passes, immediately carry off worms.
It is all due to killing and harm for clothing and food,
which is why I returned unwilling to encounter such sights."
The King said, "You are gravely mistaken.
In the human world,
poverty and wealth are determined by karma.
Everyone needs clothing to cover their bodies,
and also relies on food to nourish themselves.
If one does not spin, how can one obtain clothes?
If one does not plant, how can one seek grain?
As for flying birds and walking beasts,
it is largely the same.
Though their forms and manners differ according to karmic retribution,
they are destined by karmic conditions to feed on each other.
Rats are killed and harmed by cats,
not by human instruction;
butterflies are entangled in spiders' webs,
all by divine command.
You should not sigh in sorrow;
this is a common rule.
If you trouble my spirit,
how can that be called filial piety?"
The poem says:
How can human life, arranged by Heaven, be free?
There are relatives, loves, and enmities.
Deep blessings are all due to much cultivation in the past,
meager portions are all because one did not cultivate widely.
Poor women make clothes, diligently spinning and weaving;
plowmen plant seeds, working in the fields.
Considering all this, it is always the usual way,
why must you return and be uniquely sorrowful?
The Crown Prince said, "If that is truly the case,
I dare not disobey the King.
I wish to make a request to you,
please grant me one wish."
The King said, "Just follow my will,
entertain yourself with music.
Whatever you need,
I will grant it to you.
I cherish and pity only you,
all the gold in the kingdom is not as precious.
Why are you uniquely worried about the world's hardships,
and why do you particularly pity people's toil?
In Jambudvīpa (Yánfútí),
all follows karmic power.
Just be peaceful and do not be tormented.
You also speak of nurturing a great vow,
I will comply with whatever you wish, without objection.
When I first saw you return burdened with sorrow,
I could not fathom the reason and was very doubtful.
Nobility and humbleness are not determined by this life's actions,
longevity and short life all follow past karmic conditions.
Why bother scratching your cheeks and adding to your grief and resentment?
Just relax your mind and maintain a good disposition.
If you have a wish, speak it quickly,
I will definitely comply with whatever you desire."
The dragon-face frequently observed, the matter difficult to decide,
the son's unexpressed words always weighing on his mind.
When will the step-by-step hesitation end?
When will the clustered sorrow in his brows dissipate?
The officials, respectfully wary, awaited in their ranks,
the palace ladies, nervously arrayed outside the hall.
They only waited for the officials' reports and responses,
so that everyone could sing of peace and joy.
(Sūtra) The Crown Prince respectfully said, "I wish to obtain all the treasures, food, and drink from my Father King's treasury,
to bestow upon all."
The Crown Prince said, "The King is my father,
I am the King's son.
Since I have a private vow,
it is fitting that I fully present it.
I wish to obtain the King's food and drink
to help the hungry;
I wish to obtain the King's pearls and gold
to distribute to the poor.
To enable weavers to no longer toil at their looms,
plowmen to cease laboring with their oxen,
fishermen to break their hooks in rivers,
hunters to unstring their bows in forests.
To let butchers release the lives of pigs and sheep,
avoiding enmity;
to let fowlers abandon the lives of swallows and sparrows,
eliminating fear.
To make everyone prosperous,
and bring peace to all.
I humbly beg your sacred mercy,
to permit the opening of the treasury."
The gathā says:
"I am constrained by the suffering of living beings,
all due to clothing and food creating hardships.
Plowing and sericulture busy everywhere at all times,
officials' gates everywhere serving the nine thoroughfares.
I wish to make all killing and injury completely cease,
I want to make all the weary and exhausted revive.
I beg the King to bestow all from the treasury,
but I do not know if Heaven's heart will allow it?"
The King said, "Whatever you wish,
I will not go against your will."
The Crown Prince was then delighted,
and chose a day to open the treasury and move the goods.
He used five hundred great elephants to carry them out beyond the four city gates,
and proclaimed throughout the land
that whatever was needed,
he would not go against their wishes,
as fully recorded in the sūtra.
Thereupon, locks were simultaneously opened,
and seals were all broken.
Pearls and gems were piled up,
treasures divided into mounds.
All the laborers carried them to the imperial court,
their hands bustling to move them from the imperial treasury.
Various brocades and exotic embroideries,
all tributes from powerful vassal states;
auspicious silks and fragrant satins,
all expressions of gratitude from great prefectures.
Jade belts and sashes piled up like houses,
golden vases bundled like mountains.
The number of carved flower stacks was endless,
the raised relief boats were innumerable.
The pile of coins was immeasurable like boat tips,
the assorted silks were as vast as the sea.
Five hundred elephants carried them, continuing from night to day,
piled up at the four city gates from high to low.
Summons were issued to the lonely and destitute,
who flowed in like a river on the roads;
bells called together the farming populace,
who gathered eagerly from villages and gardens.
They were allowed to take whatever they desired,
and were not obstructed in coming and going according to their wishes.
What can be said of a year of great plenty,
or of years far removed from worries?
The King, for his son, emptied all his treasuries,
five hundred elephants carrying goods along four roads.
Coins, silks, satins, and brocades were heaped everywhere,
the number of gold, silver, pearls, and jade was endless.
He summoned distant vassal states,
and proclaimed to nearby prefectures,
the imperial decree widely disseminated throughout the world.
But the poor and destitute were quickly sought out.
Regardless of good or bad, they must all come.
The King should wish and care for the people,
the Crown Prince gives wealth to provide relief.
Once they come and ask, there is no obstruction,
whatever they desire, there is no withholding.
Everyone knew,
and flocked together,
like clustered stars or a surging stream.
To replace the young, orphaned, cold, and lacking people,
all were made content without greed or envy.
Elephants carried treasures out of the country and spread the word,
the holy lord searched and made a proclamation.
Firstly, it showed the Emperor’s practice of pure giving,
secondly, it displayed the Crown Prince’s forming of good connections.
At the appointed time, scholars gathered like clouds,
day after day, wealth was moved like ants circling.
It must be that all households were joyful,
scattering piles of money from door to door.
Every prefecture and county had ample treasures,
only engaged in sheng and ge music, getting drunk from jade cups.
Suddenly abandoning the busy months of farming and sericulture,
forever casting aside the toils of commerce.
Ashamed and grateful for the Emperor’s pervasive grace,
feeling indebted for the Crown Prince’s opened treasury.
Just as the people of the country were carrying things away,
who would dare to advise against it and bring it up?
(After some) time, the treasury minister immediately reported to the King: "Of all the treasures in the treasury,
the Crown Prince has now used one-third;
Your Majesty should consider this."
This minister was upright in his heart,
loyal and filial by nature,
not out of stinginess with treasures,
but for the diligence of the King.
He worried about the emptiness of the national treasury,
which would surely lead to chaos in the court.
So he reported to the King, saying: "The Crown Prince has been taking treasures to give to the poor;
for several months now,
one-third has already been used.
I dare not obstruct him,
but it is my duty to report it fully.
I ask Your Majesty to admonish him,
and not let him go beyond reasonable limits.
Ministers and lords of precious treasures must be utterly loyal,
and be prepared to provide for urgent needs.
Maintaining locks and keys requires effort,
and scrutinizing villains allows no quarter.
Districts and counties are depleted to fill the treasury,
and the blood and fat of the people are brought into the royal palace.
For several tens of days, the Crown Prince has been moving and distributing,
already one-third has been emptied."
The King said: "My son,
I do not wish to refuse him."
After another ten days,
even more was taken.
All the royal ministers discussed in worry,
saying: "Any capital city,
must rely on its treasury;
if the wealth is exhausted,
how will the country's strength fare?
We cannot conceal this out of human sentiment,
we must report it to the heavenly ears."
The minister in charge of the treasury reported again.
The verse says:
"Wrongly I hold the position of treasury minister to the King,
wearing the fish tally and purple robes, I enter the court gate.
To hold back words is disloyal and unfilial,
when there is a matter, one must speak directly and report first.
If I am punished, I am willing to die by the sword,
if my family is executed, why fear burning in fire?
Just now I checked all the treasures,
the Crown Prince has exhausted two-thirds."
When the King heard the minister's report,
he again said: "My son, I do not wish to refuse him.
However, you should slightly delay and slow down,
so as not to fully satisfy his heart;
the valuable thing is to perhaps gain some time and stop him from taking it."
Although the treasury ministers temporarily slowed down according to the King's instructions,
the Crown Prince, opening the treasury at the usual time, found it unavailable,
and became angry, saying: "How dare these petty people go against my wishes?
Most likely, my royal father instructed them."
The Crown Prince then pondered for a moment,
and said: "A filial son
does not go against his sovereign's will.
It is not right to selfishly form connections,
emptying my parents' treasury.
I must seek other wealth,
to relieve the poor;
if I do not devise a plan,
what name would I have as a benefactor?
I now vow not to take any treasures from the treasury,
and wish to gather wise people to discuss how to manage other ventures.
To be loyal and filial to one's parents,
one should not go against the King's will.
Unworthily acting as a man's son,
how can one go against heaven and earth?
If one has a compassionate heart for the suffering,
one must possess a different, heaven-born wisdom.
To avoid the King's heart being troubled,
and to prevent ministers' words from boiling over.
Only wealth and power must be personally acquired,
only blessings and connections cannot be sheltered.
I wish to gather all the elders in the city,
to devise other plans to carry out dānshī (charitable giving).
To avoid incurring accusations of disobedience that trouble the King,
and also to ensure the treasury remains full as before.
To immediately satisfy the wishes of all officials,
and forever remove the managers, leaving a separate name.
Deeply knowing one's own faults is to be human and wrong,
do not blame others' grievances when issuing commands.
Why not gather the wise to discuss,
and jointly offer wisdom and strategies for livelihood?
To help people, one must have abundant wealth oneself,
how much to give depends on one's will at the moment.
If I have much, I can give sufficiently,
if I have little, others will not add to it.
How can resentment arise from circumstances?
Only joy can open wisdom.
May I ask the ministers in court,
which path brings the most profit to be sung about and brought forth?
(After some) time, the Crown Prince Shànyǒu immediately gathered all the ministers and officials to discuss, saying: "Among all professions, which is the most excellent for seeking wealth?"
The Crown Prince reflected earlier,
then chose a day to visit the ministers and asked:
"Advising ministers of the court are praised by all generations,
their fame known in many countries, their plans unsurpassed.
They support the state with loyalty and righteousness,
shaping the lives of the people with harmony.
In governance and chaos, no harm befalls the multitude, no tyranny,
when taxing fields, the people do not complain of harshness.
You should also know the ways to seek wealth,
which door offers the most profit?"
As soon as the Crown Prince finished asking,
among them, the first minister reported to the Crown Prince, saying: "I heard that for widespread wealth, nothing surpasses farming.
If this year one plants five shēng,
next year one harvests ten hú in profit.
It doesn't require far-reaching human plans,
only the effort of oxen for plowing.
A large part comes from the weather,
and a large part from the moisture of the earth.
No village field is better moistened and yields more,
regardless of summer wheat or autumn grain.
Three shēng this year for three mǔ of land,
one grain next year yields one plant.
Though the oxen are tired on planting day,
when ripe, the abundant ears cannot be stopped.
Since Your Highness deigned to ask,
only farming yields the most profit."
Shànyǒu replied,
in a verse:
"Many thanks for the strong prior plan,
but upon reflection, it is not an excellent suggestion.
If by chance the harvest is good, who will feel ashamed of the land?
But if drought suddenly comes, one must resent heaven.
Even the morning sun is hard to guarantee for the evening,
how can this year's harvest reach next year?
Lately, I've been afraid to see the people suffer,
why specially ask people to farm again?"
Another minister said: "If you don't want to farm,
nothing beats raising livestock.
Whether cattle, sheep, camels, horses,
or geese, ducks, chickens, pigs,
they thrive with water and grass,
and grow fat through grazing.
Oxen can be used to pull carts for transport,
horses for riding on roads,
pigs and sheep for sacrificing to the gods,
geese and ducks for serving ministers and prime ministers.
Those who need them will surely buy them,
not a day passes without demand.
This clearly shows great profit,
nothing can surpass this."
The verse says:
"Raising livestock entirely depends on rich water and grass,
even the Crown Prince in the deep palace should know.
Oxen carry loads for public and private use on important roads,
horses are ridden in and out of the court gate.
Geese and ducks are cooked and prepared for advisors,
pigs and sheep are slaughtered for sacrificing to the gods.
Households needing them must buy them,
the profit is particularly great, doubt no more."
At that time, the Crown Prince heard this,
and replied again:
"This plan, upon reflection, is even more disgraceful,
it greatly promotes wrong views and contaminates the court.
Why did you speak and make me ask again?
It makes people plug their ears and become lazy to listen.
It's lamentable to receive salary in vain since coming of age,
it's a pity for those with fish tallies to confuse the officials.
Lately, I've been afraid of accumulating bad karma and resentment,
why now specially advocate killing living beings?"
This did not please the Crown Prince.
Finally, there was a minister,
of vibrant spirit,
and clear eloquence.
He bowed and stepped out from the ranks,
looked up and spoke directly: "Crown Prince!
I see that the Crown Prince is no ordinary person,
possessing compassion and pity,
wisdom and intelligence.
You dislike creating karmic debts through killing,
and do not wish to kill;
you know the hardships of cultivation and planting,
and do not wish to cultivate and plant.
You now intend to make all sentient beings
peaceful and untroubled,
wearing natural clothes,
and eating heaven-bestowed food.
You wish to destroy the dwellings of greed, hatred, and delusion,
and emerge from worldly toil;
to re-establish the body of precepts, concentration, and wisdom,
and perfectly practice the Dharma.
Why not enter the great ocean,
pay homage to the Lóngwáng,
seek the Móní pearl,
and bring benefit to all sentient beings?
If they want food, it will rain food;
if they want clothes, it will rain clothes;
if they want gold and silver, it will rain gold and silver;
if they want jewels, it will rain jewels.
No lives will be harmed,
no schemes will be used.
Unless a Púsà can accomplish this,
it is difficult for an ordinary person to achieve.
I know the Crown Prince laments birth, aging, sickness, and death,
and greatly extends his good and mighty compassion.
How could this be the achievement of an ordinary person's understanding?
It is truly the path of a Púsà's practice.
Though slow,
the merit will be abundant,
and will surely remove the afflictions of sentient beings.
If you wish all to be free from suffering and hardship,
there is nothing better than obtaining the Móní pearl.
The sea dragon's jewel is called Móní;
among a thousand seekers, few obtain it.
If food is desired, it will cause fine food to pour down;
if clothes are needed, it will immediately rain exquisite garments.
All kinds of silk and fine cloth can be produced,
and all sorts of gold and silver will follow.
If you are determined to go and obtain it yourself,
this will be called the Crown Prince's inconceivable act.
The practice of a Púsà,
and compassion,
cannot be known by ordinary, petty people.
The Crown Prince's comings and goings will be without hindrance,
and his abilities will become even more inconceivable.
Though urgent,
it is still slow;
many good deeds should not be delayed.
I am just afraid that sentient beings have little merit,
and will not meet the Crown Prince and turn back.
Although this humble servant has made a plan with all his humble heart,
it is best to make a decision about going or staying at the moment.
Rather than seeking personal peace and hoping for reward and salary,
do not let the king be angered and cause disaster.
Wandering in disarray and only fearing shame,
sweating and trembling, I dare not turn back."
When the Crown Prince first heard these words,
he expressed his satisfaction or dissatisfaction.
(Sūtra) Shànyǒu Tàizǐ said: "Excellent!
Excellent!
This alone is delightful."
He immediately entered the royal palace,
and reported to his father, the king.
The Crown Prince now wishes to go to the great ocean to gather precious treasures.
Shànyǒu was extraordinarily delighted upon hearing this minister's speech.
For a while, he passionately praised it as "Excellent!",
and repeatedly extolled it as "delightful."
He thanked him repeatedly,
truly recognizing him as a wise person.
Unconsciously, he rose,
joined his palms, and praised him in verse:
"Now I believe there are wise people in the court,
this grand plan I have never heard.
On the path to Bódí, I encounter a good friend,
in the city of afflictions, I see a cloud of wisdom.
Truly, we are united in heart to bring benefit and salvation,
truly, we are united in strength to rescue those sinking.
May my comings and goings be without obstacles,
and I shall offer half of my merit and power to you."
After Shànyǒu Tàizǐ finished reciting the verses of praise,
he immediately entered the royal palace
and reported to his father, the king, saying: "To help the poor,
I opened the royal treasury;
but I also feared it would become depleted,
and did not wish to deplete it.
Since I am powerless and have no other way,
I wish to enter the sea to seek treasures.
Please allow me to go,
do not worry.
At most half a year,
I will return for an audience.
I now enter the sea to seek jewels,
to universally benefit the lonely and old in Yánfú.
To largely transform worries and anxieties,
and widely clear away poverty.
The day is not far,
the roads are full of people,
I should arrive with my traveling provisions according to what is needed.
I specifically came for an audience to bid farewell to my father, the king,
may the king allow me to go without worry or sorrow.
The path is smooth and flat with no mountains,
merchants are numerous, so there will be no difficulty.
I plan to go for several tens of days to seek and investigate,
and will return in half a year for an audience.
Why worry about dispatching royal meals,
I will have my own journey provisions to eat as I wish.
I only wish my father, the king, to deeply understand,
and not let worries and sorrows hinder me.
I will return safely and peacefully,
and surely no dragons or spirits will cause disaster.
Those who harm living beings will ultimately suffer calamity,
while those who benefit them will surely have their divine eyes opened.
Please allow me to communicate from time to time,
and temporarily grant me this kindness, do not be anxious."
It is to be imagined that his father, the king, hearing these words,
must have been greatly displeased and expressed it.
(Sūtra) The King heard these words,
like a person choking,
who could neither swallow
nor spit out.
He said to the Crown Prince:
"The kingdom is yours,
the treasures in the treasury,
take and use as you wish.
Why resort to this method,
and go into the great ocean yourself?
You are my son,
raised in the deep palace,
sleeping under canopies,
eating whatever you desire.
Now you speak of traveling far,
experiencing hunger, thirst, cold, and heat,
who will know of it?
Furthermore, in the midst of the great ocean,
there are countless dangers.
Perhaps there are evil spirits and poisonous dragons,
turbulent waves and fierce winds,
whirlpools and surging eddies,
mountains of water bubbles,
and Makara great fish.
Thousands go,
but only one or two succeed.
How can you now wish to enter the great ocean?
I will not allow you."
《Fúbào'ēn Jīng》Chapter 7.
《Bào'ēn Jīng》Chapter 11.
(Sūtra) When he reached this shore,
he saw his younger brother, Èyǒu,
and asked: "Where are your companions and party now?"
Shànyǒu, having been sent out to the coast by the Lóngwáng's ghost soldiers,
who then returned.
He saw his younger brother, Èyǒu,
and asked: "Where are the five hundred merchants
now?"
The following sūtra answers:
"Shànyǒu!
The ship sank,
everyone died,
only I alone survived by holding onto corpses,
all companions and wealth are lost."
The verse says:
"Whether life is short or long, do not conclude definitely,
how can one distinguish smoke a mere foot away?
Those long familiar with boats might be alright,
but those who first see waves will surely lose their souls.
Regardless of overturning, it is said to be heavenly treasure;
in danger, who cares for the revered one in the kingdom?
Many merchants all sank,
only I, cultivating my mind, happened to survive."
Shànyǒu heard this and said: “Deep joy, deep joy!
Wealth and treasures are trivial matters.
What the world values most
is nothing like one’s own body.
As long as one’s body is safe,
why worry about pearls and jade?”
Èyǒu said: “I am not like that.
I now wish to die rich,
not live in poverty.
How do I know this?
I once went to a graveyard
and heard the ghost-corpses
discussing thus:
‘What I value are treasures,
not my body.’ ”
The meaning of the scripture was originally to entice the elder brother to go after the pearl.
The gāthā told the elder brother:
“Brother, you see pearls and gold as mere trifles,
but for me, it is most difficult to abandon them here.
With wealth, my desires will be fulfilled upon reaching the country;
returning empty-handed, my heart would be utterly disheartened.
Ignorance of such matters appears persistently dull;
seeing people and speaking little also becomes tiresome.
How can dying in wealth and nobility
not greatly surpass living in poverty in this world?”
Shànyǒu’s heart was sincere and straightforward;
what he valued was comforting his younger brother.
Fearing the treasure might be lost in the sea,
his sorrow doubled.
He then said to his brother: “You need not be sad;
the sinking of the ship
is truly a minor matter.
I have already obtained the Rúyì-jewel of the Dragon King.”
Èyǒu immediately asked his brother: “Where is the jewel now?”
He replied: “The precious jewel I obtained
is currently in my topknot.
Morning and evening I guard it,
in every movement I take precautions.
It can fulfill the worries and affections of my parents,
and also relieve the poverty and hardship of sentient beings.
It will assist your joyful celebrations,
so you need not labor your mind.
When we obtain the jewel,
we will all be rich and noble.
The precious jewel is always in my topknot;
today I clearly tell you, my brother.
From dusk till dawn, enduring hardship,
I must keep it hidden with anxious care.
It rains pearls and gold,
broadly giving relief,
equally benefiting sentient beings and removing their suffering.
When boorish people come, do not let them know,
to avoid being robbed and violating our oath.
Our coming here already had a set date;
our bustling journey must not be delayed.
Every time I recall initially departing the country,
how could I have hoped to return with the jewel now?
I pour my heart into great acts of vast compassion;
the jewel rain is especially able to save those in distress.
Except for the path, I entrust it to you, my brother;
if others ask, do not let them know.
For this, sorrow and joy fill my heart;
my great vow has been fulfilled this morning.
Since there is such an inconceivable jewel within,
why cling to the wealth in the sea?
To seek beyond what is due is a grave error;
ordinary losses are not worth lamenting.”
When Èyǒu heard his brother say this,
he calculated that he should make a plan and present it.
(Sūtra) When the younger brother heard these words,
envy arose in his heart,
along with worry, resentment, and vexation.
He thought: “My parents always loved and favored him partially,
and now he has obtained the Maṇi jewel again.
As for me, my parents now despise me,
more than a tile shard.”
Èyǒu continued to dwell on these thoughts,
and so a new thought arose.
Gāthā:
Shànyǒu receives grace and all look up to him;
at every turn, he is loved and recognized with increasing favor.
When he walks, thousands of court ladies follow;
when he sleeps, his canopy is adorned with a hundred treasures.
Before he arrives, cowrie shells are arranged;
as he approaches from afar, crystal curtains are rolled up.
Now he returns with the jewel,
and I am regarded as an enemy, even more detested.
As soon as he finished speaking this gāthā to himself,
he immediately clasped his palms and said to his brother: “Excellent!
Very good!
You have obtained this precious jewel.
This path is perilous;
it is fitting to increase our guard.”
Shànyǒu, with his straightforward heart,
said to Èyǒu: “Take this jewel,
and guard it diligently.
When I rest,
you should watch it;
when you sleep,
I will watch over it myself.”
They continued thus for several days,
all as previously described.
“Take down the precious jewel and receive it,
guard it diligently, keeping it in your mind and heart.
Whether walking or sitting, carefully maintain it together;
when sleeping, carefully entrust it to each other.
Guard against wicked people,
watch the dangerous paths;
those who see, hear, and know will certainly be jealous.
If it is suddenly lost or dropped due to carelessness,
by what means will we file a complaint?
This jewel is rare and truly difficult to obtain;
it is not easily kept if it isn’t from the Dragon King.
When you sleep, your brother will certainly guard it with full attention;
when I sleep, I entrust it to you, my brother, to take to heart.
Wicked people are cunning and have endless schemes;
the treacherous and rugged path cannot but cause worry.
If it is lost due to negligence,
Dānapāramitā will be extremely difficult to cultivate.
Do not sleep, do not be careless, do not hesitate;
do not trust negligence, do not make false excuses.
Do not let my brother err due to my lack of attention;
do not let me blame my brother for a lost item.
How many lonely elders hope for this strength,
and countless poor people long for this wealth!
They continued thus for several days,
and then it reached the part where 'who is watching' was sung.
(Sūtra) At that time, it was Èyǒu’s turn to guard the jewel.
When his brother was asleep,
he immediately rose, found two dry bamboo sticks,
stabbed his brother’s eyes,
and took the jewel and left.
Èyǒu made a plan,
calculating that his brother was asleep,
and it was his turn to guard the jewel.
He found two dry bamboo sticks.
The gāthā says:
The journey was arduous; in the deep night,
Shànyǒu fell into a profound sleep and dreamed.
Though the superior man’s mind was set on guarding,
the wicked man’s scheme had already arisen in his heart.
Considering the terrain, it would be difficult to catch him;
looking up, the Milky Way was surely not yet bright.
He took two bamboo sticks and damaged his eyes,
then stole the jewel and left first that very night.
Once Shànyǒu’s eyes were damaged,
he repeatedly called Èyǒu’s name: “Èyǒu!
Èyǒu!
There is a great thief here
who has harmed my eyes!”
He did not know that he had already left.
Since there was no answer to his calls,
he cried out even louder: “Wicked person!
Wicked person!
My eyes are already harmed;
if you want the jewel,
just take it.
Do not harm my younger brother;
my younger brother is foolish and young.”
He cried out to the sky,
saying to the thief:
“You may take the sea jewel, the Maṇi, as you please;
it’s just that I don’t know how to hide it elsewhere.
But I worry that my younger brother is foolish and simple-minded;
I humbly pray for your compassion, do not harm him.”
As he called out and pleaded thus,
still no one answered.
Then the tree spirit was moved.
Thus the sūtra says below:
As he cried out loudly,
his voice shook the deities,
but for a long time there was no response.
At that time, the tree spirit immediately spoke: “Your younger brother Èyǒu is your wicked thief;
he stabbed your eyes,
and took the jewel and left.
Why are you calling Èyǒu now?”
It announced in a gāthā:
“Do not cry out loudly and frequently;
in the deep night, it only needlessly disturbs the dragon spirits.
It was not the jewel’s wish to be stolen away;
the one who harmed your eyes is your own kin.
Stop wasting words begging for his life;
it is foolish to cherish his body with affection.
If you wish to know the news of your worthy brother,
he is the one who wielded the sticks.”
Shànyǒu said: “Alas!
Alas!
How could I have known this!”
Looking up at the sky in the deep night, he wept even more bitterly;
his double eyes ached, a pain unbearable to touch.
It was not easy to know his jealous feelings;
how could I have removed the dry bamboo?
What grievances and animosities,
what kinsmen,
joined faces, blood flowed over the grass.
They were supposed to be true brothers,
who knew there was such poison in their hearts?
Mistakenly thought they were invading bandits,
this aberrant act, sighed throughout ancient and modern times.
The pearls were taken by the wicked man and departed that very night,
blood dripped onto the grass from the dry bamboo.
So many words, endless pain,
cries broken, the deeper the sorrow.
Thought he was my truly compassionate brother,
who knew he harbored such a poisonous body and mind?
With body and face joined, too lazy to turn back,
even a heart of stone would be crushed upon seeing this.
Running beasts with bent legs all gazed in dismay,
flying birds with folded wings were all sorrowful.
Not only did he perish innocently in the endless night,
but he was also buried by the master (digging earth) on the long road.
The wicked friend having taken the pearls and fled,
to what country did he return, let him sing it out.
(Sūtra) At that time, the wicked friend, carrying the jewels,
returned to his own country,
and met his parents.
He reported to his parents: "My body's fortune and merit
allowed me to be completely saved.
The good friend, the prince, and all his companions, due to their meager merit,
perished completely by drowning in the water."
This is the wicked friend, the prince, who stole the pearls and left first,
returned to his own country,
and reported to his parents:
"Good friend, due to the karma of his previous life,
was in danger alone amidst the vast waves.
How many pearls and jades were engulfed by the wind,
countless merchants were swept away by the water.
Before setting sail and arranging things, one could still be cautious,
but having boarded the boat, regret is hard to recall.
Human fate, one knows it is (is known to be) predetermined,
only I, safe and sound, was able to return."
Question: What did the parents do when they heard this?
The following sūtra says:
When the parents heard these words,
they cried out loudly,
fainted and fell to the ground.
Cold water was sprinkled on their faces,
and after a long while, they revived.
They said to the wicked friend: "How could you bring this and come back?
Once, he cried so much, blood filled his cheeks,
his heart and guts were torn into a thousand pieces.
Instead, the wicked person extended his life's fortune,
while the good friend was made to conceal himself in the underworld.
Never harmed anything, why should things be angry?
Without reason, offended Heaven, Heaven sent disaster.
Had he been swept away by the water, he should have gone along;
why come back today, doing what?"
The wicked friend, being rejected by his parents,
became even more regretful.
He had intended to take out the pearls and say he got them,
but after hearing these words,
he buried them in the ground.
Having been rejected and ill-treated by his parents,
he increasingly pondered, giving rise to malice.
Though he walked outside the gate (walked outside) with forced composure,
dwelling in the palace, he had no reliance.
His sorrow redoubled,
he secretly deliberated,
it was already a result of indifference in a past life.
Do not foolishly give the pearls to him,
it is better to dig a hole and bury them deeply.
If I were to present the pearls now,
it would be difficult to avoid sorrowful tears, only recalling my elder brother.
All contempt and dislike are not from this world,
all criticisms and curses come from many past lives.
Desiring to devise a plan to leave the palace,
yet also fearing that news would spread and the capital city would weep.
Even if the pearls are unique in their myriad forms,
pondering it, they are still not regarded with affection.
How can it compare to burying them deep in the ground,
cutting off the many lives crushed by fate?
Showing affection to me is not the wish of this world,
being a son to him is decreed by Heaven.
Half a year abroad brought a thousand worries,
one day returning to the palace brought a hundred curses.
This, too, is an idle matter;
let him sing about where Shànyǒu found peace.
(Sūtra) At that time, Prince Shànyǒu had both his eyes pierced,
pierced with dry bamboo splinters,
and no one was there to pull them out.
He wandered and turned,
not knowing where to go.
At that time, suffering greatly,
he was intensely hungry and thirsty,
unable to live,
unable to die.
He gradually walked forward,
until he reached the borders of the kingdom of Lìshībá Wáng.
The wicked friend brought the pearls to the palace,
and was scorned and defiled by his parents.
The pearls had already been buried.
The elder brother, supported from behind, gradually walked.
He got up from the grass,
groping for a path.
Though dazed and half-awake,
how could he express the pain?
He wandered, comforting himself,
who would care for him in his exhaustion?
He was like a blind beggar,
with nothing to protect himself.
How did the foolish and wicked friend conceive such malice,
suddenly arising with this intent to pierce his elder brother's eyes?
Though I walk slowly,
I worry that he calculates the journey to be fast.
His heartlessness towards me is trivial,
but I fear my precious pearls might be damaged.
The foolish youth was completely deluded by spirits and ghosts,
looking up at the sky, he unconsciously cried repeatedly.
One cry ceased, then another cry,
thinking of his foolishness, lamenting his name.
My heart will never see his fault,
I wish to return safely to the imperial capital.
May saints and sages protect him from harm,
may his parents, seeing his return, cherish him.
When he grows up and understands,
he will come to seek his elder brother, regardless of the distance.
Thus crying,
he traveled for several days with a companion,
reaching the borders of the kingdom of Lìshībá Wáng.
Before Prince Shànyǒu entered the sea,
his father, the king, had promised Lìshī Wáng's daughter in marriage.
Later, he learned of his drowning at sea.
When the prince was tens of miles from the kingdom,
he sat on the road, feigning to be a blind beggar.
He happened to encounter a cattle superintendent,
who was tending five hundred cattle for the king.
The king bull then rode over the prince's body with its four hooves,
letting all the other cattle pass.
It licked his eyes with its tongue,
and pulled out the bamboo splinters.
After a long while,
the king bull departed.
Later, the cattle herder looked back and noticed something unusual.
He asked in a gāthā:
"Though you are blind in both eyes,
you are able to make a bull pull out the bamboo splinters and walk.
Although previous auspicious signs were trivial,
how can one not be surprised by this wonder today?
Are you secretly hiding magical arts within?
Or have you served deities and spirits in a past life?
To dispel all my doubts,
I hope you will tell me your name."
Shànyǒu, being asked,
immediately thought to himself:
"If I tell the truth,
that wicked friend will surely suffer harm.
For Lìshī Wáng is his maternal uncle."
So he simply replied: "I am a blind beggar.
Deeply ashamed of my humble and lowly state, I have no name;
begging for food, I happened to wander to this place.
I have never mastered any magical arts,
nor have I ever served deities.
I was fortunate to have the king bull
pull out the splinters for me;
it must be that my broken body is not yet meant to die.
Kind sir, why must you doubt today?
I am merely a solitary and impoverished son.
I have no home, no place to return,
I beg for food, letting my feet carry me where fate allows.
In this life, I am cold and alone, content with my lowliness;
in a past life, hunger and scarcity led to this poverty and danger.
It is not due to any profound art hidden in the bamboo splinters,
it is all because the king bull possesses great compassion.
Seeing my appearance is seeing it completely;
why then do you suddenly doubt again?
Do not vainly speculate about my surname and given name;
this body of mine is surely useless.
I do not know the appearance of the mother who bore me,
and my born body wanders in the dust all day long.
Encountering bamboo splinters is to repay karma,
meeting the king bull is to avert disaster."
But the cattle herder did not believe him,
and repeatedly expressed compassion, let him sing it out.
(Sūtra) At that time, the cattle herder observed his whole body,
and saw that his human appearance was unusual.
He then said: "My home is nearby,
I will provide for you."
The cattle herder then took Shànyǒu back to his home,
and gave him various foods and drinks,
and instructed all the men and women, old and young, in his family: "You all should serve this person
as if he were me, without difference."
Although Shànyǒu explained himself thus,
the herder still did not believe him,
and so took him home.
The gāthā says:
“Though my eyes are blind, I rely on this humble body.
Alas, how can I not accept hunger and poverty?
My thick eyebrows enter my temples,
and my long earlobes hang down like wheels.
My philtrum is straight, and my nose is high like a phoenix's beak.
Clear spiral patterns are on my fingertips.
Do not dislike my living in a village garden;
I will use this body to nurture you until the end.”
The
blind man then agreed to go.
The herdsman brought him home and raised him,
telling his family,
big and small, not to be disrespectful.
This is an excerpt from the previous text.
After a month like this,
his family became weary and began to complain.
Shànyǒu heard their voices and was unhappy.
He immediately thought to himself,
“Tomorrow morning I will bid farewell and leave.”
The herdsman said, “Is it because of my young children?”
Shànyǒu replied, “No,
it's not that your family, young or old, is not caring;
it's just that I am without a share,
so it is not suitable for me to stay long.”
The
verses of farewell:
“I humbly assess my hunger and poverty,
and my blindness makes distant objects impossible to grasp.
The mat I sleep on was sent by your wife;
the water for washing my face was added by your virtuous son.
They silently complain about my begging;
they clearly attend to me for your sake.
The reason I bid farewell today
is that I cannot simply wait to be disliked.”
The
herdsman said, “You cannot leave!”
Shànyǒu said, “No,
I must go!”
After this exchange repeated several times,
he could not be persuaded to stay.
So the herdsman asked, “What do you want when you leave?”
The blind man said, “If you pity and care for me,
make a *zhēng* for me,
and send me to a crowded place in the provincial city to settle down.
I will play tunes and beg for food!”
The herdsman then acquired a *zhēng* and gave it to him,
sending him to a place within the city of Lìshīwángguó.
Though the reluctance to part was strong, he had no intention of staying;
with sincere bows, he asked to leave.
The blind scholar knew he was causing trouble,
and the herdsman could not help but feel doubt and worry.
“My home is poor,
and it is a village dwelling;
it is difficult to provide jewels or gold to assist you.
I offer you the *zhēng* from my home,
and will send you to a crowded place to settle.”
The
host clearly pitied the guest,
and such a host-guest relationship is rare today.
The guest felt indebted for the trouble, speaking earnestly;
the host was ashamed of the loneliness, with tears in his eyes.
His home lacked even three meals,
yet he offered a *zhēng* as a parting gift.
Both observed the rituals completely,
and accompanied him all the way to Lìshīchéng.
Leaning on a shoulder, he entered the city and sat on the main street,
bidding the herdsman farewell and asking him to return.
Relying on others, he could not dislike the hustle and bustle;
passing through, he trusted in enduring the dust.
He caressed his head and face with private joy,
and subtly arranged the tunes by plucking the *zhēng* strings.
How many people all came to watch?
How could the sound arise (sound arise) from his fingers and be sung?
(Scripture says) Shànyǒu was skilled at playing the *zhēng*,
its sound was harmonious and elegant,
pleasing all hearts.
All the multitudes provided him with food and drink,
until he was fully satisfied,
and the five hundred beggars in Lìshībáwángguó all became full.
Once he arrived in the kingdom,
he played the *zhēng*,
and everyone watched,
including the five hundred poor people.
He played with even more emotion, moving people,
but never revealed his name.
He could perfectly divide the beats in his tunes,
and skillfully arranged the sounds on the strings.
Not only was his fame heard within the palace,
but it also spread throughout the capital city.
It seemed the neighborhood invited him,
and regardless of status, all came to listen.
Because of this, the people of the neighborhoods
passed the word to each other,
prepared clothes,
and provided tea and food.
Not only was the blind scholar himself fed,
but also the five hundred poor people were universally helped.
All received assistance because of his tunes,
and all were sheltered by his virtuous songs.
Every day he played songs in the neighborhood streets,
and thousands of crowds gathered everywhere to watch.
All said he must have another family,
all said it was a pity he was blind.
Plates filled with rice,
clothing piled up,
regardless of status, all paid attention.
Not to mention his own abundant well-being,
he also provided for the five hundred poor children.
Every morning he sat in the market, playing strings and singing,
women rushed like clouds, unable to resist.
The elegant tune was both high and steady,
the clear sound was both beautiful and harmonious.
Not only was everyone satisfied with the taste of food,
but clothes also increased day by day.
The five hundred poor men were all fed and warm,
whose good fortune could compare to his?
He was happy and joyful, his heart content;
every day people listened, filling the six streets.
His appearance immediately shed its thinness and weariness,
his clothes were completely changed from dusty rags.
He never allowed his name to be heard by others,
only using his songs as wealth for the world.
It was precisely during this time of carefree peace and joy,
that he was invited to sing by someone.
(Scripture says) At that time, the King had an orchard,
which was lush and flourishing,
but was constantly troubled by birds.
At that time, the orchard keeper said to Shànyǒu, “You should protect the birds for me,
and I will provide well for you.
I wish…”
“Fó Bàōrēn Jīng” Chapter Eleven.
Shāmén Yǐ said: A thousand years, the river changes;
a myriad-chariot ruler is born.
Drinking the auspicious light of the raven and rabbit,
embracing the righteous *qì* of heaven and earth.
Every year on the ninth day,
auspicious smoke is specially arrayed in the crimson court;
every Chongyáng festival,
the whole world rejoices in the joyous occasion.
His position is noble, like the nine-five hexagram line,
his sagely response is like one thousand years.
If not a Bodhisattva in disguise,
then he is a Cakravartin King in his rightful position.
Having cultivated blessings and wisdom over countless eons,
he is then made ruler of men to govern heaven and earth.
If he resides in a Buddha-land, he is called a controller;
coming to reside in the divine land, he is called the Most Honored.
He seeks the peace of the world and promotes the imperial way,
desiring that weapons cease under heaven's gate.
As long as the sun and moon shine,
where can sentient beings not feel gratitude?
Golden autumn, jade dew dampens the dust,
golden palace, jade steps arrayed with precious platforms.
Golden wind sweeps away the fog, quieting the frontier,
golden chrysanthemums, holding mist, open towards the sky.
Golden-branched relatives surround the imperial screen,
golden-purple ministers offer longevity cups.
May golden words be praised to support the emperor's longevity,
forever singing like gold and stone.
Chú'àn:
According to the phrase in the present text, "The sūtra title chanted by the Dūjiǎng who just arrived
is called 'The Sūtra of Prajñāpāramitā for the Benevolent King to Protect the Country, Chapter One: Preface,'"
it is known that this text is a讲经文 (jiǎngjīngwén) interpreting the 《仁王護國般若波羅蜜多經》 (Rénwáng Hùguó Bōrě Bōluómìduō Jīng).
Therefore, the latter title is 《仁王般若經抄》 (Rénwáng Bōrě Jīng Chāo).
《仁王般若經》 (Rénwáng Bōrě Jīng) is the abbreviated name for 《仁王護國般若波羅蜜多經》 (Rénwáng Hùguó Bōrě Bōluómìduō Jīng).
It is also a common practice in Dunhuang manuscripts for a jiǎngjīngwén to be directly titled after the sūtra's name.
The former title, 《長興四年中興殿應聖節講經文》 (Chángxīng Sì Nián Zhōngxīng Diàn Yìngshèngjié Jiǎngjīngwén),
was named based on the occasion of its use.
"長興" (Chángxīng) was the reign title of Hòutáng Míngzōng.
"長興四年" (Chángxīng Sì Nián) was 933 CE.
"中興殿" (Zhōngxīng Diàn) was where Hòutáng Míngzōng held court.
《舊五代史·唐書·明宗紀二》 (Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ·Táng Shū·Míngzōng Jì Èr) states: "(Tiānchéng Yuán Nián) Xīnhài,
the emperor first held court in the Zhōngxīng Diàn."
Hú Sānsheng's (胡三省) annotation to 《資治通鑑》 (Zīzhì Tōngjiàn), Hòutáng Míngzōng, Chángxīng Sì Nián, cites 《五代會要》 (Wǔdài Huìyào):
"In Táng Zhuāngzōng's (唐莊宗) Tóngguāng Èr Nián,
Luòyáng's (洛陽) Chóngxūn Diàn (崇勳殿) was renamed Zhōngxīng Diàn." "應聖節" (Yìngshèngjié) was Hòutáng Míngzōng's birthday (the ninth day of the ninth month).
《冊府元龜》 (Cèfǔ Yuánguī), Volume Two, "帝王部·誕聖" (Dìwáng Bù·Dànshèng) states:
"In the sixth month of Tiānchéng Yuán Nián,
the Central Secretariat proposed: 'The ninth day of the ninth month, the emperor's birthday,
by old custom, has a special festival name, and this day is called Yìngshèngjié,
with three days of holiday.
Furthermore, let the capital and the whole realm set up music
to express congratulations for longevity,'
which was followed."
Note that "天成" (Tiānchéng) was Míngzōng's (明宗) reign title when he ascended the throne.
Every year on Yìngshèngjié, it was customary to summon monks and Daoists to lecture and debate in the Zhōngxīng Diàn
to celebrate.
《舊五代史·唐書·明宗紀三》 (Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ·Táng Shū·Míngzōng Jì Sān) states: "(Tiānchéng Yuán Nián, ninth month) Guǐhài,
on Yìngshèngjié,
all officials set up a vegetarian feast at Jìng'ài Sì (敬愛寺),
and summoned monks and Daoists to lecture and debate in the Zhōngxīng Diàn,
following a recent precedent."
The "recent precedent" mentioned
refers to the common practice of lecturing on sūtras on the emperor's birthday
since the mid-to-late Táng dynasty.
The Japanese monk Yuánrén's (圓仁) 《入唐求法巡禮行記》 (Rùtáng Qiúfǎ Xúnlǐ Xíngjì), Volume Four, states:
"National custom: every year on the emperor's birthday,
venerable lecturers and Daoist priests from the two streets are invited to the inner palace to set up vegetarian feasts and burn incense,
invite monks to discuss sūtras,
and hold debates between Buddhism and Daoism." 《僧史略》 (Sēngshǐ Lüè), Middle Volume, "生日道場附" (Shēngrì Dàochǎng Fù) states:
"The practice of naming the birthday a festival
began with Táng Xuánzōng (唐玄宗).
In Wèi Tàiwǔ Dì's (魏太武帝) Shǐguāng Èr Nián, a daochang (道場) was established.
By Shén Sì Nián, an imperial edict commanded all prefectures and garrisons to establish daochangs to celebrate the emperor's birthday.
During Shǐguāng (始光) was the beginning of the emperor's self-veneration of blessings,
and during Shén (神) was the beginning of subjects offering congratulations for the emperor's longevity.
Since then,
when subjects offer auspicious congratulations, they must arrange vegetarian feasts and recite sūtras,
calling them 'Birthday Festival Daochangs,'
which are still widely practiced today."
Furthermore,
the lecturer and author of this jiǎngjīngwén,
according to Mr. Liú Míngshù's (劉銘恕) conjecture,
should be Yúnbian (雲辯).
This is discussed in 《敦煌遺書叢識·〈長興四年中興殿應聖節講經文〉的講經者》 (Dūnhuáng Yíshū Cóngshí·〈Chángxīng Sì Nián Zhōngxīng Diàn Yìngshèngjié Jiǎngjīngwén〉de Jiǎngjīngzhě),
published in 《敦煌語言文學論文集》 (Dūnhuáng Yǔyán Wénxué Lùnwénjí)
by Zhèjiāng Gǔjí Chūbǎnshè (浙江古籍出版社) in 1988.
Yúnbian was a famous monk of the Five Dynasties period,
also written as Yúnbian (雲辨).
His deeds are recorded in Zhāng Qíxián's (張齊賢) 《洛陽女紳舊聞記》 (Luòyáng Nǚshēn Jiùwén Jì), Volume One, "少師佯狂
(楊公凝式)" (Shàoshī Yángkuáng [Yáng Gōng Níngshì]):
"At that time, the monk Yúnbian was skilled in popular lecturing,
had literary talent,
and was quick-witted in response.
For sacrificial or congratulatory texts,
depending on the rank of the individual, he could compose a thousand characters on the spot,
all as if they were pre-arranged.
The Shaoshi (少師) particularly esteemed him.
When Yúnbian was lecturing in the fifth month at Chángshòu Sì (長壽寺),
the Shaoshi went to the lecture hall and sat opposite Yúnbian.
Singers were at their side.
Suddenly, a large spider descended on a thread from the eaves,
directly in front of the Shaoshi and the monk
(this sentence has missing characters).
Yúnbian smiled and said to the singer: 'Try to mock this spider.
If you can do it well,
I'll give you two bolts of silk.'
The singer, without a moment's thought,
mocked it immediately,
his words entirely about the spider,
but the mocking lines
were actually a satire of Yúnbian.
The Shaoshi, hearing this,
collapsed in laughter for a long time,
and loudly cried: 'Monk, bring five bolts of silk!'
Yúnbian, also laughing,
then presented five bolts of silk.
The singer's mockery of the spider went: 'With a belly so swollen from eating,
you spin silk and walk around the temple,
setting up a net in the air,
only waiting to kill living beings.'
(This was to mock Yúnbian)
(because he was corpulent with a big belly).
Yúnbian's dharma name was Yuánjiàn (圓鑒).
Later, he became the Sīlù (司錄) of the Left Street,
and after a long time, he passed away."
Yúnbian's popular Buddhist literary works,
preserved through Dunhuang manuscripts,
besides this text,
also include Sī Qī (斯七), Sī Sānsānqī'èrbā (斯三七二八), and Bó Sānsānliùyī's (伯三三六一) 《二十四孝押座文》 (Èrshísì Xiào Yāzuò Wén) (selected for the first volume of this book),
Bó Èrliùlíngsān's (伯二六〇三) ten poems of 《讚普滿偈》 (Zànpǔ Mǎnjì),
Sī Sìsìqī'èr's (斯四四七二) 《修建寺殿募捐疏頭歌辭十首》 (Xiūjiàn Sìdiàn Mùjuān Shūtóu Gēcí Shí Shǒu),
Sī Sìsìqī'èr's (斯四四七二) 《十慈悲偈》 (Shí Cíbēi Jì), etc.
Sūtra:
May the Emperor live ten thousand years... ... ... ...
With these accumulated merits generated by praising the Mahāyāna,
we respectfully offer them to the solemn and honorable Emperor, His Imperial Majesty.
We humbly pray that the sacred lineage may have ten thousand leaves,
and the sacred lifespan a thousand springs;
as deep as the Bohai Sea,
and as firm as Mount Sumeru.
Dedicated to
(Recite Buddha's name)
the Empress,
we humbly pray that her noble example may ever be new,
and her grace, like Kūn's (坤) virtue, be eternally spread.
May she receive the favor and glory of the myriad chariots,
and extend kindness and love throughout the six palaces.
To the Shūfēi (淑妃),
we humbly pray that her life be as long as the spirit-tree,
and her years equal to the Kalpa-stone.
May the praise for her benevolence be further spoken,
and her name for good governance within the palace be renowned far and wide.
Then we wish that the ruler sings and the ministers harmonize,
heaven be accomplished and earth be level.
May beacon fires cease and the world be at peace,
may sun and moon shine bright and weapons be still.
(Recite Buddha's name)
The sūtra title chanted by the Dūjiǎng who just arrived
is called 《仁王護國般若波羅蜜多經·序品第一》 (Rénwáng Hùguó Bōrě Bōluómìduō Jīng·Xùpǐn Dìyī): Rén (仁),
is the foremost of the Five Constants;
Wáng (王),
is the most revered of all nations;
Hù (護),
is the blessing bestowed by sages;
Guó (國),
is that which unites China and barbarians;
Bōrě (般若) is perfect and brilliant wisdom;
Bōluómìduō (波羅蜜多) is crossing the river of love;
Jīng (經) reveals the true doctrine.
This is a brief explanation of the title.
This sūtra explains thus: The Great Sage, long ago on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa,
gathered sixteen great kings,
followed by hundreds of thousands of various holy beings.
At that time, there was the Bodhisattva-prince, King Prasenajit (波斯匿王),
who bowed his golden crown amidst the assembly on the ocean of dharma,
and saluted the compassionate form upon the lotus throne.
He requested the declaration of the Ten Bhūmis,
and wished to understand the Three Voids.
He hoped for the golden words for protecting the nation,
and longed for the jade verses for pacifying the times.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One proclaimed the wondrous truth,
and entrusted it to enlightened rulers.
From afar, it leads to Buddhahood and the salvation of beings;
up close, it pacifies the people and governs the nation.
It commands the practice of the Ten Virtues,
to quell the Three Calamities.
When the mind and conduct are harmonious, the winds and rains are also harmonious;
when laws and decrees are just, the stars naturally align.
Ultimate truth and conventional truth go hand in hand,
like fish and water needing each other;
royal law and Buddhist sūtras transform together,
like clouds and dragons meeting in accord.
We wish for heaven and earth to be eternally peaceful,
with pure hearts seeking explanations and devoutly listening;
that the nation's weather and winds be unerring,
and the sun, moon, and stars in the sky suffer no eclipse.
Though the charioteer's compassionate guidance is earnest,
the king's search for dharma is even more fervent;
the Tathāgata speaks of the law for securing the country,
hence it is named 《仁王護國經》 (Rénwáng Hùguó Jīng).
The king earnestly salutes the flower throne,
only hoping for golden words to be revealed for the multitude;
may the sun of wisdom shine to dispel evil in the heart,
and the wind of compassion scatter calamities in the nation.
Diligently, we dare to hope the compassionate Venerable One grants permission,
then with understanding, the jade palanquin may return;
We wonder where this sūtra was taught,
and who heard the Dharma and brought it forth.
Sūtra
“與大比丘衆千八百人俱”者，
第五眷屬成就也 。
世尊行化，
徒衆相隨。
梵Wáng Dìshì and the dragon-gods,
the rulers of states and the heavenly kings, together with their men and women,
dignified Bodhisattvas,
surrounded and accompanied the Tathāgata.
With jeweled crowns on their heads and lotus flowers under their feet,
their words flowed like a mighty river and their hearts were like a vast ocean.
Majestic Arhats,
distinguished true monks.
Two points of snow on their brows never melted,
a strip of cloud on their kasāya always remained.
They marched in formation,
they sat encircling the flower platform.
Like the sea surging around a golden mountain,
or stars clustering around the bright moon.
Also like our Emperor's sacred lineage, with ten thousand leaves,
and the imperial throne with a thousand people.
When he exits, all the officials rejoice,
when he enters, the six palaces gaze upon him with reverence.
Empresses and princesses,
linger in the light of the sun and moon;
Princes and royal grandsons,
surround the shadow of the imperial carriage.
Cultivated over several lifetimes,
a karmic affinity over many kalpas.
The Buddha has Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas,
the king has golden branches and jade leaves.
Whenever the Merciful One turns the Wheel of Dharma,
sages and worthies surround his purple-gold body.
The breeze of compassion ripens the fruits of past cultivation,
the sweet dew cleanses the dust of delusion.
Mountains are like emerald screens supporting palaces and pavilions,
the Buddha is like the bright moon ruling the stars.
It is solely because of cultivation in past lives
that one can forever follow the undefiled person.
The Emperor oversees the world, revered by all within the four seas,
the sacred lineage continuously receives new rain and dew.
The hearts in the inner palace are like those relying on the winter sun,
the civil and military officials are like those bowing to the North Star.
In the Hall of Shùn, the thousand-year ruler lingers,
the heaven of Yáo offers shade to countless relatives.
All because of karmic affinities accumulated over many kalpas,
they are able to always be close to the sage.
Your minister hears: the Buddha's words are known as Sūtras,
the king's words become Edicts.
If Sūtras are practiced, one abandons the mundane and becomes a sage;
if Edicts are implemented, the distant are awed and the near are peaceful.
The king's grace reaches scholars, peasants, artisans, and merchants,
the Buddha's beneficence spreads to dragons, devas, Śakra, and Brahmā.
The Buddha's mind is pure,
enabling those with divine powers to save people;
the king's intention is clear,
sending loyal and filial ministers to assist the state.
At the Buddha's assembly at that time,
the reunion of the four types of adherents was already clear;
in the king's palace today,
the accomplishment of the five teachings is also flourishing.
The karmic affinity of the Dharma assembly reaches the imperial palace,
the achievement of the five teachings should be similar.
Buddha's Sūtras are respected everywhere,
the king's Edicts are revered by all people.
They can understand and uphold the law to eliminate calamities,
they can rely on the Dharma to attain spiritual powers.
If not for the Emperor's heart being like the Buddha's,
how could the Buddha's disciples reach this place?
Therefore, Sòng Wéndì said to Qiúnà Bámó: “This disciple always wishes to observe fasting and戒 and not kill,
but being compelled to sacrifice myself for things,
I cannot follow my will.
What does the Dharma Master teach about this?”
The Emperor of Sòng, with his doubts unresolved and unopened,
asked the expounding Buddhist monk on the jade steps.
It is difficult to practice the king's way, knowing there are no factions,
but I often worry that my compassionate heart may still be inconsistent.
Our national laws make it difficult to stop killing,
and occupying the king's position, one cannot observe fasting.
Today, I dare to ask the eminent monk to speak,
to clarify my mind with a single word.
Bámó said: “The cultivation of emperors and commoners differs.
A commoner's status is humble, their name obscure,
their words and commands lack authority.
If they do not exert themselves with hardships,
what benefit will there be?
An emperor takes the four seas as his home,
and the myriad people as his children.
When he utters one good word,
men and women are pleased;
when he implements one benevolent policy,
humans and gods are harmonized.
Therefore, punishments should not take lives prematurely,
and labor should not exhaust strength.
Then the wind and rain will be timely,
and the hot and cold seasons will follow their cycles,
the hundred grains will flourish,
and mulberries and hemp will grow lush.
Such observance of fasting is indeed great,
such non-killing is also abundant.
Is it really necessary to omit half a day's meal,
or save the life of one bird or animal,
before it can be considered extensive deliverance?”
The Emperor stroked his table and said: “What the Dharma Master has said
truly illuminates and enlightens,
one can speak with you about the affairs of humans and devas.
How admirable is such a person!
Not only does he attract and advance people into the Buddhist path,
he also helps to promote the king's transforming influence.”
Thus, it is known that the Tathāgata's wondrous conduct
can be practiced by rulers of states,
it is not measurable by minor sages,
nor can common people comprehend it.
As soon as a word is spoken,
the four seas comply.
It causes those who hold loyalty and practice filial piety to have their Dao broadened and virtue renewed,
and makes those who betray righteousness and lack benevolence fearful and terrified.
The great Roc flaps its wings,
crossing ninety thousand li of mountains and rivers;
the jade rabbit soars into the sky,
illuminating ten thousand layers of the universe.
The transformations achieved are
as vast as this,
shaking and stirring like clouds and thunder,
moistening and nurturing like spring rain.
The Buddha's conduct and the king's heart are comparable,
their profound vastness is clearly praised endlessly.
Just half a day's goodness from the ruler of a state,
is equivalent to a commoner's cultivation over ten thousand kalpas.
Suddenly, his decrees bring peace to the great nation,
abundant rain and dew sprinkle upon the feudal lords.
With robes hanging down, he sits calmly in his deep palace,
a single compassionate heart covers the nine provinces.
The holy ruler's cultivation of goodness is inexhaustible,
one must know that common, petty people can hardly compare.
Below, he is the master of the universe, both Chinese and barbarian,
above, he aligns with the achievements of yin and yang and creation.
Abundant harvests in the four seas return to his sacred virtue,
all nations are peaceful and prosperous, benefiting from his sagacious wisdom.
The king's blessings are the blessings of all living beings,
he holds the universe in his palm.
Our Emperor wishes to purify the four seas,
first he admonishes the six palaces.
He makes them aware of the toil of weaving women,
and teaches them to understand the urgency of silkworm households.
Their faces are without adornment,
their hands have calluses.
When the shuttle is thrown, it is laborious,
when brocades and silks are worn, they should be cherished.
The hardships of silkworm farmers are hard to describe,
when do they ever approach a dressing table all day long?
Leaves are like fly heads, [so small] that they must grow large,
silkworms are like ant legs, [so small] that they must be nurtured.
Half the cocoons are formed when new cicadas chirp,
a skein of silk is made when old debts are pressed.
Therefore, the sage admonishes the palace women,
not to sweep dust with brocades and silks.
Whenever our Emperor partakes of fine meals,
he always remembers the farmers.
He worries about the imbalance of floods and droughts,
and fears the difficulty of paying taxes.
Therefore, whenever he announces meals,
he does not excessively cook.
He values every grain like a pearl,
and cherishes all living beings like his own children.
He always remembers the farmers' busy four seasons,
supporting themselves to fill their granaries.
Hair on their temples has already turned white,
wheat in the fields is only then turning yellow.
The setting sun illuminates their bodies as they return to their distant homes,
at dawn, orioles chirp in the trees as they go to reclaim wasteland.
Officials see the farmers' hardships,
and instruct them to measure their own contributions.
Our Emperor, when the nation is extravagant, shows people moderation;
when the nation is frugal, he shows people礼.
Therefore, he is cautious and vigilant in his position,
anxiously worrying about the people.
His actions align with the will of Heaven,
he cultivates the kingly way with simplicity and reverence.
He desires to forever empty the prisons,
and permanently cease the beacon fires.
He promotes the compassion of releasing nets,
and initiates the governance of knotted cords.
Sagacity and wisdom are both present,
awe and love are equally manifest.
He is truly the most esteemed of the five phases,
truly the ruler of the myriad people.
His balanced mind attracts national peace,
rewards and punishments all follow the way of Heaven.
Rain and dew wash away all grievances,
the imperial wind blows and auspicious mists rise.
For years, no words of war are spoken,
only the sounds of music fill the ears.
[He] is as unmoving as Sōngshān,
forever guarding Luòyáng City for ten thousand years.
Your humble servant hears that myriad streams flow,
ultimately converging into the waves of the four seas;
the nation is divided into nine *zhōu*,
and must pay tribute to the lord of the Central Plain.
Thus, having felt the cessation of disaster in Dōngchuān,
Xīshǔ's heart turned.
From afar, gazing at the sun and moon, [X] they return to the Lónglóu;
from afar, imperial edicts descend to pacify the Guījùn.
Cultivating virtue and benevolence is never-ending;
mountains and rivers, once barren, are now opened.
From now on, merchants will enter through Jiàngé;
henceforth, tribute will come from Dāozhōu.
Several imperial ministers, bearing mandates, went forth;
several times [X] memorials of gratitude returned.
The Sage further conferred titles upon kings;
thus relieving the southwest of much disaster.
Our August Emperor has cast off extravagance and excess,
encompassing the eight directions;
without affairs or actions,
all nations pay homage.
Take the example of the two Zhès,
far separated by blue waves;
they felt the great grace of the great nation,
and received noble ranks from the enlightened ruler.
For a long time, they have paid tribute;
their integrity will not waver.
Imperial envoys travel without concern for wind and water;
tribute arrives with safe passage for ships.
Dragons assist and spirits help,

The two Zhès have heard proclamations many times,

People gather at the cinnabar palace, a thousand years of arrival;

The whale's eyes glow, shaking the sun and moon;

It is because they know to pay tribute to the enlightened lord,

Now, a revered title is added,
once again spreading heavenly merit.
Displaying the complete loyalty of the myriad officials,
manifesting the true virtue of the One Man.
The characters "Shèngmíng"
signify the merit of [X] far-sightedness;
the words "Shénwǔ"
praise the achievement of pacifying chaos and securing the nation.
Virtue is taken as the rule, broadening the Way and benefiting humanity,
benefiting humanity, broadening the Way is taken.
When literary virtue shines, heaven and earth are tranquil;

Virtue surpasses a thousand ages,
beauty permeates Huá and Yí.
When the One Virtue is proclaimed, all within the four seas rejoice;

Seeing that the monarch aligns with Heaven,

One person surpasses all ancient and modern rulers,

It already shows the nation is prosperous and the customs are abundant,

Following Heaven, broadening the Way, and being honored as a sage,

Our August Emperor secures the ancestral temples,

The righteousness of the capital's defense is firm,

Thus, the enlightened ones of several *zhōu*,

The wind of Yáo wafts, and golden pistils are fragrant;

East, west, north, and south,

Enfeoffing kings in several *jùn* makes the state stronger,

The clear jade rivers nourish the great nation,

Suddenly ascending the imperial chariot, the grace is known to be extreme;

How can one repay the power of Heaven and Earth?
Only by loyalty and filial piety can one repay the monarch.
Our August Emperor's words are not vainly spoken,

Feeling the auspicious removal of disasters by the hundred spirits,

On Yùquán Shān,
the Sage re-adorns the precious Lotus Palace;
by the Jīngǔ River,
the Empress [X] the Scripture Repository Hall.

It manifests the shared brightness of the sun and moon,

The temple on Yùquán Shān is renovated,

At dawn, the rainbow beams' light is already joined;

What can a humble *shìzǐ* achieve with little power?

Our August Emperor's western palace quarters,

The light of the jade rabbit slants,

[X] terraces and pavilions,
arranged as if by heavenly design;
imperial roads through forests and mountains,

Ten thousand kinds of beautiful flowers,

a thousand types of auspicious birds,

The imperial residence is not far,

Rowing boats, breaking through lotus flowers;

The clear waves are like a mirror,

Everyone points to the Yellow Dragon boat,

Monarch and ministers gather,

The azure sky just sent down a thousand-year ruler,

Every festival, banners and flowers adorn the imperial palace;

Knowing that Heaven assists the ruler of Heaven and Earth,

This day, people celebrate,

From the highest generals, ministers, princes, and marquises,

Where there are people,
incense and flowers are arrayed;

The shade of protection is vast,
the devout prayers are one in heart.
Only wishing the nation to be forever peaceful,

Today, many sounds of music are heard,

Grace is like jade dew, dripping into every home;

Circling above the palace, it is not heavy fog;

Your humble servant, the monk, prays to augment the heavenly lifespan,
wishing to see the Yellow River clear a hundred times.
For three years, Qínwáng dispatched your humble servant;

Polishing a scroll without private words,
offering tribute to a virtuous ruler of a thousand years.
Only by proclaiming and expounding the ultimate Way,
is there no other path to display merit.
And from today, lecturing before the screen,
may my name also be heard throughout the four seas.
Sòngwáng is loyal and filial, serving Yáo's heaven,

Without an imperial edict, it is difficult to enter the palace;

Lùwáng is distinguished and courageous, residing in Qízhōu,

Since there are heroes to assist the state,

Giving utmost loyalty and integrity to serve the enlightened ruler,

From ancient times, the classics clearly state,

Several families' joyous dreams have already come true,

Troubled people are all happy,

At this time, grace reaches west and east,
merits and virtues are as countless as the sands of the Ganges.
Not counting all *zhōu* and *xiàn* and towns,
all are surprised that prisons are empty at once.
Having received extraordinary grace and favor,
at night, facing the stars, I burn precious incense.
By what path can I again express my loyalty and filial piety?
Opening a sūtra collection to repay the sovereign.
All beings cultivate good deeds without error,
only then can they pass into the Emperor's household.
The Emperor suddenly bestowed a horse,
commanding his minister to ride it and boast throughout the capital.
Who does not understand the love for glory and splendor?
Fierce in body and mind, and fond of boasting.
How enviable are loyal ministers who prolong vast [land],
abandoning glory, shaving their heads, and repaying the government.
The holy compassion is like the opening sun,
illuminating with bright light throughout the nine heavens.
All are imperial favors that align with gods and Buddhas,

Having traveled over a hundred thousand lǐ of shifting sands,
monks from the Táng [Dynasty] came to pay respects to the Emperor.
A purple robe and the title of shī were graciously bestowed,
