intending to admire the [incomplete]
After the Buddha entered the city,
the Buddha saw all sentient beings,
all like children encountering their kind parents,
or like sick people meeting miraculous medicine.
The assembled officials danced,
the Son of Heaven walked slowly,
bowing to the Tathāgata amidst the five-colored light of his white urna,
gazing at his auspicious marks within the thousand lights of his purple-gold body.
There was no noble son with a golden saddle
who did not turn from extreme joy to sorrow upon seeing the World-Honored One;
no beautiful woman in a painted pavilion
who did not feel her heart sway as if drunk upon seeing the Great Sage.
High and low, vast and numerous,
rich and poor, bustling about,
some gouged out their eyes to offer to the Tathāgata,
others burned their bodies before the Great Sage.
They sacrificed their lives, yet their lives were not exhausted—
such is the unfathomable power of the Buddha;
they burned their bodies, yet their bodies could not be harmed—
〔□〕the immeasurable compassion of the Sage.
Strange indeed, strange indeed!
Holy indeed, holy indeed!
When the Buddha entered Viyé to save sentient beings,
then myriad rare and wondrous things were felt.
(Et cetera).
(Upper part)
(Lower chant):
In the Saha world, suffering scorches and boils,
seeking profit and fame, when will it end?
Clinging to self, clinging to others—what is the cause?
All due to the pervasive calculating deluded mind.
Like a person descending a high platform in the middle of the night,
stepping on a broken, snapped rope in the dark.
Suspecting it to be a poisonous snake a foot long,
ordering young and old to bring a lamp.
When has there ever been a snake?
It is all the deluded mind arising and clinging.
Just like my disciples, greedy for illusory realms,
the deluded mind calculates and perceives them as real.
One must truly understand this for oneself and for others,
that it is the broken, snapped rope of the night.
The deluded recollection of wife and children, and the clinging to their appearance,
is just like mistaking the rope for a poisonous snake.
Summon the boys and girls to come down from the hall,
and bring a lamp of wisdom to illuminate.
Breaking through the darkness of ignorance and afflictions,
then one first knows that all things are impermanent.
Forming enmity and hatred is due to delusion and ignorance,
contending for qi and emptiness is due to karmic obstructions.
Not understanding that this body is not the ultimate,
worrying about family and nation, ever busy.
Chanting poetry and playing flutes in the red pavilions,
getting drunk, then taking it as bodily pleasure.
This is precisely finding joy within suffering,
because illusory dharmas defile the mind-king.
One must know that alcohol is the gate of all resentments,
when gathering, do not drink.
Moreover, it is a harmful substance for people,
therefore, absolutely do not give rise to greed for it.
The pit of fire will fill up without rest,
the attainment of Buddhahood seems still distant.
Not falling into the three evil paths and suffering torment,
such a one is no ordinary person.
If one were to speak from the beginning, when would it stop?
All people understand transmigration in saṃsāra.
Taking Śākyamuni, the master charioteer, as example,
who then transformed sentient beings in this world.
Prince Śvetaketu descended from the heavens,
feigning to take refuge in King Śuddhodana's palace.
Even cultivating ascetic practices in the snowy mountains,
and attaining supreme great physicianhood.
He constantly uses wondrous Dharma to liberate sentient beings,
lovingly teaching us the right causes.
Enabling us to awaken to the priceless jewel of tathātā,
to help people transcend the body of deluded conditions.
Pouring ghee throughout the three thousand worlds,
showering Dharma rain in the sixteen kingdoms.
On that day, he intended to lead all the sages and saints,
driving the three carriages within the city of Viyé.
Many worthies and saints all accompanied him,
striking chimes and blowing conch shells to lead the Buddha.
As the Buddha moved his noble and auspicious body,
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas all followed.
Heavenly boys offered celestial flowers in golden bowls,
heavenly girls presented exotic fruits on jade plates.
Śakra, in stately procession, praised the holy lord,
Brahmā, soaring in order, circled the Compassionate Honored One.
The seventeen assemblies all lingered,
celestial flowers rained along the long road.
Who envies your spreading brocade and displaying silk?
Who pities you in the heavens and all directions?
A dense cover of auspicious clouds shrouded Saha,
overflowing joyous colors invaded the blue sky.
Clear and mournful celestial music resounded through the universe,
heavenly beings gathered, scattering widely.
Sages and saints from the ten directions all sang praises,
awesome is Śākyamuni Buddha.
In Viyé, the karmic causes were profound,
thus, a thousand kinds of wondrous things arose.
Kings, in phoenix carriages, came out to welcome him in the suburbs,
ministers, in chariots, ascended the road to greet him.
They wished to see the Greatly Compassionate Lord of the Three Realms,
just like children longing for kind affection.
People, vast and numerous,
came out of the city,
to gaze upon and venerate the solemn and splendid jeweled platform.
With vows and compassion, he came to teach and transform,
sacrificing body and life countless times.
The red sun shone brightly,
white clouds swirled back,
heaven and earth shook and roared like thunder.
Dense incense smoke and auspicious qi,
gently enveloped this great Tathāgata.
People leaped and danced,
laughing boisterously,
a hundred birds in the sky sang as if mournfully.
What did the Jīvājīvaka birds say?
Chirping and twittering, they praised the Tathāgata.
Many wondrous things,
truly extraordinary!
All living beings, sentient and insentient, all arrived.
With eyes full of tears, they looked at the Holy Lord,
each wishing to relinquish their fetal womb.
Why was it so?
Because the World-Honored One, through immeasurable kalpas, never in the slightest went against sentient beings,
thus such things were manifested.
(Et cetera).
Also, because the Tathāgata's entourage entered Viyé,
sentient beings rejoiced and looked up.
They asked, what kind of entourage?
(Recitation of the Great Sage Vimalakīrti Bodhisattva).
(Vimalakīrti Bodhisattva).
In days past, the Tathāgata entered Viyé,
the entourage was truly splendid and beautiful.
Clouds dispersed in the blue sky, revealing the auspicious sun,
the road became a pure realm, raining celestial flowers.
The Compassionate Honored One walked slowly, supported by golden lotuses,
Bodhisattvas walked gracefully, their faces radiant with joy.
Śakra's majestic bearing was never disorderly,
Brahmā's retinue was without disarray.
Auspicious clouds supported their feet, worthy of reverence,
auspicious qi gathered around their bodies, worthy of praise.
Flower bowls were arranged like lions' bones,
incense plates were formed like elephant kings' tusks.
Celestial immortals were graceful like spring willows,
jade maidens were solemn like evening clouds.
Mist dampened the heavy necklaces on their chests,
wind swayed the jade crowns askew on their heads.
Śrāvakas all circled the golden form,
Pratyekabuddhas all rode white deer carriages.
Upāsakas held flower parasols,
Upāsikās offered purple kāṣāya robes.
As they walked, yellow leaves were often spread,
crossing water, old rotten wood was often seen.
Their journey along the road was hurried,
the distance to the city was vaguely a little.
The king departed the phoenix palace with solemnity (far),
the emperor left the dragon palace, the road was long.
The Buddha's intention has always been to teach and transform,
but people's hearts only love glory and splendor.
How do they know that such is but a dream,
not yet realizing that humans are like four poisonous snakes?
The comings and goings in saṃsāra are countless,
sinking and submerging like dust and sand.
Who can equal the lofty Holy Lord?
The vast multitude of ordinary beings cannot fathom his boundlessness.
The Buddha proclaimed the wondrous Dharma on the lotus platform,
instantly bringing them into the family of the Dharma King.
High and low,
laughing boisterously,
dragging purple and trailing red throughout the nine heavens.
Joyous colors, shallow and deep, enveloped the sun and moon,
auspicious clouds, dense and light, locked around towers and platforms.
Resounding through the universe,
roaring like spring thunder,
manifesting the arrival of our Compassionate Honored One's teaching and transformation.
Throughout a hundred billion worlds, the net of resentment dispersed,
throughout three thousand worlds, the flowers of awakening bloomed.
Heaven and earth,
gleaming white,
everywhere piled with celestial flowers.
Like brocade and silk, this [evil/filth],
like frost and snow, covering dust.
The seventeen assemblies,
arranged themselves,
following the Empty King, unmatched in their formation.
High fans blew fragrant breezes, dispelling heat and affliction,
light dew fell, settling dust.
People leaped and danced,
urging each other on,
to quickly enter Viyé and extinguish obstacles and calamities.
Brahmā, offering grass, walked majestically,
Śakra, holding flowers, appeared grand and towering.
Dragons competed in dance,
ghosts and spirits pressed forward,
the King of Gandharvas, a hundred million myriad.
Frequently performing clear songs, elucidating the Four Noble Truths,
or playing elegant music, dispelling the three calamities.
The Golden-winged Gaṛuḍa
has unmatched power;
it grasps high mountains, shattering them to ash.
Because it eats many dragons, its body is like (fire),
and heaps of demonic hosts roar like thunder.
The eight divisions of dragons and devas are all majestic,
as the Buddha comes and goes like a gentle breeze.
Playing with its shadow and body, it turns left and right,
driving clouds and singing thunder with mighty (force).
The Lord of the Three Realms
sings "How wonderful!"
"This dignity cannot be surpassed."
For the four kinds of beings, it removes arrogance,
and for the six paths of humanity, it acts as a ladder and matchmaker.
Rulers and ministers
bow to the Tathāgata;
how dare one doubt words free from defilement?
They dance and burn incense, vying to make offerings,
cleansing their hearts and purifying their minds, circling the flower platform.
Men and women,
troubled in heart,
their many afflictions should be crushed this day.
In the golden light, they behold the auspicious marks,
and in the fragrance of the uṣṇīṣa, they bow a thousand times.
Truly it is excellent,
difficult to fully describe;
how many noble and humble beings awaken from the illusory womb!
The Buddha enters the Aṃravana garden to proclaim this Dharma,
and someone holds a canopy and sings it forth.
The Sūtra says: At that time, in the city of Vaiśālī, there was a householder's son,
named Ratnakara (Bǎojī),
who, with five hundred other householder's sons, held seven jeweled canopies.
(And so on).
The lay practitioner (Vimalakīrti) knows that the Buddha has entered Vaiśālī,
because "I am here to teach sentient beings in this country,
and the Buddha wishes for me to help propagate the great teaching,
so I must display a little divine power today."
"Whose karmic affinity is ripe today?"
Then he perceives Bǎojī and others pursuing joy and pleasure.
"I must teach them,
to fulfill their aspiration for the Way."
Moreover, when flowers scatter in the three springs,
they still rely on sweet dew to wash them clean;
when the Buddha attains perfect enlightenment,
he (still) relies on Bodhisattvas for support.
Thus, one knows that flowers rely on spring warmth,
and the Buddha relies on assistants.
The lay practitioner (Vimalakīrti) praises, saying: Within the three thousand realms,
and in billions of specks of dust,
there is a venerable one who walks majestically alone,
acting as a boundless, peerless lord.
Holding the pestle of compassion,
he can crush the mountain of arrogance;
spreading the cloud of wisdom,
he covers the sea of greed and anger.
The four kinds of beings and six paths,
the eight difficulties and three lower realms,
he saves sentient beings without beginning or end,
and transforms surrounding creatures inexhaustibly.
His mind is like a great pickaxe,
able to uproot the roots of affliction;
his intent is like a surging wave,
extinguishing the fire of ignorance.
His deportment is rarely matched,
his auspicious marks hard to equal.
His uṣṇīṣa-jewel is like the full autumn moon,
his wristlets are like freshly pure cold ice.
On the lotus platform,
his twin eyebrows secretly bear a smile;
in the hall of seven treasures,
his two cheeks always contain joy.
He acts as the guide for sentient beings,
and the model for Bodhisattvas.
He enters Vaiśālī not for others,
but proclaims the wonderful Dharma entirely because of me.
"Today, I must
display a little divine power,
observing in this city,
whose karmic affinity is ripe?"
He happens to see golden branches and jade leaves,
imperial sons and royal grandsons,
playing pipes and singing in the three palaces,
making music with strings and flutes within the nine palaces.
Behind embroidered curtains, they sleep by day,
while consorts add incense from golden ducks;
in the imperial garden during spring outings,
attendants pick the stamens of magnolias.
Regardless of season,
not choosing autumn or winter.
They return drunk before moonlit screens,
and wake from dreams beneath the hall of clear breezes.
Straddling fragrant saddles and shaking jade reins,
not caring about their status;
drinking fine wine and throwing golden cups,
knowing only wealth and nobility.
The lay practitioner (Vimalakīrti) shouts from afar,
reprimanding Bǎojī, saying: "You are greedy for feasting,
attached to sights and sounds,
because the seeds of affliction run deep,
and the karma of ignorance is heavy.
Without any shame,
how can you know of the poor and humble?
Embodying (pure) heroes,
you only love extravagant affairs.
Your treasuries hold precious and exotic brocades,
your perfumed kitchens prepare fine meals.
When you take a step, a thousand people follow;
one utterance, a hundred assents.
Clad in splendid brocades,
how can you know the toil of the weaving women?
Eating gourmet delicacies,
you do not remember the suffering of the farmers.
These are: guests who come and go in the six paths,
and people who guard the shops in the three lower realms.
Secretly you are foolish and ignorant,
unable to comprehend.
I must teach now,
I want to guide and support,
to make you abandon this clamor,
and attain the wonderful fruit of non-action (nirvāṇa)."
(And so on).
(Chanting Bodhisattva).
Vimalakīrti (Jìngmíng) suddenly ponders,
"For whom does the Buddha enter Vaiśālī?"
He sighs for sentient beings, many of whom are arrogant,
and pities creatures who are utterly foolish.
They mistakenly believe their appearance remains joyful and youthful,
and imagine their stature will not change.
They do not realize that in the end, they will grow old,
how can they know they will ultimately be destroyed by death?
With slow, frequent steps, full of grace,
with measured, vast strides, full of dignity.
His hands are like white jade reflecting an autumn mirror,
his eyes like blue lotuses emerging from a morning pond.
Leading sentient beings, he never tires,
guiding creatures, he never wearies.
This coming is a day of meeting,
now is the time for me to teach.
I see the sons of the householder in the ninefold palace,
and they are five hundred imperial sons.
They are greedy, opening golden locks in the phoenix palace,
and getting drunk with jade consorts in the red tower.
Beneath the window, green maids chant imperial poems,
among the flowers, red-faced women sing palace lyrics.
Parrots hide in green willows as the morning glow disperses,
swallows chirp on red beams as the scene fades.
Peach blossoms by the steps are washed by spring rain,
bamboo before the curtain is blown by wild wind.
In the fragrance of silks and satins, the lamps are dim,
amidst the sound of strings and flutes, the pillow is half-tilted.
Below the palace, drunk, they wake and shout "Long live!",
in front of the courtyard, after drinking, they call for their consorts.
They only crave pleasure, wishing it to last forever,
not considering that the human body has its rise and fall.
I must enter the palace to teach,
to make them take refuge in the Great Muni (Buddha).
Jūshì had finished his meditation,
then entered the royal palace.
Seeing Bǎojī chasing pleasure and seeking joy,
he expediently spoke words of reproach,
causing him to tire of extravagance,
and teaching him to return to the Three Jewels.
Jūshì meditated in his dwelling,
and having finished speaking, he departed.
He picked up his jílì (coconut wood) staff before the curtain,
and donned his wūshā jīn by the mirror.
He brought no attendants,
yet his dignity was as it always was;
he brought no household servants,
yet his bearing was exactly as before.
With white hair stirred by the wind,
and a long gown sweeping the ground,
he raised his head like a star moving at midnight,
and moved his feet like an ancient cypress, an immortal plant.
Gazing afar at the Imperial Palace,
thousand-fold auspicious qi billowed and enveloped it;
looking from afar at the Imperial Palace,
a single cloud of auspiciousness obscured and illuminated it.
He repeatedly walked slowly,
moving his body leisurely.
He saw the willows by the imperial embankment, their colors blending with the mist;
he beheld the peach blossoms in the Forbidden Garden, smiling at the sun.
No sooner had he entered the nine-layered depths [of the palace]
than he heard sheng and song;
as he slowly approached the three halls,
he observed brocade and silk everywhere.
Jūshì saw Bǎojī and others,
each displaying martial arts,
all competing in literary talent.
They captured the wind and moon in five-character poems,
and discussed enchantment and folly beneath three-foot swords.
By the steps and along the path,
clear springs gurgled around the bamboo;
beneath the trees and by the stream,
snow-capped cypresses rustled in the wind.
None failed to boast of wealth and nobility,
competing in extravagance.
Riding fine steeds on long roads,
they draped brocade robes in wide thoroughfares.
Beneath the curtains of concubines,
spring parrots cried out 'Long live!'
Before the hall of the imperial attendants,
autumn swallows chattered with myriad melodies.
And then, after getting drunk in red towers,
they returned home with fragrant parasols.
Golden whips waved among willow trees and flower branches,
jade reins held high in the clear wind and bright moonlight.
Accompanied by those in vermillion and purple robes,
they sang in unison words of imperial virtue;
attended by those in official caps and robes,
they sang together songs of gratitude.
On coral pillows,
before jade curtains,
they heard a single strain of a qín when half-awake from drunkenness,
and awakened from dreams to the rain of the third watch.
The monarch's favor
particularly bestowed the grace of rain and dew;
the empress's affection
frequently granted the benefits of pearls and treasures.
Jūshì said to Bǎojī: "This is indulgence in luxury and desire,
vexation and ignorance.
You consider it the glory and splendor of the world of forms,
I consider it the bitter sea of sinking.
You enjoy yourselves to the extreme,
how can you know the suffering of the myriad common people;
you are uniquely noble and lofty,
how can you contemplate the oppression of all living beings?
I now specially bring sincerity,
to awaken your deluded emotions.
You must truly accept my words,
they are like the Buddha's words on a flower platform.
Do you not know there is a Buddha in the ān yuán,
saving all sentient beings?
He is adorned with a thousand kinds of blessed virtues,
and embodies ten thousand kinds of majestic bearing.
You should completely eliminate greed and attachment,
and develop a good heart.
Abandon the illusory heart of an empty show,
and prostrate before the golden-adorned countenance.
You must discipline yourself,
and be firm and self-observant.
If circumstances bring about a peaceful outcome,
I will accompany you and travel as you please."
(Et cetera).
(End)
Wéimó finished speaking and exited the palace courtyard,
holding his藜杖 (li杖, staff of wild goosefoot) in his hand, clapping it.
He walked slowly out the gate, repeatedly bowing,
and with a smiling face, greeted the dukes and ministers on the road.
Scholars one by one paid respects at the Dragon Palace,
Jūshì watched them arrive at the Phoenix City.
The road was already bustling with carriages and horses,
and from the nine avenues, he heard the distant sound of pipes and strings.
Those going to and fro on the golden steps knew people,
but who ever asked their names in the jade halls?
Just seeing brothers boasting of their skills and accomplishments,
each competing in military and literary brilliance.
The joy in the deep palace was unrivaled,
there was wine poured for those pursuing pleasure.
When flower petals fell, people were half-drunk,
where willow mist was deep, the rain had just cleared.
From high towers, only words of peace and security were heard,
how could war be mentioned from the twin gate-towers?
Colorful maids smiled and chided the golden-pavilion swallows,
concubines idly called the jade-cage parrots.
Below the Zǐyún Lóu, songs and dances were performed,
before the emperor's curtain, ball games were arranged.
Washing their faces with jade mirrors, they presented their plain countenances,
in the sunny window, they teased the red parrots under the shining sun.
Puppies chased wildly, biting people,
servants frequently pinched, startling wild pigeons.
At sunset, they played tricks before the window,
when the moon was high, they learned to play the sheng by the tower.
Indulging in pleasure, they were unwilling to worry about old age,
chasing joy, who could think of life and death?
From afar, seeing Jìngmíng, all went to meet him,
from afar, encountering Jūshì, all came to welcome him.
Wéimó then said to the royal prince: "The old ways must be changed from the beginning.
Blindly coveting the sea of foolish desires,
hastily pushed into the muddy pit.
A thousand thoughts understood are all like a dream,
two eyes clearly seeing are just like being blind.
The water of karma accumulates with vast waves,
the mountain of sin adds to its rugged grandeur.
Unaware of the Buddha of Miàojué Ānyuán,
who always speaks of true conditions to save sentient beings.
His body is like golden radiance shining in the sun,
his mind is like a clear mirror illuminating a deep pool.
His teeth are arranged densely like mountain snow,
his intentions are pure and clear like crystal.
His sacred sword always carries heavy compassionate vows,
his Dharma boat is always propelled by the pole of wisdom.
One glance, one bow, removes calamities and obstacles,
whether laughing or singing, all are equally calm.
If you wish for glory and splendor, seek to worship the Buddha,
I will practice cultivation with you today."
(白) Bǎojī (寶積) and others, having received the lay practitioner's teachings,
immediately turned their hearts.
Before the lay practitioner,
they recounted their past days,
pursuing pleasure through the four seasons,
chasing joy through the eight festivals,
unaware that all this was illusory and empty,
foolishly believing it to be eternal bliss.
Now, having been exhorted,
they immediately follow his guidance,
wishing to accompany the Mahāsattva (大士) on his journey,
following him to the monastery garden to worship the Buddha.
The lay practitioner said: "It is heard that tender shoots blossom and flourish
all because of the sequence of seasons;
ordinary people cultivating practice
are entirely taught and transformed by the Buddhas.
As for you all,
you are precisely greedy for joy and pleasure,
competing for glory and splendor.
Through the four seasons, you enjoy the flower pavilions,
through the eight festivals, you wander in jade palaces.
In spring,
willow mist first falls,
and enchanting scenery is deeply hidden.
Parrots with chattering words fly about,
flower buds half-open as if splitting.
Rain adorns the colors of the terrace,
wind sways the sound of curtains.
The spring shadows of one window are warm and bright,
the sunlight filling the ground is soft and flowing.
In the beautiful palace,
the opening of the gate adds to the flow of the verdant pond;
in the glorious light of the hall,
the stacked high mountains on the pillow press upon sentient beings.
In summer,
it can be said that the gentle warmth is light,
and the heat is deep and strong.
A railing of green bamboo sways in the wind,
ten thousand cherry trees are bathed in rain.
Long-spread woven mats
are like a stream of green water just beginning to flow;
cleanly swept jade beds
are like eight feet of cold ice not yet melted.
Thin gauze makes up the curtains,
lightly transparent dyed clothes.
The hall is deep so the heat does not invade,
the pavilion is distant so the coolness is self-contained.
Leisurely clouds at the door
are like countless strange peaks;
old cypress trees leaning against the eaves
are like deep, flowing cave waters.
In autumn,
it can be said that frost carves red leaves,
and rain drips on sparse paulownia trees.
Geese cry in the cold wind of the high sky,
crickets chirp on distant steps under the bright moon.
The verdant mountain colors,
wearing clouds, entirely enter the dragon towers;
the faint sounds of cicadas,
mixed with dew, loudly fill the phoenix palace.
The vermilion courtyard at midnight,
the Forbidden City in early evening.
Hearing the sound of pounding cloth from a thousand homes,
listening to the music of pipes and strings from ten thousand households.
Golden chrysanthemums leaning on the railing,
their fragrance reaching the silk curtains;
cold pines reflected in the pavilion,
their sounds constantly penetrating the embroidered canopies.
(云云)
In winter,
it can be said that frost congeals on jade steps,
and ice clarifies the golden pond.
Snow taps on the window of the night pillow,
wind shakes the bamboo in the cold courtyard.
As stars shift in the azure sky,
how can one know the cold of the cave dwelling?
Lamp shadows on silver screens,
one does not perceive the coldness of the brocade quilt.
These are what I called joy,
what I made into splendor.
I took myself to be ultimately firm and secure,
I took myself to be originally real and existing.
I saw myself as rich and noble,
a thousand years just like this moment;
I saw myself as preeminent,
ten thousand years just like today."
Bǎojī (寶積) and others felt fortunate for a hundred lifetimes,
and that it was difficult to repay through countless kalpas.
Suddenly meeting the elder Vimalakīrti (維摩),
joyfully encountering the noble lay practitioner.
Truly, his demeanor was dignified and solemn,
a pure breeze radiating towards people;
his appearance was grand and imposing,
his virtue a towering mountain standing against the sun.
Now, by the lay practitioner's skillful means,
he guides us.
Taking a firm and sturdy rope of compassion,
he tames the five hundred wild "heart-monkeys".
From this day forward, we
shall play no more drums, strings, or songs.
We will have no mind to enjoy ponds and pavilions,
but will earnestly seek profound joy.
The clear sounds of wind instruments and songs,
we hear as wind in our ears;
pairs of beautiful women,
we see as thorns in our eyes.
Golden cups and jade goblets
will not be tilted before painted boats;
fine wine and clear spirits
will not be drunk in the company of red towers.
Vermilion bridle tassels and white horses,
brocade saddles and red saddle cloths.
A thousand men will not lead the way,
ten thousand cavalry will cease to follow behind.
Pepper-scented silver duck censers
will no longer add fragrance to the five watches of the night;
beautiful women in powder chambers
will not be reflected in the sunset mirror.
Thus, the traces of ignorance will cease,
and craving will be gone without a trace.
Eliminating all doors of defilement,
we will contemplate the principle of non-action.
All this is Vimalakīrti's (維摩) instruction,
the lay practitioner's teaching.
Suddenly, with one voice,
they bowed and gazed at the lay practitioner.
The lay practitioner gratefully said: "Excellent, Bǎojī (寶積)!
You are truly a guiding teacher.
You are an imperial prince and a royal grandson,
you are an heroic and eminent scholar.
You should only crave glory and delight,
driving sun-chasing chariots on the imperial embankment;
displaying your talents and competing in ability,
running wind-chasing steps on the purple-paved streets.
How fortunate that this old man's humble words
have touched the elder's noble mind.
Merely a few insignificant words,
yet they have received such extraordinary esteem.
This is a great fortune in life and death,
a karmic connection from past kalpas.
Having already received and accepted my words,
how dare I further accept your respectful thanks?"
It is like the full bright moon
yielding its light before the stars;
ten thousand-foot green mountains
resigning their towering height below hills.
Bǎojī (寶積) and others, hearing Vimalakīrti's (維摩) words,
all aroused their spiritual resolve.
This morning they must leave the royal city,
on this day they want to return to the Buddha temple.
Having finished speaking,
they composed their dignified demeanor.
Each holding dragon-phoenix robes,
they changed into fresh new clothes.
Accompanying the lay practitioner,
they themselves held precious canopies.
The court officials in the palace were bustling,
the women throughout the country were in formation.
They then had the imperial road leveled,
and the celestial streets swept clean.
The spring rain in the nine avenues had just ceased,
auspicious smoke in ten thousand wells was gathering.
As for the precious canopy,
it was made of a thousand treasures,
composed of ten thousand jewels competing in beauty.
It was like a forest of flowering trees suddenly blossoming,
like ten thousand auspicious lotuses already split open.
Gold formed its frame,
with pairs of coral parrots;
white jade made its spokes,
with pairs of emerald jīṅgājīṅga birds.
Its craftsmanship was superior to that of master craftsmen.
Delicate intertwined branches and stems,
fine raised floral patterns.
Pearl tassels swept the ground,
fragrant breezes caused a gentle clattering sound;
its brilliance shone in the sky,
auspicious energy locked in its shimmering colors.
Thereupon, [the lay practitioner] led the way,
Bǎojī (寶積) followed behind.
They were about to leave the royal city,
but it was not yet clear where they intended to go.
Varied brocade robes were made for clothing,
solely to adorn impure bodies.
Even if you pluck your eyebrows and eyelashes,
and apply powder and oil,
Xīshī (西施), the enchantress, could win people's pity,
and bewitch King Xiāng (襄王) to abandon his throne.
But when the demon of death comes one day to take you,
it matters not how beautiful or talented you are.
Even if you are as handsome as Pān Ān (潘安),
whose fruit-filled carriage everyone knows,
when the four elements shift and the body perishes,
only an impermanent name remains.
Even if Hán Xìn (韓信) was heroic,
destroying Chǔ (楚) at Gāi (垓) and assisting the Hàn (漢) Emperor,
you should all ponder this in your hearts,
it all proves to be an empty illusion.
Fán Kuài (樊噲) was mighty and capable,
overturning the Hóngmén (鴻門) banquet to save his lord.
A fierce mind and coarse appearance increased my arrogance,
but now it is all for naught.
Former emperors and empresses for ten thousand years,
who died, their numbers unknown.
You look towards outside Cháng'ān city,
and behold imperial tombs covering mountains and plains.
Since Wéimó thus converted the royal grandsons,
he then asked all the royal grandsons to awaken.
With one voice they thanked the lay devotee,
saying, "We are especially grateful for you removing our deluded minds."
From then on, they awakened to impermanence,
and no longer delighted in the five worldly pleasures.
I regret my heavy afflictions from before,
when I pursued pleasure endlessly through the four seasons.
Though summer was indeed scorching and humid,
I was fortunate to be in the deep palace.
A chill permeated the bamboo mat,
the jade bed, quietly brushed, felt like light ice.
In autumn, leaves withered and scattered,
clouds dispersed, wild geese flew, and much wine was drunk.
The autumn wind filled the hall, waking me from my dreams,
a bright moon shone as I sobered from my drunkenness.
I realized that all phenomena ultimately become empty,
and understood that only the three vehicles are real.
How can it compare to paying homage to the Lord of the Three Realms?
It is better to draw near to Shìjiā Zūn.
On this day, the royal grandsons made their arrangements,
so that the people of the nine palaces were vast in number.
They wanted neither colorful maids nor imperial concubines;
all the officials and lay devotees followed them.
All holding jeweled canopies, they came out of the city,
sweeping the heavenly street like a mirror.
Rows of pipes and songs heralded them,
noisy red and purple robes walked on both sides.
A thick auspicious cloud covered the pavilions and terraces,
spring light lightly enveloped the Fèngquē.
Willow smoke on the paths attracted sweet dew,
flower trees on the road played with the morning light.
Tens of thousands of maidens circled the long street,
their hearts leaping with joy upon seeing the path to paying homage to the Buddha.
They wished to form good karmic connections on this day,
and send the princes to the hermitage garden.
Heaven and earth,
all became bright,
the jeweled canopy was truly magnificent.
Golden threads formed a double phoenix dance,
silver bars were woven into a flower-offering immortal.
Cold jade was ground and carved into branches,
琉璃 was sculpted as the canopy's peak.
When the mist dispersed, it seemed woven by heaven,
when clouds enveloped it, it seemed naturally formed.
As it was held and moved, jade rings jingled,
and the moving canopy caused jade pendants to clink.
On this day, the sound of the Buddha resounded through the universe,
at that moment, heavenly music filled heaven and earth.
In a snap of the fingers,
and with utmost reverence,
Viyé transformed into the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Heaven rained down four flowers, presenting auspicious signs,
and the earth shook in six ways, which the Buddha immediately knew.
It was truly splendid,
new jade flowers,
brocades, silks, and seven precious treasures.
Amidst the fragrant shore, they beheld the Emperor's son,
within the light of compassion, they saw Wéimó.
At that time, Bǎojī developed the Bodhi mind,
and all instruction came from Jìngmíng.
Their eyes did not gaze at alluring colors,
their ears did not listen to instrumental music.
All held jeweled canopies, departing from the Dragon Palace,
each wearing a golden crown, exiting the Phoenix City.
Royal grandsons crowded the road, vast in number,
unsure where they were all heading.
People in droves,
tens of thousands,
came out to pay homage at Viyé's dharma platform.
Men and women filled the streets, gracefully moving,
heroes crowded the road, laughing and lingering.
Auspicious smoke rose from the gates of myriad homes,
and joy opened in front of thousands of courtyards.
Intending to enter the assembly and meet the holy lord,
what kind of homage should be sung?
The sutra states: Bǎojī and others recited in verse: "Eyes pure, vast, like blue lotuses,
minds pure, having surpassed all meditations.
Long accumulated pure karma, called immeasurable,
leading the multitude to tranquility, hence we bow our heads."
One scroll of Wéimó Suìjīn.
Recorded by Sāmén Kuāngyìn, who lectured on sutras at Lǐngzhōu Lóngxīng Sì.
When Yuán Zōngjiān came,
he stayed for many days,
writing countless documents.
Because he was a monk,
he did not wish to obstruct him.
Shuòfāng Shìkè □
Sutra: The Buddha told Ānán,
"I observe sentient beings,
though they possess human form,
their minds are foolish and ignorant.
They do not reflect on their parents,
who have great kindness and virtue,
they do not show reverence,
and have no benevolence or compassion.
This chanted scripture
is the World-Honored One's reprimand."
The ten kinds of parental kindness and virtue mentioned earlier,
all relate to the parents' nurturing,
and the toil of the two parents.
(etc.)
The World-Honored One said: "Ānán,
I observe all sentient beings in the Suōpó world,
though they possess human form,
they do not know their parents have great kindness and virtue,
they do not repay them,
and do not understand how to requite their kindness.
At the end of their lives, they will surely fall into the three lower realms,
never to escape for kalpas.
Alas for men and women in the world,
who, having grown up, cannot reflect.
They have not cultivated a filial heart,
and idly learn things without basis.
Even if foolish,
and often resistant,
if parents scold, they throw spoons and chopsticks.
They only indulge their temper at home,
how can they know that reputation is spread outside the door?
When it is too hot, out of love and pity,
when it is cold, they are taken care of entirely.
When the child is happy, the whole family is at peace;
when the child is angry, the whole household is disheartened.
They drive themselves to exhaustion,
and endure suffering,
how can they gauge even a little bit?
Easily abandoning them and unwilling to return,
casually deserting them for a foreign land.
They have never made good acquaintances,
only befriended evil companions who cause harm.
At home, they constantly resent their parents' words,
but outside, they believe others' words.
Greatly foolish,
and not awakening,
they indulge body and mind, giving rise to ingratitude.
The Buddha says that such five-rebellious people
should not seek a good place to be reborn.
What is the cause of the endless hells?
It is only for the five-rebellious people in Yánfú.
Do not ask about the sins of winter's boiling and roasting,
nor about the years and months of pounding and grinding the body.
Knowing they are unreasonable, they submit to being beaten and broken,
humbly requesting pity and enduring the bitter hardship.
Even if you return to the human world,
from birth to old age, you will be poor and destitute.
The Buddha said: "Ānán,
if a person commits the five heinous crimes,
at the end of their life, they will surely fall into the evil paths.
Even if reborn into the human world,
they will suffer from illness and poverty,
and all their endeavors
will not succeed as desired.
All these are due to
If one wishes to achieve ten perfect forms in the next life,
to have wealth and much fortune,
to have clothes and food,
one must, in this life,
practice filial piety and care
(etc.).
If you aim for perfect karmic reward,
with much fortune, much wealth, and much righteousness,
may your actions always meet with auspiciousness,
and your endeavors never encounter calamities.
Enter as a marquis,
exit as a general,
protected by the earth, revered by all.
It is regrettable to neglect this in other paths,
there is no faster path than practicing filial piety and care.
If one understands how to deal with one's parents,
the earth gods and dragons will all be pleased.
There will be no calamities year after year,
and many kinds of auspiciousness every day.
One's actions and retreats will all succeed as desired,
one's comings and goings will bring peace everywhere.
Even if one's life ends and returns to the great night,
the three lower realms will still not harm one.
The Buddha said, "Ānán,
if a person understands and practices filial piety,
in this life, they will receive reverence from others,
and at the end of their life, they will not enter the Three Lower Realms.
Generally, there are many unfilial people in the world.
At home, they trouble their parents' hearts and spirits,
and they do not return at regular times.
This causes the father's heart to be sorrowful,
and the mother's mind to be anxious.
All day long, they lean against the gate,
shedding tears of blood in vain
(and so on).
The classics say: 'Store grain against famine,
raise children for old age.'
Even when they grow up,
knowing east and west,
they abandon their parents,
heading south and north.
Although children are unfilial,
parents never resent them.
Such acts of kindness are most abundant;
how can one bear to abandon them and go out?
(While parents are alive),
(I advise you not to live in another land).
People in the world are unfilial, which is lamentable.
They show disrespect to their parents.
They do not remember the extreme hardship of pregnancy,
nor do they know the great fatigue of breastfeeding.
They indulge in wrongdoings,
follow bad companions,
lightly scold their elders and destroy good people.
The Buddha says that such people,
life after life, will find it very difficult to see the face of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said that people in this turbid world
indulge in wrongdoings beyond discussion.
They rejoice when they see evil people,
but become angry when they meet good ones.
Have they ever listened when relatives advised them?
Do they seem deaf when parents teach and instruct?
They are entirely unwilling to engage in official careers or business,
but spend long periods idle and indulgent.
Parents worry all day long,
seeing their children associate with bad companions of the current trend.
They pursue pleasure and entertainment without cease,
and gamble at *chūpú* endlessly.
Day after day, they lean against the gate, shedding tears of blood;
morning after morning, troubles plague their hearts.
The Buddha said that this kind of person is not a true child,
and their death will lead them to the Three Lower Realms, which is sorrowful to lament.
From conception to infancy,
until the body grows to six feet tall,
they abandon virtue, betray kindness, and act unfilially.
They crave sounds and chase after colors, indulging their hearts.
Three years of breastfeeding are truly lamentable,
and ten months of pregnancy are truly pitiable.
They do not remember the nurturing efforts of their two parents,
but ungratefully abandon and turn their backs on them, even singing about it.
The sūtra says: 'Abandoning virtue and betraying kindness.'
This passage from the sūtra
describes the five rebellious beings mentioned by our World-Honored Buddha,
who abandon kindness and virtue.
Being unfilial to parents,
they roam in other lands,
abandoning their esteemed parents,
and do not return home.
At the end of their lives, they enter evil paths,
suffering great hardships.
This is only because they were unfilial to their parents in a previous life
(and so on).
The sūtra says: In a past life,
there was a sinner
whose head was constantly circled by a hot iron wheel.
He asked Mùlián
(and so on):
('This is only because I was unfilial to my parents in a previous life.')
His appearance was terrifying,
and all who saw him said his karma was heavy.
A hot iron wheel rotated on his head,
constantly causing pain regardless of the time.
He did not know why he suffered this calamity;
it was all due to what he personally cultivated and sowed in a past life.
He had no reverence for his uncles and aunts,
and showed no devout respect to his two parents.
The Buddha said that the karma of this ghost is difficult to describe;
a hot iron wheel constantly rotates on his head.
Day after day, he suffers various afflictions,
morning after morning, he endures hardships without cease.
All because he was unfilial to his compassionate father,
entirely due to his ingratitude towards his mother.
I earnestly urge all who hear the Dharma today
to quickly become filial and not procrastinate.
For example, serving parents,
loving and caring for siblings,
seeing them brings joy,
meeting them elicits praise and admiration.
Greeting them twice a day,
respectfully serving them day and night,
fanning the pillow and warming the bed,
one must know the proper timing.
(This is a truly filial child).
If one's heart is unfilial,
abandoning parents,
staying outside for years,
with no intention of returning home,
this is not a filial child.
Furthermore, when parents give instructions,
they do not believe their words.
They respond with a loud voice,
and their actions go against their parents' wishes.
Sweet and delicious foods,
are always eaten by their wives and children,
while bitter and astringent foods
are given to their father to eat.
(This is not a filial child) (
(not a filial child))
(at all).
The classics mention Zēng Shēn
(and so on).
The Buddha teaches that men and women in this turbid world,
upon growing up, must be filial to their parents.
In the evening, visit and in the morning, attend, do not shun labor.
Warm the bed and fan the pillow (fan the pillow), do not refuse hardship.
Do not let parents harbor resentment,
obey their commands and observe their expressions to act appropriately.
Not only will everyone praise you,
but also the sages will grant you protection.
Respectfully serving and nurturing brings peace of mind,
and the name of filial piety will surely spread throughout the world.
Zēng Shēn is mentioned by everyone in the classics,
and Luóbo is widely proclaimed in the sūtras.
All are ashamed of the great kindness of breastfeeding,
and all feel the deep compassion for the suffering of pregnancy.
The Buddha says that if one can practice filial piety and nurture,
in this life and the next, there will be no misfortunes.
Unfilial people,
are hard to describe.
Instead, they reverse the roles of their two parents as if they were dull.
Inside the house, they quarrel and argue with their parents;
outside the gate, they scold and involve their ancestors.
As soon as one intends to advise (teach and instruct), they become enraged;
if one tries to gently restrain them, they harbor resentment and anger.
The Buddha says that such five rebellious people,
at the end of their lives, will find it very difficult to escape suffering.
The Buddha said that the five rebellious evil beings,
their karmic retribution in the future will truly not be light.
They come and go among the Six Realms,
dying and being reborn in the Three Lower Realms.
This is precisely because they do not appreciate the virtue of pregnancy,
and entirely lack feelings of upbringing.
Therefore, in the Three Lower Realms,
they suffer continuously without cease.
Pitiable,
and sorrowful indeed!
Forgetting profound kindness is a great tragedy!
Even birds and beasts still act with filial righteousness;
how can humans indulge their hearts?
Three years of breastfeeding is still understandable,
but the suffering of ten months of pregnancy (carrying) cannot be measured.
The Buddha personally explained in the sūtras,
how carrying a heavy burden is sung about.
The sūtra says: 'When a mother carries a child,
during the ten months,
she is restless whether sitting or standing,
as if carrying a heavy burden.
She cannot eat or drink,
like a long-term invalid.'
This passage from the sūtra
is the World-Honored One further explaining the hardship of pregnancy.
(This is the first of the Ten Nurturing Graces: the Grace of Pregnancy) (
(and))
(Protection).
According to the *Huāyán Jīng*,
our bodies are formed from the red and white substances of our parents,
completing this physical form.
It has five colors.
In the beginning, it is a *kǎlālán*
(and so on).
(After thirty-eight weeks),
one finally understands how much suffering
we endured in our mother's womb.
The mother's appearance becomes emaciated
(and so on).
In ten months, carrying disciples,
countless hardships and pains are daily occurrences.
Morning after morning, her body feels like a mountain whether sitting or standing;
day after day, her mind is like one intoxicated in her actions.
She never touches phoenix hairpins or dragon mirrors,
and her jade-like face and flower-like complexion become withered.
She has the heart to chant Buddha's name and pray to gods,
but no desire to enjoy flowers or seek pleasure.
In ten months, carrying the disciple's body,
like carrying a heavy burden, the suffering cannot be described.
Her emerald eyebrows and peach-blossom face secretly grow thin,
her jade-like face and flower-like complexion suddenly lose their spring vibrancy.
Her cloud-like hair bun is left uncombed for months,
and her mirror stand is left to gather dust.
Because she yearns to protect the child in her womb,
her brows are constantly wrinkled, and there are traces of tears.
My hands are cold to the bone, my heart is sore,
my ten fingers are cracked from the tips.
One hand feeds the child,
serving always according to the season.
My paternal uncles and aunts, and parents-in-law,
still find me foolish and clumsy.
Often my tears are like falling rain,
constantly my heart feels torn.
Nowhere to speak my true feelings,
how can this suffering ever end?
It’s all for the little infant,
washing him at all hours.
Late at night, still not asleep,
my body is frail and collapsing.
Among these, the most bitter is the mother's body;
how could she fear lifting the child frequently?
Washing, she never declines cold or heat;
holding him, she never tires of bitterness and hardship.
Always, she is criticized by her parents-in-law,
frequently, she faces the anger of her paternal uncles and aunts.
All because she is bound by this infant,
causing her to exhaust her mind and spirit day and night.
Therefore, the sutra says: "Enduring such suffering,
swallowing bitterness and spitting out sweetness,
holding and nurturing"
(and so on) to "not shirking hardship."
This describes the first [act of] diligent protection.
Second,
returning to dryness and enduring dampness.
The sutra states: "The child sleeps in a dry place,
the mother sleeps in a damp place.
For three years,
she drinks her mother's white blood."
If it is washing during the nine summer months,
it seems somewhat less difficult,
but the three winter months are
exceptionally arduous.
If there are servants to command,
it can still be managed diligently,
but if there is no one,
all must be done by oneself.
In the hall, parents-in-law and paternal uncles and aunts
are served daily.
Embracing the foolish and silly child,
and lifting him morning after morning,
one hand washing the filth,
the other hand feeding the boys and girls.
The mother sleeps in a damp place,
the child sleeps in a dry place.
Within ten months,
she endures boundless hardship;
within three years,
she drinks immeasurable quantities of blood and milk.
This causes the mother’s appearance
to become frail day by day;
the loving mother’s complexion
to become thin and haggard morning after morning.
Returning to dryness and enduring dampness is a constant task,
for three years, her diligent efforts never cease.
Hardship brings tears daily,
torment causes sleepless nights.
Her appearance is frail,
her figure thin and haggard,
she abandons her phoenix hairpins and phoenix mirror.
Often she seems foolish before others,
constantly she appears drunken while seated.
This is all because for a long time,
she has toiled and suffered,
her physical form and spirit
have all fallen into disarray.
On one hand, she serves her parents-in-law,
on the other, she dresses and ties up the boys and girls.
She is never idle day and night,
often weeping like rain.
Returning to dryness and enduring dampness is the most difficult,
busy all day, never idle.
Washing, she considers not morning or evening;
toiling and running, how can she fear heat or cold?
She always lets her child sleep in a dry, warm place,
while she herself regularly sleeps in a damp place.
For three long years, it is always like this;
how can one feel at peace without repaying such deep kindness?
Therefore, the sutra says,
"The child sleeps in a dry place,
the mother sleeps in a damp place.
For three years,
she drinks her mother's white blood."
From the child's birth,
until three years of age,
he drinks the white milk from his mother's breast.
Gradually leaving her embrace,
becoming a toddler,
he increasingly tugs at his mother's heart,
with a hundred kinds of worries and concerns.
Near rivers and by wells,
she constantly worries about the danger of drowning;
playing with dogs and handling knives,
she frequently fears the pain of being bitten or injured.
(and so on)
As the child gradually grows into a toddler,
the loving mother’s worrying heart never leaves him.
Near fire, she specifically worries about burning flames;
by the river, she fears falling into the clear waves and dying.
Catching butterflies,
chasing puppies,
playing with dirt and piling mud in the street.
Because he is innocently foolish at this age,
it is precisely because he is young and silly that he is like this.
Gradually leaving her embrace to become an infant,
crawling and taking his first steps by the steps.
His speech is like a charming oriole first trilling its tongue,
his laughter like spring trees with wild flowers blooming.
The whole family cherishes him with boundless affection,
relatives dote on him with immeasurable tenderness.
Suddenly, crying is heard outside the door,
the loving mother rushes there quickly.
The infant gradually grows into a child,
the peach blossom color on his cheeks shines brightly.
Fives and fives follow each other, riding bamboo horses;
threes and threes gather, chasing puppies.
Eager to pursue butterflies, they stray far from home;
to fish for green moss, they forget to return.
The loving mother searches a thousand times, leading the way,
her heart constantly fears he will be bullied.
Thus, we know the loving mother cherishes her infant,
her tender thoughts and instructions fill her mind.
Days and months pass, years gradually advance,
scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants each take their place.
On one hand, she instructs and teaches benevolence and righteousness,
on the other, she seeks marriage and entrusts matchmakers.
The Buddha speaks of this in the sutra,
please chant it according to the text.
Sutra: Infants and children,
even into adulthood,
are taught etiquette,
marriage, official career, and scholarship.
To seek wealth,
they endure hardships,
toil diligently to the end,
without speaking of their parents’ kindness.
This chanting of the sutra text
is divided into two parts.
The first explains growth and instruction,
the latter speaks of the mother not mentioning kindness.
Growth and instruction is again divided into two,
the first explaining teaching etiquette,
the latter speaking of marriage, official career, and scholarship.
Growth and instruction.
The sutra states: "Infants and children,
even into adulthood,
are taught etiquette."
The boys and girls of a household,
from small to large,
must be taught etiquette.
For boys, from seven or ten years old,
they are taught to enter school.
(Sutra clearly states it is appropriate)
(to enter school),
(children of noble families must strive diligently).
The Analects says: "Plow,
and food is in it.
Learn,"
(and so on).
The Qūlǐ says: "If a junzǐ desires to transform the people and establish customs,
he must certainly proceed from them."
Moreover, the Book of Documents says: "Jade not cut
(and so on),
high achievements come from
(and so on)."
There are good boys and girls,
and weak boys and girls.
Household boys and girls are also like this.
(and so on)
As boys and girls gradually grow into adults,
their father and mother personally instruct each one.
To raise them is still for them to establish themselves,
to instruct them is simply to cultivate benevolence and righteousness.
They entrust teachers,
to teach literacy,
filial piety and etiquette must be complete.
Before they have been taught for one or two years,
they easily read through all books and histories.
Everyone, high and low, says they are fine young men,
near and far, all say their spirit is extraordinary.
Having grown into a true man,
a graceful and cultured true noble.
A dignified six-foot tall man,
with snow-white clothes befitting a jǔrén.
He will certainly receive favor in the high heavens,
pass high examinations and emerge from the dust.
Most likely, he will soon encounter new joys,
no different from a dragon shedding its old scales.
Wine matured, flowers blooming in the third month,
he knows only to participate in the spring banquet at Qújiāng.
This section is about promoting and teaching proper etiquette.
Hence, the sūtra says: "From
infants and children
to adults,
promote and teach proper etiquette." What are marriage, official careers, and studies?
Marriage is one thing,
and official careers and studies are another.
Huàn (宦) means holding an official position,
and xué (學) means pursuing academic studies
(etc.).
Today, speaking of marriage:
The scriptures say: a man, once he is strong, has a household;
a girl, at her first hair-pinning age, follows a man.
When a man has grown up,
he must seek a spouse
(etc.).
(If they are good boys and girls, etc.)
There is a type of household where the son
does not practice filial piety,
and does not understand proper etiquette
(etc.),
even when it is time for marriage
(etc.).
There is a type of disciple
whose dealings with people are erratic and distant.
They do not cultivate benevolence, righteousness, or the Five Constants,
nor do they care for warmth, gentleness, respect, and frugality.
They sometimes forget how to clasp their hands,
and their bowing is always unfamiliar.
At the vegetarian feast, they are quick to leave their seats;
at a funeral, they sometimes laugh inappropriately.
How many times has Mother arranged a marriage for you,
but people are unwilling to hear about it?
No sooner is an official career arranged for them
than they are casually scolded by their superiors.
Otherwise, they are entrusted with the family business,
the value of which is to establish the son.
But estates and properties are all squandered,
how can lazy, greedy, and ill-mannered heirs become proper adults?
The above describes how, once a boy has grown up,
he must be married.
From here, when a girl is taught and grows up from a young age,
she must be betrothed to another family.
Being a girl
is even more difficult.
First, she must be taught needlework.
She skillfully uses thread and needle with great concentration,
and boasts of her ingenuity as she embroiders birds and phoenixes.
She learns to sing,
and plays musical instruments,
making the whole household joyful.
When she grows up, she is chosen and betrothed to a man,
and all her relatives and clansmen rejoice.
Born with extraordinary wisdom,
she is like a descending cloud from Wūshān.
Her temples are like winter cicadas spreading their wings,
her face like the full autumn moon.
Her eyebrows are like willow leaves, green with mist,
her cheeks surpass peach blossoms, fresh with rain.
Betrothed to another family, she brings glory to her nine generations of relatives,
such joy and celebration are hard to describe.
If a person's wisdom is meager,
and from beginning to end she is extraordinarily foolish.
Meeting people, she never knows what is good or kind;
conversing, she never understands etiquette.
She has no interest in learning embroidery or tailoring,
and never puts on makeup.
She finds her own sewing clumsy,
which household would be willing to seek her?
A loving mother's heart
is always full of grace and pity;
she cherishes and watches over all alike.
For a daughter, she arranges a betrothal;
for a son, she celebrates a wedding.
A son must have literary skills and benevolence,
a daughter must have tailoring skills and musical talent.
Only after each one has been established,
can Mother begin to worry less.
The above concludes the first part,
explaining the teaching and guidance of growing up.
From here, the second part,
Mother does not speak of her kindness.
The sūtra says: "Despite endless toil,
she does not speak of her kindness or virtue."
The meaning of this sūtra is simply to say that a loving mother carries
a child for ten months,
nurses it for three years,
moves it from wet to dry,
and swallows bitterness to spit out sweetness.
Even after her children have grown up,
she showers them with a thousand kinds of affection,
and ten thousand kinds of instruction.
Whether it's a daughter's betrothal or a son's marriage,
all are thoroughly prepared.
Having endured such hardship,
she has never, before anyone,
spoken of her nurturing kindness
(etc.). It is like the World-Honored One's compassion for all sentient beings
in the Dharma-realm:
those who fly,
those who walk,
those with no feet,
two feet,
four feet,
many feet,
those in the three evil paths and six destinies,
the five realms and four modes of birth,
in heaven and among humans,
whether noble or lowly,
high or humble,
monks, nuns, and the assembly,
good women and good men,
each and every one taught to escape the source of suffering,
everyone ascending to eternal joy.
Our Buddha has no intention of speaking of a slight kindness,
or a slight hardship,
just like a loving mother in a household,
nurturing all sentient beings, daughters and sons,
not speaking of kindness, there is no difference.
The compassionate power of Shìjiā Shèngzhǔ
pities all sentient beings.
He leads each one to attain Nirvāṇa,
never intentionally speaking of his kindness.
A loving mother's heart
knows no opposition or conformity;
she cherishes all daughters and sons.
She teaches each one to establish themselves,
never intentionally speaking of her kindness.
The Buddha pities sentient beings,
the mother pities her children.
They both extend their feelings alike,
loving and protecting from the beginning.
The Buddha's intention is no different from a mother's,
a mother's heart can be compared to the Buddha's.
Today, everyone in this assembly
must clearly understand this.
Shìjiā Zūn of the three thousand realms
shows immeasurable pity for sentient beings.
He delivers and saves them everywhere,
guiding them to cross the ford of delusion.
He does not show favoritism to the foolish or wise,
nor treats enemies and loved ones differently.
He teaches each and every one to attain Buddhahood,
never having the intention to slightly mention his kindness.
A loving mother's virtue
is hard to describe,
nurturing the bodies of her disciples and children.
She suffers hardship for ten months of carrying,
and endures toil for three years of nursing.
She does not feel aversion towards her daughter,
nor does she show special affection for her son.
She teaches and protects each one,
never having the intention to slightly mention her kindness.
A loving mother's virtue
is hard to measure; ten thousand treatises and a thousand sūtras cannot praise it enough.
It is only that sons and daughters often commit the five heinous crimes,
casually run away and do not return.
Relatives daily worry and hope,
a loving mother's heart breaks every morning.
When her child travels ten thousand *lǐ* far away,
Mother's heart follows behind, singing:
The sūtra says: "A child travels a thousand *lǐ*,
the mother travels a thousand *lǐ*;
a child travels ten thousand *lǐ*,
the mother travels ten thousand *lǐ*."
"If children are sick,
parents are also sick;
if the child recovers,

This chanted sūtra text
is divided into two sections:
first, the mother's heart does not forget;
second, the worry over a child's illness,
these two sections are different.
Let's talk about the mother's heart not forgetting.
The sūtra says, "A child travels a thousand *lǐ*,
the mother travels a thousand *lǐ*"
(etc.).
After children have grown up,
each must pursue official careers and manage affairs.
As soon as they leave their hometown,
the mother's heart follows them.
When deployed to defend the northern frontier,
for three years her gaze is fixed on the Great Wall;
when building a life in Jiànlǐng,
for half a year her soul follows the Jǐnshuǐ.
(The Book of Rites says):
(One must not be ignorant of the age of one's parents.)
Thinking of our own birth mother,
all day long she worries and pities her sons and daughters.
When her son goes out,
Mother weeps sorrowfully.
Perhaps for an official career,
holding a position,
they are separated from their parents for years.
Seeing the four seasons and eight festivals pass without their return,
Mother weeps sorrowfully.
Some manage businesses,
chasing profit, leaving;
some dwell in other lands or on the road.
Although their sons find peace abroad,

Some are in the capital,
dispatched to guard frontier garrisons,

News is sparse, the road is distant,
their mothers weep, devoid of joy.
While the son is ten thousand *lǐ* away, the mother is already…
All day long, anxious tears fall like rain.
Reciting the Buddha's name, praying to gods, she tries a hundred ways,
hoping only for protection in the dark.
Her body wasted,
her heart torn,
she begs for her son to return so they can reunite.
Pondering this kindness of a loving parent,
how can disciples bear to be ungrateful?
Some seek official posts, dwelling in other lands,
or are in the army, guarding distant regions.
Though the son is well and healthy in another province,
the mother at home is always anxious and fearful.
Her heart follows a thousand *lǐ*, wasting her appearance,
her mind resents three years, weeping until her intestines break.
Only when he returns and they meet again,
will the mother finally regain her light.
A loving mother's virtue
is extremely difficult to repay;
the thought of her never ceases.
I sincerely advise all disciples
not to abandon their parents and dwell in other provinces.
This is the first point:
A mother’s heart never forgets.
Second:
Parents worrying when a child is ill.
The *Jīng* says: "When sons and daughters are ill,
their parents are also ill.
If the child recovers from illness,
only then do the parents feel better."
When a family's son or daughter
is cherished and loved by their parents,
if they suddenly lose their protection
and contract a disease,
it makes the father's heart anxious,
and the mother's mind fearful.
They stop sleeping, cease eating,
neglect their lives, forgetting to live.
Frying broth, cooking porridge,
they do not shirk the labor of day and night;
worshipping ghosts, reading books (of divination),
how can they dread the fatigue of coming and going?
If the son or daughter recovers slightly from illness,
the parents' anxious hearts are instantly relieved.
The parents' kindness to their children is especially profound;
they love their sons and daughters twofold.
Day after day, they instruct (teach and admonish) with unwavering intent;
morning after morning, they protect with unceasing care.
If sons and daughters suddenly fall ill,
parents are consumed by worry, their hearts almost broken.
They recite the Buddha's name, pray to gods, begging for protection;
they seek doctors, consult diviners, hoping for recovery.
They have no sleep,
no radiance,
their minds are tormented, their appearance changed.
Only when their child's body is at ease,
does the mother finally feel relieved and calm.
When sons and daughters fall ill, mothers worry;
it is not taught that eventually blood and tears must flow.
Tea and meals are not taken in order;
they stop applying makeup, too lazy to comb their hair.
Seeking doctors and divining never ceases;
worshipping ghosts and praying to gods never stops.
Only when their sons and daughters are well and healthy
does the mother finally cease to worry.
Pondering the affairs of the human world, they are difficult to fathom;
a parent's profound kindness cannot be surpassed.
As soon as they see their son or daughter afflicted with illness,
they immediately fear for their life, that they will be buried in the underworld.
On one hand, they administer medicine for treatment;
on the other, they invite monks to avert disaster.
After recovering from illness, they should surely practice filial piety,
yet they commit the five heinous crimes, which is also sung about.
The *Jīng* says: "Having been raised thus,

When conversing with respected parents,

They roll their eyes and glare,

Those who do not remember profound virtue.
The *Jīng* says: "Having been raised thus,

The previous *Jīng* text describes the parents' various ways of raising children,
a thousand hardships and ten thousand difficulties,

A family's parents nurture with much kindness;

They beg for them to grow up and become adults,

Who knew that as they gradually gain understanding,

The Buddha says that such a person in the *Suōpó* world,

To be unfilial to others and neglect Heaven,
to treat parents with disrespect as if it were nothing.
Serving them all day, there is not a single act;
instead, there are a thousand ways of being contrary every day.
Carelessly shouting loudly in the house,

The Buddha says that as soon as such a person dies,

Therefore, the *Jīng* says: "Having been raised thus,
wishing them to grow up quickly,
when they reach adulthood,
they turn out unfilial."
Above, the first point,

From here, the second point:
Turning against kindness and violating affection.
The *Jīng* says: "When conversing with respected parents,

They roll their eyes and glare,

These are all people who betray kindness and forsake virtue,
people who commit the five heinous crimes.
They do not consider the profound kindness of upbringing,

From childhood, a mother held them aloft;

Who knew that recently, as they somewhat become adults,

Day by day, they constantly follow bad companions;

Constantly, their hands do not copy;

When parents call them to set rules,

Sometimes they roll their eyes and glare,

(etc.)
People who do not understand how to reflect on kindness and virtue,

When conversing, they respond loudly to others,

They associate with bad people,
commit evil deeds,
drink alcohol and gamble, difficult to persuade.
They constantly cause their loving parents to shed blood and tears,

Shìjiāzūn [Shakyamuni Buddha]
left teachings and commands;
one must carefully examine the *Jīng* text.
If one persists in committing the five heinous crimes,
it will be impossible to find this body (human life) again, by all means.
Why do people not carefully reflect?
How can they turn their hearts against their parents?
Responding loudly can still be forgiven,

They do not think of the hardship of ten months of pregnancy (carrying),

The Buddha says that such people who commit the five heinous crimes

I sincerely advise disciples
(etc.),
the repayment of the loving crow.

Fortunately, through preaching the words of all Buddhas,

Even birds and beasts know the kindness of upbringing;

Ten months of pregnancy (carrying),
three years of breastfeeding.
Speaking of hardships, there are many kinds;

Now that you are adults,
you must repay;
do not learn from foolish people,

When admonished, listen carefully;
when scolded, do not talk back.
Why bother seeking the Western Paradise?
You will naturally be born in the Land of Utmost Bliss.
Where is intelligence for a human?
There is none better than repaying the feelings of upbringing.
Not only will you long encounter auspicious blessings,

All your undertakings will be harmonious,

You must accept this exhortation,
do not doubt or speculate,

Do not imitate foolish people who are stubborn and resistant,

When admonished, they utter a thousand kinds of disordered words,

Even if it is relatives and kin,

The Sūtra says: bullying paternal uncles and aunts,
beating and scolding elder and younger brothers,

Sixth Exhortation to the Laity
Written on the seventh day of the eighth month of Tiānchéng second year (927 CE).
How can one be unfilial at home?
Honoring evil people everywhere.
Not knowing human sins and blessings.
□□□□□ and so on,
These are the lowest of the low.
□□□□□ avenues,
Clashing with people of virtue.

Banding together, leaving home, in the streets and alleys.

From being held as an infant,
growing into a six-foot adult.
Abandoning virtue and turning against kindness, committing many of the five heinous crimes,

Three years of suckling is still a minor matter,

Constantly seeing both parents treated disrespectfully,

The Sūtra says: lacking reverence,
abandoning virtue and turning against kindness,
lacking benevolence and compassion,
not observing filial propriety.
Ninety-one kalpas ago,
there was a sinner who was unfilial to his parents,
and constantly committed the five heinous crimes.
After death, he was to fall into the great pit of hell,
with an iron wheel constantly revolving on his head,
never leaving his crown.
Precisely because his karmic roots were deep and heavy,
all due to his unfilial conduct towards his two parents.
From then on, he was thrown into the pit,
always with an iron wheel on his head.
Moving through thousands and tens of thousands of kalpas,
he does not know when he will regain a human body.
Once fallen into this, for thousands upon thousands of kalpas,
day and night he constantly endures suffering and hardship.
Because of unfilial conduct, he falls into the deep pit,
suffering without cause for even a moment's pause.
Day and night, the iron wheel rests on his head,
already for hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes.
I urge you to practice filial piety, do not procrastinate,
carefully ponder this body.
Fed with sweetness and nursed through bitterness,
do not disappoint your mother's kindness.
Serving and obeying brings peace of mind,
parents always see happiness.
Filial conduct will be forever recorded in history,
and widely spread for ten thousand generations.
Ten months of pregnancy bring a thousand kinds of hardship,

The Dhūjā Acarya (都講闍黎) exerts effort,

The Sūtra says: when a mother is pregnant with a child,

Sitting and standing are uneasy,

Ten months of carrying the child's body,

Her beautiful brows and peach-blossom cheeks subtly change,

Worried when walking,

Ten months of carrying the child,

Several times, relatives and friends call,

Even if guests are entertained at home,
she is truly too lazy to join in the laughter.
Her long hair is uncombed for months,
her phoenix hairpin is not inserted for ten days.
The dressing table is visibly dirty,
the phoenix mirror is left covered in dust.
Since carrying the child in her womb,
she no longer desires her former makeup and adornments.
Pondering the ten months of raising you,
how can you bear to procrastinate and not repay her kindness?
My mother's beautiful face wastes away like a flower,
transforming to withered yellow, plagued by many illnesses.
Her cloudy hair is uncombed for several months,
her phoenix hairpin is discarded as if it were nothing.
She does not follow the young girls to enjoy the flowers,
too lazy to accompany her aunt to chase puppies.
Several times, relatives invite her to see flowers,
and repeatedly play hidden-hook games at night with laughter.
This body, though not ill, is like being constantly ill,
resting her chin in her hand and frowning all day.
All kinds of delicious foods do not appeal,
she does not taste any rare delicacies.
Even sweet things taste like bitter huángniè,
her mouth is bitter and tongue dry, she does not wish to eat.
As the ten months of pregnancy draw near,
the sounds of bitter pain are unbearable to hear.
A thousand times she recites the Buddha's name, seeking protection,
ten thousand times she burns incense, inviting the World-Honored One.
As the ten months approach, she fears bodily calamity,
only fearing that impermanence might hasten her fate.
Over there, the sound of worshipping Buddha is loud and clear,
on this side, the golden Sūtras are opened in sequence.
Pigs and sheep are slaughtered together, no different,
blood flows everywhere.
The Sūtra says: when the month is full and birth is at hand,
one endures various pains,
in a fleeting moment of good or ill,
one only fears impermanence.
Like slaughtering pigs and sheep,
blood flowing everywhere,
one suffers such pain.
I advise the disciples present,
you must greatly nourish and serve your parents.
In the morning, inquire about their well-being,
and do not fail to show respectful expressions.
If parents suddenly give instructions,
do not contradict them.
Entering and exiting with reverence,
this is a filial child.
Even weeping for bamboo shoots and sleeping on ice are not enough,
do not let your hundred years of service fall short.
Ten long months in the mother's womb,
praying for safe delivery of the infant.
After three days, there is joy for the safe passage,
at full moon, monks are invited to dispel obstacles.
Neighbors compete to admire, never getting enough,
relatives gaze with lingering affection.
From then on, the mother's love is endless,
feeding with sweetness and love.
The Sūtra says: having obtained this body,
she endures bitterness and offers sweetness.
Washing impurities,
she does not fear toil and hardship.
Enduring heat and cold,
she does not shirk suffering.
The child sleeps in a dry place,
the mother sleeps in a wet place.
For three years,
drinking the mother's white blood (milk).
She does not fear offering sweetness and enduring bitterness,
washing is simply routine.
Sometimes enduring heat and cold,
the loving mother does not shirk hardship.
How can this body, after growing up,
indulge in unfilial acts and forget profound kindness?
Sweet and delicious foods are given to the child,
the mother eats the bitter ones herself.
Enduring heat and cold, she does not think of weariness,
holding and carrying the child, sitting and standing, she forgets her pain and hardship.
Turning from dry to wet is common;
nursing for three years is not barbaric.
Who knew that when they grew up, none would be filial,
forgetting the former kindness of nurturing and raising.
Gradually leaving the embrace,
as a child,
they are always on a mother's mind,
with all sorts of worries.
