The Western Pure Land is good,
but difficult to discuss thoroughly;
it is truly luxurious and beyond hearing.
Suddenly, this body is born there,
and for a thousand, ten thousand years, it will not sink into samsara.
The defiled world is weak,
no need to discuss it;
how can one bear to hear of the eight sufferings and three disasters?
Good deeds are not yet performed even a little,
not following justice, yet hoping for a thousand springs.
Mountains of knives glow in the sun,
forests of swords pierce the clouds;
how can there be peace and joy,
with karmic fires burning the body?
One speaks of ten kalpas, five kalpas,
never truly happy for a moment.
How can this compare to the Pure Land,
where Bodhisattvas are neighbors?
Idly playing in the water of the Eight Meritorious Pond,
when bored, wandering among the seven-fold trees in spring.
Or ascending the jeweled palace,
or bowing to the sutra texts.
Or riding peacocks,
or carrying Kalaviṅkas on one's arm.
Or coming up on auspicious rainbow lights,
or going into propitious clouds.
Or ascending the jeweled palace in the morning,
or bowing to the Compassionate Honored One at night.
Constantly hearing the wondrous Dharma,
always passing through the ear.
Arriving there, one forever transcends birth and death,
thereby gradually attaining the Buddha-body.
As evening falls, one must return;
Grandmother is dryly scolding in the house.
And indeed, a person's life in this world
is like a drifting tumbleweed;
though noble and humble differ,
impermanence treats all the same.
From the emperor above,
down to the common people,
wealth and status may have highs and lows,
but impermanence is still the same for all.
Therefore, the Wúcháng Jīng (Sutra of Impermanence) says: "
(Born in the realm of neither perception nor non-perception)"
(etc.)
The Three Sovereigns above,
the Four White-Heads below;
Pān Yuè with his beauty, Péng Zǔ with his youth—
thinking their youthful faces would last a lifetime,
they too were driven and worn out by white hair.
Wénxuān Wáng (King Wénxuān),
the Five Constant Virtues taught,
boasting of his elegant writings and beautiful prose—
thinking his family would endure long,
he too was driven and worn out by white hair.
Speaking of Xī Shī,
and Dájǐ's beauty,
when alive, their youthful faces boasted of slenderness and charm—
only their names remain in the world,
they too were driven and worn out by white hair.
Whether a monk,
or a Daoist,
holding to the pure lotus platform and Shakyamuni's teachings—
thinking to escape impermanence,
they too were driven and worn out by white hair.
Or engaging in business,
or skillful crafts,
competing with novel and excellent styles—
even if one is as rich as Shí Chóng,
they too are driven and worn out by white hair.
Upholding precepts and fasting,
truly essential and wondrous,
listening to the sutra texts of the Mahayana teaching—
do not remain intoxicated and muddled in this defiled world,
for in a moment, impermanence will arrive.
All the teachings above must be heard;
thinking it over, they are good for one's body.
Do not cling to foolish thoughts and delight in the physical body,
for in a moment, impermanence will arrive.
Great man,
consider for yourself,
why are you so eagerly pursuing the ten evil deeds?
Seventy years of life are already rare,
why make a promise for a thousand years?
Force yourself to listen to the sutras,
and discuss them with each other;
this illusory body has no true master.
Even if you are greedy for beauty and the body,
when your time comes, you will be taken by impermanence.
The Cakravartin (Golden Wheel King),
lord of the four continents,
ruling over myriad lands and nourishing the populace—
no king's wealth and status surpass his,
but when his time comes, he too is taken by impermanence.
Shùtígā (Śuddhodana),
Shí Chóng's wealth,
their names passed down through generations to this day—
consider that glory and honor are temporary;
when their time comes, they too are taken by impermanence.
Speaking of Hèng'é,
and talking of Luò Pǔ,
their beauty in the human world is hard to compare—
thinking their dignified beauty would last for hundreds or thousands of years,
when their time comes, they too are taken by impermanence.
Great man,
with truly admirable demeanor,
if you wish to make a move, cast your shadow and look back diligently.
In youth, do not boast like a rogue,
for when your time comes, you too will be taken by impermanence.
Or a monk,
dwelling in a Gālán (temple),
with an ancient appearance, slowly like a dragon or tiger—
a pure temple is a good place to settle,
but when his time comes, he too is taken by impermanence.
Or entering the Dao,
seeking immortal companions,
burning and refining elixirs of longevity in a furnace—
even if you have many methods to preserve youth,
when your time comes, you too will be taken by impermanence.
Regardless of noble or humble, high or low,
regardless of monks, nuns, or Daoist companions,
except for Mùní (Shakyamuni) alone,
all others are taken by impermanence.
I have spoken for a long time,
my words are based on evidence;
the sun is already slanting, one cannot stay.
Recite the Buddha's name loudly and return quickly,
just receive the gāthā at the steps.
If you do not practice,
or comprehend the meaning of the sutras,
pursuing sights and indulging in sounds,迷 and drunk—
a person's life is but a fleeting moment,
not cultivating is truly a foolish intention.
Whether poor,
or rich,
the first is to cultivate self-benefit in body and mind.
When impermanence suddenly arrives, life ends;
not cultivating is truly a foolish intention.
If you have money and wealth,
but do not practice generosity,
and are even more avaricious and stingy with yourself—
suddenly, your hands will be torn apart on both sides;
not cultivating is truly a foolish intention.
A great official,
clearly prosperous,
rejoicing in his five concubines and three wives—
all the future consequences he will bear himself;
not cultivating is truly a foolish intention.
Brothers dwelling together,
sons and young children—
do not hastily dispute right and wrong.
Born from the same womb and nursed by the same milk, growing up as humans;
not cultivating is truly a foolish intention.
If you do not cultivate,
seeking liberation—
a hundred years of life are like a dream.
Every single suffering will be borne by oneself;
not cultivating is truly a foolish intention.
Worldly affections,
never ashamed,
clutching at one's heart, striving and competing—
suddenly one stumbles and falls into the three lower realms;
not cultivating is truly a foolish intention.
All the exhortations above must be heard;
each person must use their own intention.
When you return home, each examine the differences;
encourage each other and directly discuss good matters.
I have spoken for a long time,
the sun is already dim.
Esteemed disciples, arise from your seats!
Come early tomorrow at the appointed time to listen,
and receive the gāthā while reciting the Buddha's name at the steps.
A person's life,
in but a fleeting moment,
is like a spark from flint or a flash of lightning,
unable to endure long.
I sincerely advise disciples,
to quickly seek liberation.
I advise disciples,
to cultivate blessings and goodness,
and not love the beauty of spring to admire and play.
Consider how long it can last—
ultimately, it is a great misfortune for the body.
Many family members,
who will manage them?
One must bear the hardships of the road ahead oneself.
When idle, place your hand on your heart and reflect;
it is also a great misfortune for the body.
In love with Xīshī,
admiring the moon-like face,
many are swayed by beauty, giving rise to reverence and goodness.
Restrain the heart and purify the mind, ponder this:
this too is a great calamity for the self.
Slaughtering pigs and sheep,
ashamed of fine delicacies,
forcing relatives to indulge in banquets,
cooking, roasting, killing - doing it oneself,
this too is a great calamity for the self.
A lax mind,
hard to persuade,
picking and judging monks and masters, debating their worth,
[]凡道聖有偏坡 (missing character: 說 Shuō, "discussing mortals and saints, having biases and slopes"),
this too is a great calamity for the self.
A mind of birth and death,
boasting of cultivating goodness,
chanting sūtras with the mouth while the heart does not turn,
the Buddha said such are icchantika people,
this too is a great calamity for the self.
Shìjiāshī (Śākyamuni Buddha),
with skillful means,
expounded the seven scrolls of the Fǎhuā Jīng (Lotus Sūtra),
using a thousand methods and ten thousand expedients to transform sentient beings,
his intention is to universally guide them to the other shore.
Be diligent,
be refined and disciplined,
sincerely and reverently make vows repeatedly,
not only will you see Āmítuó in the void,
but you will surely go to the Tuóshuài Yuàn (Tuṣita Palace) in the heavens.
I intend to speak more,
but the sun has set in the west,
the disciples beneath the seat all wish to return,
suddenly encountering the familiar vinegar vendor,
fifty eggplants and two baskets.
Our disciples,
good men and good women,
born in this Sahā (Suōpó) world of five turbidities and evil,
only indulge in birth and death,
not realizing impermanence.
(The four phases change),
(the minor four phases).
Speaking of the five aggregates as a metaphor.
The sky clears,
a metaphor for debate and discussion.
It is just like a person's life,
greedy for sights and sounds, no different.
White hair at the temples arrives,
where can one hide one's body?
Deafness, blurred vision, aching back,
still worrying about family and livelihood,
limbs heavy and difficult to move,
appearance gaunt and emaciated.
When the King of Death suddenly arrives,
what preparations are there for the road ahead?
When Yánwáng (King Yama) questions you,
what words will you prepare to respond?
Do not defer to children arranged in rows,
hoping for others to cultivate on your behalf,
even if you offer vegetarian meals daily,
how can it compare to preparing it yourself?
Instructing children and grandchildren,
to practice filial piety and righteousness,
reciting prayers six times a day in the golden hall,
even if they follow your words thus,
it is not as good as preparing it yourself while alive.
Leaving further instructions,
entrusting and remembering,
drawing pictures of Yánwáng's sons kneeling,
even if you draw a thousand pairs kneeling,
it is not as good as preparing it yourself while alive.
Advising disciples,
to cultivate blessings,
to attend to matters of the next life one by one,
to avoid instructing children and grandchildren after death,
prepare it yourself while healthy and able.
Chant Guānyīn (Avalokiteśvara),
seek Shìzhì (Mahāsthāmaprāpta),
the gate of Sukhāvatī (Jílè) opens as you wish,
in an instant you arrive in the Western Pure Land,
the Great Sage Mítuó (Amitābha) will see you with joy.
Further hearing the sūtras,
and receiving predictions (vyākaraṇa),
you will surely encounter Císhì (Maitreya) in the future.
Forever abandon the suffering Sahā (Suōpó) world of impurity,
and not fall into the three lower realms of suffering.
I intend to speak more,
but the sun has stopped in the west,
there are many profound and abstruse principles.
Come early tomorrow morning and I will discuss with you,
for now, receive this verse before the steps.
The Buddha recorded five thousand scrolls of sūtras,
to awaken people to the urgency of life.
A hundred years, how is it different from a spark from a flint?
A lifetime is much like a candle in the wind.
Once awakened,
one must strive,
stop giving rise to greed and desire at every turn,
even if riches fall like the stars of the Northern Dipper,
the heart will still be insatiable.
Piling up pearls,
stacking white jade,
a treasury full of silks and brocades, thousands of bundles,
if someone brings more,
the heart will still be insatiable.
Buying estates,
building houses,
selling off all the good trees of others,
even if the whole country is your livelihood,
the heart will still be insatiable.
Filling granaries,
collecting wheat and millet,
ten thousand *shi* and a thousand carts stored in winter,
all that others plant and harvest are brought to you,
the heart will still be insatiable.
Digging more pits,
tying up all bundles,
when eyes are opened, acting deceitfully,
even if you are as rich as Shíchóng's family,
the heart will still be insatiable.
Fearing the setting sun,
hating the shortness of time,
just because there are many family members at home,
teaching them to ride horses and wear fine silks,
the heart will still be insatiable.
Fearing to see people,
intending to seek affiliation,
frowning, difficult to approach,
unnecessarily giving rise to good thoughts without cause,
seeking masters to divine in pure places when calamity strikes.
In the sky are always benevolent dragon spirits,
in heaven there are no malevolent constellations.
When discussing this emotionally, do not be annoyed,
when speaking of curing ailments, it is for admonition and encouragement.
Constantly eliminate karma,
always tame the mind.
Respecting masters and monks,
pitying the lonely,
otherwise, you may flee into hell.
Even if your children and grandchildren are lined up in full rows,
when you depart, they can only weep empty tears.
If you wish to see it with your own eyes,
learn the sūtra texts, then it will be in accord.
Swallowing the ocean's water with a hair, entirely without difference,
a mustard seed containing Sumeru, these matters are compatible.
If one can change where it is possible to examine,
still, the body and mind are entirely unsuitable.
In the evening, chant Buddha's name and return home,
it is necessary to convey this message to relatives and remember it.
The entire Jambudvīpa (Yánfútí) world is empty and false,
regardless of whether one is rich or poor, noble or base.
The rich give rise to greedy minds daily,
the poor give rise to deluded thoughts every morning.
Becoming rich,
without shame,
in the next life, becoming poor, blaming heaven and earth.
This is all stated in the sūtras,
regardless of rich or poor, all will sink and fall.
In the pot of boiling water, who cares about your abilities?
The fiery coals do not depend on your will.
White jade makes one respected in life,
gold is hard to hold onto after death.
Actions performed in vain,
no way to avoid,
bit by bit, enemies are encountered,
therefore, the Tathāgata advises the people of the world,
it is better to prepare it oneself daily while healthy and able.
Hoping for children and grandchildren,
instructing spirits and ghosts,
kneeling to Yánwáng's sons a thousand times,
even if you kneel a thousand pairs,
it is not as good as preparing it yourself while healthy and able.
Hoping for children and grandchildren,
burning more paper money,
together to find a way in the underworld,
drawing a bow after the thief has passed is a wasted effort,
it is also not as good as preparing it yourself while healthy and able.
Hoping for children and grandchildren,
practicing filial piety and righteousness,
to protect me from my lifelong misguided intentions,
even if your protection is entirely without fault,
it is also not as good as preparing it yourself while healthy and able.
Hoping for children and grandchildren,
ashamed of the taste of food,
accumulating offerings for the seven-day periods and observing distant taboos,
even if your accumulated offerings for the seven-day periods are all thorough,
it is also not as good as preparing it yourself while healthy and able.
Hoping for children and grandchildren,
practicing giving and charity,
casting images and copying sūtras for profound mutual benefit,
even if you cast a thousand images,
it is also not as good as preparing it yourself while healthy and able.
What is done in life, one receives seven parts,
what is done for one after death, one receives one part,
that one part of action,
is often wasted and abandoned.
Greedy for oneself,
greedy for one's own,
who remembers the two parents suffering scourges?
This Fū-rén's appearance was both beautiful,
and her wifely virtues were even more manifest.
Wherever the sun and moon shone, all knew of her;
the whole universe fully admired her.
The Wáng's thoughts of her
never left the jiāo-fáng day or night;
morning and evening, he rejoiced in the jīn-diàn.
Such wealth and honor,
yet sorrowfully, it was especially severe.
Suddenly one morning,
he heard of another misfortune:
The Wáng's beloved concubine, who was favored by him,
was fated not to live long.
Suddenly, during a song and dance performance,
the sign of death appeared by her ear.
A deep qi appeared,
and in seven days, she was gone.
When the Shèng-jūn saw it,
two or three streams of tears flowed.
Suddenly, the Fū-rén's complexion grew dim,
tears flowed like threads, uncontrollable.
He knew for sure that her jade-like countenance would eventually return to dust,
how could he bear to see his Fū-rén turn into dust?
This time, the blue phoenix had just lost its mate;
who would the flowers smile for in the next spring?
The Guó-wáng was shocked and surprised by this sight;
all the pín-cǎi said they understood the one person.
This Yǒu-xiàng Fū-rén had a proper face and appearance,
and she was also good at singing.
One day, she was dancing in the hall,
and while she was singing,
the Huān-xǐ Guó-wáng saw a stream of qi on her face and by her ear,
and knew that her death was imminent within seven days.
The Wáng then contained his sorrow,
his heart filled with melancholy.
The Yǒu-xiàng Fū-rén saw the Wáng shedding tears,
unaware of the reason,
and after the dance, she composed herself.

Or is it because my comings and goings are clumsy?

The Huáng-dì, having been personally asked,

Yǒu-xiàng bade farewell to the Wáng and left,

All the ten thousand people lost color,

When her parents first heard,

Initially, gazing at the moon, my spirit felt refreshed;

To know the mind's jewel, one must first make a vow;

Simply by understanding the path upon hearing the words,
I vow to learn the six *pāramitā* gates of Muni.
The *fūrén* heard this
and thereupon went into the mountains,
bowing to this *sēng*,
begging for the extension of her lifespan.
Then, reverently joining her palms,
she took refuge without reluctance to travel;
she confessed sincerely,
revealing all without a moment's delay.
The *fūrén* said: "Héshang!
My humble self was born in the wilds
and grew up in the royal palace.
Three or five days ago,
the great king, by interpreting my physiognomy, said
that I would die seven days hence,
sending me home
to bid farewell to my parents.
I just heard people say
that the Héshang is compassionate;
therefore, I have especially come
to beg for the dharma of extending life."
The Héshang said: "Fūrén,
Fūrén!
Floating life is fleeting
and cannot last long.
It is regrettable for your mind and spirit
to seek the dharma of extending life."
The *fūrén* said: "Human life is short,
your disciple understands this.
But in what direction
is life long and distant?"
The Héshang said: "The lifespan in the heavens
is different from this.
Joyful and free,
it surpasses the human world."
The Héshang then spoke to the *fūrén* about the places where people are born in the Three Realms and Nine Grounds,
and matters such as limitless lifespan.
(Guānshìyīn Púsà)
(Fózǐ)
Side comment: Floating life is hard to prolong;
born, one busies oneself with dying.
How can it compare to the blessings in heaven,
where happiness is commonplace?
Thinking of eating heavenly cuisine,
thinking of wearing fragrant precious clothes.
If one seeks to be reborn there,
the Eight Precepts are the bridge.
Break: The *sēng* spoke to the *fūrén* of this cause,
wishing for long life, wishing to be reborn in heaven.
Departing, auspicious clouds supported her two feet;
returning, a radiant form encircled her body
The sounds of five instruments filled her ears daily;
the seven treasures filled her eyes every morning.
One must know that the floating world is ephemeral;
turn your heart early, do not be idle.
Thereupon, the *bìqiūní* of the stone chamber persuaded Yǒuxiàng Fūrén,
teaching her to seek rebirth in heaven,
not to seek the lifespan of the floating world.
The *fūrén* asked the Héshang: "For those born in the human world,
what dharma principles should they cultivate?
For those born in heaven,
what dharma practices should they cultivate?"
The Héshang replied: "To be born in the human world,
cultivate the Five Precepts.
Those who seek rebirth in heaven
must uphold the Eight Precepts.
For one day and one night,
if one can wholeheartedly
receive the Tathāgata's pure Eight Precepts,
one will certainly be reborn in heaven,
happy and free."
Thereupon, Yǒuxiàng Fūrén, having heard this,
sought to receive such pure Eight Precepts
from the *bìqiūní* of the stone chamber.
After receiving the Eight Precepts,
when she returned home and the day was complete,
she then passed away,
reborn in heaven,
receiving all kinds of happiness.
(*yúnyún*)
Break-side comment: On that day, the *fūrén*, having heard it,
immediately upheld it day and night.
Indeed, after seven days, she passed away,
reborn in the terrestrial heaven.
Bowing to the *bìqiū*, she returned home;
her human years were coming to an end.
Since the *fūrén* had passed away,
her household arranged her funeral.
Break: The *fūrén* returned after receiving the precepts;
after seven days, her body rested on the night platform.
The *Guózhǔ*, upon first hearing, felt acute pain;
the court officials, upon knowing, shed tears profusely.
The six palaces were terribly mournful, their feelings boundless;
the nine clans, facing the funeral, were all grief-stricken.
A day and time were chosen for the burial;
the funeral procession blocked the fragrant streets.
Yǒuxiàng Fūrén, having received the precepts from the *bìqiūní* of the stone chamber,
returned home, and after seven days,
her life ended.
Huānxǐ Guówáng went out with the heavenly host,
and after the funeral according to dharma,
the *fūrén*, after another half year,
was reborn in heaven.
In heaven, she suddenly reflected:
"By what cause in my past
did I come to this jewel realm?"
After a long time, she entered *dhyāna*,
and observed that her former self was the *fūrén* of Huānxǐ Guówáng.
Because the king divined my fate
and knew I would die in seven days,
I then returned to my parents' home.
And I went to the *bìqiūní*'s place in the stone chamber in the mountains,
heard the wonderful dharma, and received the Eight Precepts.
After seven days, my life ended,
and I was reborn in heaven.
Today, I must
descend from the heavenly realm
to Huānxǐ Guó
to repay the heavenly grace of their offering."
Having said this, the *fūrén* then, with the celestial maidens,
descended to the lower realm together.
(Guānshìyīn Púsà)
(Fózǐ)
Break: Since the *fūrén* received the precepts and returned,
her life ended, her body gone, unseen again.
The cause and condition had ripened for her to be reborn in heaven;
the karmic reward naturally brought blessings.
In receiving life, why discuss years and months?
In joy, how can there be right and wrong?
Suddenly entering *dhyāna* to observe her past life,

Recalling, she must descend to the heavenly realm,

Four kinds of auspicious flowers shone brightly, scattered;

Approaching the imperial seat,

mist-driven carriages filled the blue sky, majestically.
Simply throwing precious objects from within the clouds,

The king said: "Why are there various famous flowers, exotic fragrances,

Thereupon, Yǒuxiàng Fūrén, from the void,
called out to the great king,
comforting each other.
"At that time, I heard;
amazed and flustered,
and within the kingdom,
all the common people
all saw Yǒuxiàng Fūrén."
Side comment: In Huānxǐ Wánggōng,
suddenly, it was heard.
Suddenly, startled and sighing,
and needing to regain one's spirit.
Stepping out of the hall, bowing to the sky,
asking the person from the sky.
What cause brought forth this auspicious vision?
Please explain the reason it occurred.
Break: The king and *fūrén*, though different,
met happily between human world and heaven.
He earnestly inquired about the original events,
the winding path that led to this day's achievement.
She said it was due to the power of the Eight Precepts,
which attracted her rebirth in the heavenly palace.
Today, she has come expressly to repay him;
hastily cultivate, do not be lazy.
The great king said to the *fūrén*: "Fūrén, since you returned home,
and died after seven days,
by what cause have you descended to the lower realm?"
The *fūrén* said: "After I left the palace,
I entered the mountains,
bowed to the *bìqiūní*,
and sought to receive the Eight Precepts of Purification.
For one day and one night,
I sincerely and respectfully upheld them,
and thus was able to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.
Today, I have come here
to report to the great king,
humbly hoping you will not cling to Jambudvīpa,
but seek rebirth in heaven,
to be together with me,
and fulfill our heartfelt desires again.
A thousand, ten thousand times, again and again,
quickly seek liberation."
Side comment: The great king, hearing this, then changed his mind,
burning incense and bowing to the sacred platform day and night.
It had been several months since the *fūrén* departed,
and thinking of it, it was good to keep fasting diligently.
He always thought of the *fūrén* leaving home,
and searched for her bedroom path every night.
Her jade-like countenance, where did it go, I wonder?
Yet I rejoice in the grace bestowed, speaking of cultivation.
If today one can ascend to the upper realm,
one will bestow wealth within the Tathāgata's country.
Exhort one another,
quickly observe the precepts of purity,
do not cling to Jambudvīpa, but hasten to emerge!
All seated here must listen to this teaching,
and in the future will surely avoid transmigration.
The King asked for the details of the cause,
leaning on the railing, he looked with tears streaming down,
"Since parting with my Lady, it has been a lifetime apart.
How could I expect her to return to my residence again?
I often think of my Lady leaving home,
night after night, making people weep like rain.
Her jade-like countenance quickly turned to ashes,
yet I hoped for grace to be prepared with composure.
How could I expect her to enter the back palace this morning?
How could I hope to see the Golden Horse again?"
If the zither and se were long-lasting then,
I too would cultivate and abandon the nine heavens."
Thereupon, the Great King accepted the admonition,
and Yǒuxiàng returned to the faith.
All who came after,
also observed the Eight Precepts,
and were reborn in heaven,
their blessings and virtues following them naturally.
(And so on)
Aside, Lady Yǒuxiàng reported to the Great King:

People who hear of a beauty that could overthrow kingdoms and cities
still have to part from their king.
Diligently make vows,
quickly cultivate,
do not cling to the defiled world of Suōpó.
You must accept the precepts and return to the true Dharma,
then in the pure land of heaven, you will meet again.
Infinite thoughts of parting, with a profound meaning,
quickly awaken and bow to the King of Emptiness.
On the three eighth days, you must abstain from wine and meat,
on the ten fast days, you must diligently burn incense.
If you can also constantly recite the Tathāgata's name,
you will attain auspiciousness at all times.
A good doctrine,
inconceivable,
remember to cultivate and do not be negligent.
Before the Buddha's seat, receive the gāthā,
and diligently scatter offerings, all must know this."
Recorded from "The Happy King" (Huānxǐ Wáng Yuán Yī Běn Xiějì).
Written by the monk Jièjì of Sānjiè Sì on the sixth day of the seventh month of the Yǐmǎo year.

Once I chant, once my heart is grieved;

I speak of hardships,
express urgent pleas;
several monks stand ranked before the gate.
Just because I have not a single garment,

Perhaps in late autumn,

Not a single qīngmín in my pouch,

Most heartbreaking,

A cold window, a chilly mat, no clothes;

Disturbed by the sound of cicadas,

Great work, grand reputation, yet unachieved,

Monks,

Never before believed in the courage of the three armies,
on this day, I finally knew the decline of the Jiǔxìng.
The Xiongnú, in their haste, fled first,
Han generals, like clouds, pressed close in pursuit.
A man would rather fight a hundred battles without complaint,
only fearing that an enlightened ruler would not know.
At that time, the Xiongnú lost their advantage,
yielding to the Han's convenience.
Until dusk,
the troops could not be withdrawn.
Those struck by swords were repeatedly struck by swords,
those struck by arrows were repeatedly struck by arrows.
Seeing the battle lost, the Chányú
was deeply distressed.
Until the next morning, he discussed with the old minister Yīzhìzī Píngzhāng: "Yesterday, I saw that the Han generals' soldiers were few,
their banners and drums tattered,
their movements slow and cumbersome,
like farmers.
My original intention was to dispatch three to five thousand men,

How is it that over a hundred thousand cavalry
could not defeat five thousand?
How can I blame his boasting!
Looking at the terrain,
it is like a long victory,
sufficient for maneuvering.

pursue and gather several hundred thousand soldiers and horses under the Zuǒxiánwáng,
surround them from four sides,

they will report to the emperor,

The Chányú personally led an army of ten thousand,
arriving at Fàn Fūrén Chéng.
He then pursued Lǐ Líng.
Hán Yánnián reported to Lǐ Líng, saying: “The great general is temporarily withdrawing his troops,
and setting out on the road.”
Lǐ Líng heard these words,
and immediately set off southward.
After traveling for three days,
he was overtaken by the Chányú.
The barbarians were now entirely strong,
while the Hàn forces were half defeated.
Unaware of those behind them,
they had lost about five hundred men.
Lǐ Líng called to his左右 (aides), saying: “Why do we not fight?”
His aides replied: “General,
our soldiers are almost all exhausted,
how can we fight any further?”
Lǐ Líng reported: “Those with three or four spear wounds
are to be carried on carts;
those with one or two spear wounds
are to continue fighting fiercely.”
When they had not yet [finished setting up] camp,
and were in the midst of eating,
Líng wished to rally the army.
He then ordered the drums to be beaten,
but at that moment, the drums did not sound.
Lǐ Líng sighed to himself: “Heaven is destroying us!”
Before he finished sighing,
from his younger cousin’s three carts,
three streams of black qi
shot up towards the sky.
Lǐ Líng ordered his aides to search,
and they found two women,
aged sixteen,
also in front of the horses.
He ordered his aides to execute them,
each cut into two pieces.
The drums, though not beaten,
then sounded a roaring cry on their own.
Yú Xìn’s poem says: “Two women in the army,
Fūrén Chéng beyond the frontier.”
There are no other texts;
this event is exactly what it refers to.
The Hu barbarians retreated swiftly,
the Hàn also raced to pursue,
slaughtering the Xiongnú,
over three thousand cavalry.
They immediately cut off their ears,
and carried them on horseback,
intending to use them as proof
when recording the achievements.
Looking northwest by night,
looking southeast at dawn,
they took to the road,
and thus hoped to escape.
Suddenly, they arrived at a flat plain,
where the plain was quiet and the grass deep.
Lǐ Líng reported to his aides: “Why do we not burrow into the grass,
and avoid disaster by returning south?”
The officers and soldiers heard his words,
and all immediately entered the grass.
At that moment, Lǐ Líng suddenly encountered a great roaring north wind,
which blew the grass southward.
The Chányú said: “The Hàn bandits will die on their own without fighting.”
His aides heard this and said: “Great King,
if the Hàn bandits are not fought,
how will they die on their own?”
The Chányú’s men then started a fire from behind,
the smoke billowed,
and the blazing flames steamed towards the sky.
“Great General,
the fire is coming from behind,
how can we escape death?”
Lǐ Líng asked: “How far is the fire from here?”
His aides reported: “The fire is one lǐ from here.”
“Are there fire-starting stones in the army?”
They quickly brought out fire,
and burned the grass in front.
When the fire from behind came,
it would naturally stop.
As the fire in front ignited,
the fire from behind was extinguished.
See how Lǐ Líng and the Chányú fought amidst the fire:
Líng’s army pressed forward,
the barbarian cavalry pursued fiercely from behind.
Battle clouds first gathered across the sea,
the northern qi in Yānnán could not be seen through.
At this time, their provisions were exhausted and the soldiers were hungry,
they had already fought and their strength was broken.
Then they were burned by the Chányú’s fire,
if they wanted to flee, where would they go?
The plain was certainly full of jackals and wolves,
blown by the wind, hairy at night.
Red flames raged fiercely and intensely,
each gust blew them higher.
White snow fell thickly across the Zǐsài,
black smoke rose in dense plumes into the mournful darkness.
The grass in front was all gone, unconnected,
when the fire from behind came, it naturally stopped.
“It is said that the Hàn general of old was covered in dust,
accustomed to much hardship at the Great Wall.
Even an army of three hundred thousand feared death,
how much more so Líng with five thousand men!
When there is trouble in the army, assistance is needed,
several generals traveled together but did not fight together.
Rushing far and pursuing the north, I know this well,
erasing traces and clearing away…
All my life I wished to emulate the achievements of a humble minister,
only in the mountain passes did I realize the fire curtain was empty.
Even if the sagely lord were to descend today,
could he know what Líng is going through?
At that time, the general suffered adversity,
I sent men to gather the scattered soldiers behind.
If the felt blankets were heavy, we abandoned them;
if light, we kept them as we wished.
When encountering water, one must eat parched grain mixed with it;
when encountering ice, do not let it pass down the throat.
Since it is the barbarian court, one must be determined to fight to the death,
killing each other is no more than dying and resting.
In what year will I see the sagely lord of the country?
I have not yet been able to bow to my kind mother in the hall!
Today I will die and become a Hàn goose in the barbarian sky,
flying ten thousand lǐ towards Bàtóu.”
The Chányú reported to his aides: “Upon entering the Hàn territory,
we have already traveled two thousand [lǐ].
Gather the troops and return,
each to his own safety.”
Before his words were finished,
there was a captain named Guǎn Gǎn under Líng,
who was negligent in his duties.
Lǐ Líng angrily struck him five times,
saying, “If you are negligent again,
I will execute you and make an example for the army!”
Guǎn Gǎn feared Líng would execute him,
so he deserted the army and fled,
straight to the Chányú’s tent.
He danced and twirled,
shouting loudly,
confessing his capital crime.
The Chányú asked: “Who is this person?”
“It is Lǐ Líng’s captain, Guǎn Gǎn.”
The Chányú said: “Why have you come?”
Guǎn Gǎn reported to His Majesty: “Lǐ Líng’s troops
have exhausted their arrows and broken their bows,
they have no provisions at all,
they are extremely close to here,
why does Your Majesty not capture them?”
The Chányú saw Guǎn Gǎn surrender,
and laughed heartily.
He called to his aides, saying: “Travel another two or three hundred lǐ,
and Lǐ Líng will surrender and become a slave on his own.”
The Chányú’s aides heard these words,
and immediately pursued Lǐ Líng.
Lǐ Líng immediately drew his crossbow and shot,
hitting the left eye of the Tūqíshī Fān King with an arrow.
The Chányú was startled and afraid,
not daring to advance.
He hesitated on horseback,
and reported to his aides: “We have been fiercely pursuing the bandits,
everyone is exhausted.
Although we have traveled a thousand lǐ,
we have lost about ten thousand men.
Even if we capture the Hàn soldiers,
what use will they be?
It’s better to return quickly.”
His aides replied: “Your Majesty came with one hundred thousand men
to defeat five thousand.
If you do not achieve glory,
but instead suffer humiliation,
and return, letting them come back again,
if the small ones are not punished,
there will surely be greater trouble.
Your Majesty, fight again,
and the Hàn will surely be defeated and surrender.
Before noon,
Líng’s army will be routed.”
The Chányú heard these words,
and immediately pursued Lǐ Líng.
Lǐ Líng had exhausted his arrows and broken his bows,
and had no provisions at all.
With a loyal heart, he sought a single blade.
Lǐ Líng ordered his aides,
to urgently instruct men to dismantle the carts.
Each man took a cart spoke as a club,
and beat the enemy, covering their heads and faces with sand.
How can one describe Lǐ Líng and the Chányú fighting in the third battle?
The mad Hu barbarians surged northward to the ends of the sky,
the great Hàn traveled southward, the road still long.
When engaging in battle, they wished for favorable winds,
facing the enemy, they hated the slanting sun.
Though the rear army fought desperately,
the Hàn general knew his strength was insufficient.
Alas, bows and swords were all used up,
so they wielded their bare bodies to block left and right.
At that critical moment, nothing was quicker than clubs,
they urgently instructed men to dismantle the broken carts.
Each man took a cart spoke as a club,
and beat the enemy, covering their heads and faces with sand.
Suddenly, plants and trees were cut down by frost;
On that day, mountains and rivers were ravaged by blood.
At night, I watched barbarian stars fly like lightning;
In the morning, I saw the deadly aura resemble clouds.
Today, I am a general of the yellow-bearded barbarians;
Year after year, I am like a red-beaked crow.
How could Guǎn Gǎn act so unreasonably,
Sending my general away to never see his home again?
This morning, everything beyond the frontier was lost;
With what face can I still see the imperial capital?
The battle ended.
A moment later, dusk fell,
and each returned to their camps.
Late in the night,
Líng himself came out
and called to his attendants, saying, "If I do not die now,
I am no true brave man!"
The attendants reported to the great general, saying, "Since you tied your hair (came of age),
you have long been raiding the Chányú,
penetrating the barbarian court
over two thousand *lǐ*.
You swore to pacify the desert,
to eliminate the clamor and dust,
and with this small achievement,
to serve the enlightened lord.
Who would have thought that the general would suffer defeat,
and the soldiers would perish in vain,
bearing a strong heart in vain,
deviating from their original vows?
At this very moment,
we are truly isolated and in peril.
Like a fish swimming in a cauldron,
or a nest beneath a curtain;
when the cauldron boils, the fish perishes;
when the curtain moves, the nest collapses.
Since the situation is not intact,
it is difficult for us to survive.
The great general's original intention
was not to labor people in vain.
Please consider what is appropriate,
and seek a path to survival."
Líng said, "I have heard that Emperor Gāo himself led an army of three hundred thousand
to campaign north of the frontier,
and was trapped at Píngchéng.
At that time, brave generals were like clouds,
and strategists like rain.
Once they entered the Chányú's territory,
tens of thousands of the three armies
were completely routed.
Fortunately, Chén Píng used wooden figures of women to deceive them,
and they narrowly escaped.
How much more so for me today, with five thousand foot soldiers,
to resist an army of one hundred thousand?
How can gnats resist a strong wind,
or ants cling to a great tree!"
"Great General,
a snake cannot move without its head,
a bird cannot soar without its wings,
an army cannot fight without a general,
and soldiers cannot survive without provisions.
Even if the general possesses the *Sānlüè* of Huángshí
and the *Liùqí* of Chén Píng,
the methods of concealing divine arts,
and ghost-like disappearance, it would still result in loss of men and defeat.
Without rescue for the troops,
Heaven itself condemns us.
Since the soldiers are not guilty,
we beg the great general to surrender."
Líng said, "My three armies' command,
my six ministers' banners and drums –
the Son of Heaven entrusted me with a mandate
to defeat the barbarians and return to court.
Alas, the Hàn is weak and the Hu are strong,
banners and drums are scattered,
the command is distressed.
Though people's lives remain,
the army has no provisions.
Watching our food run out,
it is logical that we must surrender.
You must go,
strive to return together,
do not abandon each other.
Have you not heard the saying: 'For a thousand generations, there is one lord;
for ten thousand generations, there is one hometown.
If things are good, we share the glory;
if bad, we share the shame.'
Sleep restlessly tonight,
rise early at dawn.
If you reach the Hàn court,
be wary of the barbarian ants.
My fate is meager now;
the way of Heaven is like this.
If by chance you reach the imperial court,
clearly explain the situation.
Pay respects to my compassionate mother in the northern hall,
and bow twice to my Son of Heaven in the southern court.
Say that Líng lives as a man of a foreign land,
and dies as a ghost without a homeland.
Forever parted from relatives and old friends,
long farewell to confidants."
He wished to say more and more,
but could not stop himself.
Let us see how Lǐ Líng and his soldiers bade farewell:
"A husband leaving the frontier must be ready to die,
O multitude, the barbarian wolves are truly difficult.
Bidding farewell to the lord, I intended to cut down the Xiongnú bandits,
mounted on my thousand-gold bright moon saddle.
A husband losing control and surrendering to the wild barbarians,
has truly failed the August Heaven and the Lone Earth.
Not only do I have no face to see the Heavenly King,
but in the Yellow Springs below, I shame my ancestors.
Alas, sighing, I chant a long lament,
only because deceiving the barbarians led to deep trouble.
What does the Lord of Heaven know of this path?
Your Majesty should know Líng's true heart."
His attendants, hearing these words, all shed tears: "General, how many times has this happened today?
How could you alone lead five thousand men
to fight against a hundred thousand Xiongnú cavalry?
Red blood flowed abundantly like water,
barbarian soldiers lay dead everywhere.
Even if you have no face to see the Heavenly King,
you should leave your name in the historical records.
Where is the true man (son) now?
You must be ashamed of the kindness of your upbringing.
General, hereafter do not act wrongly,
return to our country and pay respects to the Son of Heaven."
Líng, hearing his attendants speak of his esteemed mother,
cried aloud, shedding thousands of lines of tears.
"If there were ten more arrows for men,
we might still unevenly see our homeland again.
Attendants, you must now scatter like birds and beasts,
lost on the path, gaze at the moon and flee.
If by chance you return south and see the Son of Heaven,
report that Líng has failed Your Majesty's grace."
Lǐ Líng finished speaking,
sighed several times,
and reported to his attendants, saying, "I have heard that a bird in the sky
still relies on its six wings.
If the skin is no longer there,
what can the feathers cling to?
We must employ an unforeseen strategy,
an extraordinary plan:
first surrender, then break out,
behead the barbarians and face the emperor.
Will the Emperor discern Líng's true feelings,
or will he not believe it?"
Thereupon, they collected valuable treasures,
took down the banners,
and buried them in the ground,
so that the bandits would not see them.
Lǐ Líng and his attendants,
each trusting their fate,
knew that by dawn,
they would surely be captured.
The attendants, hearing his words,
immediately scattered like stars.
Just as dawn broke,
the Hu soldiers arrived.
Líng's deputy, Hán Yánnián, was struck by an arrow, fell from his horse, and died.
Lǐ Líng, without bow or arrows,
whipped his horse and fled,
beating his chest and looking towards the Hàn kingdom,
crying loudly.
With red eyes and a clear heart,
he swore by the mountains and rivers
not to betray the Hàn house's enlightened lord.
He cast aside his bow and saber,
and surrendered to the Tūjué.
Hesitant to speak for fear of anger,
the Chányú shouted at him,
asking how Lǐ Líng's surrender came about:
Lǐ Líng finished speaking and surrendered to the barbarians,
running to the front of the Chányú's great tent.
"First, I will recount yesterday's battle,
then I will reveal my true intentions."
"My armor, bows, and soldiers are all used up;
I willingly desire to dwell forever by your jade frontier wall.
If the barbarian king would grant me a glance,
then I would have no heart to face the Hàn Heaven.
Since I took command as a general for my lord,
one battle has passed as if hundreds of years.
It was the Hàn Emperor who instigated the conflict;
as an envoy, how could I dare to act on my own?
Your foolish minister's schemes incurred immeasurable guilt;
now I present my humble life before the king.
It is truly because I have no achievements that I thank the barbarian lord;
I humbly wish for your lenient grace to forgive this transgression."
The Chányú, seeing Lǐ Líng surrender,
then questioned why he had entered the frontier land.
"Time and again you led soldiers to attack,
frequently commanding your troops to tread the battlefield.
Your sallying army was not even ten thousand strong,
how then did you dare to penetrate the border region?
Until recently, you could still be called a Hàn general,
so why have you come to surrender today?"
“Previously there was a general named Sū Wǔ.
Early on, he bravely sought confrontation in the Hú court.
Because of his lofty ambition, he defied our state,
and was made to herd rams by Běihǎi for a long time.
If you, my lord, are now determined to come and submit,
I will reluctantly keep you here to guard the captured frontier.
Henceforth, you need not trouble yourself to be a Hàn general;
you shall immediately be enfeoffed as Right Grand General (Yòuxiào Wáng).”
The Chányú said: “Looking at you, a general of the Hàn house,
you do not understand profound strategies,
merely [seeking] a temporary achievement,
traversing thousands of lí.
In the past, when the Hàn house flourished,
it made peace and kinship with my Tūjué.
The Chányú, by an extraordinary custom,
sat above all our vassals.
My ancestors still did not bow,
their names were not used in commendations,
their attendants approached the steps,
and they wore swords and shoes into the palace hall.
They were even granted beautiful horse trappings,
a white jade-adorned bridle and girth,
their retainers were enfeoffed,
they rode floating dragon-like mounts,
and dined on the rare delicacies of all officials.
They were bestowed by imperial decree with twenty thousand strings of red-rimmed cash
and ten thousand ingots of purple-refined gold.
Furthermore, embroidered garments,
patterned silk, coarse silk, and plain silk,
all kinds of miscellaneous goods,
amounted to over five hundred carts.
The annual provisions were extremely generous,
more than enough to use.
The Hàn house said it was excessive,
but Mòchuò himself was still dissatisfied.
Since Emperor Xiàowén passed away,
the frontier has been spared trouble.
The Hàn generals,
you truly specialize in plundering the borderlands.
Now that you have been captured and surrendered,
what [shall] your life be [like]?
Lǐ Líng replied: “I am a humble person,
undeservedly receiving great favor.
My conduct was not careful,
and as a general, I was not discerning.
I rashly led a single company of men
to confront a lord of ten thousand chariots.
I have heard that since the Zhōu and Qín dynasties,
this region has flourished.
To the north are the Yīnshān Mountains,
stretching a thousand lí east to west.
Grass and trees grow lush,
and birds and beasts form flocks.
This was originally the dwelling place of my great king’s supreme ancestors,
which I also fully know.
I see the sand curtain blocking the way,
how can it cut off communication between the western regions and the sacred institutions of the middle and outer lands?
Your Majesty today,
I only yield my heart to your command.
My life and death are entrusted to the great king;
how can I, a humble person, decide my coming and going!
The cauldron is near,
and the axe is not far.
If there is any urgent difficulty,
please use me.
However, a defeated general
cannot speak of bravery;
a man who has lost his body
cannot plan for survival.
Life or death, two paths,
I earnestly hope for a swift decision.”
The Chányú heard these words,
and deeply admired Lǐ Líng.
Seeing his heroic talent,
he looked up to him as to a high mountain.
He enfeoffed him with an office and gave him a title,
and had him wear Hú clothing,
to travel with Wèi Lǜ,
pushing and pulling to his left and right.
Of Lǐ Líng’s dispersed men,
there were about a thousand.
Those who were ordered and able to reach the Hàn court
totaled four hundred.
When the Hàn emperor heard this,
he sighed with emotion, saying: “My General Lǐ must have been captured!”
The emperor summoned the Grand Astrologer Sīmǎ Qiān,
and also summoned Lǐ Líng’s elderly mother and wife.

The emperor asked Sīmǎ Qiān to go forward and observe the faces of Lǐ Líng’s mother and wife to see if there was any color of death or mourning: “Does Lǐ Líng have a deathly color in the barbarian lands?
If there is no mournful color,
then Lǐ Líng is in the barbarian lands.
You report back to me.”
Sīmǎ Qiān observed and reported to the Hàn emperor: “Lǐ Líng is in the barbarian lands.
There is no deathly color on the faces of Lǐ Líng’s mother and wife.”
When Emperor Wǔ heard this,
he suddenly flew into a great rage.
“How could such a scoundrel
betray my Hàn state
and surrender to those Hú barbarians!
Deliver Lǐ Líng’s elderly mother and wife to justice.”
Sīmǎ Qiān saw that Lǐ Líng was a general from a family of three generations,
and spoke before the emperor’s palace: “Your Majesty!
I have heard that Lǐ Líng’s ancestor, Lǐ Guǎng,
was renowned throughout the land,
and his bravery was unsurpassed in the three armies.
For over twenty years,
he accumulated merits on the sand curtain (frontier).
If he caused bitter fighting at the border,
the Central Plains gained peace,
his achievements were like this.
I also heard that Lǐ Líng, by chance, in a critical situation, surrendered to the Hú.
His scheme has not yet succeeded;
he should return soon.
Since his mother is not guilty,
I humbly beg for leniency in her punishment.
If he does not return later,
I will willingly accept the cauldron.”
Emperor Wǔ heard these words
and remitted his mother’s crime.
The following year,
he dispatched Gōngsūn Áo to lead fifty thousand cavalry.
The troops reached the north of the Lónglè River
and the south of Jùnjī Mountain,
and battled with the Chányú’s forces,
saying they sought Sū Wǔ and Lǐ Líng.
At that time, Lǐ Xù, a general who had been defeated the previous year, taught the Chányú’s troops military tactics,
and defeated Gōngsūn Áo’s forces,
piercing them from left to right.
Gōngsūn Áo, in his urgent fear,
asked: “Who is the general commanding the troops in the barbarian lands?”
It was Lǐ Xù who could not help but say: “The general commanding the troops in the barbarian lands
is none other than
me, Lǐ Líng.”
Gōngsūn Áo then returned to the Hàn court, saying:
“My forces should not have suffered defeat.
It was all Lǐ Líng who taught the Chányú’s troops,
and they defeated my forces,
resulting in a loss of troops.”
When Emperor Wǔ heard this,
he suddenly flew into a great rage,
and consequently castrated Sīmǎ Qiān,
and delivered Lǐ Líng’s elderly mother and wife to justice at the horse market.
Blood flowed throughout the market,
unjustly executing Lǐ Líng’s mother.
The sun and moon lost their light,
and tree branches snapped.
How can the execution of Lǐ Líng’s elderly mother and wife be described?
“I, in my secluded chamber, served my lord in the past,
hoping to share the beginning and end for a thousand years.
How could I expect him to perish in the barbarian court,
leaving me to raise our young lord alone to continue the sacrifices?
When I was first married as a new bride,
our young lord deeply pleased the monarch.
His favor, honor, and splendor were boundless,
entering and exiting the court without restriction.
We married hoping to prevent misfortune,
and raised a son expecting him to serve with sweet and savory offerings.
How could I expect him to perish in the barbarian court,
his life or death unknown, in what land he resides?
The elderly mother and wife were executed at once—
since ancient times, there has been no such event!
All this is due to shallow karma from previous lives;
the new bride (wife) need not harbor resentment or regret.”
The wife, facing execution, spoke to her revered mother-in-law: “Unjust law and severe punishment, what can we do?
The monarch is swayed by flatterers and there is no recourse;
our lives and deaths this morning are entirely up to him.
Alas, there is nothing to cling to in heaven above!
I and my elderly mother will share this calamity.
You, my lord, in the Chányú’s land, must not know;
I will meet you underground.”
After the execution of Lǐ Líng’s elderly mother and wife,
the official in charge reported to the king.
The next year,
Fùpíng Jùnwáng was sent to the barbarian lands
to see if Lǐ Líng was there.
When Wáng Jìncháo reached the south bank of the Yellow River,
he wrote a letter and entrusted it to Lǐ Líng.
When Lǐ Líng, in the barbarian lands, heard that his mother had been executed,
he did not know whether it was true or false.
Upon receiving Wáng Jìncháo’s letter,
he wept bitterly and sorrowfully on the battlefield,
and then went forth with his attendants to meet him, as described:
Lǐ Líng heard that a Hàn envoy entered the Hú court,
and so he led his attendants out to meet him.
He dismounted, gazed towards his homeland, and bowed to the emperor,
then immediately wailed and burst into tears.
“My Lǐ family has been generals for generations,
serving in the army and campaigning for the country generation after generation.
When the heavenly troops suffered defeat and I tried to kill myself,
at the moment of death, it was out of resentment.
Five thousand foot soldiers encountered savage barbarians;
what suffering like this has ever been experienced?
Although my body yielded to the Xiōngnú,
my heart never forgot the Hàn capital.
I heard from afar that the Hàn lord executed my mother;
the pain pierces my body, it is deeply bitter.
“You have just arrived from the imperial capital.
Have my kinsmen, who reside in Líng, truly been executed?
Wáng Jìn advanced, bowed, and replied, saying: “I wish to speak, but thought makes my voice choke.
Fortunately, Sīmǎ Qiān sent a letter,
and before the imperial hall, he openly presented his plea.
Emperor Wǔ heard it and his anger subsided,
considering carefully the general’s plight.
Later, he sent Gōngsūn Áo into the barbarian court,
but he lost the battle and returned.
The fault was pushed onto the general,
and the Hàn family's military strategy was given to the 'mad' barbarians.
It was always Gōngsūn Áo who spoke slanderous words,
and then the general’s mother was killed.
Líng heard that his old mother had been executed by the sovereign,
crying out in bitter anguish, his breath catching in his throat.
Tears streamed down his face as if he were about to die,
his guts twisting as if cut by a knife.
He made people weep and support him,
and from the desert, he shed blood from his bowels.
After a long time, he was roused and began to recover,
looking south towards the Hàn empire and sorrowfully crying:
“I recall when I first arrived north of Jùnjī,
the barbarian cavalry pressed in, numerous and relentless.
Drawing my saber, I split their faces, making blood flow like a stream;
this was to repay the sovereign’s grace and virtue.
Unable to control myself, I surrendered to the Hú barbarians,
planning day and night to return to my country.
Today, Heaven must surely know
that the Son of Heaven of Hàn has betrayed Líng's virtue.
Thereupon, weeping, they bade farewell to each other,
gradually passing Jùnjī.
They saw thousands of towering peaks,
and myriad fathoms of steep cliffs.
To the east, it connected to the Bóhǎi Sea;
to the west, it bordered Yànmén.
Spring grass did not flourish;
snow still fell in summer.
Apes cried like weeping;
cranes called like singing.
Wild trees grew withered;
cold flowers scattered chaotically.
White clouds dispersed loosely;
yellow leaves flew faintly.
Ice formed in secluded ravines;
wild geese cried, seeking their mates.
At times, the Qiāng flute was heard,
and listening to it brought sorrow.
At dawn, they crossed the Hú River,
then followed the winding roads.
Sometimes they met shepherds,
but saw no woodcutters.
Ambassador Sū was enraged when he saw the Chányú;
General Lǐ was ashamed to look at the Hàn banner.
Sometimes sorrowful, sometimes resentful,
sometimes laughing, sometimes chanting.
Knowing the countless precious things,
how much more so with rivers and passes blocking the way.
At this time, the three faced each other, weeping,
drinking farewell wine by the roadside,
and playing a farewell zither on their laps.
Sū Wǔ raised his cup and thanked Hán Zēng, saying: “I am a general of the great Hàn,
long trapped and fallen in the battlefield.
If not for you,
how could I ever return?
My gratitude is etched in my flesh and bones;
how could I ever betray this kindness?
” Before he finished speaking,
he turned to look at Lǐ Líng.
He saw Lǐ Líng,
wearing barbarian furs,
with a barbarian hat on his head,
and red thorn-bush boots on his feet.
He asked Lǐ Líng: “General, you are a general of the great Hàn,
do you not remember Lǒngxī?
For generations,
your name has shone brightly.
Red gates with arrayed halberds,
facing south to command others.
Entering and exiting fragrant palaces,
high officials crowding the roads.
Why, General,
do you wander aimlessly in the desert,
as if your own flesh and blood
are trapped in the barbarian court?
Would you not be laughed at by people?
When Lǐ Líng heard the reproach,
his body felt as if his skin and bones were dissolving.
Having betrayed his lord and left his kin,
Líng, though once powerful,
was now burdened with his actions.
Now he had no home to return to.
He beat his chest with his hand,
and cried out to Heaven.
Lǐ Líng took off the barbarian hat he wore
and threw it onto the sandy ground.
Then he drew a blade from his waist,
and spoke of the past years,
looking afar towards Cháng’ān.
He then said: “I remember when Líng first led foot soldiers,
less than five thousand,
deep into the barbarian court.
We fought over ten thousand battles.
We marched until we reached the south of Jùnjī Mountain,
north of the Lónglè River.
The land was vast with no springs;
empty sands had no water.
Líng’s forces were not yet settled,
when we saw the Chányú’s army of over one hundred thousand men,
advancing like rain,
completely surrounding us at once.
Líng intended to fight that day,
but their numbers were many, and ours few.
Líng decided not to fight,
Sū Gōng was herding sheep,
and I deeply recalled our worthiness.
I had no choice but to follow the standard bearers,
the battle cries echoing across Huá.
We shot to the right, feinting to the right.
The Xiongnú poured forth their troops,
charging forward at that moment.
Hàn generals vied for merit,
drawing their swords and rushing in.
From afar, they seemed like floating clouds and jade emptiness, with starry blades,
slashing barbarians and seizing flags.
On that day,
Heaven sent forth battle clouds,
and the earth produced battle mist.
The Xiongnú were utterly defeated,
and immediately withdrew their army.
The Hàn generals won,
marching about twenty li,
yet had not yet turned back their flags.
Helplessly, they immediately withdrew their army.
The Hàn generals had won,
but were then set upon by the mad bandits who used the wind to spread fire,
red flames reaching to the sky.
Líng was in the fire,

I have heard that the King's Law (Dharma of Kings) is vast and expansive,
and Buddhism is majestic;
the King's Law is impartial,
and the Buddha's actions are equal.
The King leaves behind political teachings,
the Buddha expounds the true doctrine.
All are the twelve venerable divisions of scriptures,
all are the ferry to enlightenment from Shìjiā.
After the Tathāgata entered Nirvāṇa,
all the sages concealed themselves during the Age of Semblance Dharma.
There was a monk,
named Zhāntán.
He had a disciple,
named Huìyuǎn.
This Huìyuǎn, it is said,
lived in Yànmén,
with two brothers,
and no other relatives.
The elder brother, Huìyuǎn,
left secular life to become a monk;
the younger brother, Huìchí,
stayed to care for their mother.
Huìyuǎn, at Venerable Zhāntán's place,
constantly recited the True Dharma,
and often saw the True Sūtras,
knowing the joy of the three meditative states,
and thus perceived that the world was not far off.
So one day,
he pressed his palms together and addressed the Venerable One: "Disciple has served the Venerable One,
for many years,
my studies and skills are neglected,
I am truly foolish and dull.
Now I intend to visit a famous mountain,
seek streams and cross waters,
visit masters and consult monks,
and retire to the side of a mountain valley,
to fulfill my lifelong wish."
The master said: "Since you are going now,
which mountain do you intend to reside on?"
Huìyuǎn replied: "But disciple cannot distinguish east from west,
how would I know north from south?
I only have the intention to go,
but do not know the destination."
The master said: "Since you are going now,
just go to the left of the river,
focus your mind on pilgrimage,
and wherever you encounter a mountain, reside there;
that will be your place of cultivation."
Huìyuǎn heard these words,
and was overjoyed beyond measure.
Having received the master's instruction,
how could he dare to disobey such careful advice?
He immediately stepped forward,
pressed his palms together and bowed,
bowed again to bid farewell to the Venerable One,
and then set off on his long journey.
Yuǎn Gōng (遠公) journeyed on,
carrying a complete *Nirvana Sūtra* (*Nièpán Jīng* 《涅槃經》),
traveling through the mountains to cultivate the Way.
At this time,
the spring light was bright and warm,
the air fragrant with blossoming flowers.
Green willows swayed gracefully in the wind,
the distant mountains seemed boundless,
and the returning wild geese hurried along.
With a resolute heart set on learning the Way,
he wished to quickly grasp the true principles.
After several days of travel,
Yuǎn Gōng (遠公) arrived at Jiāngzhōu (江州).
He traversed various lanes and streets,
rested for a few days,
and then set off again.
After traveling west for over fifty *lǐ* (里),
as he was traveling,
he encountered a mountain.
He asked someone, "What mountain is this?"
A local replied, "This is [unnamed] mountain."
Yuǎn Gōng (遠公) said, "When I took leave of my master,
he instructed me to settle down wherever I encountered a mountain.
This must be the place for my cultivation."
He saw that the mountain was extraordinary.
What kind of wondrous landscape was it?
Yuǎn Gōng (遠公) was captivated by this mountain.
As the sun began to set in the west,
he entered deep into the mountain
to find a place to stay.
He then temporarily built a thatched hut
on the north side of Xiānglú Fēng (香爐峰) peak.
Taking out the flint from his waist,
he struck it,
and then lit priceless incense.
He sat in the lotus position,
and began to recite the *Nirvana Sūtra* (*Nièpán Jīng*),
which consisted of several volumes.
At this time,
the sound of the sūtra was loud and clear,
heard far and wide.
The dharma melody resonated beautifully,
and the Buddhist chant echoed afar.
This caused large rocks to shake,
and all the grasses to grow.
Auspicious birds and spirit creatures
all came to offer praise.
At this time,
the mountain deity in the temple suddenly saw these auspicious signs,
and was greatly surprised and bewildered.
The mountain deity said, "Who is on duty today?"
At that moment, Jiānláo Shùshén (堅牢樹神), the steadfast tree deity,
rushed to the front of the hall and bowed,
with a voice like a bursting thunderbolt.
He had one head and three faces,
eyes like hanging mirrors,
and held an iron rod as tall as himself in his hand.
He said, "I am on duty."
The mountain deity said, "Since you are on duty,
just now, in this temple,
I suddenly felt the mountain rocks shaking,
and birds and beasts startled.
Go patrol this mountain for me
and see what auspicious signs there are.
Perhaps some worthy sage from another land
has come to my mountain.
Or perhaps some unusual spirits
are taking refuge in this mountain.
If they bring peace and harmony to my mountain,
then let them be.
If they bring unrest to my mountain,
you must immediately send them out of this mountain."
The tree deity bowed,
then traversed all the mountains and rivers,
crossed streams and waters.
He searched everywhere under the trees in the mountain forests,
inspecting all such places,
but found no one.
He then arrived at the north side of Xiānglú Fēng (香爐峰),
and saw a monk
who had built a meditation hut,
and was sitting in the lotus position,
reciting sūtras.
Upon seeing him, the tree deity
immediately concealed his divine and ghostly form,
and transformed into an old man.
His age was like a decaying willow,
his hair white like mulberry and elm.
He went directly to the front of the hut
and loudly asked, "May I respectfully ask, Reverend?"
Yuǎn Gōng (遠公) replied, "Myriad blessings."
The old man gradually approached,
and said, "This disciple does not know where the Reverend has come from,
to arrive here,
and what he seeks?
I humbly pray for your compassion,
please enlighten me."
Yuǎn Gōng (遠公) said, "This humble monk has come from Yànmén (雁門),
and has temporarily settled on this mountain
to reside and cultivate the Way."
The old man asked again, "Just now I heard the Reverend's wonderful sound,
what was that sound?"
Yuǎn Gōng (遠公) said, "The sound just now
was this humble monk reciting sūtras.
It is my wish that all sentient beings who hear it
may be liberated from suffering and attain release."
Upon hearing this, the old man
repeatedly praised, "Excellent!"
He then asked the Reverend, "Since the Reverend has arrived here,
what does he need?"
Yuǎn Gōng (遠公) said, "If this humble monk could obtain a temple or monastery to reside in,
to be shielded from wind and frost,
that would be this humble monk's wish."
The old man said, "If you need anything else, I cannot provide it,
but if you need a temple or monastery,
that is a small matter.
This disciple lives in a village to the west.
I will go to the village and discuss it with the other elders,
then I will return to build a temple for the Reverend."
After the old man finished speaking,
he bade farewell to the Reverend and departed.
Thereupon, the old man took leave of the Reverend,
and after walking about a hundred paces from the hut,
he suddenly disappeared.
At that moment, he changed back from the old man's body,
and resumed his ghostly divine form.
He came to the front of the mountain deity's hall,
bowed and announced, "Your servant, acting on Your Majesty's command,
traversed all the mountains and rivers,
searching for spirits and fox demons,
but found no one.
When I reached the north side of Xiānglú Fēng (香爐峰) peak,
I saw a monk
who had built a meditation hut,
and was sitting in the lotus position reciting sūtras.
He said he had come from Yànmén (雁門),
and had temporarily settled on this mountain
to reside and cultivate the Way."
Upon hearing this, the mountain deity
exclaimed, "How extraordinary!"
"For countless eons
I have guarded this mountain,
and I have never seen a monk come to settle on this mountain.
They always bring blessings and avert calamities for my mountain."
The mountain deity asked again, "What does the monk need here?"
The tree deity reported, "I just asked him,
and he doesn't need anything else;
he only said he wants a temple or monastery to reside in."
The mountain deity said, "If he wanted anything else, it would be difficult,
but if he wants a temple to reside in,
that is a small matter.
You too, without delay,
gather all the mountain spirits and deities
to build a temple for this Reverend."
The tree deity obeyed the command,
and then, on the western slope,
knocked three times loudly.
Clouds and mist gathered darkly,
and all the mountain spirits and deities
arrived.
That night, they gathered their divine forces,
with flashing lightning of various kinds,
and thunder rumbling in a thousand ways.
They worked noisily until dawn,
the spirits building the temple.
By daybreak,
a temple was built,
truly extraordinary.
It had multiple stories and towering pavilions,
no different from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven (*Dāolì Tiān* 忉利天);
precious halls and platforms,
identical to the Western Pure Land.
Trees and clusters of plants
were luxuriant with blooming flowers,
regardless of the four seasons;
springs flowed beside them,
never ceasing in spring or winter.
Moreover, famous flowers with tender stamens
grew beside the path to enlightenment;
auspicious birds and spirit creatures
flew above the exquisite monastery.
Thereupon, Yuǎn Gōng (遠公) emerged from his hut and looked out,
suddenly seeing a temple completed.
He sighed in great wonder,
pondering for a long time.
Yuǎn Gōng (遠公) said, "This is not by my own ability,
but by the power of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* (*Dà Nièpán Jīng* 《大涅槃經》)."
Seeing this rare wonder,
Yuǎn Gōng (遠公) composed a verse:
Slender bamboos rustle, spring in all four seasons,
Intersecting waters flow clean without dust.
Ivy climbs the walls, every branch green,
Moss covers the ground, each speck fresh.
Secluded and wild, free from city clamor,
Pure and tranquil, not neighbors with the vulgar.
The mountain deity built this exquisite monastery here,
To invite the monk to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
Thereupon, Yuǎn Gōng himself entered the monastery,
going through every room,
and every courtyard.
Everything was present
except for water,
nowhere to be found.
Yuǎn Gōng said: "This monastery is very good and conforms to the Dharma,
but without water,
how can one reside here?
When monks arrive later,
how will there be water?"
So he went down in front of the Buddha hall
and saw a large stone.
Might there be water beneath it?
Yuǎn Gōng then poked it with his tin staff,
and only then did he get water,
which gushed out from the ground.
To this day, it is called Xīzhàng Quán (Tin Staff Spring).
The monastery is called Huàchéng zhī Sì (Monastery of the Transformed City).
Below the monastery, water flows,
known as Báilián Chí (White Lotus Pond).
Yuǎn Gōng entered the monastery to settle for his summer retreat.
After several months,
listeners from all four directions
flocked to this monastery.
On that day, Yuǎn Gōng extensively expounded the meaning of the Dà Nièpán Jīng (Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra) to his disciples and followers.
For a year,
listeners were like clouds,
and offerings rained down.
Among all the listeners,
at the assembly,
it was said that there was an old man
who listened to the sūtra for a year.
It was said that this old man
never announced his name when he came,
nor mentioned his courtesy name when he left.
He sat down as soon as the lecture began
and only departed after it ended.
Yuǎn Gōng found this very strange,
so he told his companions to call this old man for him.
The old man, upon being called,
came directly before Yuǎn Gōng.
Yuǎn Gōng said: "Old man, where do you live?
You have listened to the Dharma for a long time.
I do not know your name
and wish to know it clearly."
The old man replied: "Although this disciple has listened for a year,
I have not understood the meaning of the Nièpán Jīng
and thus cannot tell you my name."
Having said this, the old man
walked out of the monastery gate.
When looked at afterwards,
there was no trace of him.
Who could he be?
He was the dragon of the Qiānchǐ Tán (Thousand-Foot Pond) in the mountains,
who came to listen to Yuǎn Gōng preach the Dharma.
After the old man left, Yuǎn Gōng
often pondered and
felt remorse: "This old man listened to the Dharma for a year,
yet he still did not understand the meaning of the Nièpán Jīng.
How much less will ordinary sentient beings
who hear it be able to understand?
I must now compose a commentary (shūchāo) on the Nièpán Jīng."
Having said this,
he appealed to the Buddhas of the ten directions: "This disciple now, for the sake of sentient beings whose minds are confused and cannot comprehend,
and have not yet awakened to the Mahāyāna,
intends to create a commentary on the Nièpán Jīng
to enable all sentient beings to open their minds and understand,
to clearly grasp the Buddha-dharma,
to abandon evil and return to righteousness,
and forever sever the traces of doubt."
Then, in front of the Buddha hall,
taking a purple cloud divine brush (zīyúnháo shénbǐ),
he appealed to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions,
and to the local spirits and deities,
wishing them all to bear witness.
"If the wise and holy ones do not permit it,
may the brush immediately fall."
Having spoken, he burned incense and offered prayers,
appealing with utmost sincerity.
He then threw the brush into the air.
At that moment, the brush remained suspended motionless in the air.
Yuǎn Gōng knew that this accorded with the minds of all Tathāgatas,
so he then asked the brush to descend from the air.
How can we know this?
To this day, there is a Zhípǐ Fēng (Brush-Throwing Peak) in Jiāngzhōu that still exists.
Yuǎn Gōng then composed the commentary.
It took three years
to complete.
Still fearing errors in the text
or unclear meanings,
he took the commentary, more than eight hundred scrolls,
placed it in a fire outside the eastern gate of the monastery,
amassed abundant incense,
and repeatedly appealed to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and wise sages of the ten directions: "This disciple now, for the sake of sentient beings whose minds are confused and cannot comprehend,
and have not yet awakened to the Mahāyāna,
and wishing to awaken their doubts,
has therefore compiled this commentary.
If the sūtra and the meaning are identical,
may the fire be unable to burn it.
If the sūtra and the commentary are identical,
may water be unable to drown it."
Having spoken, he began to burn the commentary.
At that time, red flames reached the sky,
and black smoke billowed,
but the sūtra within
suffered no damage whatsoever.
Yuǎn Gōng knew that the commentary profoundly accorded with the Buddha's mind,
yet he was still not satisfied.
So he took the commentary again, went to the edge of the Báiliánhuā Chí (White Lotus Pond),
and threw it into the water.
The commentary remained suspended about one *zhang* above the water,
motionless.
Yuǎn Gōng knew that it profoundly accorded with the Buddha's mind.
Afterwards, he retrieved the commentary and brought it into the monastery,
placing it in the sūtra repository.
Thereafter, his disciples were numerous,
and listeners were extremely many.
Yuǎn Gōng then expounded the meaning of the Dà Nièpán Jīng to the assembly,
so much so that listeners came from all directions,
like a sudden rain or rushing clouds,
competing to hear the Dharma.
He continued to preach
for about several years.
Suddenly, within the borders of Shòuzhōu,

Yuǎngōng said, "When you did not know,

I am here,

Yúnqìng saw that the Venerable Master repeatedly refused to avoid them,

Yuǎngōng saw that the monks had left,

without any fear.
Soon after, Bái Zhuāng led his followers to the monastery.
Bái Zhuāng arrayed his formation on the transverse ridge,

Their shouts made the mountains crumble and rocks split,

When Bái Zhuāng entered the monastery,

Bái Zhuāng exclaimed, "How strange!

Who informed the monastery,

Bái Zhuāng ordered his subordinates, "Search everywhere inside and outside the monastery for me.
