Thereupon, Bái Zhuāng grabbed the reins and mounted his saddle,
and went directly outside the east gate of the monastery,
where he indeed saw a monk sitting in meditation posture
inside the hermitage.
Bái Zhuāng loudly called out,
ordering his subordinates to bring him before his horse.
He asked Yuǎngōng, "What money, valuables, or clothes
are there in your monastery?
You must quickly bring them out!"
Yuǎngōng stepped forward
and replied to Bái Zhuāng, "This monastery has always been poor and empty,
with nothing at all.
Even if there were some small offerings,
they were immediately used for meals and provisions,
so there is truly no wealth.
I dare not deceive the general."
Thereupon, Bái Zhuāng carefully observed Yuǎngōng,
and admiration arose in his heart.
Because Yuǎngōng had the appearance of a Bodhisattva,
his body had a silvery radiance,
he was seven feet tall,
his hair was like lacquered paint,
and his lips were like dotted cinnabar.
Upon seeing him, Bái Zhuāng
said to his subordinates, "This monk
is fit to be one of my servants."
Bái Zhuāng then said, "I want you to be a laborer.
Will you agree to this?"
Yuǎngōng stepped forward,
"I am willing to offer this body to be a slave to the general,
and willingly serve before your horse."
Yuǎngōng added, "There is a small matter
that should be reported.
Does the general want this humble monk's body,
or does he want this humble monk's profession?"
Bái Zhuāng asked, "What is 'body'?
What is 'profession'?"
Yuǎngōng replied, "This humble monk's profession is reciting scriptures.
If you want this humble monk to serve you,
it is only this body.
If you want this humble monk's body,
then you only need not hinder this humble monk from reciting scriptures."
Bái Zhuāng said, "As long as I have you to serve me,
who would hinder you from reciting scriptures?"
Yuǎngōng acknowledged with a "Nuo!"
and followed behind him.
About a hundred paces from the monastery,
Yuǎngōng again addressed the general, "Allow this humble monk to return to the monastery,
take off these monk's robes in the monastery,
and then return here,
willing to follow the general's banner."
Bái Zhuāng said, "Then come back quickly!
Do not make me suspicious.
If you are late,
I will send my subordinates to capture you
and cut you into three pieces before my horse. Don't say I didn't warn you."
Yuǎngōng acknowledged with a "Nuo!"
and entered the monastery, standing before the main hall.
At that time, his chief disciple, Yúnqìng, was on a high peak,
and saw his master inside the monastery.
He rushed down the mountain,
and went directly before his great master,
reporting to the Venerable Master, "Just now, the mad bandits charged,
causing great fear.
But fortunately, the bandit army has retreated,
and I share the Venerable Master's joy."
Yuǎngōng said, "According to the meaning of the Nirvánà Sūtra,
there is fundamentally no fear;
if there is fear,
how can it be called Nirvāṇa?
From now on,
you must diligently cultivate
and be a good abbot.
I am now taking leave of you for another life."
Yúnqìng asked the Venerable Master, "Why do you speak in such a way?"
Yuǎngōng replied, "Just now, outside the gate, I vowed
to become a slave to that general,
and can no longer stay here.
You must strive hard in my absence."
When Yúnqìng heard these words,
he threw himself to the ground,
and fresh blood flowed from all seven orifices.
After a long time, he revived
and rose from the ground.
Then he composed a gāthā, saying:
"We are like overturned birds,
the Venerable Master is like a great tree.
Now that the great tree has moved,
where shall the flock perch?
Where is your manifested body?
Only the verse of Nirvāṇa remains.
May your lamp of wisdom shine down,
and not forget the lost path."
Yúnqìng finished speaking,
and wept even more sadly.
Yuǎngōng said: “I fear the General will find it strange if I delay.”
He walked out of the temple gate,
caught up with his banners,
and followed closely behind him.
Days and months passed,
and they accompanied each other for several years.
After Yúnqìng saw the Venerable Master leave,
he gathered the monks again,
and began a lecture series on the "Níèpán Jīng Shūchāo" (Commentary on the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra).
All the listeners,
without exception, shed tears,
as if they saw the Great Master himself.
Then Yúnqìng, seeing that there was no news from the Venerable Master for several years,
entrusted the "Níèpán Jīng Shūchāo" to Dào'ān Heshang.
After Dào'ān received the "Níèpán Jīng Shūchāo",
he immediately took it to the Fúguāng Sì in Dōngdū to begin a lecture series.
No one knew what kind of person Dào'ān was,
but he attracted listeners as numerous as clouds,
and offerings poured in like rain.
At that time, when Jìn Wén Huángdì's royal influence reached Dōngdū,
Dào'ān began his lectures,
which caused heavenly flowers to fall in profusion,
and brought forth delightful fragrance.
Five-colored clouds appeared,
and even more people came,
countless listeners,
who trampled the lecture hall,
making it impossible to begin.
Dào'ān then wrote a memorial to Jìn Wén Huángdì, saying: “Your servant, by imperial decree,
is lecturing on the "Níèpán Jīng" at Fúguāng Sì.
The number of listeners has increased,
disrupting the dharma assembly,
making it impossible to proceed.
I humbly beg for an imperial decree,
to give further instructions.”
At that time, there was an order: “If one wishes to listen to Dào'ān lecture,
each person must pay one bolt of silk
to listen for one day.”
At that time, due to the peaceful reign,
all goods were inexpensive,
and those who paid one bolt of silk daily
numbered about thirty to twenty thousand people.
The temple courtyard was small,
with no place to accommodate them.
He then wrote another memorial to the Emperor: “Your servant, by imperial decree,
is holding a lecture series at Fúguāng Sì.
I humbly believe that the previous order to pay one bolt of silk,
has led to even more listeners,
making it difficult to regulate.
I humbly beg for further instructions.”
At that time, there was an order: “Those who wish to listen to Dào'ān lecture,
each person must pay one hundred strings of cash
to listen for one day.”
Despite such restrictions,
the daily attendance did not fall below three to five thousand people,
who came to hear Dào'ān lecture in Dōngdū.
Where was Yuǎngōng then?
Yuǎngōng always followed Bái Zhuāng, raiding prefectures they encountered,
and counties they encountered.
In the morning, they roamed the plains,
and at dusk, they lodged in the mountains.
With dishevelled hair and eyebrows,
and wearing coarse garments,
he always followed behind him.
More than several years passed,
and he longed for the monastic life,
but had no way to return.
Moreover, Bái Zhuāng had committed numerous evil deeds,
associating with violent criminals,
delighting in killing and violence,
and living by plunder.
Suddenly, one day,
while in the mountains,
Bái Zhuāng settled on the east ridge,
and Yuǎngōng lodged on the west slope.
It was at this time
that the autumn wind suddenly arose,
fallen leaves drifted,
the mountains were still and the forests sparse,
and frost covered the vegetation.
The wind passed through the forest,
blowing the bamboo like strings,
the moon shone in the clear sky,
and the red clouds were like brocade.
By the side of the flowing stream,
his heart was filled with melancholy.
As he fell into a hazy sleep,
he dreamt of Buddhas from the ten directions,
all appearing amidst the clouds,
and countless sages,
all coming there.
They called out: “Bodhisattva, arise!
Do not cling to the sleep of ignorance,
attain the state of Nirvāṇa.
Why do you not recite the "Níèpán Jīng" for the sake of sentient beings?”
Yuǎngōng prostrated in his dream without ceasing.
Yuǎngōng was a mere ordinary person,
yet he moved Akṣobhya Tathāgata to grant him a prophecy,
calling Yuǎngōng closer: “Do not let your heart be filled with sorrow.
You have an old debt yet unpaid.
Because in your previous life you were a guarantor,
in this life you are destined to settle accounts.
The creditor is not far,
it is Chánglín Xiànggōng, the current Prime Minister.
Later, sell this body of yours,
get five hundred strings of cash to repay Bái Zhuāng,
then return to the mountain,
and I will meet you.”
Yuǎngōng awoke from his dream with a start,
feeling extremely distraught.
He then sat up,
and recited several scrolls of the "Níèpán Jīng".
Bái Zhuāng awoke with a start on the east ridge,
and immediately asked his attendants: “What is that sound from the west?”
The attendants replied: “Reporting to the General,
from the west is the sound of the lowly slave you captured reciting sutras.”
When Bái Zhuāng heard this,
he became extremely angry.
He summoned Yuǎngōng directly before him,
and loudly reprimanded him: “If you were in a monastery or temple,
reciting would be permissible.
But now you are following me,
how can you recite sutras!”
Yuǎngōng said: “When the General captured this lowly slave that day,
you permitted me to recite sutras.”
Bái Zhuāng said: “When did I ever permit you to recite sutras?”
Yuǎngōng remained silent,
but the attendants said: “General, you indeed permitted him to recite sutras.”
Bái Zhuāng said: “Reciting sutras is an idle matter.
We are all engaged in killing,
and do not wish to hear the sound of sutra recitation.”
Yuǎngōng said: “Since I am not allowed to recite aloud,
and not to raise my voice,
would it be permissible to recite silently?”
Bái Zhuāng said: “No,
the reason I captured you then
was, firstly, because I got no money or goods,
and secondly, because I had no men under my command.
Therefore, I became angry
and captured you.
Now I have many men,
and great strength.
I will release you to return to the mountains,
and practice as you wish.”
Yuǎngōng said: “I offered myself to serve you as a slave,
and I must serve you for your entire life.
To abandon me midway,
how can that be called an offering of oneself?
If you still wish for my service,
I shall say nothing further;
if you no longer want this lowly slave,
then sell me wherever you wish,
and use the money to buy wine and meat for yourself,
would that be permissible?”
When Bái Zhuāng heard this,
he laughed heartily: “You are greatly mistaken.
If I had bought you from various places,
I could then use the old contract
to sell you.
But since I captured you,
how can I sell you?”
Yuǎngōng said: “If you will not sell,
then I shall say nothing further;
if you wish to sell me,
then just sell me as a born slave,
who has no contract.”
Bái Zhuāng said: “Where can I sell you?”
Yuǎngōng said: “If you wish to sell this lowly slave,
then just take me to Dōngdū to sell.”
When Bái Zhuāng heard this,
he became furiously angry: “This despicable fellow has not changed his treacherous schemes!
He intends to go to Dōngdū,
meet with high and low,
and lodge a complaint at the sutra registry,
claiming I am a thief,
and have me arrested.”
Yuǎngōng said: “If this lowly slave has such an intention,
or plots against you,
may I in this life and future lives,
fall into hell,
with no hope of release.
Please do not worry,
there will be no such thing.”
When Bái Zhuāng heard this,
he believed him.
He then dismissed his followers,
keeping only three or five men.
Posing as merchants,
with three or five bolts of cloth,
and various goods,
they headed straight for Dōngdū,
to sell Yuǎngōng,
taking him to a horse market to sell.
At that time, Yuǎn Gōng came to the city market
holding a sign and selling himself.
At that time, tens of thousands of people,
all sighed with admiration.
And they saw Yuǎn Gōng's sign:
his height was seven chǐ,
his radiant features were like white silver,
his forehead was broad and his brows high,
his face was like the full moon,
his hair like lacquered paint,
his lips like dotted vermilion.
He walked with the gait of a bull king,
his hands hung past his knees,
he walked with steps moving east and west.
The onlookers sighed in wonder,
all filled with love and admiration.
At that time, people formed groups of threes and fives,
saying, "In this world, I have seen tens of millions of people, good and bad,
but I have truly never seen anyone like this."
As they sighed with admiration,
the crowd grew even larger.
At that time, Yuǎn Gōng felt dejected in his heart,
resenting himself,
knowing that his karmic debt was not yet settled,
and specifically waited to sell himself to repay Bái Zhuāng.
In a short while,
the god Dì Shì was moved and manifested to descend,
appearing as an envoy of Prime Minister Cuī,
and went straight to the horse market,
calling out loudly to the horse broker,
"This person [referring to Yuǎn Gōng]
is not to be sold anywhere else.
Prime Minister Cuī's residence in the imperial court
needs only this person.
If it were any other family,
they would not be able to buy this person."
The broker heard these words
and fully affirmed that this was true. The broker then led Yuǎn Gōng to Prime Minister Cuī's residence.
At that time, Bái Zhuāng also followed behind.
Yuǎn Gōng said, "Master, you don't need to come.
No matter what happens ahead,
your humble servant is here.
If the Prime Minister is pleased,
whatever money and goods are obtained,
Master, you can take them all."
Bái Zhuāng said, "You must answer well to the matters ahead,
do not make any mistakes."
Yuǎn Gōng bowed.
Then he followed the broker
straight to the Prime Minister's gate.
The gatekeeper asked the broker, "Who told you to come?"
"I was commanded to come personally,
because this person [referring to Yuǎn Gōng]
is not to be sold elsewhere,
so I specially brought him to be taken in by the Prime Minister's residence."
The gate official said, "Wait here for now;
allow me to go in and report to the Prime Minister."
The gate official went to the front of the hall and reported to the Prime Minister, "There is a servant broker at the gate,
now leading a humble person to see you, Prime Minister;
I dared not fail to report."
The Prime Minister said, "Let him be brought in."
Thus, the gate official received the Prime Minister's command.
The broker led Yuǎn Gōng in,
straight to the front of the hall.
He then saw the Prime Minister,
bowed deeply,
and stood to one side.
The Prime Minister, upon seeing him,
exclaimed in great wonder, "Last night in a dream, I saw a divine being
enter my residence.
Today, seeing this person,
could it be an fulfillment of my dream?"
The Prime Minister asked the broker, "Is this a servant born in Bái Zhuāng's household,
or was he bought from elsewhere?"
The broker reported to the Prime Minister, "He is a servant born in Bái Zhuāng's household."
The Prime Minister said, "Since he is a servant born in Bái Zhuāng's household,
there should be no contract."
The Prime Minister asked the broker, "This servant,
how much money is he being sold for?"
Before the broker could speak,
Yuǎn Gōng stepped forward and reported to the Prime Minister, "If you wish to buy your humble servant cheaply,
I only ask for five hundred strings of cash from Your Excellency."
The Prime Minister said, "What skills do you possess
to be worth five hundred strings of cash?
That's quite a lot.
Please briefly describe your skills."
Yuǎn Gōng replied, "Your humble servant can discern a family's prosperity for three hundred years in the past,
and also know a family's poverty for two hundred years in the future.
I can fold clothes,
and prepare medicines for all four seasons.
I can relay messages,
and answer all questions.
I have a rough understanding of several styles of calligraphy.
On horseback with a single spear,
I am ready for any challenge.
I have a slight knowledge of hoeing crops and reaping wheat.
I know all the ins and outs of trade and transactions.
If put to work,
I will come like the wind,
truly not sluggish.
If Your Excellency does not believe me,
your humble servant will write his own contract of sale,
and you will know the truth."
The Prime Minister instructed his attendants
to bring paper and brush and hand them over.
Yuǎn Gōng received the paper and brush,
then requested an incense burner,
passed it over immediately,
bowed and thanked the Prime Minister,
and then, in front of the hall, wrote his own contract of sale,
which was unlike that of ordinary people.
Yuǎn Gōng reported, "In a certain year, certain month, I sell myself to Your Excellency as a servant,
to serve with utmost loyalty,
and must serve my Master for his entire life.
If I am abandoned halfway,
in the coming future lives,
I shall die and fall into hell.
Once the suffering is complete,
I shall be reborn as an animal,
with saddle and stirrups,
iron in my mouth,
bearing the faults of the past.
If I serve my Master for his entire life,
in the coming future lives,
the fruits of the ten bhūmis will be complete,
and we shall be reborn together in the Buddha's assembly."
After the contract was written,
he handed it to the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister received it,
and exclaimed in great wonder,
"Could this be a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva come to my residence?"
He then ordered money to be brought and gave five hundred strings of cash to the broker,
which was immediately given to Bái Zhuāng.
After Bái Zhuāng received the money,
he dared not stay any longer,
and returned to the border of Shòuzhōu.
The Xiànggōng bought the humble slave.
He then ordered the retainers of the West Courtyard to lead him into a room to settle down.
Yuǎngōng, knowing himself to be repaying a debt,
dared not resent others.
Coming and going,
he submitted entirely to being driven by whips and stirrups.
One day, Yuǎngōng
sat alone in his room.
It was late at night, and the hour was deep.
He trimmed the remaining lamp.
He saw the Milky Way serene
and the moon bright in the vast sky.
After sitting for a long time,
he drowsily fell asleep.
Then, in his dream, he saw the Buddhas of the ten directions,
all manifesting in the void.
Countless saints and sages
all gathered like clouds,
calling out: “Bodhisattva, arise!
Do not cling to the sleep of ignorance.
Attain the state of Nirvāṇa.
How can you not recite sūtras for sentient beings?”
Yuǎngōng was thereupon startled awake.
He rose and sat, reciting the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*
until dawn.
At that time, the Xiànggōng, in the hall,
suddenly heard the sound of sūtra recitation and arose.
He gradually walked alone
to the front of the West Courtyard gate,
listening to the sound of sūtra recitation.
He then ordered his attendants to summon Fūrén Qū.
Fūrén, on receiving the summons,
came to the front of the West Gate.
The Xiànggōng and Fūrén came to listen to the sūtra recitation
until dawn.
The next morning,
the Xiànggōng returned from court,
ascended the hall, and sat down.
He then ordered his attendants to summon the retainers from the West Courtyard.
At that time, thirty retainers all arrived before the hall.
The Xiànggōng asked: “Last night in the West Courtyard,
whose retainer was reciting sūtras?”
A retainer, at the head of the group, reported to the Xiànggōng, saying: “Last night’s recitation
was none other than
the sound of the newly bought humble slave reciting sūtras.”
The Xiànggōng heard that the new humble slave was reciting sūtras.
The Xiànggōng asked Yuǎngōng: “Last night’s recitation,
was it you?”
Yuǎngōng replied: “It was this humble slave’s sound of reciting sūtras.”
The Xiànggōng asked: “What is the title of the sūtra?”
Yuǎngōng replied: “What was recited last night
was the *Dà Nièpán Jīng*.”
The Xiànggōng asked: “How many volumes have you recited?”
Yuǎngōng replied: “This humble slave has recited one complete work of twelve volumes.
Last night, I recited it all.”
The Xiànggōng said: “Do not speak carelessly.”
Yuǎngōng replied: “How dare I deceive the Xiànggōng?”
The Xiànggōng then ordered Yuǎngōng to sit again
and recite the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Thereupon, Yuǎngōng again began the title,
and recited the sūtra once more.
From beginning to end,
there was no error.
The Xiànggōng saw this
and repeatedly praised, “Excellent!”
He then summoned all the household members, high and low, free and slave, over three hundred people,
all to the front of the hall.
The Xiànggōng issued an order:
From now on,
no one shall
look down upon the new humble slave.
Furthermore, give him an external name,
calling him Shànqìng.
The Xiànggōng, every day after morning court,
often went to Fúguāng Sì to listen to Dào'ān lecture on the sūtras,
donating one hundred strings of cash.
Then, on the following day,
he brought Shànqìng along to the temple.
Because Shànqìng had only recently begun serving the Xiànggōng,
he was not allowed to enter the temple to listen to the sūtras,
but instead stayed outside the temple gate to look after his horse.
After a short while,
he saw the audience gathering like clouds and rushing like rain,
all entering the temple.
Soon the sound of the bell ceased,
and then the sūtra topic was announced,
the Buddhist chants echoing far,
gradually reaching his ears.
When Shànqìng heard this,
his heart was filled with melancholy.
Yuǎngōng said: "I do not know how Dào'ān
can lecture and praise so skillfully.
I wish that one day I could ascend the high platform again,
and once more attain the fruit of the ten bhūmis,
and dispel disasters for all sentient beings.
Whether form-ful or formless,
with characteristics or without characteristics,
all are extinguished and liberated through Nirvāṇa."
After a short while,
he then descended from the lecture,
and men and women dispersed together.
The Xiànggōng returned home,
and after settling down in the hall,
he ascended to the hall and sat down.
His Fūrén covered her sleeves and approached the Xiànggōng,
and addressed him, saying: "Just as the Xiànggōng, for several years,
in Fúguāng Sì,
has listened to the venerable Dào'ān lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
what teachings have you heard?
It is said that the meaning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*
is immeasurable and boundless.
How much of the sūtra text does the Xiànggōng remember?
Why are you silent and say nothing,
and do not explain even a line or two of gāthā to your concubine?"
The Xiànggōng said: "Has the Fūrén ever read the *Lotus Sūtra*?"
The Fūrén said: "I have read the *Lotus Sūtra*."
The Xiànggōng said: "The sūtra says: 'Do not speak without being asked;
if heard, it will certainly not be listened to.'"
The Fūrén said: "I wish the Xiànggōng would briefly explain a little to the noble and base in the household,
to enlighten their minds and help them understand."
The Xiànggōng said: "Very well,
I will explain the meaning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for the Fūrén."
The Fūrén then ordered the servants to sweep and clean the hall,
set up a high couch,
and summoned over three hundred people, both high and low,
to gather before the hall,
inviting the Xiànggōng to explain the meaning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
and all these people listened in silence.
That night, the Xiànggōng first explained to the Fūrén the eight sufferings that torment.
First, he spoke of "the suffering of birth."
The suffering of birth:
the body, entrusted to the mother's care in the womb,
at the approach of the month of birth,
is like curdled milk.
Within ninety days,
it can form a shape;
a boy is on the mother's left side,
a girl is nestled against the mother's right flank,
close to the heart and liver,
receiving qi and taking form,
and thus endures all sufferings.
The wise and the foolish are the same,
the noble and the base are also alike.
The kindness of a compassionate mother
should be without distinction.
When the mother eats hot food,
it is no different from being boiled in a cauldron;
when the mother eats cold things,
it is just like the hell of cold ice.
If the mother eats her fill,
it is like being crushed between stones;
if the mother is hungry,
the child suffers the pain of being hung upside down.
When ten months are complete,
and birth is imminent,
the hundred joints open,
like being sawn apart.
The four limbs are broken,
the five organs ache,
no different from a knife wound,
how unlike a sword cut.
A thousand births and ten thousand deaths,
one faints and knows nothing,
life hangs by a thread,
with no hope of living again.
Soon the mother and child separate,
blood flows like a slaughtered sheep,
and while the mother is confused and fainting,
she asks if it is a boy or a girl.
If told it is a girl,
then the mother and child are safely separated.
If told it is a son,
she completely forgets the pain in her hundred joints,
and amidst her confusion,
she immediately smiles;
this is called a filial son.
But what if it is a child of the five rebellious acts?
How is it delivered?
Within its mother's belly,
it makes the mother uneasy,
kicking and stepping on its mother,
never resting for a moment,
sometimes on the heart,
sometimes in the waist,
reaching everywhere within the five organs.
When ten months are complete, it is born,
at which time it grasps its mother's heart and liver,
and kicks its mother's hip bones.
For three or five days,
it refuses to be peaceful.
From this, the mother's life gradually changes,
the mother looks as if she is dying,
her cries shake the earth,
like a sword carving her heart.
Brothers and mother
do not know what to do.
Enemies and creditors
will only stop once they have taken a life.
Since the child endured first,
the mother must die later;
this is called "the suffering of birth."
That night, the Xiànggōng also explained to the Fūrén "the suffering of old age."
The suffering of old age:
a person's hundred years
are like a spark.
In a short while,
at seventy or eighty,
strength declines.
In earlier times, one's voice was youthful,
and appearance was like a spring flower;
now that old age has come,
how is it different from autumn grass?
Chicken skin and crane hair
are constantly dry.
Eyes are dim and ears are deaf,
unable to distinguish colors.
The four limbs are heavy,
the hundred bones ache.
Getting farther from heaven,
getting closer to earth.
Lying in bed at night,
turning over thousands of times,
unable to do anything.
The affairs of the world
are like things in a dream.
Do you not see the peaches and plums by the roadside,
blossoming year after year?
Where is the beauty of former days
now?
If old age and sickness invade,
white hair will never turn black again.
Former youthful vigor
withers with the eight seasons;
former beauty
changes with the four seasons.
Everyone grows old,
noble and base are the same,
not distinguishing between the wise and the foolish,
all share the suffering of old age.
It is better to act early
and cultivate fields of merit,
for human life is fleeting,
and soon passes away.
One must be diligent
and practice cultivation,
for once a human body is lost,
there is no way to regain it.
This is called "the suffering of old age."
That night, the Prime Minister told his wife about the “suffering of illness.”
The wife again asked: “What is called the suffering of illness?”
The suffering of illness
is when the four great elements,
which have never truly existed,
are temporarily combined by various causes.
When earth, water, fire, and wind,
even one pulse is out of harmony,
then illness arises.
Suddenly one is gravely ill and bedridden,
the soul and spirit are uneasy,
the five spirits are all lost,
lips are dry and tongue is shrunken,
brain aches and head hurts,
between the hundred bones and joints,
it is as if being sawn apart.
One suffers day and night,
with no end in sight.
One cannot seek to live,
nor can one seek to die.
The wondrous arts of the world
only treat those whose lives are not yet over;
how can one destined to die be saved?
Medicines may be able to cure,
but cannot completely heal damage,
day after day and night after night,
enduring all great sufferings.
Even if Jīpó’s potent medicines
or Biǎnquè’s acupuncture were applied,
when fatal illness arrives,
none can escape it.
People in the world are wrongly subjected to evil words;
before they are ill and bedridden,
they offer sacrifices to gods and ghosts,
burn money and lift taboos,
and wrongly kill sentient beings.
Such people
will fall into hell.
The great limit is no more than a hundred years,
among which seventy years is already rare.
If three people all live to a hundred,
how much time can they truly have?
If one lives in the world,
and there were wondrous arts,
there should be people living for a thousand years.
Why not contemplate with careful thought,
and avoid being deceived and intimidated by masters and teachers?
This is what is called the “suffering of illness.”
That night, the Prime Minister told his wife about the “suffering of death.”
The suffering of death is when
the four great elements are about to perish,
and the soul and spirit are swept away by the wind.
Brothers part forever,
parents are separated eternally,
wife, children, and sons and daughters,
have no way to reunite.
Friends one met and associated with,
once parted, have no way to meet again.
Gold, silver, money, and possessions,
are all left to be divided;
residences, shops, estates, and gardens,
cannot be taken along.
The suffering of death due to greed and attachment,
the four great elements separate,
the soul and spirit fly away,
one knows not where they are.
When the three-inch breath ceases,
that is the next life;
once a person dies,
when will they be reborn?
In life, one struggles as a hero;
in death, one is judged by merit and virtue.
One receives according to one’s karma,
allowing it to arrange one’s fate.
Perhaps residing in hell,
or in heaven,
or becoming an animal,
or a hungry ghost;
the six paths of transmigration
have no end.
To regain a human body
is one in ten thousand, a rare occurrence.
This is what is called the suffering of death.
That night, the Prime Minister again told his wife about the “suffering of the five aggregates.”
The suffering of the five aggregates is that
when one lives in the world,
it is like day and night.
Pus, blood, and skin,
fine silks wrapped around the body;
within the five aggregates,
the seven orifices constantly flow,
inwardly harboring the foul stench of filth and excrement,
blood flowing over bones on the outside.
Just look at the pus, snot, and saliva,
constantly flowing day and night,
everywhere unbearable,
completely lacking any true form.
All desires arise from the three-inch breath,
which is the sprout of the three poisons,
the root of the five inner organs and five desires.
Therefore, the Great Master has a verse:
A thin skin bag of pus and blood,
muscles entwined around stinking bones.
From head to foot,
the entire body is a flow of pus.
Such are the many kinds of suffering
that oppress the body.
This is what is called the “suffering of the five aggregates.”
That night, the Prime Minister again told his wife about the “suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.”
The suffering of not obtaining what one seeks is that
when one lives in the world,
everyone has something they seek.
Those who wish to have blessings
seek supreme bodhi.
And within the three ages,
they seek the blessing of being born in heaven.
How many can enjoy worldly glory,
seeking human wealth and possessions,
only to meet an untimely death midway?
If one seeks gold, silver, and silk,
one's heart yearns for glory for kalpas.
Even if one obtains food and clothing,
it is never enough for oneself.
Parents and siblings
each take care of themselves.
Sons and daughters are born and raised,
each goes their separate way to seek their own.
If one did not sow in a previous life,
and did not cultivate for kalpas,
yet desires worldly glory,
one must cultivate blessings in this life.
Today, with earnest persuasion, the listeners
all know that food and clothing are predetermined by past lives.
Therefore, the Great Master has a verse:
This year will surely lead to next year,
so why not plant next year’s grain?
This life will surely lead to the next life,
so why not cultivate blessings for the next life?
There are many such kinds of suffering,
and this is what is called the “suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.”
That night, the Prime Minister again told his wife about the “suffering of encountering what one hates.”
The suffering of encountering what one hates is that
when one lives in the world,
with desire in one’s heart,
seeing another’s wife,
one desires a wife.
Once a wife is obtained,
not even two or three years pass,
and then sons are born and daughters are raised.
What is this likened to?
It is like a butterfly collecting nectar,
hovering only in the void.
Suddenly it sees a cluster of peonies,
and immediately goes to collect the fragrant pollen.
Unaware of a spider on it,
tightly weaving its web,
a hundred and a thousand times around,
the butterfly is wrapped,
trapped within,
with no way to escape despite countless efforts.
This is the suffering.
Ordinary people who love beauty
are also like this.
Seeing someone young,
they develop a heart of admiration.
As years and months pass,
then they have sons and daughters.
Once they grow up,
they are unfilial to their parents,
their five grave sins reach heaven,
they do not associate with the wise,
but keep company with wicked companions.
They speak without thinking twice,
insulting their six close relatives,
and even their elders.
If they are at home,
they immediately cause mental and physical strain.
Or if they go out,
one must constantly worry and fear.
These are called enemies from many lives,
with no end in sight from generation to generation.
Through earnest persuasion of good causes,
listeners will understand.
If one wishes to have no enemies in future lives,
it is better to cultivate pure conduct in this life.
Enemies will be separated forever,
not disturbing one’s heart.
How much there is in the karma of sons and daughters!
Therefore, the Great Master has a verse:
Since countless eons, one has received the deep current,
endlessly circling through the six paths.
If one does not fiercely sever it in this life,
when will the retribution between enemies cease?
This is what is called the “suffering of encountering what one hates.”
That night, the xiànggōng again explained the `àibiélíkǔ` to his fūrén.
As for the `àibiélíkǔ`:
For instance, if a family raises a son,
his parents cherish him like pearls and jade.
When he grows up and becomes an adult,
as soon as he can discern directions,
he immediately leaves his hometown and separates from his village.
His parents worry day and night and yearn for him.
Every morning they lean against the door,
weeping sorrowfully.
From then on, their longing makes them ill,
needing care and medicine.
When will they get to see him?
Suddenly, when the winter festivals and New Year arrive,
with all their relatives present before their eyes,
they suddenly remember the son who is far away.
Thereupon, their throats are choked and their chests filled with emotion.
This is precisely what is called `àibiélíkǔ`.
That night, the xiànggōng finished speaking of the eight sufferings,
and the three hundred-odd people, great and small, noble and humble, in the household,
all bowed and thanked the xiànggōng.
Only Shànqìng shed tears profusely.
Though Shànqìng said nothing,
she thought to herself: "I recall the day I was in the mountains,
when I first lectured on the title of this sūtra,
it caused the great rocks to shake,
the hundred grasses to bend,
and auspicious birds and numinous creatures
flew to fill the temple.
Auspicious clouds did not disperse,
but constantly hovered near the purple palace;
propitious energies swirled,
never leaving the side of the vermilion tower.
All devas heard the Dharma,
the ten classes heard the sūtra,
the form-endowed and the formless,
the endowed with distinguishing marks and the un-marked,
all acted for Nirvāṇa and attained extinction.
When Shànqìng finished her contemplation,
her eyes were filled with tears.
The xiànggōng was puzzled by this,
and asked Shànqìng, "I have lectured the sūtra to you,
what is the reason you weep so frequently?
Are you perhaps resentful of someone?
If you understand, quickly explain the circumstances,
otherwise, you will watch yourself be beaten with a stick."
Shànqìng stepped forward
and addressed the xiànggōng, saying, "This humble servant does not resent anyone else,
it is only that the Dharma teaching of Dào'ān shàngrén
is not entirely impartial."
The xiànggōng said, "It is Dào'ān shàngrén himself who came to the capital to lecture and praise,
and kings, marquises, generals, and ministers
listen to his Dharma teaching every day.
You have never heard him teach the Dharma,
how can you know that his lecture and praise are not impartial?"
Shànqìng stepped forward
and addressed the xiànggōng, saying, "Last night, Shànqìng followed my master into the temple,
but was kept outside the gate
and could not hear the sūtra.
From that, I knew Dào'ān shàngrén's Dharma teaching could not be impartial.
Though this humble servant holds a lowly position,
I have a slight understanding of the Buddha-Dharma;
though our robes are different,
the Dharma should be one without a second.
From this, I know Dào'ān's Dharma teaching cannot be impartial;
he does not understand how to transmit the Dharma to the three classes of people,
and the four births and ten classes."
The xiànggōng asked, "What are called the four births and ten classes,
and the three classes of people?
Explain them to me in detail,
so that my mind may be enlightened and awakened,
and I may understand the Buddha-Dharma clearly."
Shànqìng replied, "The three classes of people are:
first, the sick child on the bed;
second, the prisoner in confinement;
third, the person who lacks freedom.
The Dharma master on the high seat does not understand expedient means,
to universally transmit and preach to the three classes of people.
He has such faults,
which is why his Dharma teaching is not impartial."
The xiànggōng asked, "What are the four births and ten classes?"
Shànqìng addressed the xiànggōng, "The four births
are: born from the womb, born from eggs, born from moisture, and born by transformation.
These are the four births.
The ten classes are:

those with form, those without form, those with distinguishing marks, those without distinguishing marks, those neither with nor without distinguishing marks, those neither without nor with distinguishing marks, those with four feet, those with two feet, those with many feet, and those without feet.
These are called the ten classes."
The xiànggōng said to Shànqìng, "I do not understand the reasons;
explain them to me in detail,
and I will abandon heterodoxy and return to the orthodox."
Shànqìng said, "Those born from the womb
are like people who listen to the Dharma,
as when two people came to the temple to listen to the sūtra.
One person had no greed,
and entered the temple to listen to the sūtra;
the other had greed
and immediately turned back and left.
Of the person who entered the temple,
one sat down in the Hall of Good Dharma,
heard a sentence of profound Dharma,
and it entered their heart and body,
immediately filling their heart with joy.
Suddenly remembering the person who did not come,
their heart immediately forgot what they heard,
and though there were words, they could not listen,
feeling dejected.
Like a child in its mother's womb,
obstructed from the sun by floating clouds,
in the course of time,
it falls into the realm of being born from the womb.
Those born from eggs
are also people who listen to the Dharma,
who came to the temple to listen to the sūtra,
and sat in front of the Hall of Good Dharma,
their minds wishing to attach to the Dharma master,
but the Dharma master did not understand,
and instead spoke of external conditions.
Then, what kind of Dharma did he preach?
Sentient beings are bewildered and ignorant,
difficult to understand and know,
feeling dejected,
they then fall into the realm of being born from eggs.
Those born from moisture
are such people who often hoard the Dharma,
having gained a sentence or a verse,
they never speak of it to others,
greedy for their own benefit,
they do not understand how to proclaim it for the multitude.
Because of this cause and condition,
they then fall into the realm of being born from moisture.
Those born by transformation
are like those who entered the temple to listen to the Dharma,
obtained a sentence of profound Dharma,
discerned it infinitely and boundlessly,
proclaimed its meaning and taught it,
like the sands of the Ganges.
Like lighting one lamp,
which lights ten lamps, or a hundred lamps,
which lights a thousand lamps, or hundreds of millions of lamps,
the lamps never extinguishing.
This is called being born by transformation."
Thereupon, the xiànggōng asked, "What are the ten classes?"
Shànqìng replied, "First,
those with form:
seeing a clay shrine's sculpted image,
they immediately humbly bow,
directly saying the Buddha is like Mount Xūmí;
seeing form, they conceive the aspiration.
This is called having form.
Second,
those without form:
they do not establish a nature and do not see a nature,
like the moon in water,
the wind in the sky;
all dharmas are empty,
nothing whatsoever exists.
This is called being without form.
Third,
those with distinguishing marks:
if they see a person of upright appearance in the street,
they immediately say it was cultivated in a previous life.
Coming to the temple to listen to the Dharma,
seeing the Dharma master is plump and fair,
their heart immediately gives rise to love and attachment,
and they are bound by it;
once there is binding,
there are delusive thoughts;
once there are delusive thoughts,
there is ignorance;
once there is ignorance,
there are afflictions;
once there are afflictions,
there is sinking;
once there is sinking,
there are hells;
committing them for kalpas,
their body and mind are unstable,
and they suffer its pains.
This is called having distinguishing marks.
Fourth,
those without distinguishing marks:
all dharmas are empty,
how could there ever be reality?
No traces in the east or west,
no tracks in the north or south.
These matters are not within the heart and body,
the entire being transcends the three realms.
This is called being without distinguishing marks.
Fifth,
those neither with nor without distinguishing marks:
when spoken of, they exist;
when speech ceases, they vanish.
When established, they exist;
when not established, they vanish.
When believed, they exist;
when not believed, they vanish.
All dharmas are not within the heart and body.
This is called being neither with nor without distinguishing marks.
Sixth,
those neither without nor with distinguishing marks:
without words or speech,
without going or coming,
without movement or thought,
neither arising nor ceasing,
this is the true nature.
Without going or coming
is the Buddha-nature.
This is called being neither without nor with distinguishing marks.
Seventh,
those with two feet:
people living in the world,
having body and wisdom is termed 'two feet';
or one may have a body but no wisdom,
or one may have wisdom but no body.
If this body and wisdom
do not meet,
therefore one sinks into evil paths.
If body and wisdom meet,
Having finished his lament,
he prepared to introduce the sūtra's title.
At that moment, Shànqìng also rose from inside the hall,
and loudly called out,
stopping the sūtra introduction.
The four assemblies saw this
and were all greatly astonished.
Shànqìng gradually approached,
pointed, and said, "Venerable Dào'ān,
is very capable in expounding the Dharma.
Jhali, you open the sūtra and lecture,
proclaiming the true tenets of the Buddha.
You widely deliver the ignorant and deluded,
propagating the sacred teachings.
Your words are brilliant,
unequalled within the realm.
The sentient beings you benefit
are countless.
Long in the sea of suffering,
you act as a Dharma-boat,
forming great meritorious causes
to ferry sentient beings across birth and death.
May I ask what sūtra you are lecturing on,
and what Dharma you are expounding for all sentient beings?
Whose commentaries are you using
to expound the true tenets?
I wish to understand the origin;
please condescend to lecture.
The Dharmamaster's lectures
are renowned throughout the land,
praised by rulers,
first in the country.
As Xiànggōng is here,
I shall briefly offer praise,
warming the Dharma assembly,
making it a Dharma joy.
If the Venerable One would kindly confer great creation,
and arrange it for the future,
not disdaining this humble person,
it would truly be a great favour."
Thereupon, Dào'ān heard the words,
his expression changed and he was moved to anger.
He chided Shànqìng, saying, "You rashly speak!
The wondrous scriptures of our Buddha Tathāgata
have profound and abstruse meanings.
The Buddhadharma is difficult to comprehend,
not something you can understand.
I would not decline to explain it to you,
but it would be like a dull stone placed in water –
water is inherently moist,
but the dull stone has no way to absorb it.
Look at your current body;
you are lowly and base.
How can you immediately attain freedom?
The Buddhadharma is entrusted to kings and ministers.
Only the wise can grasp its true meaning.
Have you not heard the words outside the Way: 'Speak with those with whom one can speak;
with those with whom one cannot speak, one errs by speaking'?
Even the Master's teachings
are still like this.
I will not explain it to a person as ignorant as you.
Vínà, check and control,
do not allow any clamour.
The time for listening to the sūtra is precious.
You do not understand, so lower your head and be silent,
and listen with full attention.
The Sthavira lectures,
the audience listens to the expounding,
and all universally hear the Dharma.
Do not act as a questioner of the Dharma."
However, those sitting below the dais
did not defy his will.
If it were other people, they would fear you, Dào'ān,
but he is Shànqìng;
who fears you?
Thereupon, Shànqìng heard the words,
and spoke even louder,
pointing at Dào'ān from afar,
and angrily rebuked him: "Jhali, your conduct
is also that of one committed to the Way, a venerable figure.
The words you utter
do not conform to the sacred intent.
Our Tathāgata left his teachings,
the sūtras are clear:
all living beings, all sentient beings,
all partake of Buddha-nature.
Have you not recited the *Jīngāngjīng*?
Those born from womb, egg, moisture, and transformation;
the ten categories, the four kinds of birth;
with form, without form;
with characteristics, without characteristics—
all attain Nirvāṇa, that is, extinction and deliverance.
I am a human,
how can I not be allowed to hear the Dharma?
Though I am lowly,
my Buddha-nature is no different.
Though our robes are different,
the Dharma should be undivided.
Have you not heard that even Kǒngqiū, though a sage,
was long confused by the words about the sun?
Even the Great Awakened World-Honored One
suffered the calamity of the golden spear.
Vimalakīrti the householder
was still reprimanded by Prince Guāngyán.
The Immortal of Forbearance
had his body dismembered by King Kālī.
'A noble person does not deceive in a dark room'
is merely the common talk of ordinary people.
This lowly servant wishes to ask about the sūtra text,
but the presiding master rashly speaks.
It is like how lofty mountains
produce poisonous herbs,
yet from the midst of muddy mire
lotus flowers emerge.
There are bright pearls in tattered bags,
what use is a brocade bag filled with chaff?
Presiding master, do not climb the mountain to pick timber,
judging by appearance.
If you act like this,
you will lose your Zǐyǔ.
Just like the Buddhadharma,
it is broadly equitable and balanced,
like sweet dew descending,
universally moistening all.
It should not frequently nourish shallow grass in flat fields,
while pits, hollows, hills, and mounds receive no benefit.
The rain is originally equal,
naturally killing nothing.
The minds of 'self' and 'other'
are entirely without difference.
Have you not heard that the Bodhisattva Yàowáng
always marks the four seasons;
the five fruits, peaches and plums,
all arise from the eight seasons,
born from the earth.
In the 'Parable of Medicinal Herbs,'
it is clearly stated.
Great roots, great trees, great branches, great leaves,
each following their root foundation,
exist due to the earth.
You cannot say that sweet fruits,
the rain is sweet;
bitter fruits,
the rain is bitter.
The rain is originally of one taste,
their natures for receiving differ.
Just cultivate a mind of equality,
and the Dharma realm will naturally be peaceful and joyful.
Xiànggōng is here,
presiding master, do not deceive people.
Just know how to establish the meaning well,
and I wish to respond well in the future."
Thereupon, Dào'ān was scolded
exceedingly.
He was ashamed to be seen by Xiànggōng,
and embarrassed to look at the four assemblies.
So he stirred his ruler
and threw it aside.
He gradually came closer,
and angrily rebuked him, saying, "Shànqìng,
have you not heard: 'One who cannot be fought with
is difficult to withstand even in death'?
How can the fault of one mouse
cause the launching of a thousand-pound crossbow?
If you see my drum,
I will not decline to debate back and forth.
How can a cicada
fly and contend with a Rócáu?
You are wasting your energy.
If you understand, lower your head and be silent,
and listen with full attention.
If you do not accept my guidance this time,
you will inevitably be subjected to a caning by Xiànggōng,
expelled from the temple gate,
and forbidden to hear the sūtra.
If you rashly speak wild words,
what good will regret do then?"
Shànqìng heard the words,
and spoke even louder,
pointing at Dào'ān from afar: "You, sir, act so capriciously!
Presiding master, you wear the Dharma robes,
and constantly expound the true sūtras.
You should cultivate an immeasurable mind,
possess the six Pāramitās,
give rise to Bodhicitta,
benefit sentient beings,
and transcend the three realms.
How can your heart be without compassion,
your malice so deep,
deceiving ordinary people,
and intending to request a caning from Xiànggōng?
Such conduct does not conform to the true tenets.
The words you utter
are no different from external paths.
Jhali, you call yourself a Rócáu,
intending to raise your wings and touch the sky.
You lament that he is but a cicada,
dwelling among small grasses,
not understanding the Dao mind.
The coarse one loses deceit,
The striker forgets the meaning.
How much more so this morning, speak not;
one must use one's intention;
do not be careless and crude.
If the words and principles are discordant,
you will become my disciple.
Hold the rope firmly;
do not let it slip from your hand.
If there is even a single character's discrepancy in your response,
then this humble slave will request the staff from the *Xiànggōng* on your behalf,
drag you down from the high seat, beat you,
chase you out of the temple gate,
and forbid you from proclaiming among the assembly.
Do not say I did not warn you!"
Dào'ān was in distress,
his mouth shut, speechless,
ashamed to see the *Xiànggōng*,
embarrassed to face the four assemblies.
After a long while,
he called Shànqìng closer: "The words just spoken
were all just a jest with you.
You should not harbor thoughts of 'them and us,'
and I do not see your faults.
When I first heard you speak,
I was truly shocked and doubtful,
thinking you would disturb the lecture hall
and bother the listeners.
I now know that you are indeed a capable person.
If you ask about a *jīng* title,
I can respond."
Shànqìng said: "The *shé lí* claims
not to harbor thoughts of 'them and us.'
The Tathāgata left his teachings in the *jīngs*,
all because of Āshéshì.
The *Shìzūn* expounded them,
and everyone understood.
Now that you permit questions,
I dare not defy.
For now, I will just ask the *jīng* title;
later, there will certainly be more questions."
Dào'ān said: "The *jīng* text that this humble monk lectured on just now
is presumably the *Dà Nièpán Jīng*.
Shànqìng, hear this
and clearly remember it."
Shànqìng asked: "What is meant by 'Dà'?
What is meant by 'Niè'?
What is meant by 'Pán'?"
Dào'ān answered: "'Dà' means vastness,
signifying the wish to vastly benefit all sentient beings
to escape the sea of suffering.
'Niè' means non-arising,
non-arising and non-ceasing,
which immediately accords with true thusness,
without coming or going,
thus becoming Buddha-nature.
The character 'Pán'
means to transport sentient beings
out of the three realms,
enabling them to reach the other shore."
Shànqìng said: "The meanings of the three characters above are of seven types."
"Shànqìng, hear this
and must remember it well.
First,
it is like the movement of spring sun,
all grasses grow,
regardless of shallow valley or deep gorge,
flowers bloom everywhere.
Once the title of the wondrous Dharma *jīng* is established,
and the Tathāgata expounds and spreads it,
sentient beings, regardless of their status,
all develop goodness upon hearing the *jīng*.
Second,
it is like the meaning of a rope and wood,
immediately forsaking evil and returning to correctness.
Third,
it is like the meaning of a gushing spring,
deep and clear, neither perishing nor flowing away;
the *jīng* text remains long in the world,
circulating without end or rest.
Fourth,
it is like a river and sea,
capable of transporting ten thousand *hú* of boats.
Sentient beings wishing to cross rivers and lakes
must first rely on poles and oars.
The *jīng* texts circulate in the world,
enabling people to transcend and leave;
if one wishes to advance in the Dao and cultivate,
one must first rely on the power of the *jīng*.
Fifth,
it is like heaven and earth covering and carrying sentient beings;
if heaven and earth were completely absent,
upon what would the myriad forms stand?
Since the *Nièpán Jīng* text exists,
sentient beings cultivate according to it.
If the *jīng* Dharma were completely absent,
by what conduct would one emerge from the world?
Sixth,
it is like warp and weft,
capable of forming brocade, silk, and fine gauze;
even great silk and damask
all depend on the warp and weft.
Once the title of the wondrous Dharma *jīng* is established,
cultivators of the Dao are perfected through it,
reaching even to the unsurpassed Bodhi,
all depend on the power of the *jīng*.
Seventh,
it is like a road or path,
enabling people to come and go.
A person wishing to travel a thousand *lǐ*
sets out because of the road.
Sentient beings who aspire to cultivate the Dao
must first read and recite the *jīng* texts.
This is why later sages attain the Dao from this.
All seven meanings above,
each distinct,
collectively explain the character *jīng*.
Shànqìng, hear this
and still must remember it well."
Shànqìng said: "The character *jīng*
has many other meanings;
are there other *jīng* titles?"
Dào'ān answered: "The meaning of Nirvāṇa
is boundless and endless;
how can one exhaust
all *jīng* titles by abruptly stating them?
For example, the common people in the world,
with ten thousand households and a thousand gates,
how are they to be governed?
Thus, prefectures and counties were established,
each dividing land and demarcating borders.
The character *jīng*
differentiates and expounds myriad dharmas,
hence their distinctions.
Prefectures and counties need officials;
the wondrous Dharma must establish *jīng* titles.
If prefectures and counties have no officials,
by whom are the common people to be governed?
The *jīng* texts, the one who compiles their commentaries and glosses,
is like a comb.
Just as tangled hair is made orderly by combing,
once myriad dharmas have *jīng* titles established,
all saints achieve the Dao through this.
The answers given above
are all in accordance with the *jīng*.
If you have further doubts,
you may ask again."
Thereupon, Yuǎn Gōng went directly before the Chéngxiàng,
and respectfully addressed the Chéngxiàng, saying: "Although this humble servant has served the Chéngxiàng for a short time,
I have yet to perform any meritorious deeds.
To presumptuously enter the temple
and cause disruption to the Dharma assembly,
I have been blessed by the Chéngxiàng's benevolence
without being punished for my faults.
Now, before the assembly,
I request to be subjected to a painful beating."
Upon hearing these words, the Chéngxiàng
threw himself down,
prostrating with his face on the ground,
and did not rise again.
After a long while, he revived,
stepped forward,
and addressed the Shàngrén, saying: "Although this disciple is a Prime Minister,
I am incompetent in all matters.
I have fulfilled three vows,
and the imperial court has honored and employed me.
As a common mortal with fleshy eyes,
how can I discern the sagely and the virtuous?
My sins reach the heavens;
please forgive my shortcomings.
For six years, I enslaved him,
constantly ordering him about in my residence,
or even speaking harshly and scolding the Shàngrén.
How can such transgressions
be repented?"
Yuǎn Gōng replied: "It is because this humble monk, in a past life, was a guarantor
and had a debt that was not repaid.
To be free of grievances in this life,
it was fated that I come here to settle the accounts.
With one payment, all is cleared,
and there is no longer any doubt.
From now on,
we shall look upon each other with new eyes,
and there is no longer a need for worry."
Upon hearing these words, the Chéngxiàng
became even more sorrowful and wept,
humbly pleading with the Shàngrén, with compassion,
to explain the causes and effects of past lives.
Yuǎn Gōng said: "In a previous life, the Chéngxiàng was a merchant,
and another household's Bái Zhuāng was also a merchant.
The Chéngxiàng then borrowed five hundred strings of cash from Bái Zhuāng.
At that time, this humble monk was the guarantor.
Later, the Chéngxiàng died,
and this humble monk intended to repay the debt,
but unfortunately, I also died.
After several reincarnations,
we unexpectedly met again.
Because of this karma,
the guarantor has paid the debt."
Upon hearing these words, the Chéngxiàng
stepped forward,
weeping tears of sorrow,
and blamed himself for his transgressions: "This disciple, having incurred another's debt,
should have repaid it himself.
To have burdened the Shàngrén's body,
if this disciple were to die after this life,
I would surely sink into hell."
Yuǎn Gōng said: "The debt is now repaid;
do not doubt.
From now on,
do not repeat such actions.
Earnestly admonish your disciples
that a debt owed must be repaid.
This humble monk, as a guarantor,
still had to serve as a slave for six years to settle it.
Common mortals with shallow understanding
do not fear transgressions,
and widely create many sins;
how can they repent?"
At that moment, the audience shed tears of sorrow,
lamenting for Yuǎn Gōng,
all filled with melancholy.
Thousands looked upon him with reverence,
tens of thousands sighed in admiration.
On that day, the entire audience abandoned avarice and greed.
At that time, Yuǎn Gōng's Dharma teaching was not yet complete,
so he was invited by all the assembly members and the Chéngxiàng
to ascend the high seat again.
On that day, Yuǎn Gōng was like a withered tree on a cliff,
rejuvenated by spring.
He was also like a fish caught in a net,
granted release back into the rivers and seas.
His innate spirit
was not like that of ordinary mortals;
his bone structure and divine demeanor
were rare in the world.
The bells and chimes were sounded again,
the Dharma title was raised once more,
and he expounded to the assembly.
At that time, Dào Ān was also seated in the assembly.
As Yuǎn Gōng began to unveil the title of the scripture,
the earth immediately trembled in six ways,
and auspicious five-colored clouds
spread across the long sky.
Hundreds of thousands of heavenly beings
played music together,
and immeasurable saints and sages
chanted the Sanskrit sound in unison.
The sounds of the sutras were clear,
and the Dharma rhymes were beautiful.
The great assembly witnessed this extraordinary wonder,
and the audience unanimously (rarely) said it was rare.
At that time, the Chéngxiàng again hosted the Lán Gōng assembly
and reopened the Xiāngjī banquet.
Monks and nuns from both streets gathered in great numbers,
and he used a golden knife to shave their heads.
On that day, the Chéngxiàng, at Fúguāng Sì,
wrote a detailed memorial about this matter
and submitted it to Jìn Wén Huángdì.
The Emperor read the memorial with great delight,
repeatedly exclaiming "Excellent!" with his dragon countenance,
and only said "rare."
At that time, an imperial edict was issued: commanding the Zhōngshū Ménxià
to arrange for the three teachings—Buddhism, Daoism, and Confucianism—
to collectively proceed to Fúguāng Sì
to respectfully invite Yuǎn Gōng into the great palace for veneration.
At that time, another imperial edict followed, stating: "Bestow upon Yuǎn Gōng several strings of Rúyì,
a staff with six rings,
several sets of monastic robes,
and also send the imperial carriage
to welcome Yuǎn Gōng into the palace."
Once the edict was issued,
everyone, inside and outside the court, knew.
The Gōng Qīng Zǎixiàng arranged themselves,
creating a scene of bustling excitement.
With dignity, they entered the temple
and invited the Great Master to board the carriage.
At that time, Yuǎn Gōng refused repeatedly: "This humble monk is but an ordinary monk,
and I always decline the sovereign's invitation.
This monk wishes to return to the mountains;
that is my desire."
Chui Chéngxiàng stepped forward
and addressed the Heshàng, saying: "Humbly I pray for your compassion;
do not decline the invitation.
The Emperor in the great palace is eagerly awaiting,
looking up to the Shàngrén.
Firstly, for the sake of all sentient beings in the Dharma realm,
and secondly, may you not defy the Emperor's invitation."
Yuǎn Gōng, having been invited repeatedly,
then stepped forward and proceeded.
All kinds of skillful arts and immortal music heralded his advance,
and all the Prime Ministers joyfully acclaimed "Long Live the Emperor!"
As Yuǎn Gōng exited the temple gate,
after walking about a hundred paces,
he suddenly ascended into the sky
and disappeared without a trace.
The Chéngxiàng, in fear and awe, performed a ritual bow,
sincerely and reverently addressing the sky: "The Great Master possesses boundless power;
I humbly pray that you grant your compassion
and comply with the sovereign's invitation."
He continued to make entreaties as he walked,
slowly proceeding.
On that day,
Yuǎn Gōng had already arrived at the palace gate ahead of time and respectfully received the imperial edict.
Thereupon, the Emperor, knowing of Yuǎn Gōng's arrival,
came out of the palace gate,
bowing a thousand times in reverence,
and ten thousand times in solemn respect.
Upon seeing Yuǎn Gōng,
his dragon countenance expressed immense joy;
his happiness was boundless.
Thereupon, the Emperor said: "In my small nation,
I rejoice to meet the Shàngrén's arrival.
The people are peaceful and prosperous,
all thanks to the Heshàng."
He was then venerated in the great palace for several years.
The six palaces admired him,
and the five courts revered him.
The Emperor received the Three Refuges and Five Precepts from the Heshàng,
and obeyed them without exception.
Ever since Yuǎn Gōng saw, in the great palace, that the palace staff often improperly used paper with characters on it in the latrines,
he reprimanded everyone
and composed a gāthā, saying:
The Confucian child explains the Five Canons,
the Buddhist teaching establishes the Three Lineages.
Observe rites, practice loyalty and filial piety;
beat and expel them from the nine rural areas.
The "Cháng Yáng" and five strategies,
their characters are the same as those in the Buddhist scriptures.
They do not understand how to cherish and respect them,
and misuse them in the latrine.
Awakening extinguishes sins as numerous as Ganges sands;
many lives of repentance are insufficient.
Trapped for five hundred kalpas,
constantly reborn as a latrine worm.
At that time, because Yuǎn Gōng recited this gāthā, everyone in the great palace
cultivated blessings.
One day, Yuǎn Gōng
suddenly recalled that Āchù Rúlái had spoken,
and thereupon took leave of the emperor: "Your monastic servant, within the grand palace,
has for several years been sustained by Your Majesty's offerings.
Now I intend to return to the mountains.
I humbly beg Your Majesty for permission to proceed."
The emperor, hearing these words,
was overcome with tears,
and after a long while said to the Ho shang: "My small country
has provided no offerings at all.
The eminent monk has been here for several years,
within the palace.
I have never had any intention of treating you lightly.
Although I am a ruler of men,
unworthily occupying this world,
I always thank the eminent monk
for coming to my small country.
I humbly wish, Ho shang, out of compassion,
that you would stay for three or five more days.
Would that be possible?"
Yuǎn Gōng said: "As for the meaning of Nièpán,
it is fundamentally without attachment.
If there is attachment,
it all belongs to deluded thoughts.
I humbly wish, Your Majesty,
that you would not harbor sadness.
This poor monk has a wish to return to the mountains."
The emperor saw that Yuǎn Gōng's words were earnest,
and knew that his intention to depart was difficult to stop.
He issued an edict to first inform the six palaces,
secretly arranging a farewell ceremony.
At that time, the emperor was deeply attached and troubled,
and all the ministers of the kingdom
simultaneously sent him off.
Yuǎn Gōng set out on his journey,
departing the palace,
leaving the imperial residence.
Looking towards the mountains, the road was long;
gazing at the rivers, the path was distant.
On that day, Yuǎn Gōng, able to traverse long distances,
immediately manifested his spiritual powers in secret.
As soon as Yuǎn Gōng left Cháng'ān,
clouds rose from beneath his feet.
Like a strong man extending his arm,
in an instant,
he arrived at the mountains.
Yuǎn Gōng did not return to his old temple;
about ten *lǐ* away,
on a steep ridge,
he temporarily built a grass hermitage.
There, he sat in the lotus position,
and immediately resumed studying his old scrolls,
once again reciting the sūtras.
Time passed quickly,
and several months elapsed.
Yuǎn Gōng suddenly looked towards a high plateau
and thereupon ascended it.
The landscape featured steep peaks where cranes cried,
and dragons roared below in the ravines.
A hundred valleys and a thousand peaks
were all in bloom with flowers.
The flat land had continuously flowing water;
gardens bloomed with imperishable flowers.
This was a place where Tathāgatas practiced cultivation.
Thereupon, Yuǎn Gōng sat upright,
entering into Samādhi.
With a pure mind and clear heart,
he contemplated the Buddha-Dharma,
meditating on the impermanence of floating life,
and reflecting on the unworthiness of the mortal world.
He then took his inherent mind-king
and constructed a Dharma-boat
to take refuge in the higher realms.
When Yuǎn Gōng constructed the boat,
he did not use worldly materials,
nor did he require various other things.
He took the great Mahāyāna of no-outflows as his ropes,
Bodhi and Prajñā as railings,
and Vajra secret traces as (below missing).
Written by Zhāng Chángjì, Scribe, in the fifth year of Kāibǎo.

a lacuna in the preceding text) King Yán.
An envoy said (replied): “It is
because (you are now suffering) for sins not yet absolved.”
He spoke,
then startled, said: “I remember from the third to the fifth year of Wǔdé, when sixty-four thousand were collected.
I personally led the campaign,
no battle was not experienced,
no battle was not endured.
The number of people killed was vast.
In those past days,
I am still suffering for those sins, not yet absolved.
How then can I return to the path of life?”
His heart was as drunk with sorrow.
An envoy then led the way,
and the Emperor followed.
Having entered the palace gate, he stood fixed before the screen wall.
The director of official affairs (shè rén) announced: “The living soul of Lǐ Mǒu Yǐ, Tàizōng Emperor of the Great Táng.”
The envoy chanted a greeting,
and led him to the hall to prostrate.
The Emperor did not perform the bowing ritual.
A high-ranking official in the hall shouted: “Great Táng Tàizōng Emperor,
why do you not bow and dance?”
Before the Emperor was shouted at,
he was still somewhat agreeable.
As soon as he was shouted at,
he immediately spoke in a loud voice: “Who is it
who demands that I bow and dance?
When I was in Cháng’ān,
I only received bows and dances from others.
I am not accustomed to bowing to people.
Is it not a human
who demands that I bow and dance in the hall?
I am the Tīanzi of the Great Táng,
King Yánluó is a ghost commander.
Why does he demand that I bow and dance?”
King Yánluó was scolded,
and was ashamed to face the underworld,
feeling disgraced before his ministers.
So he changed his expression and moved his face,
giving orders to his attendants,
for Yánluó (Pànguān) to investigate.
An attendant, after chanting a greeting,
then led him back to Cháng’ān.
Now, I ask what is the name of that Pànguān?
The Pànguān was irritable and fierce,
and dared not speak his name.
The Emperor said: “You, come closer and say it quietly.”
“My surname is Cuī, and my given name is Zǐyù.”
“I ought to know you.”
As soon as he finished speaking,
the envoy led the Emperor to the gate of an office.
The envoy reported: “May Your Majesty please stand here for a moment,
and allow your servant to go in and report to the Pànguān to come quickly.”
Having said this,
the envoy arrived before the hall and bowed: “Reporting to the Pànguān,
by the King’s order, the living soul of Tàizōng Emperor has arrived.
The Pànguān is to investigate.
He is currently outside the gate,
I dared not bring him in.”
Cuī Zǐyù heard this,
and stood up in a panic,
only saying “Calamity!”
He also said: “Zǐyù is a human official,
to not go far to welcome the Emperor,
but instead to make the ruler wait outside the gate,
your humble servant Zǐyù has indeed transgressed etiquette!
Furthermore, I currently serve as the Prefect of Fǔyáng County,
and my household has over five hundred mouths.
We ride horses and eat meat.
This is all bestowed by the Emperor.
Now that he has arrived in the Underworld,
I have no share in guiding him,
and the matter will be neglected.
If it is found that the Emperor’s life is over,
then all matters are beyond words.
But if he still has longevity,
and returns to Cháng’ān,
then the more than five hundred mouths
will surely turn into fish and meat.
How could this not be due to Zǐyù’s transgression in the Underworld?”
At this time, Cuī Zǐyù was greatly agitated and worried.
The Emperor saw that the envoy did not come out for a long time,
and pondered in his heart: “Surely the envoy was not telling the Pànguān Cuī bad things about me?”
At this moment, the Emperor
could not avoid anxiety.
Thereupon, Cuī Zǐyù hastily
got his official attire, held his huái ceremonial tablet, and descended the hall,
calming his thoughts.
After a moment,
he announced his name and title,
chanted a greeting, and walked out.
He bowed and danced before the Emperor,
(shouted) “Long live!”,
prostrated with his face to the ground,
and waited respectfully for instructions.
The Emperor asked: “The one who just bowed and danced before me,
is he not Cuī Zǐyù, Prefect of Fǔyáng County?”
Cuī Zǐyù acknowledged himself as a subject.
“I grant you no fear,
stand up and answer me.”
At this time, the Emperor, due to his anxiety,
immediately asked Cuī Zǐyù: “Are you and Lǐ Fēng bosom friends in the court?”
Cuī Zǐyù replied: “Your servant and Lǐ Qiánfēng are friends in the court.”
The Emperor said: “Since you and Lǐ Qiánfēng are bosom friends in the court,
how is your relationship?”
Zǐyù said: “Since your servant and Lǐ Qiánfēng became friends in the court,
we are like Guǎn and Bào.”
The Emperor said: “How profound!
Lǐ Qiánfēng has a letter for you,
it is currently with me.”
Cuī Zǐyù heard there was a letter,
and seemed displeased.
The Emperor then took out the letter,
handed it to Cuī Zǐyù,
who knelt to receive it.
After bowing and dancing to thank the Emperor,
he put it in his bosom.
The Emperor asked Cuī Zǐyù: “Why do you not read the letter?”
Cuī Zǐyù reported: “Your servant is of humble status,
and it is not proper to read the court letter before Your Majesty,
which would be a breach of court etiquette.”
The Emperor said: “I grant you no fear,
read it for me.”
Cuī Zǐyù then bowed as commanded,
opened the letter before the Emperor, and read it.
After Zǐyù finished reading the letter,
his emotions were agitated,
and he no longer observed the etiquette of a subject to his ruler.
Facing the Emperor, he gazed towards Cháng’ān,
and then said: “Lǐ Qiánfēng, if you truly consider me a friend in the court,
how could you entrust such a matter in a letter?!”
The Emperor heard these words,
and his hair stood on end, his face changed.
So he humbly and submissively,
with gentle words, asked Cuī Zǐyù: “Regarding the matter in the letter,
between 'possible' and 'not possible',
please quickly report a word,
to ease my heart.”
Cuī Zǐyù replied: “It is possible,
but in reality, it is quite difficult.”
When the Emperor again heard the word ‘difficult’,
his expression turned sorrowful.
He then appealed to Zǐyù: “I was pursued by you and came here,
arriving helplessly.
Moreover, the Crown Prince is young,
and matters of state are great.
I do not forget to return to life for a long time.
If you would grant me three to five days,
I would go back to Cháng’ān with you,
entrust the altars of state to the Crown Prince,
and then return to meet without delay.”
At this moment, as the Emperor spoke of the Crown Prince,
tears streamed down his face.
Zǐyù saw the monarch’s sorrow,
and then reported: “May Your Majesty please calm your heart for now.
I will discuss it with my humble self.”
The Emperor then complied with Cuī Zǐyù’s request,
and stepped forward.
Cuī Zǐyù walked in front,
the Emperor followed behind.
They entered the east side within the screen wall,
and saw about twenty offices.
The Emperor asked his attendant,
in the sixth office there were two people crying.
For what reason were they so sorrowful?
Cuī Zǐyù reported: “They are none other than
the two Crown Princes, Jiànchéng and Yuánjí.”
The Emperor heard this,
and spoke to Cuī Zǐyù: “If I had not been pursued by you to come here,
how could I have met my brothers?”
Cuī Zǐyù reported: “The two Crown Princes have been here for a long time,
frequently submitting complaints,
bitterly requesting Your Majesty’s pursuit.
They claimed injustice,
and their statements were quite urgent,
which is why Your Majesty was pursued to confront them directly.
If Your Majesty does not see the two Crown Princes,
your servant and I can find a way for Your Majesty;
if Your Majesty enters the office
and meets the two Crown Princes,
then you will encounter your enemies,
and your servant will also have no means to save Your Majesty,
and you will likely not be able to return to Cháng’ān.
May Your Majesty not go and see them,
it will be much safer.”
The Emperor heard these words,
and dared not again,
so he hastened to the hall and sat down.
Cuī Zǐyù stood at the foot of the steps,
introducing the officials of the six departments to pay respects to the Emperor.
They chanted a greeting, walked in,
paid their respects,
bowed again and walked out.
The Emperor asked Cuī Zǐyù: “Who was it that just bowed before the hall?”
Cuī Zǐyù reported: “They are the six departmental officials.”
The Emperor again asked: “What are the six departmental officials?”
Cuī Zǐyù reported: “In the Yang realm they are called the six departmental officials,
The realm of Yīndào is called the court of the Six Cao Officials.”
The Emperor said: “Why do you not come up to the hall and keep me company, speaking with me?”
Cuī Zǐyù respectfully replied: “Because I am of humble official rank,
I am not fit to sit in the same hall as Your Majesty.”
The Emperor said: “When you were in Cháng’ān,
you were of humble official rank;
now that you are in Míngsī,
you must come up and keep me company.”
Cuī Zǐyù bowed,
and sat down.
The Emperor looked up and saw outside the screen wall.
He recognized him at first sight.
Cuī Zǐyù beckoned to him with his hand.
He walked to the front of the hall and bowed,
then went up to the hall and stood still. When you were in Cháng’ān,
what good deeds did you perform,
what merits did you create?
A boy stepped forward, clasped his hands, and informed the Judge: “The Emperor came and performed no good deeds,
nor did he copy scriptures or paint images.
The realm of Yīndào relies on merits as proof.
Now, the Emperor will return to the path of life.”
Cuī Zǐyù then asked, and the good boy informed the Judge: “The Emperor issued a great amnesty,
three times extending grace.”
Cuī Zǐyù said: “Judge, he has 36,550 days, how much merit has he created?”
The good boy said: “The official in charge of merits will know this matter.”
Cuī Zǐyù asked.
